stories.title: Gasser Plans to Take Federalsburg Police in the Right Direction
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Gasser plans to take Federalsburg police in the right direction

 January 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 539
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Joseph Gasser has taken his new role of chief of police in stride, setting goals to help further the Federalsburg Police Department amid turnover and a third-party investigation.On Wednesday, Gasser was publicly named chief of police in a Facebook post made by the town government. Gasser has been interim chief of police since October, when an unspecified incident caused the town to have a third party investigate the department.
Gasser comes into this position with a military background, and he has been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years. He believes his strong background and experience will help him serve as chief.
"The jobs that I have had throughout both my military and my police career have pointed me in this direction," Gasser said. "As not somebody simply to have a standard to take over, but someone that has the ability and the knowledge to build from."
On Oct. 14 the Town of Federalsburg made a facebook post about an unspecified incident causing the town to have a third party investigate the department.
"The Town of Federalsburg received a complaint about an incident involving the Federalsburg Police Department that occurred on October 9, 2024. We are engaging an independent third party to investigate this incident," the post said.
When asked whether turnover in the Federalsburg Police Department was related to the October incident, Mayor Kim Abner referred the Star Democrat to the Facebook post.
Gasser confirmed the October incident was a consideration in his appointment. "But that's as far as I'll go with it," he said.
In the post announcing Gasser promotion, the town stated former Chief Michael McDermott, who had served in law enforcement for more than 40 years, resigned effective Jan. 5.
"The Mayor and Council, on behalf of the Town of Federalsburg, extend our appreciation to Chief McDermott for his years of service to the Town and wish him all the best in his future endeavors," the town said in the Facebook post.
In McDermott's years as chief, the department saw a significant reduction in crime rates, the post said. Gasser wants to continue McDermott's work.
"We've had a good several years here with the former chief, and I want to expound upon that and make it even better for the future," Gasser said.
Some of Gasser's goals and plans will be executed within three years, the new chief said. He plans to shape the department better for the future.
"We have several new officers with less than a year in the field," Gasser stated. "They are the future of this department. My primary goal is to prepare this department three years down the line, five years down the line, for those individuals to take over this department and to run it effectively and in service of the community."
In addition to continuing the work that has been done, Gasser plans for some reorganization as well.
"There's certainly some internal reorganization to the department that needs to be done," Gasser said. "That's going to be a transitional point, both with me coming in as Chief, even though I've been here forever. It's also going to be a task to better serve the officers themselves, like some officers have things they like to do more than others, I want to get them headed in that direction."

stories.title: Commissioners Approve Extended MOU with Sheriff's Office for Ridgely Policing
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Commissioners approve extended MOU with sheriff's office for Ridgely policing

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Building on a temporary agreement forged in the weeks following the March suspension of Ridgely's entire police force, the Town of Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have agreed to a more permanent plan for ensuring law enforcement coverage in the town.At their May 6 meeting, the Ridgely commissioners approved a memorandum of understanding for fiscal year 2025 that will ensure the sheriff's office provides law enforcement services to Ridgely in the absence of the Ridgely Police Department.
This is a longer term arrangement than originally conceived.
On March 13, the commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely police department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor. No reason for the investigation has been indicated publicly.
"To guarantee uninterrupted public safety services, the Commissioners initiated a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office," said Ridgely in a press release. "Now, building upon this temporary arrangement, Ridgely and the Caroline County Sheriff's Office have established a long-term partnership through an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This MOU will provide the Town of Ridgely with complete law enforcement coverage, by the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, for the fiscal year 2025, with the option to renew service annually. This agreement includes a provision for maintaining 480 hours of coverage per month."
According to the first amendment to agreement for law enforcement services, a document between the town of Ridgely, the Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Sheriff Donald L. Baker, the estimated annual cost of this service is $474,971.44.
According to two versions of the town's proposed FY2025 budget, one with the town's police department and the other with the sheriff's office providing policing, posted to the town website Tuesday, the MOU with the sheriff's office cheaper the cost of maintaining a town police force.
"This partnership underscores our shared commitment to safety and community well-being," Baker said in the press release. "By working closely with the Ridgely community, we aim to build trust and ensure seamless law enforcement services to all residents. The updated MOU will take effect July 1, 2024, with the current MOU remaining in effect until then."
This matter was also addressed during the May 7 Caroline County Commissioners meeting.
"At this point in time, I plan on signing it if the County Commissioners sign it, and the (Ridgely) commissioners signed it last night," Baker said about the agreement at that meeting. "Frank Bartz was there. There was a lot of heated discussion, but that is to be expected. I look forward to the continued efforts by the county, the town and the sheriff's office. So I think that only good things are on the horizon."
Many Ridgely residents, like Lakia Harris-Pierce, who went to the meeting, are concerned about what they feel is a lack of transparency. Harris-Pierce said she is still wondering who gave the orders to suspend the police force in the first place.
Commissioner Larry Porter said, "I know there has been a lot of social media discussion about this, but basically this is going to provide 120 hours per week."
Then he asked the sheriff, "Just for clarification, how much coverage was the Ridgely Police Department providing when they were there?"
Baker said originally they were supposed to cover the town 140 hours a week. Vacancies and sickness kept them from reaching that number. The sheriff's office will cover the town as much as the police department had under the new agreement.
"Just so everybody knows, the sheriff's department is constitutionally obligated to handle and provide law enforcement services in Caroline County," Baker said. "Even if we back up the towns of Federalsburg, Greensboro or Denton, who have their own police departments… we are obligated to go in there… I do that in cooperation with the commissioners and your staff."
Baker said he takes the responsibility seriously and that he wants to give the citizens of Ridgely some peace of mind.
The county commissioners' motion unanimously passed to approve the MOU.

stories.title: St. Michaels Reorganizes Police, OKs Raises
stories.author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
stories.content:
St. Michaels reorganizes police, OKs raises

 August 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 282
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Commissioners of St. Michaels voted unanimously Wednesday to revise job descriptions in the town's police department and approve raises in light of the new organizational structure.The need to restructure the small police department came about earlier this summer after former Chief Anthony Smith retired on June 30. Newly appointed Chief Jeffrey Oswald was sworn in the same day, leaving his former position as the department's captain unfilled.Instead of attempting to locate a new officer to serve as captain, with a salary ranging from $85,000 to $100,000, Oswald suggested restructuring the department through restructuring and promoting two of his officers to sergeants.The department's old structure included a chief, a captain and two corporals, each with two officers under them. The newly proposed and now-approved structure includes the chief and two sergeants, each with two officers under them.A memo in the town's meeting agenda packet indicated that both sergeants will be able to fulfill each other's roles, but each will have a separate primary focus in assisting the chief: one to help handle patrol responsibilities and one to aid in administrative tasks.Oswald said he previously handled the responsibilities of the captain position for 12 years while ranked as a sergeant and lieutenant and wanted to provide his officers with the same opportunities for advancement.The new structure will have a minimal budgetary impact, as the total base salary impact for the restructuring is $7,200.The promoted sergeants will receive mandatory first line administrator training and will be recognized by the Police Training Commission to take command in Oswald's absence. The positions come with a two year probationary period.

The St. Michaels Police Department is located at 100 S. Fremont St.

stories.title: Talbot Board of Ed Adds Makeup Day for Snow; Approves 2025-26 Calendar
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot Board of Ed adds makeup day for snow; approves 2025-26 calendar

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During Wednesday's meeting, the Talbot County Board of Education added a day onto the end of this year's school calendar following last week's snowstorm.Talbot County Public Schools was closed Monday through Friday last week due to snow that blanketed the Mid-Shore. However, the 2024-2025 school calendar only had four inclement weather days built in, meaning an additional day was needed to comply with the state's 180-day requirement.
Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership and student success, recommended that a day be added in June, moving the last day of school for students to Friday, June 13.
The last day for teachers would be Monday, June 16. Einhorn said that historically, most teachers complete mandated training that affords them with not having to come in on the last day.
The board unanimously passed the adjusted calendar for this year.
2025-26 CALENDAROn Wednesday, the board also chose the district's calendar for the 2025-2026 school year.
At last month's meeting, Einhorn presented a draft calendar with two days off in March and a five-day spring break, which was the recommendation of the calendar committee. Board President Emily Jackson, however, expressed frustration there weren't multiple options posed.
This month, Einhorn returned with three draft calendars. The first was similar to what the board saw in December, with a four-day weekend in March and the shorter spring break. The second draft removed the off days in March and had an eight-day spring break.
A third draft included both the March break and an eight-day spring break, pushing the last student day back to June 10, 2026.
All three drafts included the typical days off in November for Easton's Waterfowl Festival, as well as a winter break from Dec. 20, 2025, to Jan. 4, 2026.
"There is no calendar that we're going to create that is best for every single person," Jackson said.
Jackson said it's clear — based on previous polling and community input — that most families favor the extended spring break. Board Vice President Amy Dodson suggested the board move forward with the second or third calendars.
Board member Karla Wieland-Cherry said she preferred the first calendar with the shorter spring break.
"You're losing a lot of school time for eight days off for students," Wieland-Cherry said. "You're losing a lot of momentum. And plus you're concerned with providing day care. Not all employers are going to allow that. That's quite a long time to take off of work and find day care and so forth."
She added that not all families are looking for a longer spring break.
"My only concern is that if 59% of our students are at the poverty level, we're really talking about more of a smaller group who are really going to financially be able to afford an Easter holiday," Wieland-Cherry said. "… You really could possibly potentially be causing more hardship for something that's more an elitist type thing, quite honestly."
Jackson said while she agrees with Wieland-Cherry's point, she has "to go with what the community is saying."
"We have asked again and again, and the majority of the respondents to any time we've asked this have said they like that spring break," Jackson said.
Following board discussion, Jackson motioned for approval of the third calendar featuring two off days in March and five days for spring break. Her motion included an amendment to the calendar that the March days off serve as two of four inclement weather days for the district.
By a 6-1 vote, with only Wieland-Cherry voting against, the board approved the 2025-2026 school year calendar.

stories.title: Greensboro Candidate: William C. Schaffner
stories.author: Staff Writer
stories.content: WILLIAM C. SCHAFFNER Age: 77 Family: Widower, granddaughter and son live with me. I have one daughter that lives independently in Greensboro and another that lives in Milford, Delaware. I have 6 grandchildren, 2 great grandchildren and am proud of all of them. Education: Graduated from Rostraver High School in Belle Vernon, Pennsylvania, and received Master's in Science degree in health care administration from Wilmington University. Occupation: Retired from Holy Cross Hospital in Silver Spring, Maryland, where I was director of patient accounting and director of payor contracting Political Experience: No previous political experience. 1. Why are you running for Greensboro Town Council? I want to bring unity, integrity and honesty to our town government and to my town. One area that I believe has been under utilized is that of oversight of the affairs of the town, from the town manager to each department and project the town involves itself with. 2. What issues will you prioritize if elected? I am keeping an open mind on what needs to be prioritized, but I do believe our eroding roads and infrastructure need special attention. 3. Transparency with the residents has been questioned by Greensboro residents. How would you plan to be transparent with the residents? Transparency is a word often used, but, in my opinion, not well understood. I do believe that our citizens need to be kept informed as much as possible on the affairs of the town but do have an understanding that that transparency cannot always be delivered in the time that our residents would like. While I do want the citizens to be informed, it is important that they are informed with correct, reliable information. Being transparent does not always mean doing what everyone wants to be done, but making sure our citizens do understand why actions are taken in the way that they are. 4. Multiple solar projects have been proposed for Caroline County. What rules should Greensboro have in place for these projects? I am not at this time knowledgeable enough to know for sure what or how the various solar projects can be affected by the town's actions, but I do believe we need to maintain as much as possible the valuable farmland we have in Caroline County. To what extent the town can affect the solar projects will require study, listening and understanding of that process in our state, county and towns to better make any decision(s) on the solar projects, if any meaningful decisions can even be made at the town level.

stories.title: Federalsburg Sees More Staff Turnover as Treasurer Leaves
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Federalsburg sees more staff turnover as treasurer leaves

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 261
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — As Federalsburg continues to work through multiple town issues, it will have to navigate the coming months without a town treasurer.Treasurer Jamie Washington informed the town she was leaving her position earlier this month. Federalsburg officials said the town is working through a transition plan to make sure the coming weeks go smoothly.
In addition to other responsibilities, Washington handled the town's billing responsibilities and oversaw town finances.
The town is working to eliminate $5 million of debt.
In a text message to the Star Democrat on Tuesday, Mayor Kim Abner outlined the town's plan to make sure Washington's transition is smooth and won't hurt the town.
"Mayor and Council have an interim treasurer in place to ensure business continues to move forward and staff and bills are paid. We have reached out to the county to assist with more complicated permits as we do not have in-house experience at the moment. Mayor and Council are committed to continuity of government and we appreciate residents patience as we work to get the right staff in place at Town Hall," the text message said.
Federalsburg has faced frequent turnover of town staff throughout 2025, starting with the resignation of Police Chief Michael McDermott on Jan. 5.
Washington was the third person to serve in the treasurer role since the beginning of the year.
Former Treasurer Debbie Lawler was laid off in February, then Mercedes Moyer served as interim town manager and treasurer before Washington took over during the summer.
With Washington set to leave the town, Federalsburg will be looking for its fourth town treasurer of 2025.

stories.title: Federalsburg Council Member Confronts Colleagues Over Emails Calling Her 'Rogue'
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Federalsburg council member confronts colleagues over emails calling her 'rogue'

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 816
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A Federalsburg council member expressed frustration with her colleagues Monday night, claiming they failed to defend her when she was accused of taking action without council approval.Council member Brandy James alleged former contractual town manager Ken Decker called James a "rogue council member" in emails exchanged with town council members.
James said that in the emails, Decker accused her of taking actions without the full council's approval.
"I've never been a rogue, as I was termed in the emails, council member," James said during Monday's Town Council meeting.
"Anything that I have done I have done with everyone's up here OK. I have a whole stack of emails where I was called these names, and you all just stood by and not said a thing, but I'm a big girl, but I have all of this that shows anything that I have ever done, it has shown that you all have said, 'OK,'" James said.
According to James, the email exchange claims James acted alone in hiring a cleaning crew to clean town hall after the building was closed for mold remediation. James said the decision to bring in a cleaning crew was approved by the Town Council.
"You all OK'd all this," she said. "Now all of this that's being alleged in here is making me a rogue council member, but none of you spoke up. So, to me it sounds like you're going along with it."
While Decker said he could not remember the emails James referenced, he said any issues he had with the town were normal professional issues, not personal ones.
Decker elected not to renew his contract with the town after he served 30 days in the contractual town manager role in September.
"I don't think there's a lot to be accomplished by trying to go in and get into the details about interactions I had with individual members of the council," Decker told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning.
Decker said he thought he worked well with the town but didn't think he could help the town do what needed to be done.
"If councilwoman James is unhappy about something I wrote, I'm not hard to find," Decker said.
Council member Ian Ferguson told the Star Democrat on Tuesday morning that Decker sent the emails James referenced. Ferguson said he did not say anything in James' defense because Decker is allowed his opinion.
"Now, I can see the point that she's making of 'Hey, you know, you don't got my back, and I feel this is wrong,' and that's fair. She has a valid point to that," he said. "But at the end of the day, I looked at it more like we have larger things to worry about than somebody throwing names and shade or whatever you want to call it at people. … My focus was getting the MOU passed, and the wastewater treatment plant up to snuff and getting rates set for that."
James' comments were raised after a discussion about the town's water billing schedule. The town discussed raising water and sewer rates in meetings throughout September, a recommendation made by Decker to increase revenues and tackle the town's $5 million debt.
During public comment at the meeting Monday, a resident raised a question about whether the town was considering switching from quarterly to monthly billing for water and sewer. Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said there was discussion by the town but there was not a motion made to change its billing schedule.
James said that she had made this motion at a prior meeting and that it was passed by the council. According to the town minutes for the council's July meeting, a motion was made by James to change water bills from quarterly to monthly and was seconded by Mayor Kimberly Abner and passed 5-0.
Ryan clarified to the Star Democrat that the motion could have been to further a conversation, but the motion to switch to monthly could not be passed without an ordnance with approved legislation.
James said that in previous meetings and closed sessions, there were conversations about potentially moving the town water billing to a monthly schedule to ensure more consistent revenue to the town.
James said when a county official visited the town of Federalsburg, the official said, "Town of Federalsburg, you have three to four months out of the year where you had zero income coming in, and that's where one of your shortfalls are."
"Three to four months, and that's one of the reasons why we couldn't make payroll," James said.
"...Y'all forgot that, and that was where the discussion with staff came in of how can we make sure income is still coming in during those three or four months that we have no income. That was where the inception of monthly billing payment, but how conveniently everybody forgot."

stories.title: Oxford Tackles Short-Term Rental Compliance Issues
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Oxford tackles short-term rental compliance issues

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford currently has somewhere between 35 and 44 short-term rentals, but according to Town Commissioner Dave Donovan, only five are licensed.Donovan proposed an ordinance at Monday's Town Commission meeting amending town code to hold operators liable for non-compliance and gather accurate data on the number, location and rental frequency of short-term rentals in town.
The information will help commissioner make better-informed policy decisions, Donovan said.
He believes the primary issue with short-term rental compliance is operators forgetting or neglecting to register.
"I suspect that the real problem with compliance, at least in the last couple years, is that people in town just forgot," Donovan said. "And, obviously that's not okay, but also, you got to do something to make sure they remember."
The town's current short-term rental rules fine operators that are not licensed $100 to $200 every day they remain unlicensed. Donovan said this is difficult to enforce, especially considering unlicensed rentals are hard to track because they advertise online without physical signs.
The proposed ordinance would fine short-term rental operators who do not comply a flat fine of $1,000 a month, which Donovan said will likely be more effective. It would also make the act of advertising a short-term rental property without a license a violation, requiring owners to remove listings if not properly registered.
"The agents are the ones that really should, and most likely do, understand the requirements of the local ordinances, whether it's here, or Easton, or Trappe, or St. Michaels or the county. And so, there's really no excuse," Donovan said.
The current ordinance restricts licenses to "natural persons," which prevents corporations and investment groups from buying multiple properties for short-term rentals.
"I think it's very clever. It really provides a tremendous disincentive to the true out-of-towners, the true real estate investment companies that just want to come into a town like ours and buy up chunks of it and run a short-term rental business, because they can't," Donovan said.
There will be a public hearing on this proposed ordinance at the Oxford Town Commissioners meeting on Oct. 28.

stories.title: Workshops Held During Oxford Commission Meeting
stories.author: Lily Tierney ltierney@chespub.com
stories.content:
Workshops held during Oxford Commission Meeting

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LILY TIERNEY ltierney@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Commissioners of Oxford held several work sessions during the town's Sept. 29 meeting. These included:Town electionsCommissioners discussed the possibility of creating a supplemental municipal voter list in addition to the county's list.
They plan to discuss the matter further at a workshop on Oct. 8 and are actively seeking the public's feedback.
Ethics ordinance recommendations from the Ethics CommissionCommissioners considered revising the ethics ordinance after the Ethics Commission said the current version is confusing from years of edits.
Additional proposals included adding an alternate member, staggering terms for continuity, and clarifying the distinction between the Ethics and Town commissions.
Members of the Ethics Commission suggested narrowing financial disclosure rules, which currently require candidates to report all global property and business interests, to instead focus on conflicts of interest within Maryland.
The Ethics Commission also discussed separate disclosure standards for elected officials, appointed members and staff, and agreed to add a campaign finance section requiring filings at candidacy, election and post-election.
The updates are slated for completion by February ahead of the next election cycle.
Economic development prioritiesThe Oxford Business Association pressed town leaders for clear economic development priorities to guide its work, particularly on tourism and use of accommodation tax revenues, now at historic lows.
Commissioners asked for detailed budgets and proof of return on investment before committing tax dollars, moving away from funding with "no strings attached."
The association's representative said they must consult members before releasing past financials. They agreed performance metrics, like website analytics, which are currently hindered by technical issues, will be needed once town priorities are defined.
Short-term rental permitting processCommissioners considered adopting a software called Granicus to crack down on unlicensed short-term rentals, estimating 35 to 44 units operate in town but only five hold permits.
The program, already in use by Talbot County, would cost Oxford $2,000 a year.
The software would also help enforce a proposed rule requiring license numbers in rental ads, which officials say are easier to track than actual bookings.
Breezeline franchise agreementCommissioners are reviewing their franchise agreement with Breezeline, weighing whether to stay with the old terms or adopt a new template that covers only cable.
The draft also drops the 2% public, educational and government funding, meaning the town would need to add a franchise fee of up to 5% to recoup costs.
Commissioners said they'll hold a public hearing, likely after the holidays, to gather resident feedback on service quality before entering negotiations.
Utility payment processingCommissioners are exploring new approaches to utilities and services, including an online portal for utility bill payments that would allow credit card use but carry a 1.5% to 3.5% transaction fee which will likely be passed on to residents rather than absorbed by the town.
An Automated Clearing House payment option through Shore United Bank is also being considered, with specific cost proposals to be discussed at a future meeting.
Electric fees paid by the townThe Electric Vehicle Institute has offered to replace the current chargers with faster, pay-as-you-go chargers that would eliminate the current expense of $600.
Commissioners will also separately review electricity costs tied to the watermen's boat slips, citing the town's commitment to its working waterfront.

stories.title: County Weighs ICE Program: Officials Seek Details on 287(g) Jail Enforcement Model Before Considering Public Comment and Vote
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein
stories.content:
County weighs ICE Program: Officials seek details on 287(g) jail enforcement model before considering public comment and vote

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 654
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County officials say they are seeking more information from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the county's eligibility for a 287(g) Jail Enforcement Model program.At an informal community forum Sept. 29 hosted by Eastern Shore Indivisible at the Kent Island branch of the Queen Anne's County Public Library, County Commissioner President Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann updated residents on the status of discussions with ICE.
Corchiarino said the county has not yet been told whether it qualifies for the Jail Enforcement Model, one of three agreements available under ICE's 287(g) program. He emphasized that no plans are in place.
"We're waiting to hear from federal officials," Corchiarino said. "We don't have clear details or expectations yet of what a memorandum of understanding would look like."
Program background
Under the Jail Enforcement Model, correctional officers can be deputized with limited federal authority to serve civil detainers within a county detention facility. Other models under 287(g) include the Warrant Service Officer and Task Force programs, though Corchiarino said Queen Anne's is not pursuing those.
On July 30, the county's Republican Central Committee hosted an informational meeting in Stevensville with James Brooks, community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices. Following that session, Corchiarino said, residents asked county leaders to seek more information about the county's eligibility.
He noted that requirements for correctional facilities vary by jurisdiction in Maryland. In Queen Anne's County, the detention center falls under the authority of the county commissioners rather than law enforcement.
"If we find out we're not eligible, then it's a moot point," Corchiarino said. "If we are eligible, then we'll need to look at requirements and a cost analysis. Any decision would go through public comment and ultimately a commission vote."
There is no set timeline, he said, adding that even if ICE responds soon, the matter would take time before reaching an agenda.
Community questions and concerns
During the forum, some residents voiced concerns about immigration enforcement and civil rights. One man who identified himself as part of the Hispanic community said he had been detained twice "on the west side of the bridge" and carried laminated copies of his birth certificate out of fear.
"What's going to be done to ensure I keep my American rights … without being afraid of the lights in the rearview mirror?" he asked, drawing applause.
Hofmann said the sheriff's office does not have authority to serve civil detainers and in his 30 years could recall only one case involving an ICE civil detainer in the county. He stressed that the role of ICE is separate from the role of county commissioners or the sheriff's office.
"Regardless of origin, whether American or immigrant, there are bad people with warrants for crimes, and we are obligated to enforce the criminal law," Hofmann said.
He added that ICE falls under the umbrella of Homeland Security Investigations and that since 2010 the county sheriff's office has had a designated desk for Homeland Security agents, used in rare but valuable partnerships on cases involving fraud, child pornography and human trafficking.
"What I don't want to do is create fear amongst our community," Hofmann said. "We want people to get the services they need here in Queen Anne's County. We are genuinely here to take care of everyone fairly and equally."
Calls for transparency
Some residents said they want more public collaboration when federal topics arise.
"This affects everyone. It's not just Republicans or Democrats. We should be working together to protect our community," one Grasonville woman said.
A Centreville woman added that she wanted reassurance county law enforcement would remain lawful and not adopt questionable tactics she had heard about elsewhere.
Corchiarino said he considers public input an important factor in any decision.
"A room full of people, that's persuasive for me," he said.
Silvia Gonzalez Roman, co-founder of Eastern Shore Indivisible, said the group invited an ICE representative to the forum but did not receive a response.
"Building community with open dialogue is what it is all about," she said.

stories.title: Easton Council Members to Host Ward Town Halls for Residents
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents

 September 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Beginning Monday, Easton council members will host ward-specific town halls in hopes of increasing transparency and engaging with constituents.Maureen Curry (Ward 1), Robert Rankin (Ward 2), David Montgomery (Ward 3) and the Rev. Elmer Davis (Ward 4) will each host town halls open to their constituents at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in the coming weeks.
The town halls were mentioned during Easton's recent election, including by Don Abbatiello, now council president and then Ward 2 representative.
Abbatiello said he aims to attend all four town halls.
"We wanted to make sure that we left no stone unturned when it came to sharing information," Abbatiello said.
Rankin will kick off the meetings with Ward 2 residents on Monday. Montgomery will host Ward 3's discussion on Oct. 9. Davis will lead Ward 4's on Oct. 23, and Curry will wrap it up with Ward 1's meeting on Oct. 27. All four meetings will be held at the Easton fire hall from 7 to 8 p.m.
Abbatiello said the idea to host semi-regular ward town halls birthed from discussions on the campaign trail, with some residents feeling like they didn't have enough access to town information or couldn't attend town meetings, which are typically twice a month at 5:30 p.m.
The council president said the town's done a good job in improving its communication to residents since he joined the council in 2019, especially on its website and social media platforms. The new town halls are a continuation of that effort, he said.
Council members will provide brief presentations to residents at the meetings, updating them on recent projects in town and their respective wards. Then, the sessions will open up for feedback and questions from the public.
"We want residents to be informed and know what's going on," Rankin said. " ... The more we can hear from folks … that really helps us a lot."
Housing, growth and traffic are expected to be major points of discussion, council leaders said.
"The central topic, for me at least, will be growth," Montgomery said. "And I think that's a topic that concerns everybody of Ward 3 because of how residents have to tend to traffic."
Rankin said he expects his discussion to touch on recent development projects and the town's comprehensive plan, which is in the process of being updated for the first time since 2010 and will lay out a vision for the town's growth over the next decade.
Davis said that in addition to growth and development, he expects to field questions on the Easton Police Department and resident concerns about safety.
The Ward 4 representative highlighted the town halls as another avenue to be open with the public.
"Everybody can be included and get some questions answered," Davis said. "Our main goal is to show transparency to the community."

stories.title: Members of Oxford Historic District Commission Removed
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Members of Oxford Historic District Commission removed

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With a unanimous vote last month, Oxford commissioners removed three of the the five members from the town's Historic District Commission.At the Aug. 19 town meeting, Commission President Katrina Greer announced that the Commissioners of Oxford unanimously voted in closed session to change the makeup of the commission. Greer said in a statement at the meeting that this decision reflects the best interest of the town.
Jennifer Stanley, Jim Wilcox and Justin Werner were removed from their roles on the commission. Their terms were not set to expire until 2026 and 2027. A fourth member of the commission, Terry Sullivan, whose term expires Saturday, has not been confirmed of a reappointment.
The commission's fifth and final member, Margaret Morris, is listed on the town's website as an "alternate member." Two new members were appointed at the August meeting.
The Oxford Town Historic Commission is a volunteer body appointed by town commissioners and has five members who have three year terms. The commission provides current and prospective property owners with guidance on how historical properties should be handled in the town.
Oxford Town Commissioner Dave Donovan said the commission will not discuss details of their decision beyond confirming unanimity of the vote and saying it was taken in the "best interest of the community."
"I think that's really all we're willing to discuss on that topic," Donovan said.
Stanley, one of the three Historic District Commissioners who was removed, said she was told about the decision in person prior to the meeting by a commissioner, who cited that she "wasn't efficient enough." Stanley did not disclose which commissioner gave her this news. She said she was never given advice on how to be more efficient.
Stanley, who has lived in the town for 45 years, said she had seen behavior like this before from town officials and expected something like this to happen. "I don't think this is an issue of transparency. I think this is an issue of control," she said.
Greer said that the decision was made in the best interest of the town, noting that the commissioners' top priority is serving all residents. She also expressed gratitude to the many volunteers on boards and commissions who help carry that commitment forward.
Stanley does not agree that this decision is in its best interest. "It's unfortunate for the town," she said.
Moving forward
Barbara Ranson and Will Cawley were appointed to the Historic District Commission at the Aug. 19 meeting. According to Town Manager Holly Wahl, there are two additional spots that need to be filled. She said town commissioners held interviews Sept. 2.
"Commissioners recently implemented a new process for the town where they are reviewing applicants for all boards and commissions in public so that there's a transparent review of how members are appointed," Wahl said. "And so after an interviewing process, members are now appointed to boards and commissions by a vote of all commissioners."
Appointments for the open two spots are planned for the Sept. 29 regular commission meeting.

stories.title: Caroline Commissioners Consider Committee to Review Their Pay
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline commissioners consider committee to review their pay

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 410
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their meeting Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed appointing a committee to review their compensation rate.According to a draft bill presented at the meeting, the committee would be created to review the commissioners' current compensation rate and make recommendations for a new rate based on state and local laws.
A potential pay raise for the commissioners, which would take in effect in the next commissioners term, was suggested by county staff, County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"Staff have brought to the commissioners' attention that it has been since 2009 that their compensation has been reviewed," he said. "The cost of living has greatly increased and so has the time it takes to be a good commissioner. So we've brought it to the commissioners' attention because it's long overdue."
The commissioners' annual pay is $15,000, and the commissioners president makes $16,000. This figure is similar to some surrounding counties. According to the Talbot County charter, county council members make $14,400 per year.
Compensation is much higher in other Maryland counties. The Montgomery County Council president makes $171,912, while other council members make $156,284.
Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter had some questions about the draft bill and how the committee would properly calculate the hours the commissioners work.
"I think the question that I would have would be, I'm not sure that committee would be able to really understand or have information on the hours," Porter said. "I mean we all serve differently.
"For example, the president of the commissioners is asked to do things that the other members are not. In other words, the president represents the commissioners… there's hours in here that we don't, I don't know if this committee would even recognize or understand."
Barroll made a suggestion that Kim Raeder of the Office of Law help make the appointments to the committee. Barroll said committee members could interview the commissioners to make a proper evaluation.
The commissioners will not have a say in whether their compensation is raised or not. The appointed committee will make a recommendation after its investigation into the work of the commissioners.
The committee would have to report back by Dec. 15, and the commissioners would have 60 days to act on the recommendation.
The commissioners voted to introduce the draft bill that would create the committee and move the legislation to a first reading at their next meeting. If the bill is passed, Barroll and Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the committee is likely to be formed in early November.

stories.title: Oxford Splits General Fund into Three New Funds
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Oxford splits general fund into three new funds

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has undergone a series of changes over the past year with a new election process, live-streamed town halls and a new town manager, Holly Wahl, who plans on streamlining more of the town's processes.Historically, the town has kept its finances in one general fund and allocated from there. But with the uncertainty of future federal funding, Oxford Town Commissioners, with the guidance of Wahl, and town staff have split the general fund into three separate funds: a general fund, an enterprise fund and the shore maintenance and protection fund.
"We had one budget that was adopted by commissioners each year," Wahl said. "And so the act this year was separating and having an ordinance for each fund being the general fund is one and then the two additional enterprise funds."
According to Wahl, the separation of funds is intended to improve transparency, finance stability and long-term planning for infrastructure projects like the Strand Beach project.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said part of the reasoning behind this decision was to appeal to federal and state grant opportunities, especially at a time when federal funding is uncertain. "Because you're showing that you can support yourself," Greer said. "You're managing the money and you're managing your expenses."
Wahl said commissioners and staff have created five- and 10-year capital improvement plans so the town can prioritize its budgetary needs.
"There may be some movement between fiscal years, but at least if we can prioritize and think about what those expenses are and plug them into a fiscal year so that staff can also prioritize their actions and work towards those projects and seek proposals," Wahl said.
Greer said that throughout the year, the town will start to allocate funds to build up reserves, look at capital and develop a capital plan. "So that means, look at all your infrastructure and all the things you want to do, have a five- or a 10-year plan, and then start to build our revenues accordingly," she said.
The new budget structure allows for proactive rather than reactive management of infrastructure needs, especially for critical systems like water and sewer which require preventative maintenance, Town Commissioners said.
Wahl said there is no plan to further restructure the budget at this time and the town will focus on effective project prioritization and adapting to funding uncertainties.

stories.title: Cambridge City Council Passes Fiscal 2026 Budget
stories.author: Lily Tierney

Cambridge City Council passes fiscal 2026 budget

 June 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council adopted its fiscal year 2026 budget Monday night after a contentious discussion over whether or not they would hold a vote or defer the budget adoption.After hearing public comments, council members considered whether or not they needed to make further amendments or deletions that would require deferring the vote.
Council member Brett Summers suggested deferring the vote because council member Brian Roche was not in attendance.
"I just want to remind you all, we're here to do the city's budget not to make sure commissioners have their camera time," said Mayor Lajan Cephas in response.
Council President Sputty Cephas pointed out that two council members will be absent at the next meeting and that deferring budget approval again would push the budget adoption very close to the start of the fiscal year on July 1.
The discussion of whether council members' schedules aligned and if they would discuss budget approval continued for several minutes.
"I just want to make you all aware, I'm very disappointed right now," said Lajan Cephas, who is not able to vote on council matters except in the event a tiebreaker vote is necessary. "I know my opinion doesn't matter, but we're here to do the city's business, and that should always matter."
Summers made a motion to defer the vote, and council member Frank Stout seconded. Sputty Cephas was joined by council member Shay Sisco-Lewis in opposition the motion. Lajan Cephas broke the tie, also voting in opposition of the motion. The council then began discussing the proposed budget.
Eventually, council members approved the budget unanimously.
The council also passed an ordinance establishing a maintenance reserve fund, which transferred $500,000 from the general fund to the maintenance reserve. Steckman and Director of Finance Perry Peregoy will maintain the reserve and deposit a minimum of $50,000 each fiscal year. No money will be withdrawn from the maintenance reserve fund until July 1, 2036.
The FY26 budget established the property tax rate of $1.69 per $100 of all assessed value, the same tax rate as the previous year.
The City Council was presented with a comically large check from representatives of Chesapeake Employers Insurance totaling $174,000 from a 2022 dividend. Steckman said the city has been working with Chesapeake Employers to help control workplace accidents and that the money will go into the general fund.
The city's FY2026 budget will go into effect on July 1.

stories.title: Caroline County Passes Fiscal Year 2026 Budget
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Caroline County passes fiscal year 2026 budget

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners adopted the county's fiscal year 2026 operating and capital budgets at a meeting Tuesday.The commissioners and county employees have been working on the budget for about six months and have balanced a $2 million shortfall. The revenue total for the county sits at $79,208,471.
Allocations to some departments and agencies dropped compared to years prior. Some organizations and nonprofits completely lost county funding in this year's budget. Among those organizations are the Human Service Council, His Hope Ministries and Big Brothers Big Sisters of the Eastern Shore.
While Commissioners President Travis Breeding wanted to cut all nonprofit funding to avoid picking and choosing organizations, Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz chose to give to certain nonprofits.
"My thought process was that that there are a lot of good nonprofits in the county, and we don't have the funding ability to support them all," Breeding said. "So, I didn't really want to get in a situation where we were picking and choosing which ones. I advocate for people to donate to all of those nonprofits, but it just didn't feel like a core responsibility of Caroline County to provide funding there."
During the end of the budget process, changes from the state impacted the proposed budget. In the income tax line item, the county's original $1 million loss due to the state allocating more cost to the county went down to only a $200,000 loss. In the disparity grant section, the legislators passed a bill to make the disparity grant gap cover 90% instead of the normal 75%.
The county decided to add money to the tar and chip fund in the infrastructure line item of the capital budget. This move left over $1 million for the county to allocate in the capital budget.
The county put $100,000 to Public Works for tree trimming and $980,994 toward a fund to purchase radios for emergency services.
In addition to the budget being passed, the county S&P grade has increased from an "AA minus" grade to an "AA." This grade is what allows the county to bond or borrow money.
The commissioners thanked county employees, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and Grant Coordinator Stacy Seward for their hard work balancing the budget and the grade upgrade.
"In an environment where a lot of government agencies are seeing reduced credit ratings, we have managed to see an increase here. I think its a testament to staff, tight budgeting and managing every dollar to make sure its used appropriately," Breeding said.

stories.title: Dorchester County Council Approves 2026 Budget
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Dorchester County Council approves 2026 budget

 May 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 434
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DORCHESTER — After receiving community feedback over removing the tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock, the Dorchester County Council worked with each other, County Manager Jerry Jones and county staff to modify the proposed county budget.The differentials, which lower tax rates in the municipalities to account for duplicated services, remain intact in the fiscal year 2026 budget passed by the County Council Tuesday.
Rather than removing the differentials, the county made adjustments to its budget including deferring all nonprofit funding to a later time.
The county's real property tax rate will increase by 3 cents across the board, bringing the overall tax rate to $1.03 per $100 of assessed value. Cambridge residents will pay 95.67 cents per $100 of assessed value, and Hurlock residents will pay 94.79 cents per $100 of assessed value.
"We came up with a product. Is it the best product in the world? Heck no. But it will suit the needs of the people in the county," said council member William Nichols in reference to the budget.
As Nichols voted in favor of the budget bill, he made a point to explain to the community that this was the worst budget he has seen in the 30 years he's sat on the council. Nichols said that there have been no hidden agendas and that he appreciates all the feedback.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer is concerned the council will end up in the same position next year, with the state of Maryland expecting to reach a $6 billion deficit in the next two years if there are no significant changes.
Council member Rob Kramer agreed with Nichols, saying this was the worst budget he's seen in the 20 years in his seat, but "we made lemons out of lemonade."
Contention between the state capital and rural Maryland was brought up often. Kramer said he doesn't think Annapolis has any hope in rural Maryland, but at the same time, he doesn't have any hope in Annapolis.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) attended the meeting Tuesday, assuring residents they have a voice in Annapolis. Hutchinson echoed the sentiments of the council members, saying there's a major disconnect between what happens in the capital and what happens in the community.
"I just ask you, please, when you hear us talking about this stuff next year, please, I ask you to write letters, please make phone calls, please be as active as possible in your community to relay to Annapolis that Dorchester County cannot continue to take the economic hits it has been," Pfeffer said before opening up the floor for comments.
The budget bill will take effect on July 1.

stories.title: Cambridge, Hurlock Speak Out Against Dorchester Tax Differential Cut
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge, Hurlock speak out against Dorchester tax differential cut

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Leading into the first public budget hearing for Dorchester County's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, Cambridge and Hurlock leaders made their appeals for a reinstatement of tax differentials."We beg you to pull out a pencil and make some changes," Hurlock Council President Earl Murphy Jr. said at the Dorchester County Council meeting May 6.
During the standing-room-only meeting, the council heard from municipal leaders as well as residents about their concerns with the state of the draft budget.
Concerns largely centered on a proposal in the county's draft budget to remove tax differentials, or lower property tax rates, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents. The proposal was one of multiple tax increases suggested in an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit.
The differentials aim to address services paid for by the municipalities instead of the county.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property. Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's proposed rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
At the meeting May 6, Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said the removal of the tax differential would only be acceptable if the county planned to provide the services to Cambridge and Hurlock residents that the municipalities currently provide.
"Let's be real, the county does not have the capacity to fulfill these necessary service needs," she said. "Therefore, why remove the differential?"
Cephas proposed the county should instead take out a loan on its reserve fund and pave three less miles of roads in fiscal year 2026. She said doing this would save the county enough money to keep the differentials.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery suggested keeping the tax differentials in place and imposing a higher tax across the county. He said that would be more equitable.
Cephas also mentioned an idea to create a Dorchester County Revenue Options Task Force. She said those in the task force would be charged with locating potential additional revenue streams. She said she would sign up to be on the task force if it was created.
"A loss for Dorchester County is a loss for Cambridge," she said. "And we're in this battle with you."
In an interview May 7, Hurlock Mayor the Rev. Charles Cephas said the duty of elected officials is to make life better for their constituents. He said with other financial concerns like inflation, the removal of the tax differential could be devastating for residents.
Charles Cephas said after the county meeting, he is still "very concerned" and "very wary" the county's budget difficulties will be an annual issue. "And the residents are unable to financially support this type of increase," he said.
In recent months, the county's budget woes have created an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair during meetings. The council has said its budget problems have largely been brought on by cost shifts from the state.
Former Cambridge Mayor Cleveland Rippons argued the county is doing the same thing to its residents that the state is doing to the county with cost shifts.
"Is that not the same?" he asked.
At the end of the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the council hears what everyone is saying and understands this is hard for residents.
"We lose sleep over this," he said. "Everybody says that we don't care. We do care."
Pfeffer said the council has made efforts to address budget problems without raising taxes, but those efforts have not been fruitful.
"If we don't pay the bills, they'll withhold our income tax," he said about the state. "That is why this is so hard for us to deal with."
The Dorchester County Council will hold its next budget public hearing May 13 at 6 p.m. The final budget hearing and budget adoption is slated for May 20. Pfeffer said the council cannot make any changes to the draft budget until after the next public hearing on May 13.

stories.title: Cambridge City Manager Presents Balanced Draft Budget
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge city manager presents balanced draft budget

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A few sentences into introducing Cambridge's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, City Manager Glenn Steckman told those at a Cambridge City Council meeting April 28 that the city is financially stable."And I think that's very important," he said. "That does not mean that challenging times may not be in the city's future. However, we should look at the glass as half full."
During the meeting, Steckman detailed the city's proposed balanced $18 million general fund budget and discussed the city's four enterprise funds, which include sewer, marina, water and special projects funds.
Steckman called the fiscal year 2026 budget a "transitional budget" as COVID-19 relief funding through the American Rescue Plan Act comes to an end.
"This year's budget preparation included transitioning away from the ARPA funds," Steckman said. "These are once-in-a-generation funds that allow the city to pay salaries, support capital projects and fund nonprofit donations."
GENERAL FUND
According to the draft general fund budget, the city expects to bring in $9.84 million in taxes at the same tax rate it did last year, 80 cents per $100 of assessed value. With no plans to raise taxes, the city's budget stands in contrast with the county's.
In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
In Cambridge, the proposed general fund budget includes a 3% raise for all city employees except Steckman and additional $3,000 raises for those in the police department so the positions stay competitive in the marketplace.
Steckman said the budget includes four new positions: a public information officer, code officer, housing adviser and GIS technician.
Steckman said the housing adviser will act as an advocate for renters in Cambridge.
CAPITAL PROJECTS
Although the city is not facing the same kinds of budget concerns the county is facing, Steckman said the city has $23 million in capital needs. He said the city will seek grants to help address this but that probably won't be enough.
Currently, the city has budgeted $2.1 million for capital projects in fiscal year 2026.
Steckman said the mayor and commissioners will "seriously" have to look into borrowing or obtaining a bond of $1.5 million to replace the HVAC system at the city's public safety complex on Washington Street and at least $8 million to renovate the historic city hall on Gay Street.
"We cannot get grants or anywhere enough grants to offset these costs," Steckman said. "And these costs are only rising each year that we don't address them."
Steckman said the city will begin setting times to meet with City Council about the budget.

stories.title: Cambridge City Council Calls on County for Tax Differential
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge City Council calls on county for tax differential

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following the introduction of Dorchester County's draft fiscal year 2026 budget, the Cambridge City Council is requesting a more equitable approach to taxes.In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
During the meeting, Cambridge Commissioner Brian Roche said the council understands the county is facing budget problems that have been brought on by "unfunded mandates" from the state.
"We're sympathetic to those challenges," Roche said. "However, the solution cannot be to place an even greater burden on Cambridge."
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
Roche said the tax differential is essentially the county acknowledging Cambridge and Hurlock pay for many of their own services — like public safety and water and sewer — so the county doesn't have to.
Roche estimated that with the county's budget proposals — which include an increase of 3 cents to the real property tax for all county residents — Cambridge residents would face a 11.15% increase on their county tax bill. He said Hurlock would face an increase of about 12%.
Roche said county residents who do not live in Cambridge or Hurlock would face a 3% increase.
"It's not equitable to ask for us to take a bigger slice of this pie when there's other areas they're not asking for them to do their share," Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said.
Before the City Council voted to adopt the resolution, Commissioner Brett Summers said he has been talking about the tax differential since his campaign. He said he has been advocating for the hiring of a consultant to determine what the "right" tax rate is.
"And I think what that'll result in doing is reduce the tax rate that city residents pay but ... increase the tax rate that county residents pay," he said, "... because we're not trying to reduce the revenue coming into the county, we're just trying to have a fair and equitable allocation of taxes bases on services provided."
Commission President Sputty Cephas agreed with Roche and Lajan Cephas, saying that he understands the county's situation, but the city is providing services that would otherwise fall on the county's plate. He said there needs to be a "fair and equitable" solution.
"So how we get there, I'm open to it," he said. "But as of right now, I'm in support of (the resolution)."

stories.title: Dorchester County Makes Its Way Through Grueling Budget Process
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Dorchester County makes its way through grueling budget process

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Over the past four months, an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair has colored budget meetings in Dorchester County.In mid-April, the Dorchester County Council introduced a $91.96 million proposed operating budget for fiscal year 2026 with proposals to increase taxes. The introduction came after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
At the same time, Dorchester County Public Schools has been working to eliminate a multi-million dollar deficit of its own. At an April budget work session, DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said the district is still $5.59 million in the hole. The district hopes to eliminate the deficit by the Board of Education's May meeting.
To balance and pass these budgets, difficult decisions — like the school district canceling summer school for 2025 and the county increasing 911 fees from $1.50 to $4.25 — have already been made.
"We hate to have to put any of this on the backs of our citizens, but these are state laws that are being passed down as a bandaid for us to pay," County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "And unfortunately we're having to pass it down onto our citizens because we have no other revenue to pay these bills."
WHAT MAKES FY26 DIFFERENT
Dorchester County's proposed operating budget is $10 million more than the fiscal year 2025 budget passed last May. County Manager Jerry Jones said the increases are in part due to new education requirements from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education plan.
Jones said another reason the county has had to increase spending include cost shifts from the state to the county for things like teacher pensions.
In an effort to lessen budget costs, the county sought a waiver for the maintenance of effort for education, which is a law that requires counties to provide as much funding per pupil as was provided in the previous fiscal year. But with a narrow window between the state passing a budget and the waiver's due date, the county had to ask for an extension, which was denied.
"It's disappointing," Jones said. "But at the end of the day, we've got to keep moving forward."
Thompson said Blueprint requirements, like increasing teacher starting salaries, are part of the reason why the school district's budget — which is separate from the county's — has been difficult to balance this year. He said inflation and recurring program costs have also hindered the process.
"No decision is easy," he said. "But I think we're all trying to make the best decision for our students."
Both Jones and Thompson said they don't see the annual budget process getting easier any time soon. Jones said he doesn't see things getting easier unless change is made at the state level.
"I don't see (the budget) easing up in years to come unless some big changes are considered at the general assembly and future sessions," he said. "We'll see how it plays out."
TAX DIFFERENTIALS
One of the proposed changes to balance the county's budget is to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for Cambridge and Hurlock. This would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full property tax rate.
Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said although the county is trying its best to balance the budget, she believes this measure is unfair to Cambridge residents. She said the tax differential essentially returns money to tax payers for "duplicated" services.
Cephas also said Cambridge is growing, which will increase the tax base and bring in more revenue for the county. She said the county should instead look into raising taxes in unincorporated areas that are "a little bit better off."
Jones said he doesn't know what the final budget will look like, but said the council welcomes input.
"We want people to come forward and contribute to this conversation," he said.
Adoption of Dorchester County's budget is slated for May 20. The county's first public budget hearing will be held May 6.
Thompson said the Dorchester County Board of Education has to pass the budget by the end of June, but he hopes the board will pass the budget in May to give staff time to make necessary preparations.

stories.title: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Passes Budget
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. passes budget

 March 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 293
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a board meeting March 19, the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors passed its budget for the 2025 calendar year.CWDI Board Treasurer Frank Narr said that although the budget is a "barebones" one, it takes into account the money CWDI has leftover from 2024 and what it projects for 2025.
Narr said CWDI — which is spearheading a project to develop land along the Choptank River in Cambridge — expects to bring in $182,000 and spend $308,000 in 2025. Although that would create a budget deficit of $126,000, Narr said CWDI had $139,000 surplus from the 2024 calendar year budget.
Narr said the board is also expecting property and transfer tax abatements and refunds from the county, which would add roughly $42,000 to CWDI's budget for 2025. Between the money CWDI has leftover from 2024 and the refunds from the county, Narr said CWDI expects to have a surplus of $55,000 at the end of 2025.
After Narr presented the proposed budget, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman expressed concern the board might be creating a false narrative that CWDI is in financial trouble with this budget.
"I just want to state as the city manager, I still see a very financially sound community development board," Steckman said. "It's just the way the numbers are reflecting right now. And that could change dramatically in five months."
Steckman shared other opportunities where CWDI could gain more income, including potential city and state tax breaks and additional funding in the new fiscal year.
"While this looks kind of negative, it really isn't," Steckman said, later adding, "So please don't post on 'Destination Cambridge' the world is ending for CWDI."
Steckman said that as CWDI brings in additional revenue, the budget will need to be amended to reflect it.

stories.title: How ARPA Funds Shaped Maryland's Mid-Shore
stories.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
stories.content:
How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 March 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 884
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."
