stories.title: Easton Planners: Amid Affordable Housing Shortage, Inclusionary Zoning May Be Useful
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton planners: amid affordable housing shortage, inclusionary zoning may be useful

 January 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1134
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through her work at the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Daisy Aguilar interacts with many prospective first-time homebuyers. Of the many challenges they face, housing prices in Easton and Talbot County are at the top of the list."The houses, they're not affordable right now," Aguilar, the center's housing coordinator, said. "And most people that are buying, they're buying in Dorchester County because it's more affordable than it is in Talbot County."
An inclusionary zoning ordinance in the works could pave the way for more affordable homeownership and rental opportunities in Easton. It would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable, defined separately for ownership and rental.
Inclusionary units in ownership developments would need to meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income, while rental developments would need to meet prices affordable for households making up to 60% of area median income.
According to Jim Bent, chair of the Affordable Housing Board, Easton's area median income was around $98,000 last year.
While similar legislation has faced hurdles in the past, town leaders and affordable housing proponents are hopeful the time is now for inclusionary zoning to be implemented.
EASTON'S WORKFORCEEaston Mayor Megan Cook is well aware of the fact many can't afford to live in town, including essential workers, town employees and police officers.
"When you're sworn to protect and serve a community, yet you can't even live in the community that you're dedicating your life to, that says something," Cook said. "That's not quite the message we should be sending people."
According to the draft ordinance, Census data shows that 42% of around 17,000 Talbot County workers commute into the county. Cook and others are hoping the ordinance can lower that percentage.
"A lot of the people who work in those fields earn wages where they have been priced out of the Easton market, and so their only option is to find housing in adjacent counties," said Miguel Salinas, Easton's director of planning and zoning.
For homebuyers, the local market is a significant challenge. According to the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors, the average home price in Talbot County in 2024 was $856,000.
Town staff's calculation of the maximum affordable home price for a family of four making the area median income is $292,000.
"There was a time, a couple years, not too long ago, that houses were affordable," Aguilar said. "I mean, they were selling fast, but they were affordable. And at least you had the possibility of actually getting a house."
THE ORDINANCESalinas, who has led the town's efforts to create the ordinance, recognizes it is just one piece of the puzzle. But it's a critical step, he said.
"This is one tool in the toolbox. And it's been discussed for 20-plus years," Salinas said.
Since it was initially presented in February 2023, Salinas said the ordinance has endured many revisions, along with being viewed by the town's Affordable Housing Board, Attainable Housing Task Force and an outside contractor.
Town planners looked at similar provisions in jurisdictions such as Queen Anne's County, Annapolis and Frederick when drafting the ordinance.
A draft version of the inclusionary housing ordinance was passed 4-1 by the town's Planning Commission last November.
Planning Commission member Michael Ports, speaking for himself and not the commission, said the inclusionary zoning ordinance would do two things particularly well. It would push the "cost burden predominantly away from existing residents" and incentivize developers to build inclusionary units.
In addition to the requirement that 15% of units fit the inclusionary definitions, the ordinance would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus.
Such aspects of the ordinance encourage mixed-income projects, which town leaders believe can help to reduce housing inequities.
"Housing segregation opens the door to other types of segregation, and you can certainly see that in many, many communities," Salinas said. "But not just racial and ethnic, but also age."
Tom Klein, the Planning Commission's sole vote against the ordinance, says he is a proponent of more affordable and workforce housing. He believes inclusionary zoning is not "necessary nor a cost-effective way" to achieve that goal.
"For the past two years that I have been on the Planning Commission, just about every new development proposal has come with a component of affordable/workforce housing," Klein wrote in an email.
Recent developments that provide the town with affordable housing include projects from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, such as Port Street Commons, a multi-use property with nine affordable apartment units that opened in December, and Silo Square, a mixed-income housing project greenlit in October.
Revitalization of the Doverbrook Apartments complex in Easton is underway and will feature an additional 14 affordable units on top of 50 existing ones. On Elliott Road, more than 100 apartments are under construction, a portion of those affordable.
Last July, the town approved the annexation of 17 acres of land for a housing project on the east side of Route 50. In the annexation agreement, developers agreed at least 50% of the project's apartment units will be affordable.
Given the number of ongoing projects, Klein says he feels inclusionary zoning would not "provide a significant number" of additional affordable units.
But Ports believes the ordinance will ensure that the limited supply of undeveloped land in the town is being used properly.
"It's really the biggest asset any community has," Ports said. "If we want to allow someone to potentially change it forever, we need to make sure that they're investing in the community in some way."
REGULATIONAt the November Planning Commission meeting, Klein and other commission members expressed concerns of overregulation prior to voting on the ordinance.
"I think that the market's taking care of it," Klein said. "I think that we're putting a lot of regulation here. Like I said, I think there could be a lot of unintended consequences that come out of that and a lot of cost for what we get out of it."
Salinas and Bent both said the market hasn't been able to address ballooning home and rental costs in recent years.
Bent said he's heard from planning commissioners in the past that a "tool" is needed to point developers toward what the town wants in terms of affordability.
While proponents of inclusionary zoning are confident it can be this tool, they recognize the housing problem in Easton is complex.
"If we got into this hole of housing deficiency over the course of decades, it's impossible to fix that in one year, let alone even 10 years," Ports said. "It will be a game of playing catch-up."
Cook hopes Easton residents, along with the Town Council, see affordable housing as a top challenge to tackle.
"I do hope that they see the importance of this issue, and I also hope that the community itself sees the importance of the issue," Cook said. "For the longevity and the vibrancy of the Town of Easton, it's an important issue."

stories.title: Grasonville proposal looks to develop farmland for infill affordable housing
stories.author: Staff Writer
stories.content:
Grasonville proposal looks to develop farmland for infill affordable housing

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GRASONVILLE — A proposed water and sewer amendment to supply a potential affordable housing development in Grasonville gained support during a public hearing Dec. 10.The proposal is to amend the property's water and sewer services to accommodate the development of 72 townhomes and 218 single family lots.
Located at 5400 Main Street, Aspire at Ewing Farm is a 112 acre property currently used for agriculture and is zoned Grasonville Planned Residential Neighborhood.
Flows from use are anticipated to be 72,500 gallons per day. Sewer service would be provided via a constructed gravity sewer pump station and water service would he provided by the Grasonville water system.
Sketch plan approval for the project was granted by the Queen Anne's County Planning Commission in October and met requirements of the Water and Sewer Master Plan.
The property has been part of the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan for a 10 year service since 2011, according to attorney Joe Stevens on behalf of developer K. Hovnanian.
The property has been ratified as part of the Grasonville Growth Area and zoned for planned residential development for decades.
The 2022 Comprehensive Plan highlights affordable housing as a high need in the county.
According to Mike Irons, division president of K. Hovnanian Homes of Maryland, LLC the Aspire Development will include "efficient homes without a lot of bells and whistles," aimed toward first time home buyers, workforce housing and affordable housing.
"We're bringing to the market something that the county needs," Irons said.
K. Hovnanian is also the builder and developer for the 55 and older Four Seasons Community.
Barry Griffith, planner with Lane Engineering, noted the location is an infill property surrounded by existing houses, schools and parks.
"We're a hole in a donut of development around us, and that's where we want new growth to go," Griffith said.
The property is located in a priority funding area, meaning the state and county have both acknowledged it as appropriate for state funding for future growth, he said.
Member of the Ewing family Mitchell Andrew noted the Ewings have been approached by local, regional and national developers over the years and "without a doubt" K. Hovnanian was the first that "really fit Grasonville," and met the needs of the county.
The public hearing saw over 10 in-person as well as six emails from residents voicing support for the amendment to move the development forward with resounding sentiment toward the county's need for affordable housing.
Agreeing the project met the needs of the county, Commission President Jim Moran noted the loose terminology of affordable housing that could change in the potentially two years before the development is ready.
Following potential commissioner amendment approval for sewer and water redesignation, the project would then move forward for additional approvals including site plan, subdivision and, Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance.
A public hearing was also held to consider amending the Queen Anne's County 2011 Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan for Barnstable Lowery Farm's proposed development of 82 townhomes on a 11 acre lot in Main Street Chester.
The property is agricultural land consisting of two farms on either side of the three improved properties that are not included in the development proposal. The proposed development is part of Lowery Farm and Dream Farm. The portion adjacent to Main Street is zoned Town Center and the parcel to the rear of the site is zoned Countryside.
All residential development will occur in the Town Center zoning district.
Sewer services would be provided by Vacuum Sewer Collection Station 'G' and water services would be provided by the Stevensville/Chester water system.
Flows from the use are anticipated at 20,500 gallons per day.
The Planning Commission granted concept plan approval for the Barnstable Townhouse development in October and no anticipated off-site sewer or water infrastructure issues are associated with this proposal.
At public comment, Tracy Schulz, on behalf of Dream Farm ownership, spoke in favor of the project, citing the development appropriate for the area.
One email voiced concern for future developments' impact on water and sewer services on Kent Island, Grasonville, and Queenstown, and recommended posting projected usage numbers.
Public comment is still being accepted and a commissioner vote is expected at the Jan. 14 meeting.

stories.title: Developers Host 3Rd Community Meeting For Easton Crossing Project
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Developers host 3rd community meeting for Easton Crossing project

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Developers and residents gathered Wednesday evening for a third community meeting concerning a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, hosted the meeting to update neighbors on its draft site plans and facilitate community feedback.
The Easton Crossing infill project is expected to add around 120 units where a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation used to sit. Additionally, there are significant plans for commercial use and open areas.
Renderings show six buildings planned for the 6.5-acre site. Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said the first building, which will have 15 residential units, is projected to open in December 2027.
Benincasa emphasized the mixed-income aspect of the project on Wednesday. Some units will be at market rate, and others down to where people "will be paying $500 to $600 a month for a new apartment."
"Unlike most developers, we don't build affordable units and market-rate units," Benincasa said. "We build the same unit across the site, and we just have specific ratio goals that we hit for that site. If I'm living in an affordable unit and Joe is in a market-rate unit, and I go over to … Joe's apartment one night, I will have no idea who pays what."
Based on previous feedback, developers and architects are looking into using bricks that are darker in color to match surrounding buildings. They also touched on other topics that were raised at previous community meetings this year, such as lighting, open space and plantings.
"You're going to be seeing a mix of pedestrian (lights) and some larger lights in the areas of the parking lot," Benincasa said. "But those larger lights, from a sizing perspective, are going to feel more like downtown Easton."
There will be a focus on maintaining open space at the property, as well as around 70% native plantings. Benincasa added that once finished, there will be "around four to 10 shrubs or trees per 50 feet."
All parking spots will be screened, some by shrubs and trees and others by buildings. While Benincasa said South Street will be a "secondary" exit and entrance for residents, developers "fully anticipate" most drivers to use Brookletts Avenue.
"But we don't want them on Brookletts. That's the point," resident Harriett Page said.
Benincasa said a traffic study was completed by Lenart Traffic Consulting last week, which did not signify worries about the traffic increase around the site. An increase of around 20 cars during peak hour on Brookletts Avenue is projected.
Resident Joe Minarick said "with Brookletts being the main thoroughclear and the main import" for the site, those projections "(seemed) a little funny."
"Brookletts might be the front of the project, but it is not the only way that people are going to go in and out," Benincasa said. Those heading east toward Caroline County may use Kemp Lane to access Dover Road, he said.
As for the commercial aspect of the site, Benincasa said developers aren't expecting national businesses. In fact, Chesapeake Community Development is looking for local businesses "emotionally invested in their success."
Developers may also encourage businesses to hire people with disabilities, a segment of the population that The Arc strives to serve.
"We have had discussions about if a business wants to hire people with disabilities, then there would be, sort of, credits for that," said Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc. "Or for hiring local as well."
"That will be coming in 2026, 2027," he continued, "as we think about what those incentives are as we begin to market the commercial spaces."

stories.title: Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Approved Silo Square housing project generates resident opposition

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 815
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maury Schlesinger knows the town needs more housing, but when he takes the short walk from his home to 410 Needwood Ave, he can't quite envision the development that's being planned for the lot.A recently approved 28-unit townhouse development has garnered mixed opinions from the Easton community, particularly East End residents like Schlesinger.
The property is currently home to 10 unused grain bins from a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation. The Arc bought the 2.36-acre lot from Perdue and received approval from the Easton Planning Commission in October to move forward with developing the site into mixed-income housing.
While not immediately surrounded by residences, the lot is close to a number of single-family homes. Schlesinger, who's been outspoken at town meetings against the design of the project, says the project is "inappropriate" and "out of context" with the surrounding residential areas.
"You're putting a tear through the fabric of our town," Schlesinger said.
Schlesinger, along with other neighbors, say they support bringing more affordable and workforce housing to Easton, and even to the lot in question. Many of their concerns stem from the design of the townhomes and the process by which Silo Square was designed and approved.
"Most all folks ... are on record supporting housing at the site, simply not as proposed, and not in the manner that this has been done," said Matt Carberry, who lives within viewing distance of the grain bins.
DESIGN CONCERNS
Planning Commission members voiced split opinions on Silo Square designs during two hearings in September and October.
Commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint, Vice Chairperson Michael Ports and Chair Pro Tem William Ryall each complimented developers for how the townhomes looked in renderings. Commission members Victoria McAndrews and Thomas Klein were less receptive to the design, though both joined the other three in approving the project at the Oct. 17 meeting.
Residents who spoke during public comment were more unified in their opposition.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said in an interview that developers want to use high-quality materials and avoid creating something that's a "faux representation of a different time period."
"We're not in downtown Easton," Benincasa said. "We didn't really like the idea of replicating just another kind of brick facade, or another kind of 1990s-looking townhome community. We want to make sure when people look back on it, they know that this was built in 2024."
Resident Loretta Hatzel-Geraci says her largest gripe with the design is that the townhomes face inwards on the lot.
"Inward-facing doesn't really promote community interaction," she said.
"I can appreciate the community's concerns around inward-facing," Benincasa said. "The reality with the site is that because we have no other homes around us, if we made it outward-facing, those homes are just going to face the back of industrial properties."
Benincasa said that of the 28 units, around 21 will start off at market-rate rent prices, with the other seven priced at workforce rates achievable for those making around $55,000 to $70,000 annually.
APPROVAL PROCESS
Since the project falls within the town's planned redevelopment overlay district, it did not require approval from the Easton Town Council. The Planning Commission could have approved it at a September meeting, though it asked developers to procure a traffic study and return one month later.
Between the two commission hearings, developers held a meeting with Silo District residents. Benincasa said two main topics were discussed: the design and entrances to the development, the latter of which was adjusted to move the main entrance onto Maryland Avenue.
Still, East End residents wish that public input played more of a role and that the process wasn't so quick.
"The public gets to see the project too late in the process," Schlesinger said. " … There's no opportunity for dialogue. There's only the opportunity to shout yay or nay."
Both Hatzel-Geraci and Carberry say they felt the approval was a done deal, whether the residents spoke out or not.
"Whatever observations or comments made by the community, if considered, were essentially dismissed by the Planning Commission," Carberry said. "The appearance was that the project's approval was basically pre-approved absent any community input."
Schlesinger says he wishes developers were required to reach out to the community before an application is sent to the town. He added that the process for Easton Crossing, The Arc's mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue, included the level of community outreach he wishes Silo Square was afforded.
Benincasa said he's heard from community members that The Arc is held to a "higher standard," a challenge the organization welcomes.
"I would agree that I think moving forward, for our projects, we're going to try and make sure there's more community outreach well ahead of time," Benincasa said.
"The normal developer kind of builds, fills, and sells, that's how they make their money. We don't," he continued. "And so we go into a project with the attitude that we're going to be neighbors. We need to make sure that we have a good relationship."

stories.title: Caroline County Creates Fund for Land Preservation
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Caroline County creates fund for land preservation

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 294
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners enacted a legislative bill on establishing a fund to receive payments of compensatory preservation contributions to Caroline County when solar energy systems are developed on a parcel of land identified as Class 1 or 2 soils.The county has discussed this bill in workshops since September. After many adjustments to logistical wording of the bill, the county passed the legislation.
"It is earmarked for an additional contribution to the Maryland Ag Land Preservation Fund, which is used to purchase Ag Land Preservation easements on existing farmland," Breeding said. "So basically, the MAUPH program enters into easement agreements with farmers that basically states that they will never develop put solar or build housing or any other form of development on the farmland, so it basically preserves it as agricultural land forever."
Caroline County has seen multiple solar arrays go up on farmland in the county,
The fee for this contribution will be determined at final site plan approval and must be paid before a building permit is issued. The county has been informing solar projects about this forthcoming change through its website and email communications since the initial discussion of the change.
The bill applies to any project with Class 1 or Class 2 soils, regardless of zoning district. However, it does not apply if the land is within town limits.
The county is happy to have the bill done, during the commissioners meeting Breeding thanked all working parties of Caroline County for their contributions to the bill.
"It's been a long process. It's been a lot of nuance details that we had to work through, and it feels good that we've been able to to get this accomplished, and we look forward to preserving the agricultural heritage of Caroline County," Breeding said.

stories.title: Kent Commissioners Oppose Striped Bass Limits
stories.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
stories.content:
Kent commissioners oppose striped bass limits

 September 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On Aug. 29, the Kent County commissioners signed a letter expressing their opposition to proposed striped bass (rockfish) limits, sending it to Maryland Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz.The commissioners voiced opposition to the Fishery Management Plan amendment that proposes a 12% reduction in the harvest of striped bass.
They said the changes would reduce the commercial fishing industry's ability to harvest striped bass by 58%.
The letter objected to new regulations allowing catch-and-release fishing from January through May, a period that has been closed the past six years to protect spawning fish. The commissioners said the policy contradicts the Maryland Department of Natural Resources' proposal last year to safeguard spawning stock biomass with a 2029 recovery goal.
They added that Kent County's recreational and charter boat industry would be hurt by a non-targeting closure from July 15 to Aug. 31, when boats would be prohibited from catching rockfish. That closure normally lasts two weeks.
"This is unnecessary and will create significant hardships for the industry, economic tourism in the county and income generated by fishers," the letter stated.
ECONOMIC IMPACTCommission President Ron Fithian, a longtime waterman, said they have already heard of cancellations and reductions in reserved trips for charter boats.
"The economic impact on our county and its waterfront businesses will bear financial losses," Fithian said. "It will erode the economic growth we have worked so hard to develop."
Although the fisheries have faced regulatory reductions in the past, commissioners called the latest proposals a "tipping point," predicting some food businesses may close for good.
Commissioner John Price said, "Unfortunately the Department of Natural Resources is not going to be satisfied until they run the commercial watermen and charter boats out of business."
Price compared the situation to waterfowl hunting, where DNR has allowed Sunday hunting instead of providing a rest and nesting period for birds.
Fithian said he has fought similar issues his entire life, calling it "death by a thousand cuts." He said DNR enacts new regulations year after year without evidence to support them.
The letter concluded with a call for state officials to support Kent County's small business community: "Kent County is open for business, and we want to keep it that way."
INDUSTRY RESPONSERob Newberry, chair of the Delmarva Fisheries Association, said the proposed amendment makes changes to Maryland's recreational season baseline that are harmful to both commercial and charter operations.
He accused the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, DNR and the Coastal Conservation Association Maryland of hypocrisy, saying their policies disturb spawning rockfish while claiming to conserve them.
"If they allow rockfish to be disturbed during the spawning season, they are not conserving anything," Newberry said. "It's counterproductive."
He criticized the Coastal Conservation Association, saying its actions prioritize finances and recreation over fish health and the industry's future.
Newberry said if the amendment is passed the industry will face "severe limitations."
"It's a complete disaster," he said. "And it is inexplicable."
PUBLIC HEARINGS
Newberry emphasized that no final decision has been made. A public hearing is scheduled for Sept. 23 at the Michael E. Busch Library in Annapolis, which has a seating capacity of 200.
"We are trying to get as many to attend as possible to tell DNR we do not support this amendment," Newberry said.
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission will meet Oct. 23-24 to make its final decision.
Maryland Department of Natural Resources Associate Director Michael Luisi said since the commissioners' letter was addressed to Kurtz, a response will come following review by the agency's Office of Communications.

stories.title: As Solar Looming on Horizon, Betterton Residents Weigh in Ahead of Public Hearing
stories.author: Will Bontrager
stories.content:
As solar looms on horizon, Betterton residents weigh in ahead of public hearing

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — For the past two Saturday afternoons, residents living near Betterton held informal meetings discussing Halo Betterton Solar LLC.Halo Betterton LLC had submitted an application in April for a 5-megawatt solar project on a 30-acre site at Howell Point Road and Still Pond-Betterton Road which, if built, will be directly across from some of these neighbors.
As brought up in previous council meetings, the town is opposed to the project because the company's plans do not fit with Betterton's comprehensive plan. It takes away any potential to have commercial development in that area.
The informal meetings were conducted by Paul Falcon and Kathryn Klvana at 13959 Still Pond Road and then at the Betterton Volunteer Firehouse, and drew out other neighbors who would be affected by building the installation.
The second meeting that took place at the firehouse was well-attended and included Mayor Donald Sutton, council member Gerry Werner, longtime residents and people passionate about this cause coming from other Maryland regions affected by these facilities.
Sutton said it is good to see so many people come out and express their concerns.
Residents raised multiple objections to the proposed solar installation during the meetings.
Douglas Cregar said his group has researched the project extensively and opposes the installation.
"We've done our research and are against this solar installation here," Cregar said. "Studies show that everyone within a mile will lose 5% in property value. Also, among 35 active solar proposals in Maryland, there is no location like the Betterton area they plan to build on, that is surrounded by residential housing on three sides."
Art Pleasanton raised concerns about emergency services, noting the proposed site would interfere with helicopter medical evacuations.
"If (solar) is built where they want to build it they'd have to do it over a helicopter landing zone," Pleasanton said. "The next nearest one is at Worton at the school. For anyone who thinks this is not an issue, last year a little girl was saved from drowning because we had a way to get her out fast."
Kathryn Klvana expressed frustration with recent state legislation that could override local zoning decisions.
"I'm shocked that with this new law Governor Wes Moore just signed, the state can override local zoning and put this huge solar farm across from our homes," Klvana said. "We moved to this beautiful place to retire. We're zoned community residential. What about our rights?"
Tracy Cameransi, who lives in a small area just outside of town, said she frequently receives calls from solar companies but will not sell to them. She is opening her home for residents to attend the upcoming virtual hearing together.
"We have a small area just outside of town and we get calls all the time from these solar companies," Cameransi said. "We will never sell to them, but what we are doing is opening up our home on Sept. 9 for the Zoom hearing and everyone is invited to attend at 13499 Still Pond Road."
As the town is preparing for a public hearing for the Halo project, a virtual meeting on Sept. 9 at 7 p.m. online, attendees gave their initial impressions concerning the project.

stories.title: Talbot County Passes DAF Restrictions
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot County passes DAF restrictions

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 303
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed new regulations on food processing residuals Tuesday.County leaders said the approved legislation helps Talbot fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, also referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, materials.
The materials often come in the form of animal waste from food processing, which then can be spread as fertilizer. State rules took effect last summer cracking down on DAF residuals, but some counties have since enacted local legislation to quell further resident concerns.
Jurisdictions like Caroline County saw tense debate over the matter. Many Caroline County residents complained of noxious odors from operations storing food processing residuals in open-top storage containers. Last year, Caroline County banned the open-top method.
Similarly, Talbot's legislation requires closed-top storage of food processing residuals. In addition to the open-top storage ban, Talbot's regulations require the storage applicant to:
Receive site plan approval from the county.Obtain an approved nutrient management plan from the state.Remain at least 500 feet from any residential property lines. If all affected property owners consent to a setback reduction, it can be decreased as far as 200 feet.
"We certainly don't want to be the only jurisdiction on the Shore that neglects to regulate this material," County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said.
Lesher, Council President Chuck Callahan and council members Lynn Mielke and Dave Stepp voted in favor of the legislation. Keasha Haythe, who was absent from Tuesday's meeting, did not vote.
Talbot's Planning Commission and planning officers Brennan Tarleton and Bryce Yelton ironed out the specifics of the regulations since it was drafted last year. Lesher thanked them for their efforts.
"This is one of the more technical issues that we've dealt with," Lesher said, "and I just want to express my appreciation for the staff and for the Planning Commission in working out the details of this."

stories.title: Queen Anne's County Eyes Solar Soil Development Fees
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
Queen Anne's County eyes solar soil development fees

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In response to the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, Queen Anne's County Commissioners considered an emergency ordinance to give a semblance of control back to the county and try to reap soil development fees. It is a tactic no other jurisdiction has yet tried.On May 20, the General Assembly put forward and Gov. Wes Moore approved Senate Bill 931/Renewable Energy Certainty Act that address specific state siting requirements of solar energy generating systems, community solar energy generating systems, establishes siting and standards, and energy storage devices.
Taking effect July 1, this Senate bill establishes a (new, higher) 5% limit to the total acreage of the combined number of solar energy generating stations that may be approved for construction in the priority preservation areas.
It also gives the Public Service Commission the power to approve solar and energy storage projects that meet specific conditions, even if local jurisdictions object; aims to expedite the permitting process for solar projects; addresses the use of agricultural land for solar development, including provisions for priority preservation areas; and also includes some minor provisions for local (county) input on project design and implementation.
While complying with the new rules in Senate Bill 931, Queen Anne's County is now pushing the envelope to try and recoup money from the state permitting solar to be placed on county Class 1 soils, Commissioner Jack Wilson said.
According to Wilson, Queen Anne's County is seeking to impose an impact fee on soils used for development of solar through a per-acre financial contribution to be made to the county when solar energy generating stations and storage devices are developed on Class 1 soils.
The fee will be based on the rates used in the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF) process, which is recognized by the state, according to Wilson.
"It's like if you were going to collect this and pay this for this land, we should be reimbursed at the same level," Wilson said.
With concerns for the Maryland Ag Land Preservation Fund not being supported by the state over the next few years, the proposed impact fee or Compensatory Preservation Contribution on solar generating systems and storage sites is a way to recoup money for further land preservation, Wilson said.
The contribution or soil impact fee will be based upon 50% of the fair market value appraisal as determined by the annual amount, according to Amy Moredock county planning and zoning director, and directed to the county Farmland Preservation Fund.
Senate Bill 931 differs from similar recent cannabis legislation because it doesn't let counties create additional use standards, Moredock said. This means the county must remove all existing utility-scale solar standards and definitions and apply new standards instead.
The Senate bill addresses community solar, which the county's ordinance did not have specific provisions for and also requires the county address energy storage siting, Moredock said.
Solar is permitted in Queen Anne's countryside, agricultural, and industrial zoning districts, according to Moredock.
The county code has kept solar out of mixed use zoning districts, and high and medium density residential zoning districts, she said.
In accordance with the law, Queen Anne's County was also able to prohibit solar in Tier One and Tier Two growth areas and surrounding growth areas often zoned agriculture. This would prohibit siting within areas that are slated for development and municipal growth, she said.
Donna Landis-Smith and Joe Pippin of Queen Anne's County Soil Conservation helped solidify a compensatory preservation contribution, a payment into the dedicated farmland preservation fund to assist with obtaining easements, Moredock said.
The law is written that the 5% applies to the definite article Priority Preservation Area and does not have a caveat as to when that calculation begins, Moredock said.
Easements already preserved are not included in the total Priority Preservation Area numbers, she said.
As listed in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan, the county has approximately 109,000 acres available for the 5% designated for solar, according to Moredock.
Of the 238,000 acres in the county, approximately 88% of it is zoned agricultural and ag use, according to Landis-Smith. At the time of the previous comprehensive plan, there were 83,684 acres preserved and since the adoption of the 2022 Comprehensive Plan, the county has preserved an additional almost 8,000 acres, Landis-Smith said.
The county currently has 1,100 acres in solar.
The commissioners have noted there is a good chance the impact fee proposal would get challenged, Wilson said.
Moredock credited the expertise of Queen Anne's County Geographical Information Systems Coordinators Sam Stanton and Tyler Pease for their understanding of land use to be able to present clear statistics.
The introduction of the ordinance will move forward to the planning commission for more discussion and a public hearing scheduled in two weeks.
The Queen Anne's County Commissioners will next meet July 8 at 5:30 p.m.

stories.title: Planning Commission Recommends Against Seafood Odor Amendment
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Planning Commission Recommends Against Seafood Odor Amendment

 May 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 613
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Planning Commission Thursday provided an unfavorable recommendation on a recently proposed amendment to a seafood odor ordinance.The ordinance, which came after a multi-year push from Ward 4 residents, aims to address complaints of odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a facility located on Maryland Avenue near many homes. The legislation was passed in December, but a final resolution hasn't been reached.
The business recently requested an amendment to the already-approved ordinance, citing that industry experts consider legislation's requirements unachievable.
It requires the business to install odor control technology so "that no odor ... can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way." The deadline to install is July 1.
Owner Mitch Hughes, attorney Zach Smith and the vendor of an odor control system explained Thursday that the ordinance isn't feasible as written.
Their amendment proposes a new standard — that engineers or industry experts confirm odor control equipment uses "best control technologies and methods designed to mitigate odor before it leaves a building."
Commission members agreed the proposed change was too vague. But they also acknowledged that the original ordinance doesn't create a clear path to compliance.
"I feel like we're trying to put a round peg in a square hole here," member Tom Klein said.
Chairperson Philip Toussaint said the business, which was legally permitted to operate by the town beginning in 2019, should've never been OK'd at that site.
"That's tough to hear when we, again, followed the town zoning codes," Smith said. "It's tough to hear that position from the Planning Commission."
Smith said the amendment is not an attempt by Hughes to avoid addressing the odor complaints. Hughes noted he's fully willing to install the odor control system, but he doesn't want to foot the cost if his efforts won't meet the ordinance.
Smith said if the "no odor" requirement isn't changed, it leaves only two options: Chesapeake Brand goes out of business or involves the town in "some sort of protracted legal battle."
Commission members, along with some residents, criticized the business for proposing the amendment so soon before the July 1 deadline.
"If we had another month or two, it could've been doable," said William Ryall, the commission's chair pro tem.
The commission voted 4-0 to advise the Town Council to reject the amendment. But in that same motion, the commission directed the council to incorporate an "enforceable standard" into the already-approved legislation. Despite much discussion Thursday, it's not yet clear exactly what that standard might be.
The Town Council will still review the proposed amendment, likely considering the commission's advice to find a middle ground on a standard that can be met and enforced.
PUBLIC INPUT
Public comment was mixed Thursday, with many of the residents affected by the odor in attendance to oppose Chesapeake Brand's amendment. Some suggested alternative ways to reach a compromise.
Shawn Nuthall said the amended wording has "no teeth, no data, no standards."
"We've been going through this for years and years and years," he said. "It's way, way too long. They should've done something before now."
Others, including some fellow business owners and seafood processors, spoke in support of Hughes and Chesapeake Brand Seafood.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Joe Spurry, owner of Chesapeake Landing Seafood in St. Michaels, said Hughes has good intent and that the town should be wary of not driving the business away.
"He started a business that nobody starts," Spurry said. "Processing seafood is a dying business. I'm one of the last in Talbot County. He's the newest."

stories.title: Talbot Planning Commission Sends DAF Legislation to County Council
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot Planning Commission sends DAF legislation to County Council

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will soon be considering new restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals.Wednesday, the Talbot County Planning Commission unanimously voted to send a piece of legislation up to the council, deeming it consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The legislation aims to help Talbot County fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, which are animal waste from food processing that are often applied to farmland as fertilizer.
Under state law, the residuals cannot be applied to land between Dec. 15 and March 1, requiring them to be stored during the winter months.
Last year, Caroline County restricted storage of food processing residuals, often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in open storage tanks.
Talbot's legislation would ban open-top storage of DAF or food processing residuals. Closed-top storage would be permitted provided it follows the following conditions, among others:
The storage applicant receives site plan approval from the county.The applicant has an approved nutrient management plan from the state.The applicant has at least a 500-foot setback from residential properties, or at least a 200-foot setback if all affected property owners consent.The applicant applies the materials on the same property where they are being stored.The applicant stores and applies the materials in a permitted zoning district.
The legislation would not ban storage of food processing residuals in a temporary storage unit — such as a "mobile, closed container" — near where they are being applied. Such temporary storage would be capped at 90 days.
Before the commission approved the legislation, the body set forth a few minor conditions to be amended.
"The one thing that we do want to make sure is that we exempt food processing residuals that are used for livestock feed," commission member Chip Councell said.
Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer, said that would be an easy amendment to make, simply by adjusting the definition for food processing residuals in the legislation.
Councell added that the county discussed the DAF legislation with the Talbot County Farm Bureau last August. The farm bureau was supportive, he said.
While the commission is recommending approval to the County Council, the bill will still require a council vote to be enacted.

stories.title: Caroline County Worried Solar Concerns Will Grow Bigger if Proposed Bills Are Passed
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County worried solar concerns will grow bigger if proposed bills are passed

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — Proposed House Bill 1036 and Senate Bill 931 have been a discussion for Caroline County Commissioners since the state's legislative session began in January.According to Maryland General Assembly website, the proposed bills state, "Altering the factors the Public Service Commission must consider before taking final action on a certificate of public convenience and necessity; establishing certain requirements for the construction of a certain solar energy generating station or energy storage device."
While at legislative sessions last week, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding and Vice President Larry Porter spoke to oppose the proposed bills, stating they did not provide enough authority over solar development to local jurisdictions.
"I think there were some valuable testimonies on both sides," Porter said. "Since some that time, we have received proposed amendments to the bill. My guess is we will receive some relief in some taxation and commissioning area, but I'm not sure they are going to give up siting authority."
The state has been pushing renewable energy in all counties in the state. To maintain some local autonomy over the effort, counties have created acre moratoriums and location ordinances for solar development.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre moratorium in place.
The commissioners' concern about the proposed bill is the lack of control in the siting of solar in the county.
"I'm gonna break some news here, I think they drafted this bill with a total give away to the solar companies," Breeding said. "To shift the starting point completely in the favor of the solar companies, that's just speculation on my part."
"I think we going to get hosed, and we are getting hosed actively right now with the amendments," he said. "We're gonna walk away thinking we've gotten something out of the deal, but we still are gonna get preempted by the state as far as siting."
Caroline County has personally experienced an issue with siting regulations for a solar company wanting to set up a solar facility in an area in the county where solar is not allowed.
Chaberton Solar requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area, where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting its application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, Barroll said.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
The county has since taken this solar case to court to block the planting of solar in the restricted area.
The county is concerned if proposed house bill 1036 and senate bill 931 are filed, they will face similar issues with siting as they face with Chaberton Solar.
"Everyone that was in that hearing room testifying against that bill was saying 'Do not stripe the counties of local zoning authority' and that message fell on deaf ears."

stories.title: ESLC Talks Land Values at Dorchester County Council Meeting
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — When it comes to acreage and land value, Dorchester County is expected to be one of the most affected counties by sea level rise and storm surge in the year 2100, according to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy.During a Dorchester County Council meeting Feb. 18, Eastern Shore Land Conservancy Land Use and Policy Director Owen Bailey presented data on land value throughout the Eastern Shore. Bailey said the data was acquired with the help of Urban3.
The land trust estimates that an average of three feet of sea level rise in 2100 would mean the loss of 270,000 acres of the Eastern Shore and $2 billion in property tax values.
"And then when you add in storm surge, then that really puts into perspective the financial distress that our communities are going to face in the future with the loss of properties and property tax revenues," Bailey said.
After Bailey showed a map that accounted for storm surge in 2100, County Council President Lenny Pfeffer pointed out that more than half of Dorchester County's land is projected to be gone.
Bailey said Cambridge alone is projected to lose 280 acres and $63 million in value by 2100.
Throughout his presentation, Bailey advocated for concentrated development on the Shore to increase property value. At the same time, he spoke about the importance of maintaining the value that could be loss to sea level rise.
Bailey said the efficiency of land use can be measured by looking at value per acre.
"You take the appraised value of each parcel and you divide it by how many acres it sits on," he said.
When the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy applied this to the Eastern Shore, it noticed historic downtowns are "much more productive than the more suburban, car-focused development" that has been popular since the 1950s. This means that those downtowns, which often are more vulnerable to sea level rise, bring in more property tax revenue per acre than more sprawling areas of the Eastern Shore.
Bailey said that before the Bay Bridge was built in 1952, only 10,000 acres of land — valued at approximately $560,000 per acre — had been developed on the Shore. An additional 163,000 has been developed at less than half of that value since.
With the additional developed land, there has been a need for more sprawling infrastructure, he said.
"So we've built all this infrastructure," Bailey said. "But we haven't really built the value to help us with the maintenance of that infrastructure, which is why a lot of our jurisdictions, pretty much all of our jurisdictions, are struggling with how to keep up with that kind of maintenance."
Bailey said many historic communities on the Shore, which bring more value per acre, are built on waterfronts, meaning sea level rise will most likely affect them.
"So we're encouraging every town to think about how are you going to account for that," he said. "How can you either move that property, protect it or replace that value somewhere else in our community?"
Along with concentrating development, Bailey recommended the county look at zoning restricting the county from allowing value to grow.
"This is something we're encouraging every jurisdiction to take a look at," he said. "It's not our job to tell you what to do. We just want to provide the data and perspective. ... Use your land wisely."
At the end of the presentation Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer asked if the land trust had any recommendations specific to Dorchester County zoning ordinances.
Bailey said they have been focusing on municipalities, looking at zoning in historic districts.
"And how can we ease up on that zoning just to allow that historic pattern to continue," he said.

stories.title: 'Just Not Here': Solar Project Tests Small Town's Growth Plans
stories.author: Will Bontrager
stories.content:
'Just not here': Solar project tests small town's growth plans

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 334
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A proposed 30-acre solar facility is sparking concerns in Betterton, an Eastern Shore town of 287 residents, where local officials worry the project could hamper future development.Halo Betterton Solar LLC has submitted a nearly 300-page application for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity to the Maryland Public Service Commission, despite objections from town leadership.
"We're not opposed to alternative forms of energy, just not in Betterton," said council member Gerry Werner. "Especially not in the only area that could be zoned residential and commercial for our future expansion."
The project, planned for property owned by Schirmer Family Farms LLC along Route 292 and Howell Point Road, would be visible from all town entrances. Town officials have sent their concerns to the solar company and await a response.
The local fire company has also raised safety issues, noting the project would use land currently serving as overflow parking and an emergency helicopter landing area.
The Betterton project is one of seven solar facilities either pending approval or in pre-submission process in Kent County, as solar companies leverage Maryland state preemption laws that limit local control over such developments. The push aligns with Gov. Wes Moore's initiative to reduce greenhouse emissions 60% below 2006 levels by 2031.
In nearby Chestertown, officials faced similar challenges when the Public Service Commission approved a 245-acre solar system on Morgnec Road, despite opposition from both town and county governments.
"If there is well-expressed public sentiment against building this here, maybe the power company will cut their losses," Werner said. He is researching what rights, if any, the town has in the matter.
Meanwhile, Millington is further along in its solar facility process. A second public hearing is scheduled for Feb. 17 regarding the KE51 project, which would occupy part of a 199-acre property. That project, designated as a Community Solar Energy Generating System, would deliver power to subscribers via the Delmarva Power electric distribution grid.
The Public Service Commission maintains final authority over solar facility approvals, though it must consider local jurisdiction input in its decisions.

stories.title: Southern Dorchester County Residents Push for a Seat at the Table
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Southern Dorchester County residents push for a seat at the table

 January 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1121
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TODDVILLE — Around a big wooden table in the back corner of Elijah's General Store in Toddville Wednesday, three generations of south Dorchester County residents outlined a plan to save their home.Dick Dawson, a lifelong resident of Bishops Head, has watched over the years as areas in the southern part of Dorchester County turn from woods to swamp. He's seen land where cattle used to graze become water holes and mud holes that would take a boat to get through.
"The ground is sinking, there's no doubt about that," he said.
Sea level rise has become a significant issue in Dorchester County over the years, particularly in the southern part of the county. Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said the area has faced environmental challenges "as the relationship between the land and the water changes."
"There's massive erosion, there is saltwater intrusion and just a variety of other really relentless environmental challenges," he said.
In an effort to protect these communities in southern Dorchester from disappearing, three men are working to incorporate Blackwater, a new town, giving the communities that call this area home a seat at the table and a chance for survival.
The communities included in the plan for Blackwater are Andrews, Robbins, Wesley, Lakesville, Crapo, Wingate, Toddville, Bishops Head and Crocheron.
Each community would still exist within the new town, the planners said. But incorporating would give the communities a voice, said Drew Dawson, Dick Dawson's 17-year-old grandson.
"Because on our own, the communities aren't large enough to incorporate," he said.
David Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, said that by incorporating, the communities would have a better chance of receiving funding from government agencies.
"As you can tell when you're driving down here, it's beautiful landscape," he said. "But unfortunately, regulations and all kinds of things have made it really hard to fix properties here."
Beverley, who owns Elijah's General Store, sees a direct correlation between critical area regulations and deteriorating roads and houses in the area. According to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the state's critical areas include land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters, wetlands, and the Bay and its tributaries.
"If you buy a property down here, if you put so much money into it based on the tax assessed value, you have to raise it," Beverley said. "And the people don't have the money to raise it. ... Why are we even going to raise it if you aren't going to put the money into the roads because of the population decrease? And would you consider a priority road fix? So it's a whole circle of problems."
Beverley and the Dawsons — who make up the organizing committee to create the town — see incorporation as the path to being able to apply for state and federal grants so residents can do things like raise their homes.
Dick Dawson said the area is in need of a good road that doesn't flood "just because the tide comes up" and drainage so that when the tide does come up, it can go back down.
The effort to incorporate isn't "a move against the county," Drew Dawson said.
"We understand that the population is very low and a lot of times it doesn't make sense for them to do everything that really needs to get done," he said. "The idea is just to do what the county can't, not necessarily drill the county for what they're not doing."
PULLING UP A CHAIR A drafted charter for the proposed Town of Blackwater sat in the center of the table where the trio sat Wednesday.
Under the charter, the town would be able to elect five members to a council for a term of four years. The commissioner with the most votes would be named mayor, and the commissioner with the second-most votes would be named deputy mayor. The town would not impose new taxes.
"The idea is to give more power to the people of the area, not add an unnecessary level of government," Drew Dawson said.
It took a couple weeks for Drew Dawson — who is a dual enrollment high school student at Chesapeake College — to write the charter. His initiative in creating it is something his grandfather is proud of him for.
"Drew has written the majority of this," Dick Dawson said.
Drew said he used other charters, mainly Eldorado's, to create Blackwater's charter. "But a lot of it was also written myself," he said. "It's nearly double the size of the charter of Eldorado."
Once they can get enough signatures on their petition, the three plan to go to the county to submit the charter for review. If the county accepts the charter, the decision will go to the registered voters within the area that Blackwater would encompass.
If those residents vote in favor of creating the town, Blackwater will become Dorchester County's newest incorporated town.
As the group moves forward with the process to become a town, other residents are getting involved. Drew Dawson said "public sentiment is positive" among residents they've spoken to so far. Dick Dawson said they plan to host a public meeting to explain the idea and what incorporating a town could do for residents.
"We're interested in their comments as well," Beverley said.
Drew Dawson said the length of time it could take for Blackwater to become a town is "hard to tell" because of all of the smaller steps necessary in the process.
"The hope is to get it done by the end of this year," he said.
Detmer said that although he doesn't know how his fellow councilmen feel about the idea to create Blackwater, the chance for residents to make a decision at the ballot box has his "full personal support."
"The best thing about their initiative, to me, is not just that it's looking to the future and the picture of how business is done with local, state and federal government, but the real advantage of their initiative is they are actually going to give the residents of the area a chance for their voice to be heard about whether or not they want to do it," he said.
If Blackwater becomes a town, both Dick and Drew Dawson are interested in serving as commissioners.
"I am one of the older people that is down here," Dick Dawson said. "And I have seen a lot of changes. And not many of them have been for the good. I'd like to be here to help get this thing started."
Drew Dawson said he encourages everyone to read the drafted charter to understand what incorporating would mean for the area.
"If we continue to do nothing, the land and the roads will continue to sink, and the land will erode away," he said. "We'll lose more and more residents and they'll just keep creating regulations until it becomes nearly impossible to live here."

stories.title: As Pressures to Increase Solar Mount, Caroline County Examines Options to Hold Its Ground
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
As pressures to increase solar mount, Caroline County examines options to hold its ground

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During a discussion of solar policy Tuesday morning, the Caroline County commissioners concluded that legal action might be necessary to get the state and the county to see eye-to-eye."I don't know if there's going to be any other avenue that we're going to go except to go to court," Caroline County Commissioner Vice President Larry Porter said. "I think that's probably where we're going to end up."
These comments were made during a discussion on the Hobbs Road solar project, a 15-acre project proposed by Nexamp Solar LLC to put solar panels on a field that is no longer usable for farming. The commissioners approved a measure Tuesday that gives Nexamp the option to lease the land, which was formerly used as a landfill.
But the commissioners were clear that despite the approval of this project, their general stance on solar development in the area had not changed.
"We know there's been a lot of concern and conversation in the community about solar projects, and we want to make it clear that the Commissioners hear you," The Caroline County government stated in a Facebook post prior to the meeting.
"They do not want to see our county overrun with solar farms. However, they also have to follow state regulations that require a certain amount of land to be used for renewable energy production," the post said. "By allowing this solar project on the Hobbs Road site, the Commissioners have actually preserved 15 acres of prime agricultural land that could have been used for this project instead."
After the commissioner's vote, Porter addressed concerns voiced by residents in the comment section of the county's post.
"There's been a good amount of discussion on Facebook about our participation in this," Porter said. "We've been called sell-outs and everything else because people for some reason think that we're in favor of this. I don't think there's just been any county that's fought harder against covering farmland with solar panels than Carolina County."
THE COUNTY'S STANCEThe county has a 2,000-acre moratorium for solar development in place, which is facing pressure as the state looks to expand solar energy use in the coming years to meet 100% clean energy goals by 2040.
In the past, the commissioners have voiced concerns that solar development threatens the area's rural nature and takes available land away from agricultural practices.
Porter mentioned throughout the Tuesday meeting that farmers receive offers from solar companies in their mail weekly offering large sums of money to use their land to place solar panels.
"I think the dilemma that we find ourselves in, I know everyone has the right of the farmer to do with his land what he wants," Porter said. "When someone comes in and says, 'we're going to make you this offer, and you have an opportunity to make money on your own land.' It's very difficult for us to sit up here and say, 'No, you can't.'"
Steve Kline, president and CEO of Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, attended the meeting on Tuesday and spoke with the commissioners on a plan that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties follow that he said could be beneficial to Caroline County.
"What ESLC encourages Caroline County to adopt is a per-acre mitigation fee," Kline said. "... In Talbot, the mitigation fee is based on Maryland ag land preservation foundation fair market appraisal averages. In Queen Anne's County, the system assesses a half percent transfer tax on projects converting farmland to solar, and all of those funds are allocated for land preservation projects.
"... While both counties have adopted a different approach, both counties use substantially all of their fees on land conservation. The ESLC strongly believes the best way to protect agricultural land against all the threats it faces is permanent conservations like the ones we write," Kline said.
Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) made a suggestion that all nine Eastern Shore counties fight together instead of separately to get communities on board with their plans to limit solar development. This, he said, will lend itself to a better outcome when it's time for legal action.
"Talbot County is going to host a meeting with all nine counties to talk about, and I think ahead of this meeting, we need to make sure that all nine counties are sharing whatever zoning laws that you all have already passed, and hopefully intend on enforcing. If there's some consistency with a lot of our zoning, as consistent we can possibly be, it's gonna be a lot easier to enforce it. It's gotta be a lot easier to message it to the public. And if you guys do it, it'll be easier to defend in court." 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

stories.title: Easton Passes Ordinance to Mitigate Seafood Processing Odors
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Easton passes ordinance to mitigate seafood processing odors

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council approved an ordinance Monday that aims to crack down on odors from seafood processors by requiring the installment of odor control technology.In a 4-0 vote, the town passed Ordinance 835, which was drafted following resident concerns about the odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis was outspoken Monday evening about bringing his constituents relief from the odors they smell during crab season.
"Constituents in the neighborhood should not have to go through another season of having to endure that kind of odor," Davis said. "And if the business is friendly and working with the community, something of this nature should have been worked out prior to now."
The ordinance, which will go into effect later this month, requires that seafood processing operations install odor control technology "in such a manner that no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood, said the business' concerns center the spray application system it plans to install — which will cost around $20,000 and may not fulfill the town's new requirements of "no odor" being detectable.
"We're confident it will address the issue, at least to some extent," Smith said. "But we're not confident, not necessarily confident, it'll meet that standard."
Smith requested a compromise, stating he thinks the ordinance should not retroactively apply to "existing, lawful seafood processing uses" such as his client. He submitted proposed revisions to the ordinance that were read aloud Monday evening.
Following a lengthy council discussion, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said he was ready to pass the ordinance as written, without Smith's proposed changes. Council President Frank Gunsallus agreed those changes were "overly specific."
Abatiello made a motion to approve the ordinance, which was seconded by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry. Gunsallus and Davis joined in voting yes. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery was absent from Monday's meeting.
TIMELINE DEBATEIn the approved ordinance, businesses must comply with odor control and storage requirements by July 1, 2025. Prior to Monday, the compliance date on the draft ordinance was Jan. 1, 2026. The change stirred discussion Monday evening.
Davis pushed for that date to be even sooner — Jan. 1, 2025 — though he was outnumbered by Gunsallus, Abatiello, and Curry, who all voted in favor of amending the ordinance to the July date.
Curry maintained that it's important the town be fair to the business since it's planning to pay up for the new odor control system to address the problem.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said she had legal concerns about shortening the period, saying that "even January (2026)" is pushing it.
"They've had time to comply," Davis said.
"But they didn't have this ordinance," VanEmburgh responded. "The ordinance is what would be challenged."
"I mean the worst case scenario is that we go to court, and is that the end result? Then so be it," said Davis. " … If you say comply by 2026, just think about this for a moment. The same people who live in Ward 4 have to suffer through this this year again until January 2026."
"I have to stand on what I believe in, and I believe that they've already had enough time to do it," Davis later stated. "It seems to me that we're more worried about going to court than listening to the people. And I think we should listen to the people."

stories.title: Residual Bill Passed by Caroline County Commissioners
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Residual bill passed by Caroline County Commissioners

 September 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday morning, the Caroline County Commissioners voted to approve the long-discussed bill that would establish county regulations for storing food processing residuals, animal waste from the food processing process.These residuals, particularly dissolved air floatation, or DAF, residuals have been the topic of several heated discussions in the county since residents began raising health complaints and environmental concerns over how the material was being stored by some in the county late last year.
The county came up with a permitting system. There will be a universal permit requirement in order to store food processing residuals. It creates limitations on how residuals can be stored and permits the county to fine violators.
It would require that those storing the material use closed-top containers, going a step further than recently passed state legislation.
Attorney Stewart Barroll said commissioners and Caroline County staff had heard "voluminous" public comments that have been taken into account.
Prior to voting, two amendments were approved by commissioners involving distances from the storage containers.
Commissioner Franklin Bartz said he would prefer the storage distance and an occupied dwelling be increased to 2,000 feet measured horizontally rather than the 1,250-foot distance that was in the bill.
After discussion, the commissioners unanimously voted to approve the change.
Commissioner J. Travis Breeding requested a second amendment that would require the storage not to be within 500 feet of a well. This way, it would allow property owners to move wells somewhere else on their property to be 500 feet away from stored residuals to not contaminate water sources.
Commissioner Larry Porter brought up the discussion of postponing voting on the act until the Maryland Department of Agriculture shares their regulations. The vote had been postponed at the prior two meetings so the commissioners could review the proposed amendments to the legislation.
Breeding said there would not be a need to postpone for regulation changes because commissioners are acting well within the parameters of Maryland statue.
"There's only so much that the Department of Agriculture can do," Breeding said. "Everything that we have done inside of this legislature is not in conflict with the statue that the state has."
The bill was unanimously approved by the commissioners and has been enacted into the county law.

stories.title: Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Seeks Funding for Firehouse
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Trappe Volunteer Fire Company seeks funding for firehouse

 July 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company is raising funds to build an up-to-date firehouse. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md. 1st) wants to secure federal funding to help.The Trappe Volunteer Firehouse was completed in 1951 and has not been updated since. "We probably have the oldest one in the county," Assistant Secretary Treasurer of the Trappe Volunteer Fire Company Cheryl Lewis said.
Lewis said a new firehouse is necessary because the current building is no longer suitable for the modern equipment.
Because Trappe has a volunteer fire company, like many towns on the Eastern Shore, projects like this rely heavily on government and local support, Lewis said.
"We've been in the process of trying to get assistance," Lewis said. "In the last budget year, the federal budget that was just approved, we had successfully worked with Andy Harris's office to be included in the budget. But with the cuts that were done early on this year, it was removed."
Harris said the appropriations bill to provide funding for the project failed due to negotiations in Congress leading to a continued delay, but she said the project has been reapplied for in the current year's legislation.
"We hope the appropriations process has a better outcome, but then that's not up to us because it involves the minority party as well," he said in an interview with the Star Democrat.
In order to qualify for federal grants, the company must match 25% of the projected project cost of $6 million. The company set a goal of $1,500,000 and set aside $450,000 to begin the efforts.
Fundraising efforts include The Trappe Volunteer Fire Company's upcoming annual fair, held on July 31 through Aug. 2 at the firehouse. The event begins at 6 p.m. and ends at 10 p.m. each day and will include fire truck rides, hay rides, food, games and prizes, and live entertainment, according to the fire company's Facebook page. Saturday's event will open with a parade.
Harris said the outcome of federal funding depends on the successful bipartisan negotiations in Congress to pass this version of the appropriations bill.
"In the end, this is going to depend on the minority party. And you know, if they're not willing to negotiate in good faith, that could end up being a problem," Harris said. "The people in Trappe have to know that their member of Congress was working hard to get that money to the fire company."
