stories.title: Talbot Sheriff's Office Operating Out of New Facility
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot sheriff's office operating out of new facility

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 281
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Sheriff's Office is operating out of new offices on Mary's Court in Easton.As part of construction of a new Talbot County Public Safety Complex, the sheriff's office relocated in October and early November from its old offices on Glebe Road.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble said the new offices are "great" and that his department now has "high-tech" filing and storage systems.
"We have an armory in there where we can clean and store firearms, ammunition, which is a very nice space," Gamble added. "All the spaces are very nice. They really did a nice job with the layout of it."
The sheriff's office is located on the first floor of the building. Above it will be the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services, which is expected to move in sometime this year. It's a phased construction project being carried out by Davis, Bowen, and Friedel Inc. and Willow Construction LLC.
Construction of the back parking lot and sally port is ongoing, Gamble said. He said the sally port — which is a secure garage for officers to enter with arrestees — is projected to be completed this summer.
"When they're getting a prisoner or somebody under arrest out, they can't take off running anywhere," Gamble said. "It's a secure garage basically, and then they can just enter our building there."
The sheriff says once the Department of Emergency Services fully moves in, there'll be an open house or ribbon-cutting event to celebrate the new building.
"Everybody's really enjoying it," Gamble said. " … Once everything's done, we should be in good shape."
The Talbot County Sheriff's Office can be reached at (410) 822-1020, located at 28640 Mary's Court, Suite 100, Easton, MD.

stories.title: Sewage Seeping onto Streets Sparks Cambridge Flood Debate
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Sewage seeping onto streets sparks Cambridge flood debate

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 506
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge city commissioners met for a work session Monday to review a presentation from the "Make Cambridge Resilient" team and to ask questions about the project — and there were many.The initiative is a shoreline and stormwater flood risk-reduction project, but some commissioners and elected officials have expressed concerns about its scope and goals. The design phase is now 30% complete, but without secured funding and support from the city, county and elected officials, the effort may stall.
Current goals include:
Designing and constructing a living shoreline.Creating a stormwater system with nature-based water storage and control features.Gathering public comments.Institutionalizing floodplain management and flood risk reduction.Developing a green infrastructure plan.Implementing additional nature-based solutions.Reactivating and maintaining the stakeholder group.Providing support to property owners to identify risk-reduction strategies.
During recent City Council meetings, Commissioner Brett Summers raised concerns about toilet paper in the street, an issue caused by floodwater entering the sewer system through manhole defects. Director of Public Works Wayne Suggs said during the meeting that three spots remain where sewage and floodwater are still connected.
Suggs said three elements must be addressed to control these issues: top-down flooding, pump station capacity limits and creek water entering the system.
The Trenton Street Pump Station, which takes in most of the city's stormwater, is 97 years old and failing. When floodwater enters wastewater lines, it is pumped to the nearly century-old station, which doesn't have the capacity to handle it. As a result, toilet paper and sewage rise onto the streets.
"So can this project help us with that problem — and when?" Summers said.
Project Manager Larry White responded that adding pumps at the end of streets, repairing older infrastructure and constructing a living shoreline will help with sewage issues, but the project itself does not cover wastewater.
The city has published a bid to rehabilitate the Trenton Street Pump Station, but it's a $7 million project.
"Even if we moved and we awarded the bid tomorrow for Trenton Street, it will be 18 months before that system can be brought online," City Manager Glenn Steckman said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said a mutual understanding of the project's goals is lacking and needs to be developed.
Del. Tom Hutchinson (R- Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) expressed concerns about the project, saying there has been mixed feedback from constituents and comparing the initiative to the "failing" Strand Beach project in Oxford.
Other concerns included insufficient outreach — particularly to Black and Hispanic communities and city park users — a lack of coordination with state agencies such as the Department of Natural Resources and the Maryland Department of the Environment, and long-term maintenance responsibilities.
Hutchinson said he contacted stakeholders listed on the project's website and many raised similar concerns.
"I had the opportunity to talk to DNR Secretary Kurtz, and he wasn't aware of the project," he said.
Some stakeholders, including Debbie Cornwell with the Maryland Department of Planning, expressed concerns about transparency.
Commissioners agreed to make the council chambers available for future public "Make Cambridge Resilient" meetings to improve transparency, but no further action was taken during the work session.

stories.title: Claiborne Residents, Operating Their Own Well, Look for Water Supply Solution
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Claiborne residents, operating their own well, look for water supply solution

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 819
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CLAIBORNE — When Rob Todd moved to Claiborne in 2013, he didn't expect to be partially responsible for the village's water services. But it's a role he and others have assumed.From 2015 to 2019, Todd was one of four volunteers for the resident-led Claiborne Water Company, a group that oversees a water system serving about 30 properties.
"I, for one, didn't envision my retirement years being a well operator," Todd said while taking a walk to the community's well on Thursday afternoon.
Todd, 77, volunteered for a relatively short stint. He credits longtime Claiborne resident Renny Johnson — the "water czar" — with the decades-long heavy lifting of maintaining Claiborne's water. Johnson handles the billing, fields questions from residents and arranges testing of the well system.
Johnson moved to his Claiborne house in 1979 and was handed the water company books just a few years later by the outgoing man in charge.
"We had a water company meeting where we invited the people that were on the system to talk about (it), and no one else would take it over," Johnson recalled. "So I said I would, not thinking that I would be doing it for this long."
Johnson, 77, and others are hoping to pass the duties off and find a long-term solution to what's become a multifaceted problem keeping the water system in line with state regulations.
As Claiborne's population ages, attracting volunteers is difficult, Johnson and Todd said. And now more than ever, the Maryland Department of the Environment is pushing Claiborne to meet standards for what the state considers "community water systems."
Community water systems aren't served by a municipal company. They are smaller-scale, like the Claiborne water well. However, MDE requires systems with over 15 properties hooked up to have a licensed operator, according to residents and county officials.
Four Claiborne residents — Johnson, Todd, Jim Richardson and Kirke Harper — explained the issue at a Talbot County Council work session on Sept. 9. While the county doesn't maintain the water system, County Engineer Ray Clarke is willing to help where he can.
"We're grateful that the county was willing to listen to our problem," Todd said.
'WE'RE AGING OUT'
Claiborne, an unincorporated village on the Chesapeake Bay, is a short detour on the drive from St. Michaels to Tilghman Island.
According to residents, a 19th-century railroad company drilled Claiborne's old water well, which was then turned over to the residents when the railroad closed in 1928.
Johnson and Richardson took over in the early 1980s, back when each household paid $18 annually to hook up and just before the railroad's well was replaced. Now, the yearly fee is $200. A second, separate water system serves 14 properties closer to the Bay and past the main Claiborne Road strip. It's not subject to all of the same MDE rules.
Claiborne Water Company's current building is a white structure housing a pressure tank and chlorine pump. It sits a handful of paces away from the well cap a few feet above ground level.
Residents say efforts to find a licensed operator in recent years have come up empty, which is why they're seeking county assistance.
MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email that the state's increased rules on water system operators were implemented in 2001.
"Maryland regulations include requirements for certification, such as passing examinations and continuing education," Apperson wrote.
Claiborne's water company volunteers aren't overly concerned about water quality. MDE's most recent review of the Claiborne water system indicated that it meets state and federal requirements. Low levels of arsenic, while in compliance, was the leading worry.
MDE inspects the water system at least every three years, Apperson said.
Residents' core concern, instead, boils down to meeting MDE's certification requirements, which likely means passing the buck off to a qualified operator.
And for Johnson, who beat cancer a few years ago, juggling the billing, testing and upkeep responsibilities continues to take a toll. "I'm older now, and I don't have as much strength or wherewithal to carry on," he said.
"We're aging out," Johnson added. "Nobody who's retired wants to take on the responsibility of running the water company."
SOLUTIONS
At the county work session, officials agreed to explore options for the Claiborne Water Company through a preliminary engineering report, or feasibility study, which could be authorized at the council's next meeting on Sept. 23.
Clarke, the county engineer, explained that homeowners connected to the community system mostly can't drill individual wells because of necessary setbacks from private septic systems.
Extending sewer services down to the Claiborne village could be a longer-term solution to make private wells a possibility, officials said. But in the short-term, the residents are still seeking a fix.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, acting as a liaison to the Public Works Advisory Board, said he understands Claiborne residents have been "clamoring for some assistance" for a long time.
"I'm well aware that, in (this) process, you've already actually explored a lot of options and are coming to us because you've come up empty," Lesher said.

stories.title: Broadband Service Expands in Dorchester County
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Broadband service expands in Dorchester County

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 308
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Historically, those living down long lanes and private roads in Dorchester County have struggled to get broadband access. However, a state funded program is working to expand high speed internet access to these areas."One of the cool things about this is that a majority of the people on this list, except for the people who came forward, don't even know they're getting broadband coming to their homes," said Dorchester County grant writer Marylin Williams.
The Maryland Homestretch — Difficult To Serve Properties Program is administered by the Maryland Office of State Broadband and provides funding for internet installation in areas where it can be particularly expensive. The program is also referred to as the Long Driveway Internet Program.
Williams referred to the program as "ever changing," saying the state modified the grant program as recently as this spring.
This came in handy when the amount initially awarded to the county was not enough to cover projected costs for the project.
Initially, the county was granted $1.1 million, but the project is estimated to cost $2,422,493. The county was recently awarded with a higher grant after Williams advocated for more homes to be covered.
However, The grant still will not cover all of the 299 homes approved to be serviced, so energy companies Bay Country and Choptank Electric are investing in the county to ensure access, Williams said.
Choptank Electric spokesperson Valerie Connelly and Williams requested two action items from the Cambridge County Council at the June 3 County Council meeting.
The first item is accepting the higher grant award of $1,217,852. The second is having the county sign a memorandum of understanding with Choptank Electric and Bay Country. The Commissioners unanimously agreed, with County Commissioner Ricky Travers leading the motion.
According to Connelly, broadband will be installed at no cost to the homeowners and all construction must be completed by Dec. 31, per the grant.

stories.title: Commissioners of Oxford Hear Plans for Portable Pump Stations
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Commissioners of Oxford hear plans for portable pump stations

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — In an effort to address flooding caused by rainy day events, Oxford is looking into setting up portable stormwater pump stations across town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, engineer Wayne Newton presented plans to install four temporary, portable pump stations in three locations in town: Two stations near the causeway, one station at Bank Street and one station at Mill Street.
Newton is the president of Messick & Associates, an engineering firm the town has a contract with. He said he expects the pump stations will relieve moderate flooding, which he defined as anything less than storm surge.
"A storm surge comes in, it comes over the bulkhead, it comes over the causeway, that's not what we're planning for here," he said. "We're just planning for rainy day events."
Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman, who has been working closely with Newton, said the pumps will allow the town to drain water faster.
"It's the plan of moving the water where it's not going to take us days, it'll be hours," Ozman said.
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said the town is trying to take a step back, look at what it would like to see in the future and determine what is needed today in order to build toward that.
"So this is more of a holistic viewpoint than what we've been looking at previously," he said.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the portable pump stations are more flexible than permanent pump stations in the ground.
"You can take our solution and move it to where the problem is instead of having a problem and saying, 'Oh, well we've got this really neat pump station eight blocks away,'" he said.
Along with placing portable pump stations in the low-lying areas Newton identified, Newton also outlined plans to address the existing drain system on Mill Street that runs through the marina. He said he would like to re-grade and rebuild some of the drain system so water drains toward the water tower and the pump station can be moved to that area.
"We'd prefer (the pump station) to be down there," Newton said about the area where the water tower is. "There's more room for it down there."
Newton said over the next month, his office plans to work on designs and cost estimates for the project that he can bring back to the commissioners for review. He said his goal is to have the project complete by the end of 2025.
The project will be funded using American Rescue Plan Act funds.
Ozman considers this project to be laying the foundation when it comes to addressing flooding issues. He said the town can hone in on these three areas first, then address flooding in other areas.
"We're trying to do the best that we can with the money that's available at the time without having to spend millions on something that can't be moved, can't be touched, can't be retrofitted," he said.

 December 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CENTREVILLE — An overview of the pedestrian bridge plans to connect the Cross Island and South Island trails were presented to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners Nov. 26.In conjunction with the Parks and Recreation Department, Southern Kent Island Trail Extension Project staff obtained preliminary construction cost information for a pedestrian bridge crossing over MD Route 50, Chief Roads Engineer Shane Moore said.
Engineering consultant Kimley-Horn was contracted to complete a preliminary evaluation of several Route 50 pedestrian crossing locations east and west of the Route 8 overpass.
Utilizing the MDOT cost estimator to estimate a pedestrian crossing construction costs, As part of this evaluation Kimley-Horn estimated a pedestrian crossing construction cost at the Cracker Barrel location at $8.1 million, Moore said.
Construction only cost estimates were taken from similar type projects including Virginia's Tysons Old Meadow Pedestrian Bridge over Route 495 at $8 million and the Lane Place Pedestrian Bridge over Route 295 at between $10.8 and $12.4 million, according to Moore.
Several locations have been selected for a preliminary study through Kimley-Horn but there has been no final decision yet, according to Moore.
For safety, pedestrian bridges have to be built at a higher elevation than a typical vehicle overpass, Moore said.
With the commissioners' approval, Public Works staff will work with the BMC and RK&K Civil Engineering to develop a scope of services and costs for a final location study of the County's proposed MD Route 50 pedestrian bridge crossing.
Next steps include meeting with Maryland Transportation Authority and the State Highway Administration to begin discussions to nail down a final location for the construction of a pedestrian crossing, Moore said.
Queen Anne's County currently has about $120,000 in Baltimore Metropolitan Council (BMC) monies to be used for this study. In addition, BMC has also federally approved pre-established consulting contracts with RK&K, Moore said.
Federal and state partners have been supportive of this project to serve as alternative transportation connecting the county, County Administrator Todd Mohn said.

stories.title: Aaron’s Place Presents Potential New Location to Caroline County Commissioners
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Aaron’s Place presents potential new location to Caroline County Commissioners

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 433

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Cheryl Beulah, executive director of Aaron's Place, discussed the food pantry's potential new location with the Caroline County Commissioners on Tuesday.The proposed location on Meeting House Road will allow Aaron's Place to work in partnership with His Hope Ministries and the Chesapeake Culinary Center to provide a year-round homeless shelter and multiple different classes, additions and food storage locations, Beulah said.
Plans for the location have been in the works for the past two years while volunteers from Aaron's Place and His Hope Ministries have resolved issues with the Environmental Protection Agency resulting from a covenant on the property.
The EPA covenant came after the property was contaminated with volatile organic compounds in the 1980s, Beulah said at the meeting Tuesday. Extensive testing has been conducted over the years, with the contamination shrinking due to a large pumping and air system installed by the previous owner, Russel Metals.
The EPA covenant is restrictive, primarily concerning water usage, but the EPA has indicated that as long as the project does not break the wellhead and uses water according to county instructions, it can proceed. The EPA also said that if three negative VOC tests are obtained after the project is on the property, it would consider removing the covenant.
Beulah told the commissioners how great the location will be for the community after all renovations were completed.
"To take that big piece of building, that building and that property, clean it all up, fix it all up and have it as a resource center to serve the people in the community. All the agencies that can come together will come together under one roof, joining forces together, joining resources together, and providing us a significant services in our community," she said.
The commissioners asked Beulah and the group questions about what services will be included at the new location. The group responded with a full analysis of the building.
"So, it's three main components, three main partners. Aaron's Place, His Hope Ministry and the Food Aggregation, those are the three main ones," Beulah said.
The group said the project requires significant funding. They are forming a capital campaign committee and exploring various funding opportunities around the state, Beulah said, and wanted to make sure they had the commissioners' support for the project before proceeding.
While the commissioners did not suggest a certain amount of money to support the project, the commissioners all said they will support the project and provide any help they can offer.
"I think it's a very worthwhile project," Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "I think if nothing else, it'll make that entrance to this town beautiful."

stories.content:
QA parks to see new inclusions and popular upgrades

 September 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 535
 Words

 CENTREVILLE — Updates for popular sports and inclusive playgrounds are on the horizon for Queen Anne's County parks.Church Hill Park will be getting a upgrade with the construction of three pickleball courts.
According to the Town of Church Hill, a layout for tennis courts was initially included in the original park masterplan back in the 1980s, but due to a surge in pickle popularity, the town felt as though pickleball courts would be a better suited facility.
The Department of Parks and Recreation are contracting with ATC Corp to construct three pickleball courts and associated storm water management facility in an amount no more than $243,245.
ATC has developed all the other county pickleball courts and has a great relationship with the county, Parks and Recreation Director Steve Chandlee said.
The project is currently in the engineering phase and officials are hopeful to have to have the community playing ball by spring or summer, he said.
Chandlee also noted the complete replacement for a more inclusive playground is coming to Mowbray Park, with equipment delivery estimated in about 12 weeks.
While the current playground is still safe, the equipment is about 23 or 24 years old with pieces much more difficult to replace, Chandlee said. The playground will be closed beginning in October to give staff about a month to remove all materials and level the surface before construction is expected through the winter.
Excited for the inclusive playground project's prospect, a poster showcasing the intended playground with estimated dates for construction is expected to be installed around the vicinity as well, he said.
"Because of the popularity of that playground, we want to make sure we get the word out appropriately and to as many different avenues as possible," Chandlee said.
Initiatives to bring forth Mowbray Park as a more inclusive, accessible, and sensory-friendly space for all children were led by non-profit Noah's Perfect Playground.
Following a public hearing held Aug. 26, the Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved upgrading the sewer service designation of two neighboring Stevensville properties Sept. 9.
The Brennan and Prevoznik properties are both single-family dwellings at 233 and 235 Great Neck Road in Stevensville under the same ownership, according to the county.
With both properties currently served via a failing on-site sewage disposal system and the remaining soils on the site are deemed to be unsuitable for a replacement system, the commissioners approved amending the properties from "No Planned Service" to "Service on Demand" with a "Limited Development" designation which would require any intensification on this site, such as a subdivision, to be required to re-amend the Plan.
In other business, county property wetland mitigation moves forward as the commissioners awarded a contract to Martin's Excavation and Hauling, LLC of Centreville to establish approximately 16 acres of forested wetland on county-owned "Tanner" property in the amount of $1,115,152.
This construction project aims to satisfy the remaining wetland mitigation deficit for permitted wetland impacts in Bay City, Cloverfields and County projects presently totaling 15.4 acres, according to the county. A total of 11 bids were received.
The Solid Waste Division of the Public Works Department was approved the purchase of a Caterpillar 926 14A Wheel Loader with 2.25yd bucket and optional 12' plow, from Carter Machinery Company, of Felton, DE, in the amount of $264,844.

stories.title: 'Only Going to Get Worse': Talbot Officials Discuss Rise in Senior Homelessness
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
'Only going to get worse': Talbot officials discuss rise in senior homelessness

 July 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 648
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials and senior care leaders met Tuesday to discuss creating a task force to address senior homelessness, a rapidly accelerating problem, experts say.The request for the task force comes from Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke. Based on council feedback, a resolution to create the task force seems poised for approval at the council's Aug. 12 meeting.
Members of the county's Commission on Aging and other health and housing experts spoke on mounting challenges faced by area seniors, from housing costs and food insecurity to mental health struggles.
Rachel Smith, chair of the aging commission, said a task force would help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department. There's currently a "disconnect," she said.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," Smith said. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."
Mielke said there's no single solution to help the homeless senior population.
"Each agency would bring solutions or suggestions, but not one agency can deal with all of the issues," Mielke said.
As drafted, the senior citizens task force would consist of representatives from the following entities: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council. Members from Mid-Shore Behavioral Health and law enforcement agencies may also be added based on Tuesday's discussions.
The task force would make recommendations to the County Council on housing, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
Homelessness is growing
Julie Lowe, executive director of Talbot Interfaith Shelter, cited jumps in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is on the rise.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range.
Talbot Interfaith has limited capacity, Lowe said. It runs a multi-year program to transition people into paying for partial rent before moving out on their own. But even when shelter residents move out, Lowe said finding a financially viable apartment in the area isn't an easy task, especially for seniors who can't work.
"Most of the people who we work with will never get to that point with the market-rate housing and where it is now," Lowe said.
Lee Newcomb, a Talbot County social worker for 26 years and the aging commission's secretary, said she's never seen senior need at such a high level.
Newcomb said the Days Inn in Easton is home to many unhoused individuals. Smith said seniors especially suffer in the winter months since Talbot County doesn't have a low-barrier homeless shelter.
Smith noted an incident at the Days Inn last December as a wake-up call. According to police, an unhoused man who was living in the woods behind the hotel was found dead on Dec. 14, 2024.
"I feel like we missed something there," Smith said. "We shouldn't have our senior residents — some of them have worked in our community — die."
Cambridge-based Delmarva Community Services has served many homeless people from Talbot County down in Dorchester, according to president and CEO Andy Hollis.
Hollis said a low-barrier, overnight shelter is a gap in Talbot County, and something that a task force could work on. Many others at the meeting on Tuesday emphasized the need for a physical location to consolidate services for the senior homeless population.
'We don't have this issue in Talbot,' we thought for so long," Hollis said. "And we truly do. It's something that is long overdue in terms of being addressed."
"The challenge is not leveling out and it's only going to get worse," he added.

stories.title: Caroline Commissioners Hoping to Nail Down Site for New YMCA
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Caroline commissioners hoping to nail down site for new YMCA

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County and YMCA leaders are restarting efforts to build a new YMCA facility after discussions fizzled out in recent years.At a county meeting Tuesday, YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill told county commissioners that the organization has always wanted to build a full facility in Caroline County. The biggest step to moving forward is choosing a location, he said.
"The goal is still to build a YMCA that can be a hub for community," Gill said. "We just haven't solved the first piece of the puzzle, which is the right site and getting everybody on board."
During Tuesday's talks, stakeholders didn't land on one location in particular, though commissioners indicated three potential considerations: land on Double Hills Road off of Route 404, the old Southern States property at Gay and Market streets in Denton, or near Denton Elementary School.
"It's probably time for us to, as you said, pick a site and start telling a story," Commission Vice President Larry Porter told Gill.
Gill briefed the commissioners on the YMCA's recent expansions on the Eastern Shore, including in St. Michaels and Centreville. A new facility serving Caroline County residents would need to be around 60,000 square feet or more, Gill said. The project could fall in the $20 million range.
The YMCA of the Chesapeake currently operates an 11,000-square-foot facility nestled in the Denton Plaza shopping center off of Route 404. Gill said it serves around 3,000 people. A full-fledged building could more than double that mark.
PAST ROADBLOCKS
Past efforts to expand the YMCA's presence in Caroline County have been met with roadblocks. Porter, a commissioner since 2010, said it's time to get the ball rolling.
"The thing that's frustrating for me is it seems like we've had this conversation several times, and we are still in the same spot we were," Porter said.
In 2018, the county and YMCA signed an agreement in which the county would donate 15 acres of land on Double Hills Road to the YMCA. It was conditioned on the project beginning by July 1, 2023.
Talks stalled, and the project didn't begin before the deadline.
Gill said on Tuesday that there "wasn't support from a (county) administrative standpoint" at the time. Other concerns, such as the fact that the Town of Denton didn't own the land, parking meters and, eventually, the pandemic, hindered efforts, he noted.
In 2022, the YMCA of the Chesapeake returned a $2.5 million donation from a New Jersey donor that was meant to go toward the Caroline County endeavor.
"We really didn't see a pathway forward," Gill said.
But now, as talks resurface, there's renewed interest in delivering a new YMCA.
Commission President Travis Breeding said it may be challenging to locate the YMCA next to a school, though he said near Denton Elementary on the south end of town could be a consideration.
When commissioners raised the idea of considering the current and soon-to-be moved Lockerman Middle School on the north end of town, Gill expressed some reservation.
"With the school going away there, and if you demo'd that and built (a YMCA) there, it's kind of tucked away," he said.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the county will look at some potential sites and put together a list. Gill said the nonprofit organization can conduct market assessments on potential sites to determine viability.
The CEO said it "hurts my heart that we still haven't solved this one," but expressed confidence that pursuing a larger YMCA facility in Caroline County is a benefit to residents and local businesses.
"There's an economic engine behind the Y as well because it gives you kind of that third place in your community to connect to people," Gill said.

stories.title: Residents Soon Will Move in to Renovated Doverbrook Apartments
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The revitalized Doverbrook Apartments were shown off to state, county and town leaders last week as final touches are completed before residents move in.Don Bibb, executive director of the Housing Commission of Talbot, said the 64-unit redevelopment project will benefit the community.
"You can see the tremendous improvement this has made to the community and the opportunity for much improved, long-term sustainable housing for the program participants that we have that are going to be living here," Bibb said April 30 during a tour of the complex.
Bibb said Thursday that move-in for returning residents is imminent and is likely to begin within seven to 10 days.
The commission and construction company Pennrose began redevelopment of the Doverbrook Apartments in late 2023. The $26 million project replaced the apartment complex's seven old buildings with five new buildings, adding 14 units to its original 50-unit setup.
"It's good utilization of open space that provides the opportunity for the growth to add more units in," Bibb said.
Located on Dover Street, the complex will accommodate households earning between 30% and 80% of the area median income, or between $21,000 and $58,000 for one-person households.
It includes one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom apartments. Project leaders said the complex was designed to bring original residents — who were assisted in finding temporary housing during construction — back once completed.
Bibb said of the original 50 tenants, around 30 will return — a relatively high percentage for a redevelopment project during which residents move elsewhere temporarily.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day toured the apartment complex April 30. He applauded the redevelopment efforts and lightheartedly pointed out how close residents will be to Rise Up Coffee across the street.
"Do your marketing materials for the remaining (units) talk about how many steps it is to the Rise Up?" Day said with a smile.
Bibb praised the public-private aspect of the project, which included state and local funding and low-income housing tax credits for the 14 new units.
"It was well worth the blood, sweat and tears," Bibb said.

stories.title: Harriet Tubman Posthumously Commissioned to Rank of Brigadier General
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Harriet Tubman posthumously commissioned to rank of brigadier general

 November 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 533
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — More than a century since Harriet Tubman served as a spy, scout, nurse and cook in the American Civil War, she has been officially recognized as a general officer in the Maryland Army National Guard.On Veterans Day, Tubman's descendants, local and state officials, veterans, military personnel and others packed a tent outside the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Visitor Center in Church Creek for a ceremony to commission and recognize Tubman as brigadier general.
The event brought an array of elected officials to the podium to speak, including Gov. Wes Moore (D), Maryland House of Delegates Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County) and Del. Edith Patterson (D-Charles).
Patterson, who sponsored a House bill that led to this posthumous commission, talked about Tubman's legacy.
"As we honor her legacy today, may Harriet Tubman inspire us all to strive for a more just and equitable world," she said. "Her life and legacy remind us of the courage that it takes to stand for and the profound impact one person's dedication can have on future generations."
Moore talked about Tubman's service to the country, connecting it to what Veterans Day celebrates.
"This is a holiday that is a celebration of those who chose to raise their hand," he said, later adding that Tubman was one of those individuals who raised their hand. "... Because she believed that you cannot just rail about a system being flawed. You actually have to be the one to go in and work to change it."
Maj. Gen. Janeen Birckhead, adjutant general for Maryland, explained why Tubman was given the rank of brigadier general and not captain or major. Birckhead said Tubman "lived the unique traits and responsibilities" of brigadier general.
"Like them, Harriet Tubman was a lightning rod, a role model," she said. "Her willingness to risk everything compelled others to action. Her actions communicated the audacity of hope and the potential of a vision."
Birckhead said generations of Maryland communities have known this about Tubman, and this commission honors that in a formal way.
Following the presentations of a resolution from the Maryland General Assembly and a proclamation from Moore, Tubman's great great great grandniece, Tina Wyatt, spoke. Wyatt said she loves her Aunt Harriet for her inspiration, faith, tenacity and ability to discern.
"And that is what helped her during the Civil War," she said.
Wyatt said her aunt was selfless.
"She gave up any rights that she had obtained for herself to be able to fight for others," Wyatt said about Tubman. "... She never thought about herself, she thought about what others needed."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Michele Jones Galvin, another great great great grandniece of Tubman, called the ceremony astounding, heartfelt and emotional.
"Her work (in the Civil War) was just amazing," Galvin said. "And to be able to see her today to be commemorated and also recognized for that work so many years later is truly amazing."
Galvin came from Syracuse, New York to attend the event along with around 20 other Tubman descendants. She said they all came to the ceremony to do the same thing: come together to recognize their ancestor.
"To be able to all be here today is just a wonderful way to have a tribute to her," Galvin said.

stories.title: St. Michaels Proposed Dog Park Must Find New Location
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
St. Michaels proposed dog park must find new location

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The long-desired dog park for St. Michaels has faced yet another barrier in its journey to becoming reality. Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, a volunteer group advocating for the park, have decided to move away from the proposed Bradley Parks location due to concerns from residents.During the Aug. 14 Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting, members of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park spoke up and suggested Bradley Park as the location for the future park. According to Mitch Ettinger, the founder of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, the one-acre park was "underutilized" with few residential homes located nearby and had the added bonus of already being maintained by the town.
But last week, St. Michaels residents were sent a message from Ettinger stating the group had requested the commissioners remove the planned dog park discussion from the Sept. 11 meeting.
Ettinger said the decision came after hearing concerns from those living adjacent to Bradley Park. These concerns included noise from barking and the effect the park would have on the property value of their home, Ettinger said.
"Quite frankly, I just couldn't see myself standing up and saying, 'disregard these neighbors.' That's not the way that I think. That's not the way that my committee thinks," Ettinger said. "And so we withdrew the proposal for Bradley Park and asked the commissioners to take it off the agenda for this week."
The effort to have a dog park built in St. Michaels has been ongoing for more than three years. Ettinger said the dog park has been volunteer-led since its origins and is widely supported by residents of the town, according to a survey conducted when an architect was coming up with a master plan for seven acres at San Domingo Park. The site did not work for a dog park due to grant requirements that would prohibit fencing.
Moving forward, Ettinger said he would like to see commissioners of St. Michaels to take initiative and assist with the finding of a new property.
"It's time for the commissioners to step up, and they've been supportive of this concept, but they have yet to propose a location," Ettinger said.
Ettinger said his group would continue to work behind the scenes to assist commissioners in picking a location, and currently there are a couple of options that are under consideration.
Dan Conway, a member of Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park, said he and the committee are still committed to the dog park project. For him, it is more than just a place for dogs to run around. It is a community building area and would benefit owners and dogs alike in St. Michaels.
"Dog parks aren't really for dogs ... They're for people, and they help make a municipality, a community," Conway said. "In my experience, it's where townspeople can get together and renew acquaintances and make friends and share experiences. And so that, to me, is the beauty of a dog park."

stories.title: Bradley Park Suggested for Future Dog Park in St. Michaels
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Bradley Park suggested for future dog park in St. Michaels

 August 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — A group of St. Michaels residents want a dog park in what they call an "underutilized park," but the town administrator and some commissioners seemed reluctant to commit to it at a Wednesday night meeting.The Commissioners of St. Michaels did not vote on the issue, and the item was moved to the next meeting in September.
Mitch Ettinger, founder of Friends of the Dog Park, came dressed for the occasion — a shirt decorated with dog drawing and a folder covered with dogs wearing sunglasses.
For over three years, Friends of the Dog Park, a group of St. Michaels residents and dog owners, have been advocating for a park to bring their dogs and create community.
Now in front of a new commission, Ettinger recommended Bradley Park for the dog park. According to Ettinger, the one-acre park is underutilized; there are few residential homes located nearby. Bradley Park is also already unkempt by the town, and it would not require additional acquisition funds.
Ettinger said the overall cost of the park would be approximately half a million dollars to remove the old playground equipment, create a fence and renovate the park to better fit a dog park. The Friends of the Dog Park has filed to become a nonprofit and will plan to raise the funds through donations and grants so the cost would not fall on St. Michaels residents.
Ettinger asked commissioners to tentatively approve Bradley Park as the future St. Michaels dog park and to direct town staff to retain an engineering firm to prepare a site plan that will be submitted to the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board and Planning Commission.
The group asked for about $7,000 for the site survey because all efforts up until now have been completed and paid for by residents.
"[Friends of the Dog Park] might feel that the town has skin in the game," Ettinger said. "That we don't have to go out and raise $7,000 in our pockets to have a site plan that ultimately could be shut down."
Rob Straebel, town administrator, raised concerns he had with the park, stating a need for more public comment from residents before moving forward.
"I know that this community, they take their parks very seriously," Straebel said. "And unfortunately, this is going to be a fair amount of people that are opposed to it, and there's probably going to be a fair amount of people that would love to see a dog park there."
Commissioner Katrina Whittington raised questions over the town's prioritizes when it comes to supporting projects. According to Whittington, the town was deciding whether to pay over $200,000 for a small plan for a dog park and yet there is concerns over funding a site plan for Bradley Park.
Straebel said the $200,000 would have been a "policy decision" by commissioners for a different property.
More questions and potential ideas were raised by commissioners. Some suggesting bifurcating Bradley Park and updating the playground equipment, others sharing concern for the price of the park and public opinion of the park.
Ettinger reminded commissioners that he had offered to do a survey the last time he was in front of the council and he was told not to.
Additionally, he said, when the town hired an architect to come up with a master plan for the seven acres at San Domingo Park, a survey of the entire town was done and from the residents who participated, their No. 1 request was a dog park.
A few resident commented that there is a responsibility from the new commissioners to work toward a dog park since during the commission election last spring they had said they would approve it.
Whittington suggested the commissioners move the subject to the next meeting but noted that the idea of a dog park has not seen much progress in years.
"This seems like Groundhog Day all over again," Whittington said. "... This is ridiculous just to get a dog park here at St. Michaels."
After a bit of back and forth from commissioners and town residents, the council decided to delay further discussion on the park until the September meeting.

stories.title: Community Development Block Grant Projects Celebrated
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Community Development Block Grant projects celebrated

 May 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Friday morning, community members and partners gathered to celebrate two Community Development Block Grant recipients: Family Support Center and Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center's Community and Commercial Kitchen Space.The Community Development Block Grant Program assists in strengthening Maryland's communities by funding projects generally falling into three types: housing, public facilities and economic development projects.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Assistant Secretary Carol Gilbert was also present for the tour.
Family Support Center, a recipient of the grant, held an open house for its Early Head Start center. This center offers year-round comprehensive early care, education and family support to children from birth to 3 years of age, as well as their families.
Mary Kay Verdery, grants administrator for Talbot County, gave opening remarks outside of the center.
Verdery told community members the renovated space, including classrooms for up to 65 infants and toddlers, office space, kitchen and laundry facilities for the program, was possible due to the grant the center received.
Maria Maguire, health officer for the Talbot County Health Department, gave a speech noting the significance of Head Start programs for the community, including research showing that children enrolled in Early Head Start programs have better social-emotional language and cognitive development.
"All babies and toddlers need positive early learning experiences to foster their intellectual, social and emotional development and to lay the foundation for later school success," Maguire said. "Talbot County Health Department's Early Head Start program offers daily, year-round services to families and young children in Talbot County. It provides a comprehensive array of services, including mental health, education, housing, referrals and linkages to health services."
Community partners and members were given a tour of the center, where they were greeted by staff and children enjoying the care and benefits of the program.
Afterward, people enjoyed refreshments and baked goods before heading to the next stop on the grant project tour, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center Kitchen and Community Space.
This full restoration of a brick warehouse provides the resource center with a much-needed space for small groups, class opportunities and community gatherings.
Adding a full commercial kitchen will allow small food businesses to expand their economic impact on the community and provide an appropriate space to create meals and food options for the community.
Talbot County Councilmember Pete Lesher, vice president of the council, shared the council's enthusiasm and gratitude for the community space and renovations made by the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center.
"This is an organization that has an important mission to a growing part of our population in this community," Lesher said. "Thanks to all of you who are already doing that. Thanks to the rest of you who have helped to make this project possible."
Attendees were welcomed to a feast of Pakistani food created by Veronica Guevara, who used the kitchen to help launch her catering business. People enjoyed a delicious array of lentils, fresh strawberry salad, seasoned chicken and fluffy naan. Guevara explained each dish and showed the best way for attendees to eat it.
Matthew Peters, director of Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, described this project as a "labor of love."
"So we've got that whole new growth take, and all really thanks to having a little bit more space to breathe and to get people together like this provided to the community," Peters said. "And hopefully, we keep finding more and more of our clients that are those secret gems so that I can create an amazing mission to share. So thank you all."

stories.title: Ribbon Cut for St. Michaels Community Center Renovation
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Ribbon cut for St. Michaels Community Center renovation

 May 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 464
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Monday morning, many community members gathered for the ribbon cutting ceremony for an approximately $4.5 million renovation project to help serve the community of St. Michaels.The St. Michaels Community Center has been operating for over 30 years and has provided various supports through community pantries, events, senior and adult programs, youth programs and community gardens.
Lori Morris, the center's board chair, said she is excited to continue serving the community 2,500 meals a week and distributing groceries to neighbors in need.
"The outstanding center staff, both past and current, many of whom are here, not only provided ongoing input to the design and construction process but kept as many of our programs running as possible while we were out of the building," Morris said.
The approximately 5,700-square-foot building now houses a modern commercial kitchen, two classrooms, a technology center, a gallery and upstairs offices for staff. The main level of the building will serve multiple uses, including cafe seating, a space for speakers or performances and a place where people can pick up items from the center's community pantry.
The 800-square-foot commercial kitchen will serve the new Culinary Arts & Hospitality Workforce Development Program and the center's Community Cafe, which serves chef-made meals free of charge to anyone experiencing food insecurity.
The two classrooms on the other side of the gallery will be used primarily for children's programming but also for adult programs.
A technology center will have desks and computers for different organizations and nonprofits.
During the ribbon cutting ceremony, Morris praised her predecessor Langley Shook, former chair of the board of directors.
Morris said that Shook's leadership was the foundation of the project. The renovation was his vision, and he and his wife, Karen Shook, threw themselves into the fundraising, representing the committee before the town commissioners and the Historic District Committee.
Shook spoke about the work that many put into the project and thanked everyone involved in making the community center what it is today.
"The programs have been expanded, the staff has been strengthened," Shook said. "Our fundraising has made this platform possible and successful, and I think our greatest days are yet to come."
One of the speakers, State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), requested that all people who had attended St. Michaels Middle or High School come to stand with him as he presented the St. Michaels Community Center board of directors a citation in recognition for the work that was put into the community project.
"Because we do citations and we do projects, and it's part of the government doing something, but this is the will of the people," Mautz said. "This is what the town needed. This is what the town wanted, and by golly, this is what the town was going to get. So it's a great day for everybody."

stories.title: Long-Awaited Easton Dog Park Officially Opens
stories.author: Natalie Jones
stories.content:
Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 467
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Not even sub-freezing temperatures and bits of ice laying on the turf grass Thursday morning could stop over a dozen dogs — and their owners — from celebrating the grand opening of Easton's long-awaited dog park.Dogs of all ages, sizes and breeds were pulling at their leashes with energetic anticipation, waiting for the ceremonial red ribbon to be cut by Easton Mayor Megan Cook.
Thursday's ribbon cutting was a welcome sight for local dog owners and dog lovers, many of whom had waited years for the project to come to fruition.
A voiced interest in a dog park first came seven or eight years ago, said Rick Van Emburgh, the town engineer.
But in 2019, Easton residents David Ferraris and Noah Matten restarted the efforts, working with Rauch Inc., a local engineering firm, to prepare concept plans for a dog park near the downtown area.
And in fall 2020, the town received $7 million in bond funding, a majority of which was required to be allocated to parks.
Almost three years later, in March 2023, the Easton Town Council voted to fully fund the dog park on Brewers Lane and to add a restroom there, Van Emburgh said.
With the legislative work completed, construction of the dog park required a true group effort from the town's public works, parks and recreation, IT, buildings and finance departments.
Willow Construction, Easton Utilities and Chester River Landscaping also lent a hand with a number of other efforts to make the park a reality.
"I believe this is a wonderful example of teamwork," Van Emburgh said. "I believe it's a wonderful example of our community working together to build something beautiful for our town residents and our dogs."
Cook kept her comments brief, acknowledging a number of excitedly yapping dogs waiting to enter the park and play.
"I really want to give an extra shoutout to all the departments," the mayor said. "Pretty much every department in the Town of Easton played a role in getting this park up and running."
Once the ribbon was cut, the dogs were unleashed and off to play.
The new park, open dawn to dusk, includes two separate play areas for the pups based on weight, with a larger area allocated to dogs over 35 pounds.
A turf grass layer on top makes for a comfortable surface for dogs to run, jump and roll around, and underneath, there's an anti-microbial infill material and an irrigation system for cooling the turf.
It was clear that the dogs were excited as they raced in circles and made new friends, and the smiles on owners' faces told a similar story.
Easton resident Scott Cohen, who stopped by the park with his two Australian Shepherd-poodle mixes Scruffy, 4, and Casey, 3, said the dogs had a great time playing Thursday morning.
"I think it's a terrific add to the community," he said.

stories.title: Easton Town Council Approves Food Truck Pilot Program
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Easton Town Council approves food truck pilot program

 September 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 286
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a meeting Tuesday evening, the Easton Town Council unanimously approved a resolution that creates a pilot program for food trucks in town.The program allows food trucks to operate on private property with the owners' permission. They will not be allowed downtown or on public property, and they cannot be located within 300 feet of a brick-and-mortar restaurant.
The effort comes as the council discusses potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
In last month, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The pilot program aims to pinpoint where town rules regarding food trucks can be revised in the future, town officials said.
"I worked with staff to try and come up with a strong pilot program for you to look at," Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh said at the meeting Tuesday.
The pilot program is set to run for eight months. There will be a one-time $250 fee for each vendor participating.
Permits must be submitted to the town with a map of the location of intention. The map can be an aerial photo, but it must clearly show the food truck is not blocking exits, fire hydrants or entryways.
The food trucks cannot remain in the same place for more than 24 hours, and truck owners' responsibility to get permission from property owners. Vendors must have trash and recycling available and ensure the space is clean before they leave.
Once permits are submitted, it should take around three days for approval or denial. The resolution is effective immediately.

stories.title: CWDI Gives Project Updates and Addresses Concerns
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
CWDI gives project updates and addresses concerns

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. gave an update on the Cambridge Harbor project at a July 31 community update meeting, outlining a vision built around four zones: Town Center, Walkable Neighborhoods, Maritime Trade, and Community Recreation.CWDI Board President Angie Hengst also addressed community concerns that have caught traction on social media regarding a potential YMCA, a board position and planning committee meetings.
Hengst said CWDI's operations are all "100% above board."
CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project aims to develop Cambridge's waterfront, similar to the Inner Harbor in Baltimore.
The first major step in the waterfront project will be a boutique hotel, which CWDI hopes will open by early 2029, Hengst said. Plans also call for new commercial and residential spaces, townhomes on Byrn Street, and a 1,000-foot fishing pier to replace the condemned Bill Burton pier.
"The biggest thing is that we showed some of the renderings and really zoomed in on those four zones so people could get a better idea of what our actual concept design is, kind of our vision for the site," Hengst said of the July 31 meeting.
These renderings are a guide to understand CWDI's vision, but they are subject to change depending on the developers{span}, she said{/span}.
At the meeting, {span}CWDI members{/span} also addressed community concerns regarding a potential YMCA on the waterfront. CWDI emphasized that no YMCA is planned, though the organization could submit a proposal in 2026.
Hengst said she believes the YMCA rumor got started because an old concept design that had a space for a potential YMCA was shown by mistake at a recent Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods meeting.
During an interview, Hengst addressed other concerns regarding CWDI Treasurer Frank Narr's appointment to the CWDI board. Hengst said Narr's seat on the board was formerly a CWDI-appointed position.
Last year, the policy was changed to have three positions appointed by the Cambridge City Council and three by the Dorchester County Council. CWDI appointed Narr before the policy change, so some people think he should have to be reappointed by the county council.
"I do want to note that when CWDI as an organization made Frank's appointment, it did have to be approved by both the city and the county, so they did approve of that appointment at the time, as with CWDI," Hengst said. "They didn't directly appoint him, but they did approve of the appointment at the time."
Hengst said CWDI has a signed letter from the county council acknowledging Narr as one of their three appointees.
The final concern Hengst addressed were CWDI's Planning Committee meetings, which she said are not open to the public.
Previously, CWDI was in hot water for not allowing the public meetings where they held discussions with elected officials. But Hengst said these specific meetings are for the Planning Committee to work with city officials to compile information that will then be publicly presented at a community update meeting.
"It's our planning committee working directly with the city as they work through the regulating planning and zoning guidelines," Hengst said.
To see the updated renderings of the Cambridge Harbor Project, visit CWDI's website.

stories.title: St. Michaels Hears Presentation on Houseboat Vacation Rentals
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
St. Michaels hears presentation on houseboat vacation rentals

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST.MICHAELS — Flohom, a company that provides vacationers the chance to stay on houseboats, presented the company's plans for St. Michaels to government officials.Flohom and St. Michaels Marina owner Michael Morgan have discussed putting one or two Flohoms in the marina.
"I run a strict place. Everyone knows my style," Morgan told the town's commissioners at a meeting Wednesday. "I was timid at first, but then a heard their rules and the type of clientele that they have. If I thought this would displease my customer base, I wouldn't even have entertained it. I think it's a neat concept."
The Flohom presentation showed how the boats are built, how the company was started, and what types of rules and regulations are enforced within the company.
Customers are not permitted or allowed to drive the Flohom boats at all, so they remain docked in the same place.
To eliminate excessive noise, Flohom monitors the sound of anyone that stays in the houseboats. If the sound gets too loud, the guest will receive a text message asking them to lower their noise level. Noise monitors do not listen or record conversation but monitor the sound decibels in the home.
Flohom staff members look to dock in places where guests can walk or drive a short distance to get breakfast or lunch and attend different town events.
"I'm new to this as well," Morgan said. "I'm willing to take the chance on it because I think it would be a unique thing for the town, it would be another option for people to come and stay and do something in St. Michaels. Not to mention the accommodation tax"
Commissioners and town residents had multiple questions for the company and for Morgan.
Commissioner David Wojiechowski questioned if Flohom would have to pay accommodation tax, and if so, if all other boats or yacht should pay the same accommodation tax if they stay overnight.
"It is an overnight rental competing against our hotel rooms," Wjiechowski said. "So if this gets approved and pays an accommodation tax, then all 200 slips that are overnight should pay an accommodation tax."
Morgan said that other slips would not be subject to accommodation tax.
Flohom staff confirmed the company does have a plan to bring business to St. Michaels after going through the proper protocols. But the company has an interest in exploring the town and gauging reception first.
"This is just an initial presentation," Jerry South Co-Founder of Flohom said. "Were not sure if this is something that requires a vote. We wanted to be very proactive and come in and say, 'hey, this is what we are doing.'"
Flohom doesn't need a approval from the town council just yet. The company first must go in front of the town's Planning Commission to ensure plans abide by the town's zoning policies.
"The use that they are proposing tonight would not be allowed with our current codes," Town Administrator Rob Straebel said. "So it would require a zoning change that would most likely go in front of the Planning Commission, then come back to the commissioners for discussion.
"So the presentation is just to see if there is enough support to move forward with consideration of a zoning change to potentially allow this."
St. Michaels residents also wanted to know if Flohom can give the houseboat model an historic look instead of a "business look."
Flohom officials confirmed they can remodel the boats to give them a historic look.
This report was updated to clarify how accommodation tax could be applied.

stories.title: Cambridge to Receive More Than $1 Million from State for Revitalization
stories.author: Staff Report
stories.content:
Cambridge to receive more than $1 million from state for revitalization

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The City of Cambridge has been awarded $1.15 million from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development for four of the city's revitalization projects.Projects receiving grant monies include the Mace's Lane Community Center, the 444-448 Race Street development project, the old City Hall renovation and Cambridge's façade improvement program, according to a news release from the city.
Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said in an interview with The Star Democrat on Friday that the grants were awarded about a month ago.
"I think this shows that city staff is working very hard to create a good first impression for people visiting our community," he said. "And that they see Cambridge as a happening place and not a sleepy backwater."
The Mace's Lane Community Center has been awarded $500,000 to complete construction and renovation at the former Cambridge high school. Founded by The Good Shepherd Association and the Mace's Lane High School Alumni Association, the community center will offer a variety of programs — including sports, arts and education programs — to support Cambridge's youth.
In November, about $8 million had been raised for the community center and $4.5 million was still needed. The $500,000 in grant money is from the Strategic Demolition Fund, which is a state program that aims to activate local economic development and create jobs.
In order to complete the third phase of the 444-448 Race Street development project, the state has awarded the city $500,000 from the Community Legacy program. The third phase of the Race Street project includes creating three retail spaces and nine apartments.
Community Legacy grants are awarded to projects in Maryland's "sustainable communities," a designation that Cambridge received in December 2023.
A total of $100,000 from the Community Legacy program was awarded to the "Old City Hall" renovation project on Gay Street. The grant money is for the creation of a community room in the building. Renovating and preserving the old city hall is a priority for the city.
The city was also awarded $50,000 to go toward improving the city's commercial building façades. The grant is through the Maryland Façade Improvement Program. Steckman said he expects this grant to benefit the city's downtown area.
"The City is grateful for these generous awards from the State of Maryland, which demonstrate its ongoing support of Cambridge's work to improve its buildings and economy for the betterment of the lives of all our residents," Steckman said in a news release. "We look forward to the continued improvements these projects will bring to the City of Cambridge over the next year."
Along with the city's awards, the Packing House received two awards totaling $550,000 from Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, according to the city. The grants, from the Community Legacy program and the Strategic Demolition Fund, will be used to furnish the building's shared commercial kitchen and to complete the building's interior and exterior event space.
Margaret Norfleet-Neff, the development manager overseeing the Packing House renovation, said the Packing House appreciates the support from the state.
"The Packing House is most appreciative of the ongoing support from DHCD and looks forward to unveiling the completed interior and exterior spaces for the benefit of the community and public use," she said.

Cambridge City Council approves tax abatement for Ocean Gateway property

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council unanimously voted to approve a property tax abatement for a property tucked between Peking House Restaurant and Advance Auto Parts on Ocean Gateway at a meeting on Oct. 7.During the council meeting, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said this property, located at 2721 Ocean Gateway, is the site of an old gas station that hasn't been operational for more than a decade. Currently on the site, there is a concrete block building, which was once the gas station storefront.
According to an Oct. 4 memo from Hesson to City Council, the vacant and underutilized property tax abatement program was created in Cambridge in 2016 to incentivize development of vacant and underutilized properties in the city.
The abatement will only apply to the improved value of the property, not the original assessed value of the property.
In the memo, Hesson said the Ocean Gateway property, owned by Delmarva Real Estate Management Group LLC, qualifies for the vacant and underutilized property tax abatement. The owner wants to remove the building to take away liability.
"If he removes the building now, without approval, the property will not be eligible for the program," Hesson said in the memo.
At the meeting, Hesson asked for approval of the property tax abatement. According to the memo, the abatement would be applied once a new commercial building has been built. There would be a "sunset" of June 2026 on the abatement in the case that no improvement has been made at the property.
"We do want to incentivize it, but we also want to incentivize it now," Hesson said.
After Hesson spoke, multiple commissioners said they were happy to see the abatement program used.
"That is prime real estate because it is right there on 50," Commission President Lajan Cephas said. "So thank you for using this resource."

stories.title: Cambridge City Council Moves Toward Creating TIF Policy
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Cambridge City Council moves toward creating TIF policy

 August 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council voted at a meeting on Aug. 26 to direct its attorney to prepare a resolution creating a tax increment financing, or TIF, policy.During the meeting, Acting City Manager David Deutsch recommended the council make this move. He brought up the Cambridge Harbor project, a project to develop Cambridge's waterfront. Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc., the group spearheading the project, has been looking into using tax incremented financing to help fund the project.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area.
CWDI's proposed TIF would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area. The TIF would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30 million bonds taken out by the city and county. According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
In March, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said they had completed a seventh run of a TIF model and it looked "very stable."
At the council meeting on Aug. 26, Deutsch said that a TIF project is different from a general obligation bond issued from a municipality.
"This is a method of financing that is unique to a specific project," he said. "And in order to position the city to be able to seriously consider that, we need to have a policy document in place."
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE POLICYIn an Aug. 22 memo to the City Council, Deutsch pointed out parts of TIF policies used in other Maryland jurisdictions that he said were "worth noting." These include creating an application process, using an outside financial advisor, requiring analysis of a test that demonstrates whether there is a need for the TIF and requiring developers to pay for fees and expenses of the city's consultants.
In creating a report with recommendations, city staff looked at TIF policies in six jurisdictions in the state. According to the report, staff recommend that the city use Bowie's policy and application, adding select practices and language from Frederick and Howard counties.
Deutsch said that if a policy is approved by the Cambridge City Council, the city would be ready with an application process in the event that a developer requests a TIF.
"And then we can sit with them and make sure that all the various elements are proper and in place so that the folks on city staff and our advisors can advise mayor and council properly," he said.
Before the council voted unanimously to direct the city attorney to prepare a resolution creating a TIF policy, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he thought the policy was an excellent idea.
"I'm delighted that we're moving in that direction," he said. "Not only will it help the city and the commissioners, but it will help a developer understand what they're going to have to go through in terms of making the application and what they're going to have to produce."
