stories.title: Pinnacle Hospitality Group Hopes to Build Hotel on Cambridge Harbor
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Pinnacle Hospitality Group hopes to build hotel on Cambridge Harbor

 August 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 600
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Less than a week after the city and Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. settled a lawsuit regarding the ability to transfer certain land, members of the CWDI Board of Directors sat in the front row of an Aug. 26 Cambridge City Council meeting.With them: a hotel developer interested in building a hotel on Cambridge Harbor, the project led by CWDI to develop Cambridge's waterfront.
The first half of the meeting, the developer, Tauhid Islam, spoke about why he would like to build a hotel on Cambridge Harbor and what he would like that hotel to look like.
No deal has yet been made with Islam to develop on Cambridge Harbor. On Aug. 23, CWDI Board President Angie Hengst told the Star Democrat that CWDI will be working with the city and county to identify the appropriate time to sign a deal after "various details" have been worked through.
Islam, the founder of Eastern-Shore-based Pinnacle Hospitality Group who started his own venture in 2016 after spending two decades with Choice Hotels, has been in talks with CWDI for the past year. Islam said that in the past eight years, his group has built seven hotels, including a Cambria Hotel and a Hampton Inn & Suites, both in Ocean City.
Islam said in an oceanfront hotel room, when you turn off the lights, all you can see from the balcony at night is darkness. By contrast, in a hotel room "on the tip of the bridge," it's not just darkness, he said.
"The rumbling of the bridge, the beauty of the dolphins swimming by and the moon actually glistening on the water," he said. "That's what attracted me to Cambridge."
Islam sees this venture as an opportunity to embrace a working waterfront. He said it's an opportunity for the younger generations to learn about a "forgotten art."
"Things that our children and their children may not have the opportunity to see first hand," he said, mentioning boat repair. "I think Cambridge does bring that and it will resonate with people who are just trying to get away from the city. ... I want to create something that will make them stop."
Islam said his plans include a rooftop restaurant and a conference center. He said he wants to bring in a franchise that doesn't exist in Cambridge.
During the meeting, Islam and his team unveiled an initial rendering that shows the project concept. The rendering included balconies that overlook the Choptank River and a pool steps away from the river.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), who sat in the front row of the meeting along with two CWDI board members, acknowledged that this hotel would take a few years to build and open if a deal is made.
"But boy, we have a great vision, and I think this is a great restart of Cambridge Harbor," he said.
Over the past year, tensions between the city and CWDI over the Cambridge Harbor project have received significant attention. With the lawsuit settlement — which includes both parties entering into a memorandum of understanding to address certain issues — representatives from both the city and CWDI Board have expressed hope about their relationship moving forward.
At the meeting, multiple City Council members thanked Islam for the presentation and shared their excitement for his approach to the project.
"There's an old adage that says a home without a heart is nothing but walls, roof and floor," Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said. "And its nice to hear you speak of the buildings, that they have heart in them as well. I think that's something we definitely want to have moving forward in our projects in Cambridge."

stories.title: City Council Discusses Cambridge Harbor TIF, CWDI Articles in Closed Session Meeting
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
City Council discusses Cambridge Harbor TIF, CWDI articles in closed session meeting

 April 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1067
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Following a Cambridge City Council closed session meeting Monday, April 22, Mayor Stephen Rideout publicly shared three decisions made behind closed Council Chambers doors that evening relating to Cambridge Harbor and Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc.TAX INCREMENT FINANCING
For one, the council has determined that it is a "worthwhile undertaking" to look at establishing a policy or an ordinance on how the city should deal with tax increment financing, commonly called TIFs.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area. The tax revenues from that increase are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area.
CWDI has proposed a TIF for its Cambridge Harbor project — a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront — that would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30-million bonds taken out by the city and county.
In October, the city expressed its concerns with the proposed TIF in a letter to CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard. It said the council had concerns that the TIF would take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades.
After the council returned to open session April 22, Rideout said that pending getting information about sample policy and getting advice from counsel, "the city will not be moving forward with any consideration of TIFs or a TIF program."
ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
The second decision Rideout shared is that he will hold off on amending the CWDI Articles of Incorporation until after the CWDI Board of Directors has had it's next meeting on May 22.
Rideout said that council had a discussion on this in closed session and that he requested direction from the commissioners. He said the commissioners voted in favor of holding off on amending the articles, with Commissioner Brian Roche abstaining.
Last week, the Star Democrat reported that Roche's brother-in-law, Mike LeMire, is an attorney with Miles and Stockbridge, a law firm that represents CWDI. In an interview April 19, Roche said he has followed protocol with this potential conflict of interest, including asking for an opinion from the Cambridge Ethics Commission.
April 16, Rideout held a meeting where he proposed amendments to the Articles of Incorporation. At that meeting, Rideout said he thought the amendments would make it more likely that the project is successful. He said he would make a decision in the 10 days following.
Rideout said CWDI has indicated its Board of Directors will discuss the proposed amendments at its May 22 meeting. He said he will hold off on amending the articles to give the board time for comment.
As mayor, Rideout is the sole member of CWDI. Similar to the a shareholder of a company, under Maryland law, a non-profit can have a member or members that represent the group which founded the nonprofit, Rideout said in an interview. As sole member of CWDI, Rideout said he has the authority to make amendments to the articles.
Before the City Council went into closed session Monday, both Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioner Sputty Cephas commended Rideout for holding the meeting April 16.
Sputty Cephas offered his support to Rideout.
"We're in support of development," he said about the CWDI project. "It's just how we get it done."
MEETING WITH HUTCHINSON
The third piece of information Rideout shared after the closed session was that he and Commissioner Laurel Atkiss would be meeting with Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), CWDI board President Angie Hengst and CWDI Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr on Tuesday, April 23.
Rideout said he told the council during closed session that he and Atkiss had been invited to meet with the others to discuss the challenges with collaboration on the Cambridge Harbor project. Rideout said he and Atkiss will report back to council with any information worth sharing.
TRANSFER AGREEMENT
Before the City Council went into closed session Monday, Roche said he wanted to make it clear that he supports the sale by CWDI of the Yacht Maintenance Company parcel and the prospect of a hotel being built on the Cambridge Harbor site.
Both of these properties were discussed in an April 12 memo to City Council from City Manager Tom Carroll.
According to council meeting documents, in his memo, Carroll said he recently learned that CWDI is in breach of the covenants of a March 2022 property transfer agreement between the city and CWDI.
In the memo, Carroll said the city conveyed approximately 10 acres of property to CWDI in the agreement. He said CWDI was supposed to issue a request for proposal, select a developer or developers and make a public summary of the request for proposal, per the covenants of the agreement. He said CWDI didn't do any of those things.
Carroll said that under the transfer agreement, CWDI can't transfer property the city has conveyed to it until all the covenants are fulfilled.
This means CWDI would not have the legal grounds to transfer the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance, a Cambridge company that offers boat and yacht services, or the land for the construction of a boutique hotel.
At a CWDI Board of Directors meeting March 20, Narr said CWDI plans to sell the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance this year. At the same meeting, Hengst said CWDI is making progress on its agreement with a boutique hotel developer to build on the Cambridge Harbor site, and she hopes the signing of the agreement is imminent.
At the City Council meeting Monday, Roche said the transfer of the Yacht Maintenance property is important so that Yacht Maintenance can invest in and install an 850-pound boat lift.
"This is a comparative economic advantage unique to Yacht Maintenance and the city of Cambridge," he said. "It is also a fundamental step in expanding the education and employment opportunities alongside the Richardson boat works facility for our citizens."
Roche said he supports CWDI's efforts to bring a hotel to Cambridge's waterfront.
"And although some members of this council and our outgoing city manager have made it known that there are other aspects of CWDI that they want to continue to discuss, that is fine," he said. "But I do think it's the obligation of every commissioner here tonight to make it abundantly clear that we will support and take whatever steps are necessary for the expansion of Yacht Maintenance and the prospect of a hotel being built at the site on the waterfront."

stories.title: CWDI Holds Community Update Meeting, Answers Some Questions
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
CWDI holds community update meeting, answers some questions

 April 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1272
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge residents packed the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Thursday night to hear from the Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors, its executive director and project partners.At the community update meeting, CWDI representatives talked about various aspects of the Cambridge Harbor — a project to develop the space along the Cambridge waterfront — before launching into a question-and-answer segment.
Resident Lauren Mross called CWDI's presentation "polished."
"I felt like they had many of the right answers," she said. "But I don't feel that they paid attention to the actual questions."
CWDI has been a major topic of conversation in the city recently.
On March 18, Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation and said he was resigning over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project. Two days later, residents lined the conference room of the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce for a CWDI Board of Directors meeting, where multiple residents asked questions and voiced concerns during public comment.
Two days before the community update meeting Thursday, Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout held a meeting where he proposed amendments to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation. As mayor, Rideout has the authority to make amendments to the articles, according to provisions in the articles themselves.
After the community update Thursday, Mross said she is excited and optimistic about the idea of the project but has concerns with the transparency of it. She called Carroll's resignation disappointing.
"I also thoroughly respect Steve Rideout," she said. "I trust his opinion on what's going on, and I want his transparent involvement in the project."
Before answering questions submitted for the event, CWDI addressed various parts of the project, including the plans for the project's first and second phases, funding and proposed tax increment financing, or TIF.
The TIF would increase taxes on the property as it gets developed to pay for two $30-million bonds taken out by the city and county.
Much of the presentation included information that has already been made available to the public through CWDI reports and previous presentations.
Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher, who led the question-and-answer portion of the event, said 65 questions —including repeats — were submitted by 20 different people. He said most of the questions fell into two categories: the YMCA and the Board of Directors. Christopher read nearly 20 questions Thursday.
YMCAThe first question Christopher read was about the current status of the YMCA and why CWDI would consider putting a nonprofit on the waterfront.
Many residents have expressed concerns about the possibility of Cambridge's YMCA, currently located at 201 Talbot Ave., moving to Cambridge Harbor. In late August, CWDI included a design for a new YMCA facility in its 2023 mid-year report.
At the meeting Thursday, CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said CWDI is not negotiating with the YMCA at the moment. He said the YMCA came to CWDI with an expression of interest that CWDI put out two years ago.
"They submitted to us what they would like to do and why they would like to do it," Leonard said. "We reviewed them like we did every other potential government partner or investor."
YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill, who was at the community update Thursday, said in an interview after the meeting that he was at the event to learn, and there were no new developments with the Cambridge YMCA.
When asked what would happen if the YMCA did move locations, Leonard said he thought it should become residential to match the rest of the neighborhood. He said that is something CWDI could help with if it "needs to be done."
Part-time Cambridge resident Steven Van Dorpe said the clarification that CWDI was not negotiating with the YMCA was "interesting."
"But it seemed like it was still a little bit vague as to whether or not they could come back into the equation," he said.
BOARD APPOINTMENTSAnother question asked at the meeting was whether the CWDI Board of Directors is responsive to the bodies that appoint them.
The seven-member board is made up of one governor-appointed member, two county-appointed members, three city-appointed members and one CWDI-appointed member. Currently, one of the county-appointed seats is vacant.
Board President Angie Hengst said part of a board member's job is to relay information to their appointing body, but their main responsibility is to CWDI and its mission. She said she hopes the appointing bodies have chosen representatives that they have full confidence in.
"At the end of the day, we are the board members of CWDI, and that's (who) we're really beholden to for any decisions that we're making," she said.
Board Vice President Shay Lewis-Sisco said she is responsive to her appointing body, the city. She said she has been in constant communication with the city manager and Cambridge City Council and called it "unfortunate" that press has gone out that does not make that clear.
Carroll, Cambridge's city manager, said in an interview that he has had a couple meetings with Lewis-Sisco, but she hasn't listened to his suggestions, which include making sure the project benefits Cambridge's workforce and its disadvantaged community.
CONFLICTS OF INTERESTAnother question brought up at the meeting had to do with Cambridge City Council Commissioner Brian Roche's connection to an attorney at a law firm that represents CWDI.
The question asked about a lack of disclosure regarding a council member and his brother-in-law, an attorney for one the law firms representing CWDI.
Leonard said CWDI uses three different law firms, including Miles and Stockbridge. He said he believes that "one of the hundred or so" Miles and Stockbridge attorneys "may be related to one of the City Council members."
Leonard said it was not a conflict of interest and quickly moved on to talk about what one of the other law firms CWDI uses has provided.
In an interview Friday, Roche confirmed that his brother-in-law, Mike LeMire, is an attorney with Miles and Stockbridge.
Roche said that when he learned of the potential conflict of interest, he reached out to City Attorney Patrick Thomas.
"There's been no votes or anything that would be, according to (Thomas), a conflict," Roche said. "But I was very careful. I take that allegation very, very seriously."
Roche said he has followed protocol with this, including getting an opinion from the Cambridge Ethics Commission to determine if it is a conflict of interest. He said the Ethics Commission has called and asked him questions, but he has not received a statement from them.
Roche said the City Council is aware of this potential conflict of interest.
LeMire did not immediately answer phone calls for comment.
ARTICLES OF INCORPORATIONRegarding Rideout's proposed amendments to CWDI's Articles of Incorporation, Leonard said CWDI appreciates when a concerned person comes forward with ideas to help the project.
Leonard said the CWDI Board of Directors will look at Rideout's suggestions at its meeting on May 22 to determine whether the amendments are necessary for improving CWDI and accelerating its mission.
At the meeting where Rideout proposed the amendments on April 16, Rideout said he would convene another meeting in the next 10 days to make his final decision on the amendments.
In an interview, Carroll said Leonard's comments at the community update indicate the board won't comment before Rideout convenes another meeting on the subject.
"So we will have no feedback on them," Carroll said about the amendments. "So it will be up to the mayor to decide what he does."
Overall, Carroll said the questions that needed to be answered by CWDI at the community update weren't. He said the city's fundamental questions still remain unanswered.
"I didn't learn anything that I didn't already know," he said.
Van Dorpe said he thought the questions were answered well. He said CWDI should have done more of these events in the past.
"Just kind of be open and direct," he said. "It's always about communication."

stories.title: CWDI Board Talks Finances, Hotel Deal at Board Meeting
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
CWDI Board talks finances, hotel deal at board meeting

 March 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 742
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cambridge — Cambridge residents lined the conference room of at the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce for a Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Board of Directors meeting Wednesday, March 20.The board addressed a variety of topics related to Cambridge Harbor — a project that will create public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River — before entering into closed session.
HOTEL DEAL
Board President Angie Hengst said CWDI is making progress on its agreement with a boutique hotel developer and hopes the signing of the agreement is imminent.
"There's just a little bit of back and forth with some final legalese with our lawyers," she said.
CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the board would meet with lawyers in the closed session portion of the meeting.
2023 AUDIT
Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr said the 2023 audit is currently underway. He gave a preview of what that report will look like when it is presented at the May board meeting.
Narr said CWDI has two separate entities when it comes to finances: CWDI Holdings, which is for real estate, and an operating entity.
In 2023, CWDI Holdings received a grant income of more than $2 million, Narr said. This income went toward pre-development costs including professional, design and consulting fees, he said.
CWDI Holdings had a net income of around $817,000, which Narr said is the cost of the Richardson Maritime Museum property that CWDI purchased in early 2023.
Narr said a lot of the operating entity's revenue for 2023 came through public sources, including a commitment from former Gov. Larry Hogan's administration and City of Cambridge American Rescue Plan Act funds. He said revenue also came through property leases and docking fees.
The operating entity had a net income of $24,000 in 2023. Narr said this would have been higher if CWDI had sold the Yacht Maintenance property to Yacht Maintenance, which it expected to do in 2023. He said CWDI now expects that sale to occur this year.
Narr said that other than an increase in legal fees "due to a couple issues we had to deal with here locally," costs to the operating entity stayed in line with what CWDI expected.
TAX INCREMENT FINANCING
Hengst said the Cambridge Harbor tax increment financing model looks "very stable," as a seventh run of the model was recently completed.
TIFs increase taxes in a certain area due to development. The increased tax revenues are used to pay for bonds, which have been issued for public improvement projects in that area. CWDI's tax increment financing would cover the Cambridge Harbor development project area.
According to a CWDI presentation at a Dorchester County Council meeting in December, the net tax increment from the TIF is expected to be around $10 million each for the city and county.
"We continue to try to work with the city and the county to provide them all the information that we can on the TIF and to hold public meetings with them," Leonard said at the board meeting Wednesday. "We did have a couple with the county already. We're waiting for the city to agree to do that with us so we can move it forward."
OTHER NOTES
During public comment, some residents said they were unhappy with the look of the fence currently at Cambridge Harbor. Cathy Hanson called the fence "unsightly and industrial looking."
According to the meeting agenda, the board discussed government relations in closed session. This came just days after Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll submitted his resignation. Carroll said he resigned over concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.
Hengst said the board is still in need of one county-appointed member and is waiting for the county to put out a request for interest.
Hengst said CWDI is waiting for final approval on the plans for the promenade extension at Cambridge Harbor. CWDI expects to bid the project before May so it can break ground in July.
CWDI agreed to having the Girls on the Run 5K take place on its property on May 4. Leonard said 85 boards on the boardwalk were replaced to make it safe for the event.
The Rotary Club of Cambridge will place 40 to 50 flags on the Cambridge Harbor property for Memorial Day.
CWDI is planning a public update meeting where people can attend in person or virtually to get a detailed update with what is going on at Cambridge Harbor. Leonard said they plan to hold the meeting sometime in the second quarter of the year.

stories.title: Cambridge Council Not in Support of Harbor Project Plan
stories.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Cambridge Council not in support of harbor project plan

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 690
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In a letter addressed to Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard, the city of Cambridge expressed City Council's concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project.The letter, signed by City Manager Tom Carroll, states that City Council does not support CWDI's current plans for Cambridge Harbor.In late August, CWDI, a private nonprofit, released a 2023 mid-year report to the community that detailed what the group has done so far and what it plans to do moving forward. The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces.In an interview in September, Leonard said the goal is for the entire project to be complete in somewhere between five and 10 years from now. By 2025, CWDI expects it will no longer need public funds to operate Cambridge Harbor.The letter from the city gives four reasons for the council's lack of support for the project. First, the council thinks CWDI seems like it wants to be the site developer instead of hiring a "capable master developer." "The redevelopment of a site of this size and complexity requires a private sector development partner with a proven track record of success in similar projects," the letter says.The second reason cited is that the proposal for the project "does not generate enough economic value" for developing the project without "an unacceptably large public subsidy."The third reason is that the proposed tax increment finance district will take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades."The city and county need to be involved in shaping these public financing plans from the start," the letter says.The fourth reason for the lack of Council support is that the council does not approve of the governance of CWDI. The letter states that CWDI is not being transparent, accountable or responsive to the Council.In a September interview, Carroll said that communication between CWDI and the city has not been enough. He said that, having spent 27 years in local governments and having been a part of two major economic development projects, he has concerns about the financial feasibility of CWDI's plan.In an interview Wednesday, Leonard said he was shocked by the letter. He said CWDI met with the city back in S eptember to discuss the project and got "relatively positive feedback."Leonard recognized that not all Council members agreed with every aspect of the project, but he said they seemed generally OK with it.While Leonard said he and the CWDI board take the concerns of all stakeholders very seriously, he said they do not share concerns with the city for the direction of the Cambridge Harbor project."Our direction has come from community input over the last three decades," he said. "We have accounted for the community development aspects ofwhat the community says they want and the economic development aspects ofwhat we believe will be valuable to the city and the county, and the state and the community, of course, at large."Leonard said CWDI is concerned about its relationship with the city, however."That means a lot to us," he said. "And we've tried, and continue to try to make that relationship positive and productive."Moving forward, Leonard hopes to address the city's concerns during a meeting scheduled for Nov. 13. Leonard said CWDI has issued invitations to all of its stakeholders and development team members to discuss some of the more confidential development matters of the project."We hope that members of the City Council and leadership of the city staff will attend the meeting so we can address, in essence, a number of the issues that they raised in the rest of their letter," he said.In the letter, it says that the City Council thinks the Nov. 13 meeting is premature and the City Council will be reaching out to Dorchester County Council to talk about how to get the project "back on track." 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
A view of Cambridge Harbor looking out onto the Choptank River on Sept. 13.

stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Branson and Perez Vie for Denton Council Seat

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 915
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Two Candidates Have Qualified to Run in Denton's Upcoming Town Council Election. They Are Lester L. Branson and Angel L. Perez.Branson Is 82 and Perez Is 38. Perez Is the Program and Events Manager for the Chesapeake Culinary Center and the CEO and Founder of Caroline Pride. Branson Is an Optometrist on Market Street.
The Winner Will Serve a Five-Year Term. the Election Will Be Held the Same Day as the General Election, Nov. 5, at the Denton Town Office, Located at 4 N. Second St. the Polls Will Be Open from 7 A.M. to 8 P.M.
The Star Democrat Spoke to Both Candidates Ahead of the Election. Their Answers to the Paper's Questions Can Be Found Below.
What Is Your Political Experience?Perez: "Here on the Shore, I Served as Community Outreach/Main Street Coordinator for the Town of Greensboro. I Presented Best Practices at Statewide Maryland Municipal League Conference in My Talk Titled, 'Partnering for Progress: Municipalities and Community Organizations Working Together,' Where Elected Officials and Municipal Staff Learned About Developing Partnerships Between Municipalities and Community Organizations Is Critical to Providing Quality Services to a Shared Constituency. in Addition to This Maryland Political Experience, I Also Bring Fresh Ideas from Serving as District Assistant for a City Council in Massachusetts. We Created a Communication Bridge Between Residents and the City Council and Community Programs."
Perez Went on to List Leadership Positions He Has Held with 19 Boards and Organizations on the Eastern Shore in the Past 10 Years.
Branson: "I Have Been Mayor Five Times and on the Board for 38 Years. So I Know Everything You Want to Know."
What Makes You the Best Candidate for the Position?Branson: "the Biggest Thing Is I Have Been Doing This for 38 Years and I Know the Ins and Outs of Everything."
Perez: "Over the Past 10 Years I Have Dedicated Myself to Working Tirelessly to Be Part of the Solution. I Come to Run as a Candidate to Bring People Together, Connecting with Our Community and Impacting It in a Positive Way, Especially Through the Creation of Different Local Programs for Youth and Families. Having the Ability to Make Decisions Based on Knowledge and Data Not Assumptions, Making Decisions That Benefit Everyone in Our Town. Direct Contact with All the Different Kinds of Residents in Denton and Knowledge of the Situations That Our Community Has, Especially Our Elderly, Youth and Small Business Owners. Being Able to Bring New Ideas and Perspectives and New Ways to Help Our Town Grow."
Why Are You Running?Branson: "I Am Running Because There Is a Lot of Things I'd Like to Get Done. And the Five of Us, Right Now, for the Last Few Years, We Work So Sweetly Together, and There Is No Rift or Anything Like That. We Really Get Things Done for the Town of Denton and the Citizens of Denton. I Am Hoping to Keep That Going."
Perez: "My Home, the Town of Denton, Has Always Had a Special Place in My Heart, and I Can Serve Better Our Community as Part of the Town Council. I Want to Continue to Work for My Community in a Respectful and Equitable Manner and Help Our Town Move Towards the Future with Strong Economic Growth While Maintaining Our Small Town Charm."
What Change Would You Like to See in the Next Five Years?Perez: "I Will Actively Listen to Small Business Owners to Develop Solutions Together. Also, I Will Provide Support and Assistance to the Downtown Main Street Office to Combine Efforts to Protect and Preserve Our Local Businesses. We Should Keep Property Taxes Low and Water Costs Affordable for All... Our Town Is Full of History and Art. the Town Council Can Create Collaborations with Organizations That Showcase Art and History in Our Town Is Essential to Expand, Promote, and Highlight the Arts and History District in Our Town by Providing Them with the Necessary Support. Thus, Making Our Town, Art and History Enjoyed by Visitors and Citizens... for the Past 10 Years, My Work Has Been Focused on Seeking the Well-Being and Impacting Our Youth in a Positive Way Through Different Programs and Community Services. as a Council Member, I Will Seek to Create Collaborations and Build Bridges of Communication with Different Organizations to Create, Promote and Expand Programs That Help Our Young People Reach Their Full Potential."
Branson: "See the Change from the Social Service Building. I Really Want to See the Road to Nowhere from Walmart Over to 404 Is Going to Be Called Commerce Drive. It Has Gone from $1 Million to $3 Million to Build the Road. I Really Want Us to Cut Taxes Again This Year. I Hope There Is a Way to Get This Road Money to Help with the Taxes and Not Have to Double Tax the People in Town. I Am Looking for Any Way That We Can Make It Better for Affordable Housing for People in Denton... Another Big Thing Is That We Are Looking with the County, They Are Going to Have to Build Another Middle School. There Is a Possibility That Where Caroline County High School Is That There Is Land to Do That Out There. in the Future, Are They Going to Keep the Middle School There or Put It Somewhere Else in Denton or Are They Going to Go Out to North Caroline and Put It There? ... Another Thing Is to Build Water and Sewer Out in West Denton. There Are a Lot of Houses Where Their Septic Systems Are Going Out."

stories.title: Cambridge Candidates Dispute Peace Order Request, Residency Requirements
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge candidates dispute peace order request, residency requirements

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With questions swirling about the residency of candidates in Cambridge's Oct. 19 election, three candidates headed to Dorchester County District Court Wednesday morning for a peace order hearing between one candidate and another's wife.Ward 4 Cambridge Commissioner Sputty Cephas, who is running for reelection, was denied a final peace order Wednesday against Natalee Bradshaw, the wife of former Cambridge Mayor and current mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw.
Andrew Bradshaw called the peace order request "a malicious use" of the court system "performed specifically for political purposes."
Cephas told the Star Democrat he had no intent behind filing the peace order other than not wanting to be bothered.
On Oct. 2, Cephas was granted a temporary peace order against Natalee Bradshaw. The peace order entailed that Natalee Bradshaw neither abuse Cephas, nor contact Cephas, nor enter his residence.
During the hearing Wednesday, Cephas asked Judge Abigail Marsh to grant a final peace order, which would extend the length of the temporary peace order.
Cephas testified that on Oct. 1, after leaving a Cambridge Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, he noticed a white Lincoln follow him to his home. Cephas said when he backed into his driveway, he saw the white Lincoln slow down and the driver of the vehicle snap photos before driving away quickly.
Cephas said he got back into his vehicle and drove behind the white Lincoln to get identification. He was able to identify the driver as Natalee Bradshaw. Cephas said he then spoke with Andrew Bradshaw for a minute or so.
Cephas then brought the issue to his sister, Commission President Lajan Cephas — who is running against Andrew Bradshaw and La-Shon Banks-Foster in the mayoral election — before going to the police department.
During the hearing, he told the judge that he felt harassed and stalked.
"I just want to be left alone," he said.
Natalee Bradshaw's attorney Philip Cronan argued Sputty Cephas' petition should be dismissed because none of his allegations was sufficient. Cronan said Natalee Bradshaw never made contact with or approached Sputty Cephas the night of Oct. 1.
Before denying the final peace order, Judge Abigail Marsh said Natalee Bradshaw is on notice that Sputty Cephas does not want any contact.
Marsh said harassment and stalking allegations require a pattern of behavior for a final peace order to be granted, and this was a single incident.
RESIDENCY REQUIREMENTSDuring the hearing, Cronan brought up statements that have been made questioning whether Sputty Cephas and/or Lajan Cephas are following the city's residency requirements for candidates.
Questions regarding the residency of candidates have circulated through Cambridge in the last month.
At a City Council meeting Sept. 9, one resident brought up the importance of verifying candidate applications. In response, Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said city staff has heard rumors regarding applicants and their residency, but no formal complaints had been filed. He encouraged residents to submit formal complaints so that they can be looked into.
In an interview Wednesday, Andrew Bradshaw alleged that Lajan Cephas has not been residing at the Cambridge address on her application. He said that his wife "may well have been" seeing about residency the night of Oct. 1. He said if that is the case, her actions were based on "real and genuine" concerns.
Lajan Cephas said in an interview Wednesday that she is not sure of Natalee Bradshaw's intent. Cephas said she has met every requirement to be a candidate in the city's election.
Sputty Cephas said during the hearing that the city has a process to do its due diligence for candidate applications.
Andrew Bradshaw said his wife has never expressed to him why she was outside Sputty Cephas's home Oct. 1. He said that in the privacy of their home, she has sworn she did not take any photos.

stories.title: Attorney General: Sheriff Has Limited Role in Electoral Process
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Attorney general: Sheriff has limited role in electoral process

 October 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown wrote a letter to Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gable detailing the "limited role of local law enforcement, including our sheriff's office in the electoral process."The letter from Brown was read aloud by Tammy Stafford, election director for Talbot County, during an Oct. 7 Board of Elections special meeting.
Although the letter is not an official opinion of the attorney general, Brown said he hopes the letter is helpful in setting forth the roles of law enforcement officers during elections.
The letter is the latest salvo on the topic of sometimes tense back-and-forth between the Talbot County Board of Elections, the Talbot County Sheriff and local elected officials in recent weeks.
Brown's letter responds to a letter sent by Gamble to the Board of Elections on issues concerning the upcoming election, in which Gamble "strongly" urged the board to follow state law.
In Brown's letter, he addresses the role of law enforcement, security, authority on election law violations and concerns involving election judges.
"State law does, specifies and carefully circumscribes the authority of local law enforcement and polling places while conferring primary responsibility for election law enforcement on other agencies," Brown said. "I understand that local law enforcement agencies do provide assistance to local boards of elections in some jurisdictions, including deploying personnel to provide security and transporting election materials. But importantly, this is done at the request and under the direction of the local Board of Elections itself."
Gamble's letter came in the midst of intense discussions centering concerns over the partisan breakdown of election judges ahead of the Nov. 5 General Election.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
In his letter, Brown emphasized state law "does not require equality in the total number of judges" recruited and trained by the local Board of Elections.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown said.
Toward the end of Brown's letter, he advised that opening a polling place, even if the number of judges from each party is not exactly equal, is preferable to "closing the polling place and disenfranchising all the voters who would have voted there."
After the reading of the letter, the county Board of Elections weighed whether to release its own letter or statement to the public addressing the election judge concerns.
Denise Lovelady, a member of the board of elections, said the issue with Brown's letter is it is still subject to "clarification." She said the letter speaks more to security issues than election judge equality.
After a bit of discussion, board members voted 3-1 to sent out Brown's letter instead of drafting their own. Lovelady voted against sending Brown's letter.
"I don't feel that it services the public, that it's giving them the full information that they need," Lovelady said. "The board is kind of skirting the issue that it needs to be defined better than what it has been in these meetings." 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

stories.title: State Board of Elections Weighs in on Election Judges Amid Concerns in Talbot County
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
State Board of Elections weighs in on election judges amid concerns in Talbot County

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After some Talbot County officials and residents raised concerns about the partisan breakdown of election judges, the Maryland State Board of Elections is telling voters that election judge affiliations will not bring about disenfranchisement at the polls in November.Discussion about the imbalance of election judge political party affiliations surfaced last week after Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp raised it in a council meeting Sept. 24. He voiced concerns the county Board of Elections was not following state law for election judges, though his motion for the council to send a letter to the elections board failed by a 3-2 vote.
One week later, Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble sent a letter to the Talbot County Board of Elections, "strongly" urging the board to follow state law.
The following day, Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, released a statement regarding the assignment of election judges. In it, he emphasized that Maryland voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," DeMarinis wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections. The party affiliation of an election judge does not stop them from casting their ballots or disenfranchise a voter. And to say otherwise is disingenuous."
DeMarinis noted in his statement the strict rules election judges must follow, bounding them "to conduct the election in a nonpartisan manner and fashion."
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
According to the most recent breakdown from the Talbot County Board of Elections, 62 judges are Democrats, 50 are Republicans and 11 are unaffiliated.
Following a closed session meeting on Friday for legal advice, the Talbot Board of Elections is set to meet Monday at 1 p.m. to discuss of a statement to send to the public, according to Talbot County Election Director Tammy Stafford. She said election judge assignments are on the agenda for a second special meeting Tuesday at 9:30 a.m.
Stafford did not respond to questions from the Star Democrat rabout the election judges and whether legal counsel has advised if the board is in compliance with law or not.
Election judges are appointed 13 weeks prior to the primary elections, DeMarinis said, and recruiting judges is an ongoing process local boards of elections undertake.
"There are never enough election judges on call to serve," the statement read. "Individuals get sick, have emergencies, have transportation issues, and a whole list of other things that might prevent them from serving on an assigned day. Having election judges assigned to being on call is the only way to mitigate this problem and ensure smooth election operations."
LETTER FROM SHERIFFIn Gamble's letter sent to the board and Election Director Tammy Stafford, the sheriff stated he's received more than 25 complaints regarding the election and "feelings of disenfranchisement."
"Complaints received highlight a clear disparity among one party over another and in this current instance, registered Republican voters are not being equally represented," Gamble wrote.
In an interview, Gamble, a Republican, explained the reasoning for his concerns and why he sent the letter.
"We provide security at the polling places," Gamble said. "We also escort ballots back. The election judges, we follow them back and make sure that the election's not tampered with by outsiders, however they might do that. I think to have free and fair elections, you need to be transparent, and you need to follow the law."
DeMarinis' statement addressed the role of local sheriff's offices in elections.
"The Sheriff's office does not have any legal authority to conduct security checks or a role in securing the ballots in a polling place," DeMarinis wrote. "Nor does the Sheriff enforce the requirements of the Election Law Article. The legal authority to keep the peace, to preserve the integrity of the voting process and maintain order in the polling place is entrusted to the election judge. In fact, a police officer must obey the order of the election judge at the polling place."
Gamble said he's not heard back from the county or state elections boards. In an interview, he expressed worry that the election judge controversy may affect safety during the election process.
"It causes me security concerns, too, because people are going to get frustrated," Gamble said. "We've already seen violence associated with this election cycle with two assassination attempts of the former president.
"And we don't want any issues here in Talbot County with people getting frustrated and then taking their frustrations out in some criminal manner," he said.

stories.title: Easton Approves Restrictions on Campaign Donations
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates in future campaigns will face new fundraising restrictions and reporting requirements thanks to a new law passed by the Easton Town Council.After nearly six months of fine-tuning, Easton passed its first campaign finance ordinance on Monday.
It will limit campaign contributions to $1,000, ban contributions from political committees and organizations, and require campaign treasurers to submit detailed financial reports before and after the election.
Council members said the ordinance is a win for transparency in Easton's elections. All five voted in favor of the new regulations.
"I think that (we) have done an excellent job of putting together an ordinance which achieves our goals of providing transparency in elections," said Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook.
The ordinance was introduced in April, amid a heated and politically charged race between current Town Council President Don Abbatiello and former President Frank Gunsallus.
There were largely no requirements for candidates to report specific contributions made to their campaigns during this year's election. Financial disclosures submitted by candidates when they filed for candidacy didn't include campaign donations. Montgomery, Cook and others argued that there should be more transparency on which organizations and people make donations to candidates.
Now, future candidates must name a campaign treasurer, who is responsible for sending the town office documentation of each donation, whether from an individual, business or organization.
The council has made several edits to the campaign ordinance since April, including raising the maximum donation mark from $250 to $1,000 and exempting spouses or domestic partners of candidates from the $1,000 limit.
Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said Monday that concerns he had about a political committee donation ban in the ordinance breaching First Amendment standards were quelled after discussion with Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh.
Rankin said individuals involved in political organization can still donate on behalf of themselves. And the ordinance doesn't stop political committees from making "independent expenditures" supporting a candidate, as long as the money doesn't go to the candidate directly.
Political groups will be required to file reports to the town if their expenses for an election cycle are $100 or more.
Town elections are nonpartisan.
Resident Lance Simon, a vocal advocate for the ordinance, thanked council members for supporting the new restrictions and said he hopes it can be "up and running" soon to allow enough time for it to be properly implemented. The town's next election is scheduled for May 2027.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who expressed concerns with the first draft of the ordinance potentially blocking some residents from running for office due to fiscal limits, said Monday that the final version is in a better place.
Davis thanked Cook and Montgomery for sponsoring the ordinance and bringing transparency to future town elections.
"I think the work has been done," Davis said. "I think we have really mulled it over a lot."

stories.title: Easton Election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello Weigh in on Housing, Growth and More
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton election: Gunsallus, Abbatiello weigh in on housing, growth and more

 April 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town Council president candidates Frank Gunsallus and Don Abbatiello both recognize the need to monitor and manage Easton's growth, but they each indicated different strategies on how to do so in editorial board interviews with The Star Democrat this week.Gunsallus, the incumbent, is being challenged by Abbatiello, the current Ward 2 councilmember. Voters head to the polls May 6 to decide the council's next leader, as well as representatives for the second and fourth wards.
During the interviews, both candidates were asked how to tackle Easton's affordable housing issue.
Gunsallus noted one of his priorities is to vote down an inclusionary zoning ordinance town leaders have expressed mixed opinions on. Instead, he said methods like removing impact fees or marking down land should be considered.
"It's a lot simpler than it's being made out to be," Gunsallus said. "Those are very straightforward, simple ways that can be done very soon to make that happen."
Abbatiello said the main issue with the lack of affordable homes is the rising price of land. He said incentivizing developers to build "middle housing" options is a solution.
"How do you get that price of land out of the equation? You have townhouses," Abbatiello said. "And townhouses become your starter home for people."
The current Ward 2 representative added that his vote against the Gannon Range project on Matthewstown Road in 2022 stemmed from the high prices of those homes.
"It was bringing us $450,000, $500,000 homes, which is not something that we needed," he said.
Gunsallus pointed out he's asked for the Town Council to have more say in approving housing projects. At a February workshop, Gunsallus and others led a discussion of how the council has only approved 37% of the town's 1,000 housing units in the pipeline at the time.
ENVISIONING THE FUTURE
The town is in the early process of revising its comprehensive plan for the first time in 15 years. The Planning Commission is currently reviewing drafts of the new plan, which lays out a vision for how the town should prioritize its growth.
Abbatiello said that in 2010, Easton was aiming to draw developers into town, but now the focus has changed.
"Tap the brakes, we need to slow down," he said of the current thought process.
The town's current comprehensive plan calls for 1% year-to-year growth. Gunsallus says he's "of the school of thought that that 1% is the ceiling, and we should not be exceeding that."
"When I graduated high school here in 2006, the town was literally half the size population-wise that it is now," he said. "So if we continue that same rate of growth, in 20 years, we'll have almost 40,000 people here."
REPRESENTING RESIDENTS
Candidates were asked questions concerning constituent representation. Gunsallus said he's given underrepresented groups a voice since being elected, such as when he voted to remove a 10-cent paper bag fee, a measure that narrowly fell short.
"That stemmed directly from a conversation with a room full of people about, 'I count my pennies when I go shopping so I can buy bags because my food stamps don't cover the cost of bags,'" Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello said if elected, he would push for each ward to have quarterly meetings. He said follow-up is critical, such as when he helped Ward 2 residents who raised concerns about safely walking to Walmart and Giant.
"I was annoying in saying, 'There needs to be a sidewalk on Elliott Road,'" Abbatiello said.
LEADERSHIP
With an election cycle that's become increasingly heated, both candidates offered thoughts on the responsibility of the council president and the disagreements that come with serving on the council.
"You can be the most amazing council president in the world, but if you can't get there with the rest of the council members, then you're going to lose every single vote that comes up," Abbatiello said.
"Sometimes you are not even part of the issue, but you still have to mediate or at least navigate the conversation," Gunsallus said. " ... Let's find common ground and go from there."
Gunsallus said it's been an honor to serve in the role since 2023.
"I'm happy with what has occurred under my administration, and I am looking forward to continuing the good work for another four years," Gunsallus said.
Abbatiello acknowledged serving on the council isn't an easy job, but he said it's an enjoyable one.
"You wonder if you're making the right decision," Abbatiello said. "But at the same time, I am still glad that over the last six years I've had the opportunity to make those decisions. And I wouldn't trade it for anything."

stories.title: Campaigning Practices Questioned at Cambridge City Council Meeting
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Campaigning practices questioned at Cambridge City Council meeting

 November 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 644
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In the final week before Cambridge's heated run-off election for its next mayor, residents are bringing up concerns with candidate campaigning practices.During a Cambridge City Council meeting on Nov. 25, two residents detailed their concerns with candidates door knocking at apartment complexes where elderly people and people with disabilities live.
Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas and former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw are both running to fill the open mayoral seat. Their campaigns have been gearing up as the city draws nearer to the Dec. 3 run-off election.
At the council meeting, resident Mya Woods read a letter from another resident, GeriLeigh Farrow, that called out Cephas and her campaign.
In the letter, Farrow said she was working at Conifer Village at Cambridge, an apartment complex for seniors, when she noticed a man standing outside.
"I noticed the man outside, which now I know as Lajan's boyfriend or husband, while she was inside," the letter read.
Before Woods could finish reading the letter, Mayor Stephen Rideout told her public comments must be made to or about the entire council, not a single commissioner.
Woods went on to ask that the city's elected officials make sure they make decisions with the residents best interests, not just their own.
"... Just remember, the town is broken and they need people who can lead them and not take advantage of them," she said.
Michael Jones, a resident of New Horizons Apartments, told the City Council he has seen people come in and out of his apartment for campaign reasons. He recounted an experience where he received a knock at his door and later found a campaign flier at his door.
Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said Conifer Village residents have been reaching out to her about "problems with their building being infiltrated."
"The measures that people go to these days to take advantage of our vulnerable and elderly and differently-abled is really heart wrenching," she said. "They do everything from selling fake extended car warranties or service contracts to stealing home equity lines of credit."
Atkiss — who has endorsed Bradshaw in the upcoming election — said she has also heard that a campaign gained access to New Horizons and the Bradford House Apartments. Atkiss later told the Star Democrat she was talking about Cephas' campaign.
Atkiss said that when she wanted to go door knocking inside Conifer during her campaign, she was told she couldn't as a security measure for residents.
"It's not up to me to decide that my cause is greater than their privacy and their right to not be disturbed," she said.
Atkiss continued on to say that no one voted for the commissioners "so they could see what we could get away with."
"But I know, if this is how elected officials act, I don't blame people for not coming out and voting," she said.
Cephas responded to the comments, acknowledging the issue has nothing to do with city business.
"But since people want to spin a narrative, I'm going to be transparent," she said.
Cephas said she was invited by a resident to do a meet and greet at Conifer on Nov. 26 and said she was invited by management to do a meet and greet at Bradford House on Dec. 2.
"I think we need to understand that canvassing is not illegal," she said. "Canvassing is an intentional way of interacting with the residents. Everyone doesn't have social media. Everyone doesn't have email. So we all knock on everyone's door that we're allowed to knock on."
She said her concern is not with "sensationalized behaviors," but with making sure everyone is able to vote.
"And I just really find it a shame that we have other people who are trying to say that (canvassing is) being used to take advantage when we're trying to engage," she said.
The Cambridge run-off election will be held on Dec. 3 at 447 Race St. The polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

 With about 1,000 mail-in and provisional ballots left to canvas in Talbot County, the future of a charter amendment extending the county's ability to raise residents' taxes for public safety hangs in the balance.The 1-cent amendment would authorize the Talbot County Council to raise property taxes one cent per $100 of assessed value each fiscal year. stories.title: Open Meetings Compliance Board Finds Cambridge City Council in Violation
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Open Meetings Compliance Board finds Cambridge City Council in violation

 July 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 694
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Maryland Open Meetings Compliance Board has found the Cambridge City Council to be in violation of the Open Meetings Act for actions made during and following a City Council meeting on Jan. 8At a City Council meeting on July 8, Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout read a portion of the board's July 3 opinion, which found that the council violated documentation requirements for a closed meeting preceding the open session council meeting in January.
"The city does not fully agree with this decision, but has read it as required by the Open Meetings Act board," he said before directing city staff to publish the opinion on the city's website.
According to the opinion, which was published on the Maryland attorney general website, the board found the city failed to prepare a written closing statement to enter into a closed session meeting, failed to put together "sufficiently detailed" minutes of the closed session and failed to put together a "sufficiently detailed" public summary of the closed session.
The board did not find that the council violated the Open Meetings Act by holding the meeting itself.
The opinion states the complainant filed an application in September requesting the city rezone several parcels of land. It says the council was scheduled to vote on the matter on Jan. 8, and at the beginning of that meeting, the council voted to postpone the vote on the application.
According to the Jan. 8 council agenda and meeting minutes, the council voted to postpone one item that dealt with rezoning: an ordinance that would have amended zoning to make four contiguous parcels at the corner of Washington and High streets the same zoning district.
At a council meeting on April 22, the council voted to deny the proposed ordinance, which had previously been tabled, in a three-to-two vote, with commissioners Jameson Harrington and Brian Roche voting against denying the rezoning.
Jim Chaney, complainant and managing member of Quality Housing Cambridge LLC — which submitted the application to rezone parcels on Washington and High streets — said he thought the Compliance Board did the best it could with the information it was able to obtain.
Chaney said it was concerning that the city did not keep "proper minutes" for the closed session meeting. He said that he didn't believe in the city's leadership.
"How do you attract businesses and people to come to the city when you're doing things like this?" he asked.
According to the opinion from the Compliance Board, the complaint alleged that the council:
Entered into closed session without convening the meeting in open session.Had discussions in closed session outside the parameters of what it said it would discuss.Failed to make required disclosures to the public after exiting closed session.Conducted business outside of a meeting that should have been conducted in an open meeting.
The complaint also alleged that the council violated the act by tabling the ordinance during the Jan. 8 open session meeting.
The Compliance Board said it could not conclude whether the council "improperly convened" in closed session Jan. 8 after the town said it made a public announcement before doing so.
The board said that although the council invoked two exceptions that allow it to enter into closed session, the council did not prepare a written closing statement, which is a violation of the act.
The board also said it could not determine whether the council talked about things outside the bounds of what it claimed to enter closed session for because the council failed to disclose anything regarding the substance of the closed meeting in its sealed minutes. The board found the council in violation of the Open Meetings Act because of that failure.
Regarding the allegation that the council conducted business it should not have outside of the meeting, the board said the question is really a matter of whether the council met in secret because the act only applies to meetings. The board said the council denies discussing the application before the regular meeting, and the board could not conclude whether the council met in secret.
The board said tabling an item is not a violation of the act and declined to find a violation based on that specific allegation brought forward by the complainant.

 The Commissioners of Ridgely suspended the entire Ridgely Police Department with pay, effective immediately, pending an investigation by the Office of the Maryland State Prosecutor, according to a Wednesday release from the town.The commissioners are developing a temporary agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Department to guarantee uninterrupted public safety services for the Ridgely residents, the release said.
According to the Ridgely Police Department website, six officers are employed by the department.
The Commissioners of Ridgely met in closed session Monday evening to discuss matters of personnel and "to consult with staff, consultants, or other individuals about pending or potential litigation," according to an agenda for the meeting posted to the town's website.
Sheriff Donnie Baker said the Caroline County Sheriff's Department is ready to continue to provide services to the town of Ridgely.
"We cover the town when their police is off the clock," Baker said. "We provide them with back up. We're familiar with the citizens."
A statement from the Sheriff's Office read, "Given the recent events involving the Ridgely Police Department, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, in collaboration with the Caroline County Commissioners and the Commissioners of the Town of Ridgely, are committed to providing continuous police services to the town's citizens, ensuring their safety remains a top priority. Together with the Maryland State Police, the Sheriff's Office will guarantee seamless and uninterrupted police coverage within the town limits of Ridgely."
Residents are asked to continue to dial 410-479-2515 for non-emergencies and 911 for emergencies.
This report will be updated as information becomes available.

stories.title: Caroline County Commissioners Advance Solar Ordinance with Amendments
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County Commissioners advance solar ordinance with amendments

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have had multiple discussions about the future of solar energy in the county. Another discussion was on the agenda for the commissioners' meeting Tuesday.They discussed a solar energy ordinance designed to help bring the county's solar laws in compliance with state laws passed by Maryland General Assembly.
The ordinance would allow the county to put certain requirements for solar electric energy generating facilities in place.
Commissioner Larry Porter has had multiple safety questions about battery energy storage systems, which he feels were never answered by the state.
"I don't want to use the word lie, but I will because we've been lied to about this from day one," Porter said. "From the time this was brought up, we have been told by various agencies, various departments, that there were going to be safety provisions that were going to be introduced in this. There isn't anything in the Senate Bill 931. There was nothing in that bill, contrary to what I was told on record in that hearing that addresses self-contained fire suppression in these systems."
"Now, I was told down it when we were at MACO, I stopped and talked at one of the booths for the Maryland State Fireman's Association, and I was told it at that time, and that was August, that there had been some changes to the bill, but the guy didn't know what they were. So, until somebody can tell me that these things are going to be safe and they're not going to propose a hazard to our firefighters and first responders, I'm not going to agree to include them in this bill," Porter said.
Commissioners president Travis Breeding said he agrees with concerns for safety, but he said the county cannot completely remove battery energy storage systems from the law because it is against state law. Breeding suggested adding some safety precautions for the local fire departments in case of solar battery emergency.
While battery solar was the commissioners' main concern Tuesday, four amendments were suggested by the commissioners to take the legislative bill into second reading and public hearing.
The amendments were:
Increase the compensation fee from 50% to 100% of the fair market value for new solar arrays and battery solar storage systems.Add fire department equipment and training fee for battery energy solar systems and self-contained fire suppression systems within battery energy storage systems.Remove the county's 2,000-acre cap on solar development to bring the county in compliance with state law.Make changes to the zoning table to reflect permitted districts within the county where solar is allowed.

stories.title: Easton Council Debates How to Move Forward with Food Trucks
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After uproar from food truck owners and residents, the Easton Town Council is considering changes to its restrictions on food trucks.On Monday, the council discussed potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
"I think that should be something we should take on as soon as we can," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
All five council members acknowledged they must keep in mind the town's existing restaurants when making any relaxations to food truck rules.
"2011 was a long time ago, and things change," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "But we have to be mindful of our brick-and-mortar restaurants. We don't want to do anything unnecessarily to compete with them."
In the last two weeks, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. A petition garnered over 3,000 signatures.
The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The council and attorney Sharon VanEmburgh agreed Monday to look at amending the ordinance by next spring. Then, they focused discussion on a short-term solution.
PILOT PROGRAM
Much of the food truck debate has centered on vendors that had been setting up outside the Shore Medical Center hospital on South Washington Street. Curry said the council received "tremendous" feedback from hospital employees who relied on the food trucks during lunch breaks.
"It's literally impossible to even go pick up a sandwich sometimes with the traffic in our wonderful, little town and get back to the desk within 30 minutes," Curry said.
Curry asked if the town could include the hospital in a short-term fix, such as a pilot program floated Monday. The program would likely be created through a resolution, VanEmburgh said, allowing certain businesses to invite food trucks to their properties.
Easton's program, if approved, would likely include a setback rule from nearby restaurants. VanEmburgh said the best mark may be around 300 feet.
Town Council members debated various provisions that could be included in a resolution to establish the pilot program.
Davis said any pilot program introduced would need to apply to other businesses in town.
"If we're gonna do it for the hospital, we got to be fair across the board to other people," Davis said. "I get the hospital has a need, but you can't just arbitrarily give them favor."
Ward 4's David Montgomery pushed back, saying a pilot program is meant to try out "in a specific time and place." He said the hospital should have "first crack" at a food truck pilot program.
Davis raised the concern that certain food trucks could be excluded from the pilot, providing an example.
"If there's a food truck that specializes in African American food that is not served at the hospital, what do we do in those instances to be fair?" Davis asked.
Montgomery replied, "It just seems to me that you're being obstructionist in these comments.
" ... The hospital has chosen in the past what food truck to invite on their private property," he added. "I think that's their right to do it."
The council also touched on transient license fees that food trucks pay when setting up at permitted festivals or events. Vendors pay $500 for the first two days and $150 for each day after up to 30 days.
"I would not be opposed to waiving that right now while we're in the pilot program," Curry said. "Because you can't expect a food truck to pay $500 to sit outside a hospital or a store or anywhere. Because they'll never recoup."
VanEmburgh said it makes sense to reduce that fee for the pilot program, though she said there probably should still be some fee.
The Town Council is expected to consider a pilot program proposal at a future meeting, potentially on Sept. 2.

stories.title: Potential Bill on Public Nuisances Workshopped at Caroline County Meeting
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 301
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners workshopped a potential legislative bill addressing public nuisances at their Tuesday meeting.The commissioners discussed a proposed amendment to the definitions section of chapter 137 of the county's code and a new section addressing public nuisances and their abatement in Caroline County.
As defined in the current legislation, a public nuisance affects an entire area or the public at large, unlike a private nuisance, which affects a single property.
Public nuisance properties can be properties that can cause harm to public health and safety or properties that have been abandoned or unkept. The main priorities for the commissioners with the potential bill are burning trash, temporary use of recreational vehicles and abandoned homes and properties.
The proposed ordinance provides framework for identifying the nuisances, which would include notifying landowners and tenants and providing due process hearings in case of disagreement.
"The county does have the power, as does the health department, the health officer and the secretary of the department of health, all have these powers under the state statutes to abate nuisance," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"It doesn't give you a great deal of direction how you're supposed to do it, but you have the power," he said. "So the purpose of ordinances at county level is to give some framework to how public nuisance is identified by the director of planning and codes."
Inspections would be conducted by the county code enforcement office, and coordination with the health department would depend on the nature of the complaint.
Concerns were raised about the feasibility of incorporating appeal hearings into the regular County Commissioners schedule, given the potential for lengthy hearings, but county officials said most of the appeals would not reach the commissioners.
County officials and the county health department agreed to work on the commissioners' concerns within the proposed legislation.
