stories.title: Caroline County Passes Fiscal Year 2026 Budget
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Caroline County passes fiscal year 2026 budget

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners adopted the county's fiscal year 2026 operating and capital budgets at a meeting Tuesday.The commissioners and county employees have been working on the budget for about six months and have balanced a $2 million shortfall. The revenue total for the county sits at $79,208,471.
Allocations to some departments and agencies dropped compared to years prior. Some organizations and nonprofits completely lost county funding in this year's budget. Among those organizations are the Human Service Council, His Hope Ministries and Big Brothers Big Sisters of the Eastern Shore.
While Commissioners President Travis Breeding wanted to cut all nonprofit funding to avoid picking and choosing organizations, Commissioners Larry Porter and Frank Bartz chose to give to certain nonprofits.
"My thought process was that that there are a lot of good nonprofits in the county, and we don't have the funding ability to support them all," Breeding said. "So, I didn't really want to get in a situation where we were picking and choosing which ones. I advocate for people to donate to all of those nonprofits, but it just didn't feel like a core responsibility of Caroline County to provide funding there."
During the end of the budget process, changes from the state impacted the proposed budget. In the income tax line item, the county's original $1 million loss due to the state allocating more cost to the county went down to only a $200,000 loss. In the disparity grant section, the legislators passed a bill to make the disparity grant gap cover 90% instead of the normal 75%.
The county decided to add money to the tar and chip fund in the infrastructure line item of the capital budget. This move left over $1 million for the county to allocate in the capital budget.
The county put $100,000 to Public Works for tree trimming and $980,994 toward a fund to purchase radios for emergency services.
In addition to the budget being passed, the county S&P grade has increased from an "AA minus" grade to an "AA." This grade is what allows the county to bond or borrow money.
The commissioners thanked county employees, Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox and Grant Coordinator Stacy Seward for their hard work balancing the budget and the grade upgrade.
"In an environment where a lot of government agencies are seeing reduced credit ratings, we have managed to see an increase here. I think its a testament to staff, tight budgeting and managing every dollar to make sure its used appropriately," Breeding said.

stories.title: Talbot County OKs $161 Million Budget
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot County OKs $161 million budget

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 685
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County made good on its promise to deliver a flat, conservative budget for fiscal year 2026. The County Council unanimously passed a $161.1 million spending plan Tuesday.It comes in at nearly $3 million under last year's budget amid what County Manager Clay Stamp calls "uncharted waters."
"The economic landscape out there is a bumpy ride right now," Stamp said. "This year, we knew that we needed to flatten the budget out, we needed to live within our means."
Stamp and other officials have emphasized Talbot County's continued financial commitments toward public safety, whether through capital projects such as an EMS station in Cordova or support for correctional officers.
In a draft version of the budget that only received a few adjustments Tuesday, the council is expected to allocate the following funds for public safety:
$11.5 million for emergency medical services.$10.5 million for the Talbot County Sheriff's Office.$7.6 million for the Department of Corrections.$5.4 million for emergency management.$3.3 million for volunteer fire departments.
Council members thanked Stamp, Finance Director Martha Sparks and Assistant Finance Director Kaitlin Foster-Clark for their work during the budget process.
"This was the most challenging budget that I've ever sat through," council member Keasha Haythe said. "The decisions were very hard on some items."
"It was definitely a heavy lift this year, but everyone bucked down, and we made it happen here," council member Dave Stepp said.
The county's property tax rate will remain largely steady at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, though residents will see a supplemental tax of just over 1 cent per $100 of value on their tax bills.
EDUCATION FUNDING
That supplement stems from education funding OK'd by the county. While most line items were ironed out through deliberations, workshops and meetings, Tuesday's discussion centered on funding amendments for Talbot County Public Schools.
The budget already included $55 million in education funding as required by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's initiative to fund and improve education. County Council members were left to consider how much the county would contribute above that mark.
In a 4-1 vote Tuesday, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding for schools, aimed at filling nine positions, including multilingual and special education roles. Council member Lynn Mielke was the sole no vote.
The approved budget change came after an amendment to fulfill the district's entire $1.1 million request — which had been scaled back from $5.5 million earlier this budget cycle — failed narrowly. Vice President Pete Lesher and Haythe favored the $1.1 million, but President Chuck Callahan, Stepp and Mielke did not.
Lesher argued it is "short-sighted" to not fund the full request. He said it'd be prudent for the county to gradually increase its education funding as even higher Blueprint projections loom in future fiscal years.
"This would be a small step in that direction," Lesher said. "And frankly, it will make next year, an election year, a lot easier for all of us up here."
"I think we should be going farther," he said of the $600,000 mark. "But this goes some distance."
Callahan sponsored the amendment to partially OK the district's request, citing the significant need for teachers. The $500,000 not approved by the council was requested by the district to increase teacher and instructional assistant salaries.
"I would ask that the school board use the money that we give you for (hiring) teachers," Callahan said. "I would like to see that, and not for something else."
Mielke said she was initially on board with Callahan's amendment. But she said she needs "more security" that the district will put the $600,000 toward the nine positions.
"I'm not advised that it necessarily would be," Mielke said. "So for that reason I couldn't support it."
A spokesperson for Talbot County Public Schools said in a statement to The Star Democrat that the district stands behind the $1.1 million request but understands the "challenges faced by council and staff in meeting the funding needs of Talbot County in these uncertain times."
"We are grateful for their support for educators' pensions and for the additional staff needed to serve our students," the statement read.
This story has been updated to include a statement from Talbot County Public Schools.

 DORCHESTER — After receiving community feedback over removing the tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock, the Dorchester County Council worked with each other, County Manager Jerry Jones and county staff to modify the proposed county budget.The differentials, which lower tax rates in the municipalities to account for duplicated services, remain intact in the fiscal year 2026 budget passed by the County Council Tuesday.
Rather than removing the differentials, the county made adjustments to its budget including deferring all nonprofit funding to a later time.
The county's real property tax rate will increase by 3 cents across the board, bringing the overall tax rate to $1.03 per $100 of assessed value. Cambridge residents will pay 95.67 cents per $100 of assessed value, and Hurlock residents will pay 94.79 cents per $100 of assessed value.
"We came up with a product. Is it the best product in the world? Heck no. But it will suit the needs of the people in the county," said council member William Nichols in reference to the budget.
As Nichols voted in favor of the budget bill, he made a point to explain to the community that this was the worst budget he has seen in the 30 years he's sat on the council. Nichols said that there have been no hidden agendas and that he appreciates all the feedback.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer is concerned the council will end up in the same position next year, with the state of Maryland expecting to reach a $6 billion deficit in the next two years if there are no significant changes.
Council member Rob Kramer agreed with Nichols, saying this was the worst budget he's seen in the 20 years in his seat, but "we made lemons out of lemonade."
Contention between the state capital and rural Maryland was brought up often. Kramer said he doesn't think Annapolis has any hope in rural Maryland, but at the same time, he doesn't have any hope in Annapolis.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) attended the meeting Tuesday, assuring residents they have a voice in Annapolis. Hutchinson echoed the sentiments of the council members, saying there's a major disconnect between what happens in the capital and what happens in the community.
"I just ask you, please, when you hear us talking about this stuff next year, please, I ask you to write letters, please make phone calls, please be as active as possible in your community to relay to Annapolis that Dorchester County cannot continue to take the economic hits it has been," Pfeffer said before opening up the floor for comments.
The budget bill will take effect on July 1.

stories.title: Caroline County Retains Tax Differentials, at Least for This Year
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County retains tax differentials, at least for this year

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held their last fiscal year 2026 public budget hearing Tuesday evening.While the commissioners received multiple recognitions for balancing the budget, municipalities brought questions about property tax rates and real property tax differential rates.
Ridgely Commissioner Brad Sears asked the county commissioners what the extended outlook was for municipal tax differentials.
"Just in terms of looking forward from my town's perspective, I would like to get your overall sense of where this might be headed, if that's appropriate," Sears said.
In Caroline County's proposed budget, the property tax rate sits at 98 cents per $100 of assessed value. For towns incorporated within the county, tax rates can sit between one cents to six cents lower than the county's rate.
The differentials were put in place to keep resident of towns from being taxed twice for services provided to these residents by the municipality instead of the county.
"This is something that was in play when I came into office, and it's been a real subject that I battle with over the years," County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "What this means is it does not affect the town's budget, it affects the money the county collects in their county property tax rate.
"I will say tonight that this will be the last year I would support the property tax differential, I know its gonna be a very controversial subject... In this year's budget, we did not collect about $600,000 in the property tax differential. We're able to balance the budget this year. Going forward, I don't have a clue."
Porter advocated for eliminating the differentials in coming years, pointing to cost shifts from the state that he says will make it more difficult for the county to balance future budgets.
"We will not be able to forgo $600,000 revenue in the next year, I don't think we will," Porter said. "I see nothing but cost being shifted every year, the Blueprint number just keeps exponentially going up every year... I'm not sure where the road is going to take us."
The situation is similar to one being seen in Dorchester County this fiscal year.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
The Cambridge City Council has voiced opposition to the county's elimination of the differentials. In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
While Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding does not fully agree with Porter, he said he understands Porter's point.
"My position is a little different than Commissioner Porter. I believe that there are redundant services that are provided by the municipalities," Breeding said. "I know the formula that generated the tax differential was generated for police protection.
"....I don't know what the fiscal situation is going to be next year, we may find ourselves in the same dilemma that Dorchester county is in this year, I don't think we will…. I am still at the maintain point, but I certainly understand Commissioner Porter's position. That's where I'm at right now."

stories.title: Easton Introduces Proposed $28M Budget for FY26
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton introduces proposed $28M budget for FY26

 April 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 367
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Mayor Megan Cook said Easton's fiscal year 2026 budget focuses on transitioning the town out of an era of one-time funding sources and pandemic-related dollars."That period of growth positioned us well, but now we shift our focus to the responsibility of maintaining what we built," Cook said. "This year's budget is lean, focused on sustaining our progress by investing in the essentials."
At Monday's Town Council meeting, Cook presented a balanced draft budget with $28 million in general funds, nearly even with last year's mark. The capital fund budget came in just above $1 million.
Easton's property tax rate will remain the same as it has been since 2008 — 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. The town is projected to bring in around $13.6 million in real property taxes, according to the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, slightly up from last year.
"When you compare tax rates across the region, Easton stands out," Cook said. "We have the second lowest municipal property tax rate among surrounding towns, but we're also the largest community and provide the most comprehensive range of services."
The budget aims to equip town government departments with the necessary tools and training to do their jobs, Cook said. While "it's not exciting as building new things," she said, it's an important focus.
In the draft fiscal year 2026 budget, just above $1 million is allocated for transfer to capital work. That's down from the around $2.2 million mark in fiscal year 2025.
Cook added that areas of government improvement will include adding safety features to town hall, providing leadership training to Easton employees and hiring a new town manager. The town has been without a permanent employee in that role since last August.
Expenditure categories in the draft general fund budget include:
Public safety (police, fire, code enforcement, etc.): $11.5 million.
Public works: $7.1 million.
General government (financial administration, IT, HR, planning and zoning, executive functions, etc): $5.3 million.
Economic development: $503,000.
Recreation: $192,000.
"This year's budget reflects a shift: from growth driven by outside funding to careful maintenance, steady service and smart planning for what comes next," Cook said Monday.
A budget hearing is scheduled for the Town Council's next meeting on May 5. The budget can be accessed online at eastonmd.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=53.

stories.title: Caroline County Officials Discuss Fee Changes for Fiscal Year 2026
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Caroline County officials discuss fee changes for fiscal year 2026

 March 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett | Section: News 
 
 599
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed potentially raising some fees as the county looks for ways to close a $2 million deficit in its fiscal year 2026 budget.""We really wanted to get into the fee schedule today and highlight a couple items that the board has brought up in conversation through past meetings that they wanted to either look at that will possibly change," Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.
County officials presented the draft FY 2026 fee schedule at the meeting, highlighting some main focuses the commissioners wanted to discuss.
The Liquor Commissioners fees were looked at by the county commissioners. While majority of the licenses and fees for the board are set by state legislation, there are three line items the commissioners can adjust: the application fee, advertising cost and TIPS alcohol awareness certification class.
The commissioners focused on the application fee.
"The reason for bringing this up is really looking at the money that's being brought in from the liquor license," Fox said. "First, what the operation is costing us. So, we're budgeting to take in about $60,000, but last year, we spent about $99,000 to operate the the board. So there's about a $40,000 gap there that is being made up by the general fund."
The commissioners suggested raising the application fee from $175 to $500 to help the board break even.
Commissioners addressed similar concerns with Jonestown Water System.
The water system, which serves residents near Preston, hasn't increased its fees in over a decade, commissioners said at the meeting.
"We have to do surveys, outreach that are now required by MDE, and it's just just continuing to push that fund into a little bit of a bigger hole," Fox said. "…Based off the 52 users that are in the system and some quick math that we calculated on last year's operation, the fee would have to be about $476 to break even."
The current resident price to have a property connected to Jonestown Water System is $300.
"I think we have got to start coming up with some type of a gradual increase here," County Commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "We are going to at least start recovering some of this money because we cannot continue to operate the system on the same amount of money every year."
The commissioners suggested raising the price to $350 this budget term and removing the $150 unconnected charge.
The last fee the commissioners and officials discussed was the Office of Finance administrative.
"This is the fee that the county charges for the Office of Finance to conduct all tax collection or property tax collection for the municipalities," Fox said.
The adjustment of the fee is being presented to account for the larger towns that require more attention and interaction. The current cap is set at $15,000.
"This costing us money to provide. I don't want to gouge anybody, but if it's costing us a certain amount of money to process these bills, we already give a differential to the towns. We already provide significant services to the towns," Porter said. "… We are going to have to get away from this subsidizing services process here if we're going to go forward with balancing this budget."
The commissioners will phase the removing of the cap in to next years budget.
"I'm fine with with implementing this next year, but letting them know that the cap is going to be phased out and they are going to need to adjust their budgeting for to come of this cost," Porter said.
The commissioners will raise the cap to $22,500, and next year they will remove the cap completely.

stories.title: Mid-Shore Counties Advocating Against State Cost Shifts
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

stories.title: In Wake of Fatal Hit-and-Run, Route 50 Safety in Easton a Concern
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
In wake of fatal hit-and-run, Route 50 safety in Easton a concern

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 826
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Safety concerns for pedestrians and bikers using Route 50 in Easton are being raised after a fatal hit-and-run crash Saturday.Donald Dawson, a 68-year-old Easton resident, was killed riding a bike early Saturday morning in what police said was a hit-and-run crash with a box truck or tractor trailer. Police are still searching for the suspect vehicle.
The crash occurred at U.S. Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
On Monday, Town Council President Don Abbatiello implored residents to drive safely.
"We already have enough people who come through town speeding. We don't need to add to that," Abbatiello said.
The fatal crash occurred just north of the Immanuel Lutheran Church and across from Saints Peter & Paul High School. Slightly north of the crash location is an overhead sign instruction drivers of the traffic light ahead, reading: "urban area stay alert." The speed limit reduces to 45 mph as drivers funnel toward the Route 50 and Dutchmans Lane intersection.
Saturday's crash is the second fatal collision on that stretch of road this year. In February, a car struck and killed a 35-year-old man near Route 50 and Woodridge Drive.
In response to questions about Route 50 safety in Easton, State Highway Administration spokesman Danny Allman said pedestrian activity near Woodridge Drive "is not encouraged as there are no sidewalks nor shoulders" on that side of the highway.
"We always emphasize visibility for pedestrians and cyclists on any road," Allman wrote in an email statement Tuesday. "Pedestrians and cyclists should always wear reflective apparel, especially in areas with no separation or lighting."
Saturday's fatal crash is also raising the question of whether speed cameras should be placed along Route 50 in Easton. Abbatiello said the cameras are needed.
"I also am pleading with the state to consider adding speed cameras on Route 50," he said during Monday's meeting. "We are talking about adding two crosswalks, one at Dover, one at Goldsborough, hopefully within the next year. We're going to have people walking across Route 50. It needs to be safe for them to do so. And so I hope that the state will seriously consider a request for a speed camera on Route 50."
Easton has its own speed enforcement program to deter speeding in school zones. School zone signs with "photo enforced" written under them indicate where the cameras may be active.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said speed cameras on town streets and roads have been successful. There are cameras near the YMCA and The Country School, he said.
"I think that speed cameras help change behavior," Van Emburgh said.
While Saturday's crash didn't occur on a town-operated road, Easton engineers are in communication with their counterparts at the state level, he said.
Allman said SHA doesn't have "enabling legislation" to install speed cameras in non-work zones. Per state law, jurisdictions can install cameras in school zones and sometimes residential and other areas, he said.
For a camera to be placed on a state route, Allman said a jurisdiction would have to submit a request to SHA and receive a permit to place the camera.
Abbatiello said in an interview Tuesday that the next step for the town to consider requesting a speed camera permit for Route 50. The precedent is already set in Salisbury Abbatiello noted, pointing to speed cameras on the highway near Wicomico Middle School.
"It's a real issue in Easton," Abbatiello said of Route 50 safety.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey said on Wednesday that the police department is working with a speed camera vendor to assess safety on the highway. "There's a lot of work to be done" before officially submitting a speed camera request to SHA, Lowrey said. Work includes gathering crash data.
"The goal is safety, the goal's not revenue," Lowrey said. "That's how the state looks at it, too."
According to SHA, sidewalks and pedestrian crossings are in the works for two Route 50 intersections — Dover and Matthewstown Roads, or Routes 331 and 328, respectively. Construction will begin in early- to mid-2026, Allman said Tuesday.
For roads maintained by the town, a draft comprehensive "Complete Streets" study is expected to be presented to town officials in the coming weeks. It will outline target speed limits, assess the need for sidewalks or bike lanes and, overall, put "safety first," Van Emburgh said.
"It's gonna tell us what we want our roads to look like," he said.
Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit that advocates for pedestrian and bicycle safety, said in a statement on Monday that the town's Complete Streets study and similar safety efforts by Talbot County officials are important.
"These efforts need to be, at their core, about saving lives," the statement read.
Talbot Thrive's statement also addressed Saturday's fatal crash.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the vulnerability of those who travel by foot, bicycle, or wheelchair in our community — and of the urgent need to make Talbot County's roads safer and more connected for everyone, not just for those in cars," the statement read.
This story has been updated to include comment from Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey.

stories.title: Greensboro Faces $300,000 Sewer Line Repair Cost
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Greensboro faces $300,000 sewer line repair cost

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 372
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The aftermath of a sewer main pipe break will cost the town of Greensboro around $300,000 to fix, but the town plans to be reimbursed for the cost.At around 3:30 p.m. last week, the Town of Greensboro received a call about sewage water in the road on Route 313 and Bridgetown Road, town officials said.
Upon arrival, Greensboro Public Works found a sewer main pipe break on Bridgetown Road. Greensboro Town Manager Cindy Yost said the sewer line runs from Greensboro to Goldsboro. Friday evening, she said the town asked Goldsboro residents to use less water while repairs were underway.
After investigation, the town discovered that a subcontractor from Sure Shot Drilling was boring on the property. Yost said the subcontractor for Cherrywood Solar hit the main sewer pipe, then covered the pipe with plywood, put orange netting around the pipe and left the scene without contacting the town.
Now almost one week after the main pipe break, the town still continues work at the site to resolve the broken pipe 19 feet underground.
According to Yost the town called Spring and Associates, a horizontal directional drilling, to begin the process of fixing the pipe on Friday. The plans state that this particular pipe is 19 feet underground and while drilling down and getting to 17 feet, the road began to slide.
The town signed a contract with Spring and Associates on Saturday night. After the contract was signed Spring and Associates began to bring more equipment into Greensboro, but equipment delivery was delayed until Monday because of the wind storm this past weekend.
After more difficulties on Monday, Spring and Associates are still bringing in equipment from Virginia.
Yost said the town has two pump trucks operating around the clock at the Goldsboro pump station to prevent any issues for the town of Goldsboro.
Yost said that with the costs for contracting with Spring and Associates, Premier, the State Highway for guard rail removal, power companies for telephone pole removal, flaggers and their town staff, the repair will run up to $300,000.
The town is fronting the bill and has reached out to CherryWood solar contractors, NextEra to request they cover the cost, but has not yet received a response and plans to reach out to confirm.

stories.title: Next Phase of Oxford's Strand Beach Project Poses Funding Hurdle
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Next phase of Oxford's Strand Beach Project poses funding hurdle

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 262

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Phase one of the Strand Beach Project has been completed, but the prospect of phase two is daunting for the town and its residents.The first phase was turbulent. Residents, commissioners and town staff were frustrated with the duration, expense and results of the project.
Funding for phase one came from the state and Department of Natural Resources. Currently, there is no additional funding for future phases of the project.
Phase two will cover stormwater mitigation, an Americans with Disabilities Act access ramp over the dune and bulkhead improvements.
"We're looking at funding options with the state to mitigate the stormwater on the roadway as well as town internal funds, which it's going to be likely that we're going to have to look at that, especially with mitigating the stormwater on the roadway and that failing bulkhead," Wahl said.
Engineering work is underway to design stormwater mitigation, like removing standing water from the roadway, creating a swale through the parking lot to channel water away and improving the failing bulkhead.
The standing water between the beach access point and the parking lot, known through town as the "perma-puddle," can be seen on sunny days and grows even more after a storm.
In addition, there's no ADA compliant entrance to the beach area.
These have been hot topics at recent town commissioner meetings. Commissioner Dave Donovan said it has been on the agenda every meeting for the past two months.
Once plans for the second phase of the project are ready, the town will seek permits. Whal said commissioners are unlikely to approve another contract with Underwood & Associates.

stories.title: Superintendent and Commissioners Discuss Lockerman
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Superintendent and commissioners discuss Lockerman

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners and Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons discussed Lockerman Middle School at the County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday.At the last commissioners meeting, the commissioners discussed their role, responsibilities and preferred location for the new Lockerman Middle School.
The superintendent came to the commissioners meeting to discuss the approval of its fiscal year 2026 budget. After the discussion the commissioners talked about Lockerman Middle School and the next steps.
"I think it'd be good for us to say that we are working together on the Lockerman Middle School construction," Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We were asking questions about what role the commissioners officially play in siting and construction, they were just questions that we were asking. It wasn't like the Board of Ed's going to run all over us and make crazy stupid decisions and we're going to be stuck with it. It was just what influence do we have over the process."
Breeding explained the consensus the commissioners have come to on their personal choice for the new school location.
"I think we talked about it, and our consensus is that the most logical place to put it is probably next to North Carolina High School for us," Breeding said. "We understand that there's a whole process that has to be going through, fact finding, the Board of Ed will review that and make their decisions based off of that. But we were just saying that that questioning what influence we actually had over the process."
Simmons clarified they understand the commissioners wanting understanding of their role and told the commissioners how the process will go.
"Board of Education selects the site," Simmons said. "The feasibility study, which was presented to the board on July 1st, indicated North Carolina High School was the better of the two locations. We did review the two sites that we were asked to review that were basically the county-owned, which is cost efficient way to do it.
Simmons said the board received the feasibility study that night and should be making its decision on a site at the August meeting. He added the site selection does not include picking what the design of the building will be.
After looking over potential designs for the new Lockerman Middle School, Breeding suggested having athletic facilities have their own location and not sharing fields.
"One of the major things that stuck out with me was, relocating the athletic facilities around there," Breeding said. "If we can get dedicated facilities so we're not sharing space like we have been doing forever, where lacrosse or soccer is using the outfield of the softball and the baseball field, if we can actually get dedicated space, that would be a priority of mine."
He noted that facilities in surrounding counties should be studied.
"We've got one bite at the apple here, let's get it right," Breeding said.

stories.title: Contractor Bringing Oxford's Strand Project Up to Specifications
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Contractor bringing Oxford's Strand project up to specifications

 April 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 318
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Efforts to complete the first phase of the Strand Beach project are underway this week after it was determined the project was not finished to the specifications originally presented to the town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting March 25, Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said work to complete the project would begin the week of March 31.
In order to finish the first phase of the project, the contractor, Underwood and Associates, will lower the islands on the beach, remove temporary access to the islands, purchase and install native plantings and install a grassy strip along the roadway to prevent sand from flowing into the roadway, Wahl said. All of these items are to be completed to match the approved permit and site plan.
Wahl said Underwood and Associates is required to complete this phase of the project by April 19.
In December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced that although the Strand Beach project was signed off on in June by previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis, the project had not been completed to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The plan for the project was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands. During the commissioners meeting in December, Commissioner Katrina Greer said not all the grasses had been planted on the islands and the islands were two feet higher in elevation than they were supposed to be.
That month, Greer brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would bring down the elevation of the islands and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands at no cost to the town.

stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Residents eager as St. Michaels considers dog park locations

 September 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384

 ST. MICHAELS — A dog park in St. Michaels has been in discussion for almost four years. Now, with a special meeting planned, the town and commissioners are turning their attention to finding a location where the dog park can properly serve the community.The commissioners want to take into account multiple factors when decided the location of the dog park, including cost of building and maintenance, liability concerns, who is allowed to use the park, and limiting the amount of people affected by the noise and traffic.
While a date is still being chosen for the special meeting, some dog owners in town said they were excited that the town is looking to get the ball rolling.
"It's exciting," said Jonathan Dietrich, St. Michaels resident and owner of two dogs, as he was walking his dogs through town. "It's exciting as long as the location is right and everybody approves of it. I know it's been a very long journey, and it's pretty complicated, but it would be great. It would be great if we could get one but we'll see what happens."
When dog park discussion started in St. Michaels four years ago, a group of lawyers in St. Michaels came together and created a group called "The Friends of St. Michaels Dog Park."
Member Devon Hewitt spoke at the August town meeting about donors for the dog park and potential locations.
According to Hewitt the group of lawyers did research and came up with multiple locations, but the conversations fell through. After the new commissioners were elected, conversations began again.
While determining the master plan for San Domingo Creek Park construction at the August Town Council meeting, discussion arose about a dog park being included in the master plan. The town commissioners decided not to include a dog park in the plan.
One of the reasons brought forward at the meeting was that if dog park plans were added to the master plan, the grant received from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources could be pulled back.
While the location for the potential dog park is unclear, St. Michaels residents say they are ready to see movement.
When Stacy Sass, a resident of St. Michaels, was asked how soon she would hope to see a dog park in St. Michaels for her dog Ginger to play in, she said, "tomorrow."

stories.title: Talbot County Approves Senior Task Force
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot County approves senior task force

 August 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 329
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed a resolution to create a Senior Citizens Task Force amid calls to address a rise in senior homelessness.Council OK'd the task force 5-0 at its meeting Tuesday after hearing from senior care and housing experts at a work session last month. Council member Lynn Mielke originally brought forth the resolution earlier this summer.
Mielke said she's pleased the task force was established and looks forward to serving on the body. Council Vice President Pete Lesher thanked Mielke for leading the effort.
"I look forward to working with the folks that we'll be calling together for that," Lesher said.
The task force will make recommendations to the County Council on housing, health care, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
It will consist of representatives from the following entities, among others: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council.
At the July 29 work session, Talbot Interfaith Executive Director Julie Lowe cited an increase in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is growing.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range, Lowe said.
Other nonprofit and health care leaders advocated for the task force's creation at that meeting. They said it's especially needed to help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," said Rachel Smith, chair of the county's Commission on Aging. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."

stories.title: A New YMCA in Caroline County? Talks Are Starting on the Topic
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
A new YMCA in Caroline County? Talks are starting on the topic

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 433
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — The Caroline County Commissioners are moving to discuss building a new YMCA in Caroline County."I just make a comment, the YMCA, there's been a lot of discussion about the YMCA building a facility in Caroline County, and I think we need to start having a serious discussion with them about why they haven't," commission Vice President Larry Porter said. "I mean, they've built them all around us, and I think it's time to have have that discussion with Robbie Gill."
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman responded saying that she had talked to Gill, the CEO of the YMCA of the Chesapeake, the day before the meeting.
Freeman said that she and Gill discussed restarting conversations about bringing a new YMCA to Caroline County and they will continue to have discussions to make sure that it happens.
On Friday, Gill told the Star Democrat that the YMCA of Chesapeake has always had "a desire to build a full facility YMCA in Caroline County," conversations sizzled out after COVID-19 hit in 2020.
"Since then we've been blessed and fortunate enough to have opened new facilities in St. Michaels, Centerville and Chestertown," Gill said. "Even with all those wonderful things that have happened and tens of thousands of people that have benefited from it, Caroline County has still been a priority for us. We just haven't quite been able to put the pieces to the puzzle together, and so I'm excited that Kathleen and the commissioners have an interest in beginning those conversations again."
The current YMCA facility is an 11,000-square-foot storefront facility that is in Denton just off of state Route 404 in a shopping center. While the facility provides service to Caroline County residents a new facility would potentially look something like the new facilities built around the Mid-Shore.
"if you look at the YMCA that just opened at Centerville, it's a 70,000-square-foot facility serving a little over 7,000 people," Gill said. "...They're really built specifically to meet specific community needs."
The new facilities around the Mid-Shore have congregate meals daily for older residents in the community. To service the elderly, the YMCA partners with multiple groups around the community.
The new facilities include a six-lane pool with a shallow depth entry, allowing chances for swim classes for kids and adults. Another feature included is a double gymnasium with an indoor walking track, giving residents options for physical activity on cold and hot days.
Two other features includes multiple program open spaces and after-school care programs that will be beneficial for Caroline County Public Schools.
While their is no timeline on a new YMCA, Gill is happy that conversations have started again.

stories.title: Groundbreaking of Millington Senior Village attended by Secretary Day
stories.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
stories.content:
Groundbreaking of Millington Senior Village attended by Secretary Day

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 MILLINGTON — "I am proud of what we achieved and am looking forward to this project coming to life and bearing fruit," Millington Mayor Kevin Hemstock told an audience of stakeholders and community leaders on Dec. 3, about the new senior housing center being built. The new facility will be located at 172 Sassafras Street — the site of the former Millington Elementary School.He along with Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) Secretary Jake Day, Chair of Home Partnership Inc. Phil Wohlfort and Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, John Price and Albert Nickerson, tossed out the first shovelfuls of dirt.
"As we break ground today, it's not just the beginning of a building project, I think this is going to be important for a lot of people in Millington," Hemstock said.
Earlier, inside the building of the school, in a spacious room with walls that still had paintings of emblematic characters from childhood, Clifford the Big Red Dog, The Wizard of Oz, Winnie the Pooh and Bambi, Hemstock pointed out the irony that the senior center will be built there.
"This is a magical moment," Hemstock said, adding that 100 years ago the location was a farm. Then in 1974 the school was built. He said it is interesting to think the first students at the school may benefit in the near-future from what is being built.
2005 was the first mention of a senior housing center in the Town.
Since then, the concept has grown significantly, he stated, plans altering from building a senior center across the street to this location.
Jamie Williams, director of Kent County Economic and Tourism Development traced the history of the property after the school closed in 2017.
The property officially transitioned to the County in May of 2019, she said, then the approximate 24 acres and 36,000 sq ft. building and property were purchased by the Town of Millington in 2022 for $1.
Williams, who told the audience the project speaks to the power of community, collaboration and vision, highlighted the partnerships involved.
The Upper Shore Regional Council provided $50,000 for a preliminary architectural feasibility report.
The Rural Maryland council approved $100,000 for design and engineering cost of the roof and fire suppression system.
The Town of Millington invested $1.4 million for repairs, maintenance, utility cost, staff time, permit fees and submitted a $500,000 community legacy grant application to the DHCD for the construction of the roof and fire suppression system.
Home Partnership Inc. committed over $630,000 towards reconstructing 2200 square ft. for senior-focused spaces.
With all that effort, Williams acknowledged, challenges still remain, estimating the overall cost is projected to be $1.5 million.
She recognized that also includes creating walking trails, a community garden, and creating other enriching open spaces. That takes partnerships, to "build a brighter future for Kent County," she expressed.
After introductions, Secretary Day spoke, expressing the need for this center in an aging population.
"Housing is critical, particularly when we have failed to build housing from 2018 until now," Day said.
Housing costs are high and not likely to decline, he added.
With supply chain interest and expensive labor costs, as all the developers, builders and government officials could attest to, it can be challenging, Day noted.
Day emphasized that with local government all-in, and the developers and community all-in, he knows that Governor Wes Moore would want the DHCD to be all-in, as well.
"We're not at the finish line yet but we are 100% committed," Day reiterated.

stories.title: Cambridge Hears Presentations About Youth Services, Day Shelter
stories.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Cambridge hears presentations about youth services, day shelter

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Commissioners heard two presentations at a Cambridge City Council meeting on Monday evening.The first was from a Baltimore-based nonprofit, Lead4Life, about a possible partnership with the city. The second was about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge.Jennifer Gauthier, founder and executive director of Lead4Life, spoke about the services which the nonprofit offers and inquired about partnering with the city."Allow us to hire people who can go into the community," Gauthier said. "Allow us to have that peer-to-peer model to be able to spend some of the resources that we have on these two initiatives in your community." Founded in 2008, Lead-4Life aims to lower the number of youth entering the juvenile justice system.According to its website, the nonprofit offers 10 different programs, including alternative placement programming, mentoring and individual and family therapy.At the Council meeting, Gauthier talked about two pilot programs, a gun diversion program and a returning citizens program, which it wants to offer in Cambridge.Gauthier said Lead4Life has the funding to provide these services in Cambridge and "all the way down to the Lower Shore." "We just want to hear any concerns that you have or any opportunity for us that you want to be able to partner (with us)," she said."We're not asking you for money." After Gauthier spoke, Commissioner Sputty Cephas said that he thinks it would be great to partner with Lead4Life and try to expand the program in Cambridge."From everything that I've heard so far, we need you here," he said. "Any way that we can continue to funnel this information and get the word out there about all that you guys are doing, I would love to." Valerie Nwakudo Davis, with Delmarva Community Services, spoke to the Council next about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge."This presentation is not for any agency," she said."It really is on behalf of our homeless population in this city, in this county." Davis said that there is a growing population of homeless people and talked about the importance of having a shelter for people to go to, particularly the aging homeless population."We cannot afford, as a community, to have people sitting on benches when it's 22 degrees outside, or when it's 92 degrees outside," she said.Davis said that although The Salvation Army provides shelter at night, those people in need of service don't have somewhere to go in the day. She said this problem is most apparent on the weekends."Sunday is the most miserable time of the week when you're homeless," she said, adding that places like the library and One Mission Cambridge are closed then.Delmarva Community Services hosted a meeting last week, Davis said. The Overflow Cafe, One Mission Cambridge and The Salvation Army were at the meeting."We talked about what was here already and what we need," she said.To get a day shelter in Cambridge, Davis said support from the local government is needed. She also said support from churches is needed."Because that could be an awesome volunteer segment of this," she said.After Davis spoke, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he had spoken with Davis about this a few weeks ago."I thought it was very important," he said. "It was something that we have not really paid attention to enough. So we're having an ongoing series of meetings with the churches and citizens and agencies to see what we might be able to do here to address this particular issue." 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Jennifer Gauthier, founder and executive director of Lead-4Life, speaks to the Cambridge City Council about a possible partnership during a Council meeting Nov. 13.

Proposed solar bill discussed by Caroline commissioners

 August 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 DENTON — Throughout the past two years, solar energy has been a major topic of discussion on the Eastern Shore.The conversation was raised again at the Caroline County Commissioners' bi-weekly meeting Tuesday, where the commissioners dissected a proposed legislative bill on solar.
The solar energy ordnance would bring the county in compliance with state law. The bill focuses on maintaining accessory solar, which is residential solar that is generating power for a property's electrical use.
After discussing several definitions they wanted to revise, the commissioners raised concerns about donating money to the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation. The commissioners have no problem with donating to agricultural land preservation, they said, but they want to make sure the money is going back to farms in Caroline County.
The county contributes $20,000 per year to the land preservation foundation. On top of that, commissioners said, when solar projects come into Caroline County on agricultural land, the solar company has to pay an agricultural transfer fee, which the county also donates to MALPF.
Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter's concern is if the state funding was cut on MALPF would the county still receive financial help to preserve agricultural land.
"If we collect money in Caroline County, I want it to be used to preserve farmland in Caroline County," Porter said.
No official decision was made on donation of the funds, and the county will continue to discuss options at future meetings, the commissioners said.
The county officials will discuss some changes to the proposed bill and move the bill to an official legislative bill with the purpose of having the first reading at the next county commissioners meeting.

stories.title: Eastern Shore Legislators Push for Gov. Moore to Veto Solar Bill
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Eastern Shore legislators, House Republicans and agricultural advocacy groups in Maryland are making one last effort to nix controversial solar energy legislation by asking for a veto from Gov. Wes Moore.Senate Bill 931, the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, was passed by the General Assembly in April. It aims to increase the state's solar generation by streamlining the regulatory process for solar projects. Fencing, setback and vegetation requirements would be standardized.
House Republicans and the Eastern Shore Delegation both wrote letters to the governor urging him to veto the bill. While Moore (D) hasn't publicly signaled whether or not he's considering a veto, some believe it could be in play given he hasn't yet signed the legislation.
"I've heard it is possible," said Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) in an interview Wednesday. "I'm hopeful that he would see the opportunity and the wisdom and just say, 'No, not yet.'"
Qualms with the solar legislation largely relate to a reduction in the control local governments would have over solar project approvals, and the increase in Public Service Commission authority.
The legislation outlines a cap on how much land the Maryland Public Service Commission can grant to solar projects in each county — 5% of land designated for agriculture and forests.
Republicans attempted but failed during session to lower that cap.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said Thursday that Eastern Shore counties could have thousands of acres up for solar development even with the 5% cap.
At a legislative wrap-up discussion in Easton Wednesday, Mautz said solar interests came into Annapolis and "cleared the decks."
"They wanted to set up their own regulatory system, they wanted to set up their own siting system," he said. "And they wanted to run this through the Public Service Commission."
"It puts an X on the Eastern Shore," Mautz added. "We are the prime target for solar investment."
The Chesapeake Climate Action Network, an environmental nonprofit that's one of the bill's many advocate groups, encouraged supporters to contact Moore's office and lobby for no veto. Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, said rumors of a veto were floating.
"The rumor mill was churning, and no one had a concrete answer here or there," Baker said.
Baker said in addition to streamlining processes that otherwise vary greatly across the state, the bill is set to codify best practices. And it could help local farmers who are looking to remain economically viable, she said.
"It provides another way for people to be able to stay on their farms and make revenue," Baker said.
PUSH TO VETO
The governor's office didn't comment specifically on whether Moore is considering a veto, but did provide a statement.
"As Governor Moore reviews the hundreds of bills put forward this session, he will continue to work with the State Legislature, local leaders, and all partners involved to ensure that we are signing legislation that will make Maryland safer, more affordable, more competitive, and the state that serves," the statement read.
Baker said despite rumors, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network believes Senate Bill 931 will become law.
"We're pretty sure at this point that the governor will not be vetoing this bill," she said.
Mautz acknowledged a veto is a tricky, party-line situation. He said it would be messy, but "less messy" than what happens down the line if the bill becomes law.
"For the governor to veto it, he's going to cross his own party," Mautz said. "He's going to cross some of his own advocates. It's going to be extremely controversial."
Adams acknowledged that vetoes are rare. But he said the bill not yet being signed may signal "at the minimum, that the governor's paying attention."
If Moore doesn't sign the Renewable Energy Certainty Act by May 27, it automatically becomes law. The governor's next slate of bill signings is scheduled for May 20.

 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford approved an ordinance to amend the town's floodplain management ordinance. The changes would loosen requirements for residents seeking to make significant improvements to buildings.Commission President Norm Bell opened the public hearing for Ordinance 2416 and shared additional information on the changes made.
Previously for buildings in Oxford, owners were required to track and calculate the costs of any construction made since July 1, 2013 prior to making changes to the structures.
If all those improvement costs equal or exceed 50% of the market value of a building prior to the start of the construction, it would require the building to be up to code and raised in elevation.
The amended ordinance revises the definition of "substantial improvement," removing the 2013 date and substituting "the previous five (5) years."
Bell said the revision allows for a lean way for owners to make improvements on their buildings.
"What this is saying is we're only going to go back five years, or 1,825 days," Bell said. "So it's shortening the period that you can take a look at the 50% requirement. It's liberalizing it."
An additional change in the ordinance was the revision of the "agreement to submit an elevation certificate."
An elevation certificate is a form on which applicants for a permit to construct a building or structure show compliance with floodplain management legislation.
Previously people looking to make substantial improvements to buildings would need to submit an elevation certificate with a building permit application upon the construction of the foundation and prior to further vertical construction; and prior to the final inspection and moving in.
The revision removes the requirement of submitting the form prior to placement of the foundation and further vertical construction.
According to Bell, the changes would make it cheaper for owners to have engineers/surveyors certify that the floor of buildings seeking improvements is above the mean high water mark and it lowers costs of the certification by a "couple of hundred dollars."
After answering clarifying questions from the public, commissioners unanimously approved the ordinance.

stories.title: Talbot County Looks into Restrictions on Food Processing Residuals
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Talbot County looks into restrictions on food processing residuals

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals are in the works for Talbot County.The county's Planning Commission and County Council held a preliminary work session Tuesday to discuss regulations for the residuals, which are animal waste from the food processing process.
Earlier this month, Caroline County passed a bill to restrict the storage of the residuals, which are often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in storage tanks.
Talbot County is looking to the neighboring county and hoping to be proactive.
"We think we need to get ahead of it," Planning Commission Vice Chairman Chip Councell said. He noted that Caroline and Wicomico counties were "behind the eight ball" in enacting legislation.
Councell said he met with the Talbot County Farm Bureau regarding potential restrictions.
"I think they would like to see some restrictions put on it, one being that any type of food residuals storage would have to be enclosed, so it couldn't be open-air," Councell said. "The storage of it would have to be used in that agricultural operation. A farmer couldn't store it for everybody in the neighborhood. He could store it for his operation only, so there wouldn't be commercial storage."
Councell clarified the county would focus on the storage of the residuals, not the land application. State legislation that went into effect July 1 created a formal permitting process for the usage of food processing residuals.
"There's a few bad actors out there that, frankly, I think see profit potential with handling the material," said Alan Girard, advocacy director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, during Tuesday's meeting.
While Wicomico County banned the storage of residuals, temporary storage for 45 days is allowed. In Caroline County, storage is allowed once a permit is acquired, as long as the storage tank has a closed top.
Councell said the 45-day allowance may be adjusted once the legislation begins to be drafted.
"I think 45 days might be a little bit tight," Councell said.
At the end of the work session, Planning and Zoning Director Brennan Tarleton said discussion of potential DAF legislation will be added to the Planning Commission's agenda in November.

stories.title: Solar Energy Discussed at MACo Summer Conference
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Solar energy discussed at MACo Summer Conference

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 543
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Solar energy was one topic of discussion that captured the attention of multiple Mid-Shore counties at the Maryland Association of Counties Summer Conference.Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said solar energy came up a lot at the four-day conference, which went from Aug. 14 to Aug. 17 in Ocean City. Breeding said there are elected officials from different Maryland counties who feel that solar lobbyists are pushing the state to take away local authority when it comes to where solar energy system sites can go and how close those sites can be from roads and neighboring structures.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre cap on solar projects. Once that limit is reached, the county will stop permitting new solar energy system projects on county land, Breeding said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said his fellow council member Ricky Travers asked about solar site acreage caps in a MACo session with the Maryland Public Service Commission. Specifically, Travers asked about how the commission feels about these caps.
Pfeffer said that after the session, the Dorchester County Council members had a conversation with Public Service Commissioner Kumar Barve, and the council was able to explain its concerns about increasing solar sites in the county. Pfeffer said the only part of the county that can host these sites is the north part of the county, and that is where the council hopes to grow the county's tax base.
"They were very interested and didn't realize some of the demographics and logistics of Dorchester County," Pfeffer said about the Public Service Commission. "So I'm hoping that is successful for us, they'll take a look at it and they won't establish any legislation that's one-size-fits-all."
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher called the conference one of the best he's been to. He said it ran smoothly and was well put together.
Breeding said that MACo's summer and winter conferences give Maryland counties an opportunity to get together, discuss and "try to come up with a unified message."
"It was a good conference," Breeding said. "We got to talk to all of our partners in other counties, bounce ideas off of them, discuss problems and issues that we're all facing and kind of brainstorm on how to resolve those issues."
Pfeffer, who is the secretary of MACo this year, said that all counties have problems.
Pfeffer said the opportunity to discuss these common problems, no matter how many zeros come after them, can benefit each county.
Breeding said he is taking some ideas on solar power back home to Caroline County this year. He talked about the systems that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties have in place, including Talbot County's point system that is used to help preserve prime farmland for farming and determine where solar sites can go.
Lesher said he didn't attend the solar session at MACo, but said the Talbot County Council tackled legislation dealing with solar energy sites last year when it put the point system in place.
"Which I think is model legislation for other rural jurisdictions," he said. "Right now we're in the testing period for this. Will this hold up? Will this have the desired impact of preserving farmland and channeling solar toward areas where we have more marginal soils that are not the highest priority for cropland?"

stories.title: Public Weighs in on Emergency Food Processing Residual Bill
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Public weighs in on emergency food processing residual bill

 August 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An earlier version of this story contained incorrect information about the status of the bill. The commissioners did not vote on the bill Tuesday.DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held a public hearing on a controversial bill concerning the permitting of food processing residuals Aug. 6.
If the bill is passed after the commissioners' third hearing on Aug. 20, storing these residuals in Caroline County would require a permit. The bill also allows for inspection and civil or criminal penalties if a storage site is found to be in violation.
"This is not banning storage of food processing residuals," Commissioner Larry Porter said. "If someone feels strongly about using it as a soil amendment and wants to store it, they can come in and apply once these regulations are set."
The bill requires the use of closed-top storage tanks for food processing residuals, going a step further than state regulations passed during this year's General Assembly. House Bill 991, which took effect July 1, created a state permitting process under the Maryland Department of Agriculture for the use, storing and hauling of the residuals.
Caroline County's bill is the latest development in what has been months of packed public hearings and extended moratoriums on residual storage tanks. For county commissioners, the main hurdle has been cracking down on a few "bad actors" that store the residuals irresponsibly.
The bill garnered mixed reviews from Caroline County residents, environmental experts and representatives of the poultry industry at prior public hearings. Several took to the podium Aug. 6 to voice their opposition or support of the legislation.
Mike Woodward, the owner of a Ridgely farm right next to an open-top residual storage facility, voiced support for the bill.
"I am 400 yards from the tank itself... We have a lot of issues with flies. The odor is atrocious at times," Woodward said. "We had a vet come out. We were having trouble with our horses. Their eyes were watering and runny and nasty. We couldn't figure out what was going on with them. The vet checked them out and the flies were laying larvae inside their eyes."
Brad Sears, a Ridgely commissioner, said, "I come before you on behalf of the Town of Ridgely in support of the emergency legislative bill. I offer this testimony to advocate for the men, women and children, who live, work and attend school and play within the town limits. We have concern because of improper storage of FPR (food processing residuals) poses well documented threats to human life, health and wellbeing."
He said open-top containers do nothing to limit "odors, the exposure to vectors, the airborne bacteria and viruses."
Holly Porter, executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, has been a vocal opponent of the county's bill in prior public hearings. She spoke again in opposition of the legislation on Tuesday.
"I really and truly would like the commissioners to consider some way of grandfathering in the farmers who are utilizing and storing food processing residuals for years without the complaints we have had in the past," she said. "If we do not do that, we are impacting other farmers who are becoming collateral damage because of one unfortunately bad actor."
Responding to Holly Porter's comments, Larry Porter said, "Grandfathering in, unfortunately would have to include grandfathering in what Miss. Porter referred to as the 'bad actor.' ... you can't enforce laws on some people and not all people."

stories.title: Solar Energy Discussed at Dorchester County Council Meeting
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Solar energy discussed at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Solar energy systems were discussed more than once at a Dorchester County Council meeting on Feb. 6.During the meeting, the Council introduced legislation that would amend a part of the Dorchester County Code that deals with utility-scale solar energy systems.
Specifically, the legislation would put a cap on how many aggregate acres in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems. The legislation would also make it so that a 75-foot-wide alive and maintained vegetated buffer must surround the solar energy systems.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he thinks this legislation is not a move for or against solar, but a move against "bad solar."
"You know, when you go driving in your car, you hope you don't need a seatbelt, but you always put it on," he said. "We need that seatbelt there for (this)."
If this legislation is passed, up to 1,800 acres of land in the agricultural conservation zoning districts of the county could be used for utility-scale solar energy systems. County Planning and Zoning Director Susan Webb said that currently, 1,574 acres are developed or being developed for these systems.
Webb said making sure the vegetated buffer is maintained and alive will be key.
"A 75-foot buffer that's alive, it's going to do its job as compared to a 100 or 200-foot (buffer) that's dead," she said. "So we just have to make sure that we're staying on it. And we will."
Webb said the requirement of a fence around these types of properties and adequate fire suppression devices on site are also in the proposed legislation. She said that any solar energy system that has not operated for a continuous period of 12 months would be considered unused and abandoned.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer asked Webb if this kind of legislation is something surrounding jurisdictions have tried to do.
Webb said it is very typical for jurisdictions to have a cap on aggregate acreage of solar energy systems. She said she understands the state has been looking into banning these caps.
"Right now, there's nothing in place," she said. "We're doing exactly like our neighbors."
PROPERTY TAX EXEMPTION
Also at the Feb. 6 meeting, Pfeffer brought up a bill that has been introduced in the Maryland Senate and Maryland House of Delegates.
The legislation, Senate Bill 783 and House Bill 1435, would make it so that nonresidential solar energy systems constructed on rooftops or parking facility canopies don't have to pay property taxes.
Personal property taxes would also be exempt for community solar energy systems that provide at least half of its energy to low or moderate-income customers at a lower cost than electric companies in the area, and are installed on a rooftop, brownfield, parking facility canopy, landfill or clean fill.
The legislation would also make it so that counties would receive $2,500 per megawatt when entering into an agreement with a solar facility owner to exempt real or personal property taxes for ground-mounted solar energy systems. This means that counties would no longer be able to negotiate individual payment in lieu of taxes, or pilot, agreements with solar developers.
Detmer said he disagrees with this legislation because he thinks the county should be able to negotiate pilot agreements.
"This is them taking away some of the scant leverage that we have," he said.
Pfeffer brought up that the negotiations the county has had with solar developers have, in some ways, set a standard.
"The pilots that we've done so far, we've set a standard, basically, on the amount of money on the megawatt-age," he said. "That's what everyone coming to us generally expects that we'll negotiate. ... So haven't we almost already set a price by doing that?"
County Attorney Chip MacLeod said he thinks every pilot agreement the county negotiates can be different.
MacLeod said he thinks this proposed legislation would result in less local control.
"I've personally been involved in many pilot agreements in various counties," he said. "And it is really one of the few (opportunities) that you get to sit face to face with these solar developers and say, 'This is what's important in my county.'"
Detmer said this isn't about banning solar.
"It's just we're trying to have some modicum of control over bad solar," he said.
Detmer said this makes the county's proposed solar legislation even more relevant.
"It just raises the stakes of us doing it now and doing it right," he said.
