stories.title: Talbot Council Discusses a Senior Citizens Task Force
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot Council discusses a senior citizens task force

 July 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council is set to consider creating a senior citizens task force to address the needs of the county's older residents, including those without stable housing.Council member Lynn Mielke asked for the council to approve the task force by way of a resolution last week, but council members largely preferred holding off until a work session is held.
"We do have a growing problem with homeless senior citizens," Mielke said at the July 1 council meeting. "They are in need of services, particularly in the Easton area but throughout the county."
Council President Chuck Callahan said he liked the idea.
"But the first thing that came to my mind was, do we get these groups and we have a work session and kind of get a game plan," he said.
The council introduced Mielke's resolution but did not approve it, opting instead to hold the work session with local senior care leaders.
As Talbot County's average age grows, nonprofit organizations like Upper Shore Aging and groups like the health department's senior care program aim to address senior housing and health needs. The county has a Commission on Aging which meets monthly; Mielke is the council's liaison to that commission.
According to census data, people 65 and older account for 30% of Talbot County's total population. The county's average age was 50.9 in 2023 and has slightly increased each year since 2020. The national average is just under 39 years old.
The task force, if created, would provide recommendations to the County Council on how to implement services for homeless senior citizens in the county.
Mielke said after talking to leaders at Upper Shore Aging, the Talbot Interfaith Shelter and the aging commission, it's clear homelessness is a problem for seniors. She said the groups are aware of 52 seniors in the area dealing with homelessness.
"I think it's extremely important that we form this task force and move forward to address those special needs," Mielke said.
Council member Keasha Haythe said a work session could be a "starting point" so the entire council can gather information and data from senior care experts.
Mielke reluctantly agreed to a work session but said it'd be "redundant."
"So because, I guess, they're senior citizens, you're putting another level of delay by having a work session rather than moving forward with the task force," Mielke said. "I hear you."
All five council members introduced the resolution, though a vote to approve was not held at the meeting. As currently written, the task force would include: a Commission on Aging member; a board member each from Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center; a person working in Talbot County Health Department's senior care program; an Easton Town Council member; and a Talbot County Council member.
A work session to discuss the potential senior citizens task force has not yet been scheduled.

stories.title: Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In her 15 years at the Neighborhood Service Center, Marilyn Neal has never faced a financial obstacle like the one the nonprofit is up against now.A delayed grant reimbursement is leaving the organization $300,000 in the hole. The center's leaders say the financial uncertainty has caused panic, sleepless nights and fear.
"Fear that we close the doors and our staff can't work," Neal said, "fear that we can't give food to a family."
Located on Port Street, the Neighborhood Service Center is a go-to for low-income residents, seniors and families. It lends emergency financial support on electric and rent bills. Staff run a daily food pantry and mobile food pantry. The nonprofit provides case managers to work directly with the county's most vulnerable populations.
The center is designated as Talbot County's community action agency, meaning its most consistent federal funding comes from a Community Services Block Grant.
That grant is administered by the federal Administration for Children & Families, a division of Health and Human Services, along with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development at the state level.
Neighborhood Service Center leaders say they've been working around that "fully executed grant," which hasn't been reimbursed yet. They expected to start receiving funds for this year's first two quarters by the end of December. That didn't happen.
In a statement Friday, the Department of Housing and Community Development said it received payment from the federal government this week for its first and second quarter block grants. First quarter funds were delayed, and payments to local agencies are in the process of approval. Second quarter funds will be on time, DHCD stated.
In the meantime, the service center says the holdup is leaving it $302,000 short, forcing it to pull from contingency funds.
Sitting across from one another late Thursday morning, Neal and fiscal officer Kathy Taylor discussed which cost-saving strategies are being implemented and the additional belt-tightening that might be on the way.
The nonprofit's 13-member staff is already trimming its hours. Full-time staff are down from 40-hour to 32-hour weeks, and part-time stuff have cut back from five to two days a week.
There's been discussion around how the nonprofit would operate with only three staff members and whether after-school offerings or programs for formerly incarcerated fathers have to shut down.
"Everything we do stabilizes a household," Neal said. "And when we don't have those funds and we don't have the Neighborhood Service Center in Talbot County, I don't know what this county looks like."
ASKING FOR HELP
Earlier this week, Neal, Taylor and many staff members attended a Talbot County Council meeting to request $150,000 in county assistance to fill the gaps presented by the reimbursement delay.
"The money's tightening down now," County Manager Clay Stamp said. "But the need is not tightening down. They run everything on a shoestring."
Council members were largely supportive of the center's work, but they remained steadfast in keeping fiscal responsibility at top of mind. Council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke preferred the council hold off on any promises until it came to understand how town governments may be helping the center financially.
Haythe asked if the center has a long-term sustainability plan or money in savings. Neal said the center operates by drawing on its available funds to help families in poverty at any given moment, making it hard to save a specific amount.
"We're scaling back," Council President Chuck Callahan, who also serves as chairman of the service center's board, said at the meeting. " … I think we also need a plan for the future on how we stabilize the Neighborhood Service Center."
The council partially fulfilled Neal's request, giving the center $50,000, which won't put the county's budget in any danger, Stamp noted.
Despite the shortened hours and growing uncertainty, Neighborhood Service Center staff have remained dedicated to their work.
To Neal, it all starts with the staff members and how their compassion spreads into the community. Taylor feels that now more than ever.
"We struggle with that balance of, 'OK should we leave?'" Taylor said. "But we don't want to because we love what we do and the impact on the community that we have."
To learn more, visit https://nsctalbotmd.org/.

stories.title: Eastern Shore Renters Face Challenges With Affordable Housing
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Eastern Shore renters face challenges with affordable housing

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1987
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Bradford House Apartments resident Linda Johnson doesn't carry mace on her keychain anymore.She doesn't feel the need to use a key or a cell phone instead of her finger to tap the buttons of the apartment's elevator.
After years of asking apartment management to address resident safety concerns, from mold and bug infestations to a lack of security, Johnson and other Bradford House residents finally feel safe.
"I feel better every day," said Johnson, who has lived at Bradford House on Race Street in Cambridge for nearly 25 years. "I'm not angry no more."
The complex — which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs — came under new management with a new principal owner in the fall, and residents started to see changes they had requested for years be made.
But as housing problems across the Eastern Shore persist, others have not been as lucky.
A SHORE PROBLEM
With a lack of affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and a need for better enforcement over housing standards, renters living in poor conditions often feel stuck.
In the eyes of Larry Rooths, the head of the Public Safety and Intelligence Committee for the Eastern Shore branch of the Caucus of African American Leaders, the lack of affordable housing is a national issue.
"But it seems a lot worse down here because there's so little housing," he said, "and there's no infrastructure in place for emergency services, emergency shelters."
Rooths said he's noticed landlords don't feel like they have to do much for tenants because there aren't many other places those tenants can go.
"And then the residents feel like that also," he said. "They don't want to stir up too much trouble because they know if somebody comes in and shuts the building down, where are they going?"
Rooths sees a need for housing legislation with more enforcement power so landlords address the issues residents face. He said the Shore also needs more housing infrastructure.
"If you create a situation where there's enough housing, then the landlords lose control," he said. "...If you don't like the place you're living in, you get up and move. But if there's no place to move or you can't move to another apartment building close to where you work, then it gets difficult."
The caucus is working to get tenants to form groups, which Rooths said would help them know their rights and push elected officials to make change.
"Unless there's some change in legislation or there's some increased funding to create a bigger pool of housing, this problem is going to be the same," he said.
In October, the Tenant Safety Act of 2024 went into effect in Maryland. The act, which places responsibility on landlords to provide safe dwelling for tenants, guarantees tenants can form groups.
Shore Legal Access Executive Director Meredith Girard considers Bradford House's tenant association a critical piece of its success in getting new management.
"I think the tenant association was critical to really letting the management and the court know what the issues were and how widespread it was," Girard said. "And that prompted some really important changes so that now the building is managed by a new company."
Girard said rural counties don't always have enough resources to support a rental inspection and licensing system. She said it would be great if counties on the Eastern Shore could pool their resources to form a regional housing commission.
"Where you could set some basic standards for habitability to make sure that if you're renting a unit, that the oven works, that the heat works, that the plumbing works, that the roof isn't leaking," she said.
Girard acknowledged rural landlords may also be strapped for resources. She said in some cases, landlords might not have the resources to make needed repairs.
"Which then becomes this really problematic cycle," she said.
At Bradford House, previous management said the property had been neglected before they took over in 2022.
In an April 2024 statement to The Star Democrat, Millennia Housing Management, the previous management at the complex, said it had invested more than $300,000 into the maintenance and enhancement of the "severely distressed property."
Girard said that when problems in complexes are fixed, tenants are often scared to complain about the conditions because they don't have anywhere else to go.
"And they don't want to upset their landlords," she said. "But at the same time, they need landlords to fix the things that need to be fixed."
Maryland Legal Aid Advocacy Director for the Human Right to Housing Zafar Shah said further protections against evictions are needed so tenants aren't reluctant to use the Tenant Safety Act of 2024. He said the Maryland legislature is considering a good cause eviction bill "that would protect tenants from lease non-renewal without a good reason."
"This is the big priority for renters in Maryland," he said.
NO WHERE TO GO
De'Auntte Clark came to Cambridge for peace.
In 2016, her 14-year-old son was killed after being hit by a car in Anne Arundel County. Four years later, her husband died from COVID-19.
In September 2022, Clark brought her family to the Eastern Shore for a fresh start. But since moving here, Clark has found anything but the peace she was seeking.
"I'm so numb, I can't cry," she said.
With concerns about the safety of her apartment at Calvin Mowbray Park and Stephen Camper Park in Cambridge and nowhere else to go, Clark spent more than a month living out of a van with her family.
A few days after her family moved into the complex, Clark noticed what seemed like mold in the cabinets along one of the walls in the kitchen.
Maintenance came to clean the cabinets out, but as the weather outside got colder and she turned the heat on, Clark said she started to see black spots pop up on the walls.
In December 2023, Clark's son, Keith Dezurn — who has a medical history of severe, persistent asthma — was airlifted to the University of Maryland Children's Hospital because he was struggling to breathe. He stayed in intensive care for five days, Clark said, displaying symptoms consistent with mold exposure.
Clark said on the way to the hospital in Baltimore, she could barely see anything and was crying.
"I don't want to lose another child," she said.
Ed Cafasso, a spokesperson for the property that is managed by WinnResidential, said on Jan. 15 that the health and safety of residents is WinnResidential's number one priority.
"Any time a household reports a moisture-related issue, it is treated as an emergency and remediated immediately by a professional, licensed specialist," he said.
Cafasso said over the past year, there have been seven instances at the complex that required professional mold remediation. He said there were zero reported cases of mold at the 190-apartment community as of January.
Before Clark and her family could move into a new unit at the complex this past fall, the unit was condemned. Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said that in condemning the unit, the city ordered mold and moisture testing be done.
An inspection report obtained by The Star Democrat from the city showed an early November analysis found aspergillus and penicillium spore counts in the unit that were "significantly higher than the baseline count and probably indicates a source of contamination."
The unit was later removed from the city's list of condemned properties after a report by Simple Mold Solutions, which was based on the analysis, found the numbers "indicated a normal fungal environment with no elevated concentrations of airborne mold spores." The report recommended the HVAC system be cleaned to prevent mold spores from circulating.
But Clark's son's health scare was enough to make her seek housing elsewhere. The search proved to be no easy feat.
Limited affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and across the state have made it difficult for Clark to find somewhere new to settle.
Clark said she went to multiple shelters in Howard County, where her children are currently enrolled in school, but all of them were full. She said the places she did find that had space required she live in the county for six months, which she had not.
Moving from place to place hasn't been easy on Clark's kids. She said they are scared to go back to the complex.
"They don't want to go back there, and I don't know what to do," Clark told The Star Democrat while they were living out of a van. "But at the same time, I know we can't keep living like this."
In mid-December, Clark and her family were able to secure a hotel room after living out of a van for more than a month. On Valentine's Day, they moved into a townhouse on the western shore.
"It's much better," she said. "No mold."
ZOOMING IN ON THE PROBLEM
Clark's story isn't an uncommon one when it comes to tenants of affordable housing on the Eastern Shore.
Residential issues at affordable housing complexes in Cambridge have come to a head more than once in the last two years.
In an attempt to attack the bigger issue at the local level, Cambridge has beefed up its Code Enforcement Department and is working on projects intended to increase and improve the city's housing stock.
Hesson said although the issues at housing facilities are all unique, there are common themes among them.
"There have been failures by agencies at the local, state and federal level to hold up the standards we've set for housing providers here," he said. "It's not my place to point fingers, because it isn't going to fix anything. The city is part of that structure, and we're committed to being better."
Hesson said building "strong relationships" with the governing authorities for the different housing facilities has helped achieve "significant progress."
"We've been able to draw attention to where these systems and processes have fallen short, and residents are seeing some of the early results of those efforts," he said.
PROGRESS
For Linda Johnson, those results are clear.
On Feb. 13, Johnson moved into a new unit within Bradford House Apartments. The move is not just a win for Johnson, who has been a loud and consistent voice of the Bradford House community, but proof of a new era for the apartment complex and its residents.
For years Bradford House residents expressed concerns about the safety of the building. In September 2023, the property — which was then managed by Millennia — received a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development inspection score that indicated health and safety deficiencies.
Three months later, Millennia received a debarment order from HUD, preventing the company from participating in any new business with the department.
In October, it was announced that Nuveen, an asset manager and subsidiary of financial planning firm TIAA, had been made principal owner of the apartment complex. Paths Management Services, a subsidiary of Nuveen, would manage the property.
Johnson's new digs, complete with a brand new, updated kitchen and laminate wood flooring, are a stark contrast from her previous unit.
When The Star Democrat visited some residents' homes last year, residents pointed out things like holes in ceilings, possible mold and problems with stoves. At that time, multiple residents had active rent escrow cases, where tenants pay their rent to a court, rather than to their landlord, until property issues are addressed.
The change at Bradford House isn't just visible in individual apartment units. The hallways have new flooring, the stairways are consistently clean, there is better lighting and new cameras and the community room has been renovated. Johnson said management is fixing the elevator that's been broken for more than a year.
"It's been wonderful," Johnson said. "I mean Paths came in here, they didn't talk, they worked."
Johnson is the president of the complex's tenant association, which was formed with guidance from Shore Legal Access.
"Just because we're low income people doesn't mean we have to live like that," she said.
Johnson said other renters going through housing issues should fight for what they believe in, adding that tenants have the right to withhold rent and form tenant associations.
"Your voice matters," she said.
Star Democrat reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

stories.title: Cambridge Aims to Improve Its Housing Stock with Programs, Projects
stories.author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Cambridge aims to improve its housing stock with programs, projects

 December 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 733
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Visiting the corner of Douglas and Bethel streets in Cambridge is an exciting trip for Cambridge Housing Program Manager Ed Crosby.The four homes being built there, in Cambridge's historic Pine Street neighborhood, are part of a plan slowly unfolding.
"We went out to the site yesterday," Crosby said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Dec. 11. "(The developer) said to me, 'You're looking at (the houses) like they're your babies.' I said, 'Yes, they are my babies.'"
The project is one of multiple the city is working on in order to achieve its goal of improving its housing stock, uplifting the community and fostering a culture where residents want to stay in Cambridge.
"Everything from renovations to restorations to demos even, if that's the case, depending on the situation," Crosby said. "But in those areas, making sure that the community is fully engaged and informed that the city is committed to having a healthier home environment."
As housing program manager, Crosby sits at the helm of this mission. His position, which he took on in March, was created out of a need identified by former City Manager Tom Carroll.
Crosby was brought on board to oversee the execution of an "umbrella program" called Healthy Homes, which provides support services to residents to help them navigate home-related challenges.
Under that umbrella program, the city offers a variety of housing-related help for residents.
The Homeowner Helper Program, for example, is a financial program that gives qualifying seniors financial assistance to make needed repairs to their homes. Crosby said that so far, a resident has had their roof replaced through the program.
"We're looking at our residents having piece of mind," he said. "We want them to know that they come first and that we care."
Another program, which the city started through a grant from the U.S Department of Housing and Urban Development, will allow the city to do lead remediation. The three-year grant has a training component so local contractors can be trained in lead remediation and even become trainers themselves.
In March, the Cambridge City Council voted to establish the Land Bank Authority of Cambridge, which will have the power to take on, manage and sell vacant land in order to stabilize neighborhoods and encourage redevelopment. Crosby said the city has identified potential board members for the land bank, but the City Council has yet to appoint anyone to the board.
After the city finishes building the Douglas Street houses, it plans to build at least 10 more homes on Chesapeake Court and School House Lane.
Crosby said it's important that Cambridge is seen as a "livable community."
"We want you to feel not only that is this a destination, but this is going to be a permanent place of residence for you," he said.
The new Douglas Street houses will be sold at 80% of area median income. Crosby said people interested in purchasing the homes will have to qualify for them based on income and HUD standards. He said they will also have to complete homebuyer education training.
As the Housing Department builds up their programming, it is focusing on community engagement. The department now has a community engagement specialist who is responsible for engaging with and mobilizing the community in different housing discussions.
Crosby said community engagement is such an important piece of the city's housing goals because there needs to be "buy in" from residents.
Commission President and Mayor-elect Lajan Cephas said the Cambridge Housing Department is the city's first housing department.
"We have areas in our community, such as the historic Pine Street community that have been, in a sense, either ignored or maybe was not a priority," she said.
With the Housing Department, the city can make those areas a priority. Cephas said she thinks the city is doing a "great job" of this.
"Of course, we can't fix this overnight because this is something that's been neglected (for), I would say, more than 50 years," she said. "But absolutely within the next three to five years, as far as that gateway street known as Washington Street — and all the other streets that feed into that — there's going to be a huge difference."
Five years from now, Crosby hopes to see Cambridge's housing that's currently in a "dilapidated state" either repaired or replaced with newly built homes. He acknowledged it's an ambitious goal, but said he thinks it's doable.
"I think the community is looking for that kind of transformation," he said.

stories.title: Queen Anne's County Seeking Input on New Recreation Center
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
Queen Anne's County seeking input on new recreation center

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 190
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Department of Parks and Recreation is seeking community input for a public engagement phase feasibility study as it draws nearer to a recreation center, the Queen Anne's County Parks Department reported to Commissioners March 26.The County's contractor, Berry Dunn, is currently assessing needs for the building phase and now wants to hear from the community about what will be viable, according to James Miller, recreation manager.
The community can expect to begin learning about the feasibility study soon, as the months-long public engagement phase of the study officially begins April 22.
"It's going to be a big push to get as much community input and outreach as possible," Miller said.
In addition to focus groups and public meetings, participants will be provided with access to an online portal to join in a community-wide conversation, he said.
Following the study, market and demographic research will be conducted of the area before performing site research, Miller said.
Strong communication and collaboration between the departments has been essential through every step of the study, he said.
"This is the beginning of something amazing," Commissioner Phil Dumenil said.
The feasibility study final report is expected in December.

stories.title: Housing Secretary Visits His Hope Ministries
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Housing secretary visits His Hope Ministries

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day, came to His Hope Ministries in Denton Tuesday to learn about the nonprofit's vision for the future.The organization, which provides services and shelter to those experiencing homelessness, wants to develop a new building and move to Market Street.
They toured bunk rooms at 409 Aldersgate Drive, where neat piles of clothes, toothbrushes, laundry detergent and ear buds lie. The shelter welcomes guests from September through the end of April, with accommodations for families, single men and women, and youths.
"They are seeking to grow because the demand is high," Day said. "Part of that is that there just are not enough housing units, particularly affordable housing units in the Mid-Shore. We have underbuilt for the last 15 years. The consequence is that people are unhoused."
Executive Director Stefanie Johnson showed Day some architectural plans for a new facility she would like to build to expand His Hope's services.
"I did show him our design so far. We have an idea in mind for land, but so far, it is not available from the town yet. We have our Senior Haven, which is a three bedroom one bath home. It has three seniors in it. Seniors or disabled — it is transitional so they can stay there for up to three years," said Johnson.
There is a vacant lot next to this senior home where His Hope hopes to build their expanded facility.
One of the barriers to completing the project is its cost. Some of the visit was talking about money.
Day said he believes the best fiscal options for His Hope to complete the project is through the Community Development Block Grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The state has $7.5 million to fund CDBG annually, he said.
"Probably for the Eastern Shore it is CDBG money. It gets to the end user when it is ready to be executed and spent for construction and design. This federal money has to serve the low income population," Day said.
The other option Day mentioned is Sowing Empowerment and Economic Development Inc., a nonprofit organization providing food, education, and training while promoting self-sufficiency and empowerment directly to low-to-moderate-income families.
"I believe both predevelopment and development costs are eligible. SEED is the institutional version of this. For the town, all it has to be is a community development goal that they're interested in. Helping unsheltered homeless be sheltered has positive health outcomes. A hospital and a shelter would go hand and glove," Day said.
Andrew Breeding, treasurer for His Hope Ministries, called their hoped-for property the Market Street Property. The land is owned by the Town of Denton and used to be a Southern States facility.
"The challenge is putting a homeless shelter literally anywhere," said Breeding.
Johnson said some local politicians are hesitant about the idea of building a shelter in town. Day said that representatives from his office, including him, could come and testify to the town council on behalf of His Hope's story.
Day asked some pressing questions about how His Hope Ministries and the community interact.
"What's that look like between you and other organizations in the community?" he asked.
Johnson responded, "It is impeccable. When we closed (for the warmer months), we called and said, 'Hey, do you have room for our families? Talbot Interfaith in Easton, and in Cambridge the Salvation Army, we are all on speed dial. Even the Christian Shelter in Salisbury. This community is so giving."
Day also toured the office and youth drop-in center of His Hope Ministries on 105 Gay Street, housed in a spacious Victorian house with a broad porch. The inside is inviting and colorful. There is room for classes on financial literacy, and there are many positive affirmations on the walls.
Amidst a big black board filled with affirmations, Day was invited to grab some chalk and add his. He wrote, "A mistake will not define you. Get back up and keep going."
This report has been updated from earlier versions to correct the name of His Hope's treasurer.

stories.title: 'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere
stories.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In August, everything came to a head at Altair Apartments.Trash piled high outside the apartments on Greenwood Avenue for an entire week. Broken water heaters and air conditioners couldn't be fixed. Even the internet stopped working.Resident Rodaisia Brummell said she felt disgusted."It felt like we were abandoned," Brummell said. "Like they didn't really care about us." The reason for these conditions: its new California-based management company, FPI Management, hadn't been paying all of the bills since taking over the property in April.Property Manager Judkya Murray said that overtime, vendors stopped showing up, causing trash to build up and plumbing to remain broken.She said the problem was all caused by one person at FPI Management, who has since been let go. That one person wasn't paying the bills to keep everything at Altair running. FPI Management could not be reached for comment."I was literally sitting here pulling my hair out because we had no internet," Murray said. "We had no phones. I couldn't call anybody.I couldn't email anybody." At the time, Murray was the assistant property manager acting as the property manager. The previous property manager had left for another opportunity, Murray said.The week the garbage trucks didn't show, Murray remembers the garbage being so plentiful that the building's maintenance worker had to take garbage cans from inside the building to fill with the overflowing trash outside."We were trying to do everything we could possibly do to keep the trash contained somewhere," she said. "It was just too much trash." The building's staff was quitting left and right."Nobody really wanted to leave but it's like, the conditions - you have no choice but to leave," Murray said.Even Murray quit.However, in about three weeks, she was back."The senior director of FPI (Management), she actually reached out to me one day," Murray said. "She was like, 'Can you please come have lunch with me.'" At the lunch, Murray explained why she quit and said the senior director told her they were already working to let go of and replace the the person within the company that hadn't been paying the bills for months.With that conversation, Murray agreed to come back in early October, this time as the official property manager.Having a boss who pays the bills has made Murray's job easier since coming back, she said. But she still has a significant list of to-dos and goals, especially because so many people quit a few months ago.In mid-October, Murray said she has hired a new assistant and interviewed a potential new maintenance worker."And if we hire him, we'll just need one other maintenance guy and we'll be fully staffed," she said. "Once we're fully staffed, everything flows perfectly." Murray also has some big picture goals in the works to increase occupancy and create new community programming.She is working to increase the property's occupancy rate by filling the vacant apartments. Of Altair's 144 total units, Murray said 20 are vacant. She hopes to bring the occupancy rate from 86% to 94% by the end of the year.While the waitlist of applicants is "a mile long," Murray said maintenance has to get the apartments fixed up and ready before new residents can move in.PROBLEMS PROMPT RESIDENTS TO LOOK ELSEWHEREWhile Murray is taking applications to fill apartment vacancies, Millie Lewis and her husband Willie are filling out applications for other apartments in Cambridge. After more than 40 years of living in the Altair Apartments, the Lewises are tired of dealing with the problems.Recently, they dealt with the outcome of a recent water leak, which affected their kitchen, living room and bathroom. In all three rooms, water spilled out from the ceiling. In the kitchen and bathroom, water filled in the ceiling lights.The edges of the carpeting against one wall in the living room has turned from beige to rusted brown.For years, even before the leak, the carpeting in Lewis' bedroom has been coming undone from the floor.Lewis covers these spaces - where pockets of air separate the carpeting and the floor - with small area rugs. She said Altair won't fix this issue, even though she has complained about it.Although the ceilings were patched up by maintenance following the leak, it took weeks and a citation from the city for the mold, which grew from one of those patched up spots in the bathroom, to be removed.Lewis has COPD and asthma, which made her even more concerned about being in a home where there is mold in the bathroom that she and her husband use everyday."I pay my rent every month," she said. "Before I'm supposed to pay it.Why can't the head people do their job? Why can't they pay? Why can't they take care of what's got to be taken care of at these apartments hereft" Lewis isn't the only resident looking to live elsewhere.Tieonna Wisher, who has lived at Altair for three years, said she has already filled out an application for another apartment.She has concerns about how long it takes for management to respond to problems.Wisher has a hole in her wall that she said management hasn't done anything about for months."They keep saying they're going to come in here," she said.Wisher remembers one day when she unplugged a cord from a socket in her home and it sparked and caused half of the lights to go out in her apartment."They told me to call the emergency number," she said. "Call it and nobody answers. Go to the office.Like, nobody wants to do nothing." Brummell, who has lived at Altair for over a year, said she has also started submitting housing applications.In the time that she's lived here, Brummell has experienced a months-long leak in her bathroom and a leaking dishwasher. She said that when her dishwasher was leaking, all maintenance did was drop off a shop vac. She has yet to receive a working dishwasher.It took about three months before Brummell could get someone to fix the leak in her bathroom. She said that gnats are still flying around the apartment because of it.A mother of two young kids, Brummell has noticed her children keep getting sick. She fears it is from the building. The one time she saw mold in her home, a previous property manager told her to spray it with bleach."That's all she told me to do," Brummell said.THE CITY's INVOLVEMENTTo get problems solved, Brummell said she has started reaching out to the City of Cambridge. She said this has been effective because code enforcement can fine Altair for property violations."A couple weeks ago (workers hired by management) came in and painted and fixed my stuff that was supposed to be fixed," she said. "Only because I called the City of Cambridge.Because, if I didn't call them, it wouldn't have been that." Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said a goal of the city is to solve quality of life issues."That's not always going to be possible from the outside of homes," he said."We need to get people to the point where (residents) trust us and they are contacting us and they're aware of their tenants rights and they're ability to call us about issues they're having with their rental homes and their apartments." Hesson said they have been able to do this at Altair and are "still very present." Since August, Hesson said communication with upper management has been satisfactory. He said they shared an action plan with multiple items they plan to address. As of Nov. 3, Hesson said he was still waiting to see if they are following that plan.Hesson clarified that communication with Altair's on-site management "has always been pretty good." Murray said she is making sure that she stays in communication with the city."I know their biggest thing is nobody was communicating anything back to them," she said about the city. "They just need to know if somebody's on top of (a problem)." With all of the issues at Altair, Brummell said residents are paying rent and not getting the services they should be getting as tenants."Everything's being prolonged," she said. "But ya'll want things from us. You want rent money from us.You want us to go in the house at a certain time. But we're not getting the things that we properly need." 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Judkya Murray, Altair Apartments property manager, was so frustrated with surmounting issues that she quit. Now she is back and trying to get the tenants resources.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Rodaisia Brummell is looking for another place to live with her husband and two kids. "It felt like we was abandoned," Brummell said about Altair Apartments management. "Like they didn't really care about us."
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Millie and Willie Lewis have lived in the Altair Apartments for 40 years. Recently they had mold coming out of a vent in their bathroom.

stories.title: The Big Pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Promenade Makes Progress
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
The big pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. promenade makes progress

 May 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. did its first "big pour," according to Treasurer Frank Narr.The concrete base for CWDI's promenade was poured May 10, a visible sign for the community that progress is underway. The project aims to develop the waterfront similarly to Baltimore's Inner Harbor.
Progress has been slower than many hoped as CWDI has faced significant headwinds.
Tensions between the developer and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit in May of 2024 over a transfer agreement. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice a few months later, and the city and CWDI entered a memorandum of understanding to address issues that were not included in the lawsuit settlement.
"And, you know, honestly, that has actually kind of been a blessing in disguise," said CWDI Board President Angie Hengst about the lawsuit. "It has allowed us to open up those doors of communication with the county and city even more," Hengst said.
The city and county managers now sit on the board of CWDI, which has helped bridge divides between the development project with the community. "It is really great to have their constant input," Hengst said.
Narr has been with the project for over 30 years and cares deeply about making sure it is done right. For Narr, it isn't about finding partners who can simply fund the project, but finding partners who care about the mission.
That mission aims to foster community engagement, economic growth and further development projects in Cambridge. "It really needs to be a place where everyone in our community feels there's a place for them," Narr said. "And so continuous access to the waterfront, public open space, no gates, no walls, nothing that would say you're not welcome."
Narr acknowledges that the negative backlash CWDI has received from the public has been tough, but he chooses to focus on what is in his control. "There's times when people question, 'Why are you still doing this? You must be getting a benefit from this,' and I'm thinking, 'No it's my commitment to my community to make sure we get what we deserve and we get what will make us all proud,'" Narr said.
Now that they've overcome the litigation hurdle, the main challenge CWDI faces, like many nonprofit organizations at the moment, is funding. "I think that's really our biggest challenge right now," Hengst said.
The promenade is slated to be finished by the end of summer and CWDI is holding a meeting on May 20 to deliver updates to the County and City Council and is open to the public.

stories.title: Cambridge City Council Hears Plans for Harriet Tubman Mural Area
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge mayor and commissioners spent a significant portion of their three-hour meeting Monday learning about Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation's plans to revitalize the area surrounding the Harriet Tubman mural behind 424 Race St.Adrian Holmes, president and program director of Alpha Genesis, said the second phase project will help extend the stay of tourists in Cambridge.
"Right now, most people who go back there stay no longer than five or ten minutes because there's nowhere to sit, it's hot, it's just not really appealing," she said. "So this is what we want to do to help the people who come to the mural extend their stay. And when they extend their stay, they'll spend more money ... and they'll just have a better experience."
The plan, which extends into Cannery Way off Race Street, is to add two retail spaces adjacent the mural. One of the spaces will be a souvenir shop, Holmes said. The building itself will also include Alpha Genesis' headquarters, three other retail spaces that face Race Street and an exhibition deck.
In front of the mural will be the Harriet Tubman Pavilion, which will shield viewers from inclement weather. Near the pavilion, there will be a community garden.
"We affectionately call this project the North Star Village, a tribute in honor of Harriet Tubman," Holmes said.
Alpha Genesis has been working with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, the Maryland Historical Trust, the Rural Maryland Council, state legislators and the City of Cambridge to make enhancements to the space. Alpha Genesis is still raising funds for the second phase of the project, which will cost around $1.5 million. The project has received funding from the Maryland General Assembly and the city.
"And then we have a couple grant opportunities that can cover the rest of it," Holmes said.
According to council meeting documents, the proximity of Alpha Genesis' property to city property has made the project a "joint venture" between the two. One document from Alpha Genesis states the city will improve Cannery Way and the adjacent parking lot, and Alpha Genesis will focus on 428 through 432 Race St.
Alpha Genesis is asking the city for the installation of public restrooms, the repositioning of the brick wall on Cannery Way and the addition of a replica of the Ben Ross Cabin on the Cannery Way property.
Holmes said restrooms would benefit tourists who come from far distances to see the mural. Alpha Genesis' proposal is to construct a "North Star Station" that includes two all-gender bathrooms, a 135-square-foot public meeting room and a small lobby space with digital kiosks that have information about the city.
RESTROOM DISCUSSIONCommissioners asked a variety of questions about Alpha Genesis' plans. Multiple questions focused on the restroom proposal.
Commissioner Brian Roche shared his concern with the North Star Station blocking the view of the water from Cannery Way. Holmes said a possible change to the proposal could be to remove the meeting room from the station to make it smaller.
Commission President Sputty Cephas asked who would be responsible for maintaining the public restrooms. Alpha Genesis Executive Director Jermaine Anderson said he thinks it would be a good idea to form a youth or recidivism program where those in the program would be tasked with maintaining areas around the mural.
"Now's the time," he said. "Let's get real creative. Let's continue planning, continue talking, developing relationships. ... I think we can find the solutions we need."
During public comment, Chuck McFadden said he supports revitalizing the area, but the city should be careful about how much it commits. McFadden also cautioned that bringing youth in to clean the public restrooms might not be an easy feat.
After council discussion, the City Council unanimously voted to have city staff work closely with Alpha Genesis on its proposal and make sure it gets through the Historic Preservation Commission and the Planning and Zoning Commission. The vote, which Cephas motioned, also called for a presentation on the fiscal impact of the proposal and made sure Roche and any other interested commissioners can work with city staff on the matter.

stories.title: St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board Holds First Meeting
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board holds first meeting

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of controversy surrounding its creation, the St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board held its first meeting at the Boy Scout Cabin in St. Michaels Thursday morning.During this meeting, members of the board, the St. Michaels Business Association and residents of the town came together to discuss the future and current condition of the tourism industry.
The board discussed potential budgets, marketing and branding strategies including combining various websites, and getting a better understanding of the tourists who are visiting and the tourists the board would like to bring to St. Michaels.
Timothy Law, the representative of retail businesses on the board, said as a business owner he is really excited for the work the board will produce.
"I love St. Michaels, and today was a huge stride forward to really understanding tourism and promoting our spectacular destination. I think it's a great group of people and we've got a great diversity of thought and diversity of background. It was just a very positive first step."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board has seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership includes residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
The members of the board were elected by the Commissioners of St. Michaels and include:
Brian Ball, managing director for the Wildset Hotel, to represent lodging.
Chris Agharabi, chief executive officer of Ava's Hospitality Group, to represent restaurants.
Katie Blaha, advancement manager of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, to represent nonprofits/museums.
Michael Morgan, owner and president of St. Michaels Marina LLC, to represent marinas.
Timothy Law, owner of American Holiday Shop, to represent retail.
Craig Bertolett, chief operating officer of COLUMBIA Technologies, and Michael McMillan, associate clinical professor of accounting at the University of Maryland, as two representatives for the residents of St. Michaels.
Included in the board is St. Michaels Commissioner Katrina Whittington as acting representative for the commission.
On Thursday, the board discussed the importance of a unified marketing message and the potential benefits of public Wi-Fi for data collection. Board members emphasized the need for a clear target audience and suggested a short-term plan to focus on digital marketing.
Ball said it's important for people to understand how tourism effects all aspects of the town's economy.
"St. Michaels is very much a tourism-based economy and it really affects everything we do from local government to all the businesses and all the restaurants and hotels," Ball said. "I think that this (board) is a very valuable economic tool to use to help the town grow."
Plans were made for the next meeting to include presentations on budget allocation and marketing strategies. The next meeting will be held on Jan. 30.

stories.title: After Months of Debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board Is Approved
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
After months of debate, St. Michaels Tourism Board is approved

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of heated discussions, revisions and compromises, the St. Michaels Tourism Board was unanimously approved by commissioners on Wednesday evening.According to Commissioner David Wojciechowski, the board will help provide additional resources in case funds from different avenues, including federal funds, are reduced after the election.
"It's a proactive measure to get ahead of the curve," Wojciechowski said. "A lot of things have happened in the past two weeks, we're counting on a lot of grant money coming into this town. There might be an administration in place right now that jeopardizes that grant money. We need to preserve and protect the revenue that's coming into the town."
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
According to the ordinance, the board will be composed of seven members including a mix of business types from the community and residents. The now approved board will recommend to commissions an annual promotional plan and budget that will manage tourism for the upcoming year.
The board would include representatives of several businesses including lodging, food and beverage, retail or service, marinas and nonprofits. The commissioners will appoint the members of the board and appoint one commissioner to participate as a non-voting member of the board.
The idea of a tourism board was suggested during the town election last May. Wojciechowski, Alexis Roiter and Jay Hudson, who were elected as commissioners, said during their campaigns that they would work with business owners to make the town more friendly to their needs.
The tourism board faced pushback soon after its suggestion. During an August commission meeting, residents raised an array of concerns over potential conflicts of interest and a lack of data supporting the board's creation.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment on Wednesday evening, Daniel Spiegel, a member of Residents Association of St. Michaels, said he and other residents have four issues with the proposed ordinance.
Spiegel said the issues include a lack of adequate data and evidence, an underrepresentation of residents on the tourism board, a "dangerous and unwelcome built-in conflict of interest," and the potential for "managed tourism."
According to Spiegel, managed tourism is a "code word" for moving tourism "upscale," which he has based on previous discussions among commissioners with business representatives.
"I think it's inappropriate for a town, which basically says, 'Bring in the Porsches and keep out the buses and day trips,'" Spiegel said. "I don't think a government policy should be advocating this type of upscale tourism. I think it's not appropriate."
Following comments included a sentiment from residents that St. Michaels is more than a tourism town and a request to focus on already existing institutions.
Debbie Jackson said she is a longtime resident and the town has "always been businesses." Jackson addressed what she described as anti-business sentiment from the residents who said the town was more than just businesses.
According to Jackson, business owners have seen a decline in sales the past two years and support the establishment of a tourism board. Additionally, Jackson said there has been a "wedge" she had seen in town between residents and business owners.
"What prompted all the citizens of St. Michael's to feel this way? Or is this just one little group that's gotten together to hype this up?" Jackson said.
After comments from residents and business owners, Commissioner Alfred Mercier brought the matter up for a vote. The commissioners unanimously voted to approve the tourism board.

stories.title: Caroline County Towns Forge Connections at Chamber Event
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Caroline County towns forge connections at Chamber event

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Around 70 members of the Caroline Chamber of Commerce met at the Greater Impact Church to have a dialogue of connection between six towns in the county.On Oct. 9 representatives from Preston, Denton, Greensboro, Goldsboro, Federalsburg and Ridgely were given 10 minutes to talk about their municipality. There were six tables, one for each municipality, and attendees rotated between them.
Everybody in the room was a stakeholder for Caroline County. A lot of business cards and handshakes were exchanged.
Tracey Snyder, executive director of the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce, coached the town leaders to "Share what is happening in your fabulous, wonderful town. Share who you are and let them share who they are."
She said, "The power is the municipalities. If they don't communicate with each other, how are we going to grow? We need each other. We are a small but mighty county. Not competing, supporting."
Although this was Snyder's idea, she had a think tank to help her.
The audience contained economic development departments, commissioners, CASA, Caroline GOP, Chesapeake College, Channel Marker, Compass Regional Hospice, Choptank Community Health and more.
Not only the town representatives showed up. There were also county, state liaisons in attendance.
Carl Anderton Jr., director of rural economic strategy from the Maryland Department of Commerce and Gov. Wes Moore's office, said, "The whole point is there is strength in numbers.
"There may be something that Federalsburg is doing well that Denton is trying to do. Then Denton uses it from Federalsburg ,and there is no need to recreate the wheel," Anderton said.
He said there are 16 rural counties in Maryland, and his goal was to be available to help counties and municipalities, especially if they are have trouble with agencies.
Amber Korell, town manager of Preston, went from table to table.
"I met so many folks that I need to invite to our Preston Connects Program. I have gotten over twenty business cards. Preston Connects is a program we offer to partners and other organizations to come out to our town and utilize our office space," she said.
Another town representative, Stephanie Berkey, clerk treasurer for the town of Ridgely, shared information about the town's upcoming events.
"We have a website www.christmasinridgely.com It is all things we do throughout the holiday season. Starting at Thanksgiving through New Year's Day. We have a lights display. They are already putting the lights up," she said.
She was very animated in her presentations.
"As a townsperson this was fun. I made some good contacts. I gave a lot of ideas about our holiday Christmas in Ridgely to people," Berkey said.
After attendees rotated to all six tables, Snyder called time and everyone clapped. All the town representatives were called up to the stage for a group photo.
Blue tote bags were given out to everyone so they could carry out all the swag and business cards. People kept talking all the way out to the parking lot.

stories.title: Urban design consultant presents analysis of Easton's economic potency
stories.author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Urban design consultant presents analysis of Easton's economic potency

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Town employees and representatives gathered at the Easton Town Office on Aug. 22 for a presentation of Easton's economic potency for land use planning.Joe Minicozzi, the principal and founder of Urban3, an urban finance consulting group, spoke during the presentation regarding Easton's potential to up its economic potency. He compared the growth of the town to the trajectory of one's DNA.
"Cities all have those moments," Minicozzi said. "They all have a DNA baked into them through their infrastructure, their growth patterns, that will have effects into the future."
Miguel Salinas, the town's director of planning and zoning, helped organize the partnership with Urban3 and last week's presentation.
"We hired Urban3 to model the potential revenue implications of various development scenarios based on different types of land use, … how we build out, … and at what densities," Salinas said.
Minicozzi pointed out the success of Easton's core downtown area. His presentation provided hypothetical examples of how much certain residential developments, businesses and homes could deliver in property taxes per acre.
"As Talbot County taxpayers, you take up 3% of the county's footprint, you're producing 26% of the county's property taxes," Minicozzi said of the town. He encouraged the town to find "opportunities for infill" and "neighborhood growth areas."
Urban3's analysis noted there was a potential $637,000 in property tax revenue from a Poplar Hill housing proposal that never came to fruition.
In August 2023, an application from a developer to build 456 residential units between Easton Bypass and Oxford Road was rescinded. A 119-unit plan was approved by the Easton Planning Commission in September 2023, but this February, Talbot County bought the 120-acre Poplar Hill Farm property.
"That was an opportunity lost," Minicozzi said. "Make sure that you account for that or find a way to learn from this and do it in another place. Maybe that's not the right place, that's cool, your decision. But don't just avoid that."
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who attended the meeting, said he felt it was "inappropriate" for the presentation to mention the canceled Poplar Hill proposal given that it was a "democratically led and made decision."
"The data are perfectly useful in their own way," Montgomery said of the presentation as a whole, "but I was disturbed by the way the presentation made it seem like the only objective we should have … is how we can maximize the amount of tax revenue we can take in. And that's just wrong. There are so many other things that matter, starting with how we preserve the character of the town and maintain our rural character, maintain our open spaces."
During the presentation, Minicozzi raised the topic of sea level rise. He noted Maryland Department of Planning projections that predict Talbot County will lose $817 million in property value due to sea level rise by the year 2100, with $8.1 million of that coming in Easton.
Minicozzi also encouraged the town to ensure underrepresented groups of people — such as those under 45 and the town's non-white population — should be heard in conversations of economic potency.
"Those folks get pushed out of the community and take on more burden in transportation to get here," Minicozzi said, "which is even more painful financially."
Salinas said the analysis and presentation brought information that can serve the town's planning and zoning department moving forward.
"This information can be important for us to add another tool to the toolbox," Salinas said.

stories.title: St. Michaels Commissioners Discuss Comprehensive Plan
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
St. Michaels Commissioners discuss comprehensive plan

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 359
 Words

 ST. MICHAELS — St. Michaels commissioners dove into the process of renewing the town's comprehensive plan with a workshop meeting on Tuesday.One of the main topics discussed was the town's priorities for the updated plan, which is revised every 10 years.
While no firm decisions were made, the commissioners said existing passages in the current plan would be taken into consideration.
Commissioners President Jay Hudson said there will be a special meeting schedule to discuss the commissioners priorities.
"We have been discussing getting together with a special session to discuss what those priorities are," Hudson said. "As you know, we've just hired a new town manager as of April, and he's been busy getting himself acclimated to his role. Now it is time for us to sit down and kind of prioritize projects moving forward."
Hudson said that the commissioners would come back to the Nov. 5 comprehensive plan meeting with priorities mapped out. Hudson also mentioned that the priorities in already outlined in Chapter 14 of the comprehensive plan will be the road map.
During the meeting, commissioners brought up multiple concerns and items they wished were included within the plan. Commissioner Alexis Roiter mentioned demographics as a consideration. Hudson said that the Planning Commission plans to add all of those to the plan before the next meeting.
"Those are easy ones. Looking at a 10 year plan, it's definitely necessary to see what the demographics are when we're writing it," Hudson said.
With federal funding in question, to make sure all of St. Michaels plan can be completed, the town plans to strengthen its relationship with Talbot County.
"I think all the municipalities in Talbot County have a wonderful working relationship with the county," Hudson said. "I think now with grant funding running out and having a better idea of what we need moving forward, I think for us now it's imperative to strengthening the relationships with the county. It's more creating these programs so that these relationships can work."
The special meeting to discuss the commissioners' priorities for the comprehensive plan has not been scheduled yet, but the next comprehensive plan meeting will be Nov. 5 at 5 p.m. at 407 St. Mary's Square.

stories.title: Easton Leans Away From Annexing New Land in Comprehensive Plan Update
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton leans away from annexing new land in comprehensive plan update

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As planners draft Easton's new comprehensive plan, the town's direction on annexing new land is becoming clear: slow down.At a workshop Monday, the Easton Planning Commission chose to retain language in the comprehensive plan update that discourages new annexations in the next 10 years.
As recently as last year, Easton annexed around 17 acres of county land east of U.S. Route 50 between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. It's expected to become an affordable housing project, though the developer will still need town approval on an application.
Town Council members have indicated concerns about annexing additional land into town, especially as Easton deals with the question of whether it's maxing out on residential growth.
The comprehensive plan, last updated in 2010, is undergoing revisions before potential council approval later this year or early next year. It outlines how the town aims to grow in the next decade, touching on areas such as annexation, population growth and traffic.
On Monday and at a workshop last month, commission and council members noted that there may be exceptions to the no-annexation rule.
"I would have a hard time with being absolute about annexation, saying that that's not happening," Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said on Aug. 25. "Because there may be exceptions."
The main exception to completely halting annexation seems to be Easton Point, the development project that seeks to revitalize Port Street and the area around the Tred Avon River. The effort hasn't significantly progressed in recent years, council members say.
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at last month's meeting that Easton Point's redevelopment is "an enigma." She advocated that annexation of the county land in that area be excluded from any no-annexation directive in the new comprehensive plan.
"The Easton Point development project's been on the board for almost 20 years," Curry said. "We have to find a way to move that forward if we can."
Town leaders largely agreed that a project like Easton Point rises to the level of an "extraordinary" annexation that should be permitted under the comprehensive plan's guidance.
Still, the plan should emphasize that annexation generally is "not a priority for the town," said Planning Commission member Victoria McAndrews on Monday.
GROWTH RATE
Hesitation to approve future annexation requests stems, in part, from the town's growth. From 2000 to 2010, the town's population increased 36%, according to census data. In the next decade, growth slowed to 7%, bringing Easton's population from 15,945 to 17,101.
When commission and council members met for a joint workshop in August, the council maintained that the comprehensive plan should include a target growth rate for population. The 2010 version has a 1% annual growth rate, which for the most part hasn't been exceeded. Bumping it up to 1.75% was discussed.
Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Monday that 1.75% "makes the most sense." But other commission members leaned toward a 1.14% annual growth rate, which is based off of historical trends.
Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint agreed with the 1.14% rate, emphasizing that it needs to be at a mark so the Town Council feels comfortable approving the plan as a whole.
TRAFFIC
When housing projects come to the commission or Town Council for approval, they include traffic impact studies. Developers typically hire a traffic engineering firm to conduct the study of the development's potential impact on traffic backups.
Planning Commission members said moving forward, the comprehensive plan needs to demand more thorough traffic reviews. Klein said studies often choose a few intersections next to the project and ignore the town's main arteries, where traffic is already an issue.
Easton Planning and Zoning Director Miguel Salinas said the best way to expand the scope of a traffic impact study for a development is if town engineers or the State Highway Administration request a larger scope during meetings with the project's traffic engineer.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said he wants to continue requiring developers' traffic studies to include a percent change in traffic based on if the development were to be built.
Toussaint said he wants the studies to include more consideration on the impact to pedestrians, not just vehicles. He added that studies should be framed around the town's ongoing Complete Streets study, which is assessing Easton's roads on a large scale.
"What we've received in the past as a traffic impact study is going to be worthless for us going forward," Toussaint said. "It's propaganda at this point, prepared by the applicant's engineers."

stories.title: New Comprehensive Plan Discussed in Cambridge
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
New comprehensive plan discussed in Cambridge

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 249
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, the City of Cambridge hosted a charette to devise a new and improved comprehensive plan.The charette was a weeklong intensive and interactive public session where Planning Director Brian Herrmann, alongside a planning committee from consulting firm Able City, began to capture a vision of Cambridge's future.
The new plan outlined five main ideas: make downtown vibrant and multi-generational, encourage great places beyond downtown, reinvent lost Main Street areas, increase waterfront access and recreational amenities, and build a sustainable and equitable future.
The last time the city came up with a comprehensive plan was in 2011. They planned to re-address it in 2021, but due to the pandemic, that never happened.
Under Maryland law, cities must update their comprehensive plans every 10 years to reflect the community's current needs.
Individuals on the planning team specialize in a variety of development topics, ranging from economic development and housing to transportation.
During the weeklong session, there was strong community engagement, said Jason King, a city planner with Able City.
"This week, we started off with that hands-on design session — 135 plus people, 18 tables, two and a half hour event. It was an epic," King said. "For the city of 13,035 people, you know, we ran out of surveys, and we didn't have enough pens."
King said this kind of turn out is expected in a city of 100,000 residents.
Planners and city officials will continue to work on the comprehensive plan in the coming months before submitting a final version to the state.

 EASTON — As Talbot County prepares to update its comprehensive plan, residents are asked to share their thoughts through an online survey.Bryce Yelton, the county's assistant planning officer, said Tuesday that updates to the actual comprehensive plan language haven't started. But the process is beginning, he said, with an emphasis community input.
The survey, which takes around 10 to 15 minutes to fill out, is available online through May 23. The county has already received 250 responses as of Tuesday, Yelton said.
"You'll put in some stuff you think Talbot County's doing well, some things you think we could improve," Yelton said. "It's an overall messaging to try and get the community's feedback before we highlight the important parts of the plan, what we really want to focus in and update on."

stories.title: Easton Town Council Hears Update on Seafood Odor Mitigation
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Easton Town Council hears update on seafood odor mitigation

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 652
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council heard an update Monday evening from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a business on Maryland Avenue that's drawn complaints from residents for its odor in recent months.At a Nov. 4 town meeting, councilmembers discussed a draft ordinance to limit seafood processing uses in business commercial zoning through special exception only.
That exception would require that seafood by-products are "stored within a closed or refrigerated vehicle," with operators required to install "odor control technology" so "no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner/operator Mitchell Hughes, spoke Monday regarding the town's Nov. 4 discussion and how the potential legislation may impact Hughes' business. Smith said finding a new site for Chesapeake Brand Seafood, as was previously suggested by Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, is not his client's preferred course of action.
"I did speak to Mitchell about that, and that is not preferable," Smith said. " … He located there lawfully. He followed the town's rules. The town zoning still allows that use in that location. So he doesn't necessarily feel like he should have to relocate."
Smith said Hughes has invested around $200,000 in "fitting the space" for his operation. Additionally, many employees live within walking distance of the current site, the attorney said.
"While things are pretty good at the moment, you never know when fisheries are going to decline, when regulations are going to cause restrictions, and so he just doesn't know," Smith said. "The prospect of investing a large amount of money to relocate just doesn't seem reasonable to him at this time."
Hughes' attorney said the business owner is "committed" to addressing the odor and has looked into an odor mitigation solution that may be viable. "I think he would hope there could be some cost-sharing in that," Smith said.
The proposed ordinance, which would require existing businesses to comply by Jan. 1, 2026, was not voted on Monday, and the public hearing was left open.
Carla Howell, a resident on South Aurora Street, asked the council to consider a compliance deadline earlier than 2026.
"I was hoping we'd get some relief when the crab season was over, but we haven't," Howell said. " … I'm hoping you all will at least change the date, and we can go along with (Smith's) idea. I think it would be marvelous if they just put in some kind of a filter system."
Carolyn Johnson, an employee at Chesapeake Brand Seafood and Hughes' aunt, vouched for her nephew and his work as a local business owner.
"He has always wanted to be a good neighbor, and whenever we've had a situation, a complaint from the mayor's office or the town, we have addressed it," Johnson said. "He's taken care of it. And I feel that that shows what he is. He wants to be in business here in Easton. And he was allowed to be in business here in Easton. You guys, the town, gave him that permission."
Councilmembers offered limited perspective on the seafood legislation Monday, as it will likely be revisited at Town Council's Dec. 2 meeting. Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he's "pleased" that a solution for all parties is in the works.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who represents the area in which the business is located, spoke to his constituents and told them "their concerns have not been brushed aside."
In previous meetings, Davis pushed for a deadline sooner than Jan. 1, 2026. He also contended that seafood processing should not be allowed in business commercial zoning at all.
"If I have to stand by myself, I will," Davis said regarding a potential council vote on the matter. "I will represent the voices and the members of that community in such a fashion that they are heard and represented at the table whether they're there or not. So I want all of my colleagues to know that's where I stand."
