stories.title: Caroline Commissioners Talk New Regional Detention Center
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Caroline commissioners talk new regional detention center

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Oct. 15 the Caroline County Commissioners discussed a plan to build a new regional detention center in Queen Anne's county.The financial burden would be split between Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties, but it is still unclear how that would be managed or what would happen to the detention center on 101 Gay Street in Denton, commissioners said at the meeting.
The new facility is being designed to hold 338 beds for men and women. The current Denton jail holds 130 inmates.
The warden of the Caroline County Detention Center, Charles Scott, said there are mental health needs among the inmates that could be better managed with a designated space, which could be incorporated into the design of the new facility.
"There should be a wing just for mental health. Juveniles and mental health are just piling up in the jail," Scott said.
He said there is plenty of land in Queen Anne's County to build this new detention center. The new facility will be located in Church Hill on the site of the Eastern Pre-Release Unit.
Commission President Travis Breeding cited the economies of scale and how the new detention center could serve the needs of the counties for less money.
The commissioners discussed who would be the authority on this tri-county project. Right now, one county commissioner and one county administrator oversee the jail in Denton. The commissioners said they wanted more clarity on how that would work in a tri-county context.
The commissioners also discussed the employment possibilities for current Caroline County Detention Center employees. Employment decisions would factor in tenure and managing workers who have fulfilled this amount of time as they work in a new county.
Scott said it is hard to find correctional officers, so everyone's job should be safe.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the new facility will offer better services at lower costs, but the devil is in the details.
The commissioners agreed to discuss this further at the next meeting on Oct. 22 at the Health and Public Services building.

stories.title: Sharp Road Park Construction Underway
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Sharp Road Park construction underway

 September 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 341
 Words

 Denton — Construction has officially started on Sharp Road Park in Denton.The park is expected to receive multiple upgrades, which started with a mural on the basketball court created by Terae Warner, a local business owner and basketball coach, and artist Shelton Hawkins.
Now Caroline County has started construction on the baseball field, softball field and multipurpose field at the park.
"It's a unique build, and we're doing it a la carte," said Jamie Beechey, director of Caroline County Recreation and Parks. "It's only so much money, so we're making sure that we get the right materials for the right price each step of the way and then decide like what we can afford and what we can't afford."
The construction starts with moving dirt for an access road and making sure the road has a good foundation for construction trucks. The next step is stormwater management.
The county has set up lighting and irrigation contracts, all of which have yet to be approved by the county commissioners. A fencing contract of $84,873 for the playing fields was approved by the county commissioners on Tuesday.
While the hope is for the fields to be finished by December, the county has plans to make the fields safer by adding nets, which could push the completion date back.
"My strongest hope is that we get finished by December, but that may not be everything," Beechey said. "One of the things that we are looking at because of the proximity of the fields, we want to put a netting up at least on one of the fields so the foul ball situation doesn't cause a safety issue for people."
The county is very excited for what the field could offer to Caroline County and other surrounding counties with games under the lights.
"It's going to be really remarkable to have a so-called it 'Field of Dreams,' where our kids go outside of the county and they get to experience these games under lights and now both the boys and the girls will get to experience that here in Denton," Beechey said.

stories.title: QA County Halts New Growth: Moratorium Tied to Sewer Capacity; Land Preservation, Park Upgrades Approved
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
QA County halts new growth: Moratorium tied to sewer capacity; land preservation, park upgrades approved

 August 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Looking at future wastewater capacity, the Queen Anne's County commissioners on Aug. 12 approved a temporary moratorium on residential and mixed-use development.With the area Wastewater Treatment Plant near capacity, the commissioners adopted a moratorium on applications, approvals, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of subdivision, concept plan, site plan or building permit applications for residential or mixed-use projects in Kent Narrows, Stevensville, Grasonville, Prospect Bay, Cloverfields, Bay City and Southern Kent Island.
During the moratorium, the county will not process, consider, review or approve any application, permit or other approval under the County Zoning Ordinance or the Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance for any project in those subdistricts where the total anticipated sewerage allocation exceeds 1,750 gallons per day.
The resolution does not apply to any pending project that already has prerequisite sewer and water allocation for its specific development.
Queen Anne's County has applied for a rerating of the wastewater treatment plant, which if granted would increase capacity by 300,000 gallons per day.
Because of federal Total Maximum Daily Load regulations restricting nutrient and sediment discharge into the Chesapeake Bay, further expansion of treatment capacity at the plant is unlikely.
The county is in the process of updating its 2011 Comprehensive Water and Sewerage Plan. Both that plan and the County Water and Sewerage Allocation Policy may be revised to reflect limited treatment capacity, limited expansion potential and the need to determine how best to allocate sewerage capacity to meet current and future demands.
The county's Adequate Public Facilities Ordinance regulates development based on public infrastructure availability. Commission President Chris Corchiarino said a number of factors have developed since the ordinance was last reviewed, including limited sewer capacity.
With Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the county has also seen an exponential increase in education costs.
"At a time when our enrollment is not going up, our costs have gone up significantly, and that's a cost that is borne by all the citizens," Corchiarino said.
The moratorium will give the county's planning and zoning staff time to take a closer look at zoning, he said.
Land preservation
At no local cost, the commissioners approved the preservation of 117 acres owned by Thompson Farms LLC for review and final approval by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.
Funding will be provided entirely by the Rural Legacy grants program through Program Open Space.
The Thompson Farms LLC property is within the Lands End Rural Legacy Area and will add to the 5,085 acres already preserved. The package includes the Agreement of Sale and Project Agreement signed by the commissioners.
Stevensville park upgrades
Old Love Point Park will see new field lighting. The Department of Parks and Recreation was authorized to contract with Musco Sports Lighting to upgrade the Field Three lights to LEDs for $200,566.
Mowbray Park in Stevensville will also receive new playground equipment. The commissioners approved a $1,139,861 contract with Kompan Inc. to replace the park's current playground.

stories.title: Caroline County Discusses Capital Transportation Priorities Request
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County discusses Capital Transportation Priorities request

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed their Capital Transportation Priorities list and drafted a letter to send to the state at their April 15 meeting.The priority list is presented to the state every year to receive funding for road work projects within the county that the commissioners and town officials believes are a priority.
The state will ultimately determine which projects it funds.
PRIORITY A
Priority A for Caroline County is maintaining and improving existing infrastructure. The county asked for a comprehensive resurfacing of Route 313 from Route 404 to Federalsburg, including repairs to pavement, shoulders and stormwater infrastructure.
Next is the completion of the resurfacing project on Route 16 from Lake Drive to Route 404.
Lastly, Caroline County asked for general resurfacing, shoulder repair, drainage improvement and signage upgrades across Caroline County's state road network. Timely investment in these areas will help avoid further deterioration, reduce maintenance costs and significantly improve travel conditions for our residents and businesses, the county said.
PRIORITY B
The county requested Route 404 be widened from Harmony Road to Route 16 East.
Previous phases of this project have led to improved traffic flow and reduced accidents, demonstrating the importance of completing the corridor, the county said in its priorities list.
PRIORITY CCaroline County requested help with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 454 (Crownstone Road) from Marydel to Templeville.
Route 454 is a vital connector for residents in the western part of the county and serves as a gateway to Queen Anne's County. This route has seen substantial wear and requires resurfacing and structural upgrades to ensure safe and dependable travel, the county said.
PRIORITY DThe county requested state assistance with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 313 from Greensboro to Goldsboro.
This is a major north-south route within the county and is essential for local mobility and emergency response, the county said. It added resurfacing and drainage improvements are necessary to restore safe travel conditions and extend the life of the corridor.
PRIORITY ERounding out the county's priority list is an effort to restripe Route 317 and add a right turn lane.
"We propose restriping MD 317 (Burnsville Road) at the intersection of MD 313 to add a right turn lane. This improvement will help enhance traffic flow and improve safety for all drivers," the county said.

stories.title: CWDI Breaks Ground on Cambridge Harbor Promenade
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
CWDI breaks ground on Cambridge Harbor promenade

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 555
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After a tumultuous year — complete with a lawsuit and mediation with the City of Cambridge — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. has taken a significant step forward in bringing life to the city's waterfront.Thursday, CWDI and the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Cambridge Harbor promenade. Once complete, the project will extend the existing promenade along the wharf, next to Yacht Maintenance, so that it stretches around what is known as Lookout Point and to the Franklin Street boat ramp.
For CWDI Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr, who has been involved with the Cambridge Harbor project for almost 32 years, it felt "unbelievable" to witness the ground breaking.
"You know, it's funny, 32 years ago Gov. Schaefer said we're going to get this done in three or four years," he said. "But the reality is — as political climate changes, as things like the hospital, changes in health care, things like that — you start to realize these things take time and you have to have patience."
Narr said passion has kept him involved with the project for all these years.
"I'm just passionate about making sure what we do here is right for the community," he said. "Because you only get one chance to do it right."
Although the groundbreaking was held Thursday, the work to extend the promenade has already started. Narr said CWDI expects the project to be finished by the end of June.
Once the promenade project is complete, CWDI plans to put out a request for proposals for Cambridge Harbor's developable parcels. Narr said the community will have the opportunity to offer input once CWDI has received proposals.
The ground breaking on Thursday brought together a variety of local and state representatives, including members of the Cambridge City Council.
In the last year and a half, tensions between the city and CWDI bubbled to the surface, culminating in a lawsuit filed against CWDI by the city regarding a transfer agreement. In August, the groups settled the lawsuit, with both city officials and CWDI board members expressing hopes for a stronger relationship moving forward.
During the groundbreaking, Cambridge Commission President and Mayor-elect Lajan Cephas acknowledged the hard work of CWDI's board.
"They've experienced a lot of abuse over the last couple years," she said, adding that it's important trust is rebuilt.
"So I think this is a wonderful opportunity for us to take the next step forward," she said about the promenade. "The best step forward."
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said the board hopes this promenade will be enjoyed by the entire community and "will be just the beginning of creating a waterfront area and experience that is accessible to all."
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer called Thursday "a great day" for the community.
"This is a clear canvas now that we're going to start building up from," he said. "And this is a great project to start with."
Chesapeake Conservancy's President and CEO Joel Dunn, called the day "bittersweet." He said it's his second to last day at the Chesapeake Conservancy, which is a project partner of Cambridge Harbor.
"I've helped create a national wildlife refuge, a national park, two national monuments, expand Blackwater Refuge, create local parks, state parks," Dunn said about his time with the organization. "But I've got to tell you, this is one of my favorite parks that I've ever been a part of."

stories.title: Federalsburg Elects First Two Black Council Members in Historic Election
stories.author: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com
stories.content:
Federalsburg elects first two Black council members in historic election

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones And Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com, njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 814
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG - Just under 300 voters braved a gray and drizzly Tuesday to cast their ballots in Federalsburg's bicentennial election, making history in electing two Black women to the town council.While the election falling during the bicentennial year is special on its own, the day was historic for a different reason - it was the first election held under the town's recently passed election plan, and it was the first time a Black resident had been elected to the town council in the town's 200-year history.According to Kristy Marshall, Federalsburg's interim town manager, 283 residents voted in Tuesday's election, accounting for 17% of the town's registered voters.The mayoral seat and all four council seats - two council members for each newly created district - were up for election.Incumbent Mayor Kimberly Abner held her position at the helm of the town, earning 191 votes and a five-year term as mayor. Jeffrey Stevenson, Jr., a first-time candidate, received 83 votes.In the newly created District 1, which has a majority Black population, representation was achieved for Black residents with the election of two Black women to the council seats.Darlene Hammond received the highest number of ballots, earning 70 votes and a five-year term on the town council.Brandy James received 52 votes, earning a three-year term on the council.James held a narrow lead over incumbent councilman Scott Phillips, who received 49 votes.In District 2, only two candidates - Debra Sewell and H. Torbert "Toby" Williamson - ran for the two open council spots, locking in their seats on the council even before the election.Sewell received 135 votes, earning a five-year term. Williamson received 90 votes and a three-year council term.The new election plan, passed in June, changed the town's former at-large, staggered term election system to a two-district system that ensured more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.No Black resident had ever been elected as a mayor or council member in the town's 200-year history until Tuesday's election.The change was spurred by a federal lawsuit filed earlier this year, which contended that the former election system discriminated against Black voters by keeping them from being able to elect their chosen representatives.Abner, who has served as Federalsburg's mayor since 2019, faced a challenge from Stevenson, a lifelong town resident who hoped to bring change, leadership and caring for the future of the community.To Abner, time already served as an elected official mattered."People look at experience and pay attention," she said.Paying the town's debt, fixing pump stations and paving roads are also among Abner's priorities.When asked why he was running, Stevenson gave a simple answer: "If not me, then who?" "Man, I always felt like I was a leader, and I was always willing to take the chances that everybody else won't take," he said."I'm getting older now, so I've had interest in politics because it matters to me now - I pay taxes, I'm invested in the city - so it's like the things that I wasn't concerned about as a child, as a man coming of age."For James, a 25-year Federalsburg resident and first-time candidate, choosing to step up and run for one of the District 1 council seats came from a simple question she asked herself, "Why not?" "It was more so like, 'Will I be here for another 25 years and just continue to complain and nag about things that need to be done, or will I be that person that tries to be a part of the change - you know, be the change you want to see," she said.To James, changing the town's level of transparency with residents is a major factor, especially when it comes to ensuring that the community knows what the town is doing, whether it's a municipal election or roadwork."I want to make sure that the information that is conveyed is information that is understood by anybody on any education level, like you shouldn't have to have a master's or doctorate degree to understand what they're talking about," she said. "I just want to make sure that it's plain and simple and understood."On a similar note, James said the town should publish relevant information in both Spanish and Creole to serve Federalsburg's Hispanic and Haitian populations.For Federalsburg's Black residents, the first election under the new plan is one they've long been waiting for."I appreciate everybody that (would) listen to me, that listened to my cry, and took interest in doing what they've done to get this," said Roberta Butler."It took a while, it took awhile - can you imagine, 200 years? That's a long time." 
 
 Caption: Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner, left, poses for a photo with incumbent Councilwoman Debra Sewell, who ran in District 2 to preserve her seat.
 
Federalsburg resident Roberta Butler spoke of the election in biblical terms. She said finally, someone had heard her cry after 200 years.

stories.title: Easton Town Council Candidates Make Their Cases at Town Hall
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton Town Council candidates make their cases at town hall

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 756
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With the election less than a week away, voters had the chance Tuesday to ask Town Council candidates a number of questions about issues facing Easton, including fiscal responsibility and housing.During a town hall hosted by The Talbot Spy and the Avalon Foundation Tuesday night, all seven candidates for three spots on the council made their pitches to voters.
For the council president seat, incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello will square off.
With Abbatiello opting to run for president, a new resident will assume the Ward 2 seat. In that race, Lynnette Keefe and Robert Rankin will face off.
The Ward 4 race will present voters with three options: incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, who has served in the seat since 2020; Moonyene Jackson-Amis, previously Ward 4's representative from 2001 to 2008; and newcomer Cameron Keefe.
Gunsallus and Abbatiello, along with other candidates, spoke about the town's budgetary outlook. The town's proposed budget for fiscal year 2026 is $28 million and includes a real property tax rate of 52 cents per $100 of assessed value. That mark hasn't changed since 2008.
One resident asked whether the candidates would consider a property tax rate cut given increasing property values, which have caused residents' tax bills go up.
Gunsallus said he would consider it and that it has been discussed by the council. He said the town could work on increasing the number of business to bring in more commercial tax revenue.
He added that since joining the council in 2023, he's pushed for detailed reviews of the town's budget.
"Through my direction, this council has done something that it hasn't done in at least 30 years," Gunsallus said, "and that is go line by line, every single line, in the $28 million budget to be just that: responsible stewards of the town's money."
Abbatiello said during this year's budget discussions, he was against a property tax rate hike. He said a tax break is dependent upon the town's fiscal need.
"If we can afford to reduce taxes, great. I'm all in favor of that," Abbatiello said. "I don't think we should just automatically say we're cutting taxes. We need to also look at other revenue sources."
Abbatiello said he's focused on keeping the Easton Volunteer Fire Department a volunteer organization — since a shift to paid would be "one of the biggest tax increases this town will ever see."
Ward 4's Cameron Keefe advocated for the town to continue funding its police department at a high level. He said he's "absolutely immovable" on fiscal transparency.
"I would like to — and I might be shooting myself in the foot — strike fear into the hearts of our representatives and let them know, the money we're spending is not ours," Keefe said. "We have to have the people of Easton's best interests in mind."
HOUSING
During both the moderated and open question portions of the town hall, the need for more affordably priced homes was mentioned. Candidates offered different ideas to tackle the dilemma.
Jackson-Amis said the town should "hold the developers responsible" by requiring a percentage of units be affordable. She vouched for smart growth, and said the Town Council should have more say in approving housing projects.
"We need to be very strategic in what it is we desire, and then how that can be implemented," Jackson-Amis said. "But the council is accountable for that. We're responsible. It's not the Planning Commission."
Davis has lobbied for that same increase in council involvement. Tuesday, he told residents the town should buy land and partner with a housing developer or nonprofit.
"So, therefore, the people who work at Wawas can get a house that's around $200,000 because the town has purchased property," Davis said. "I think we need to make that kind of investment for affordable housing in the Town of Easton, and we will meet the needs of the individuals in the community."
Ward 2 candidate Lynn Keefe emphasized the town should be thinking "outside of the box" when it comes to addressing housing and infrastructure problems.
"I really feel like we need to work on our green space here," she said. "We need to look at different parts of housing, not just affordable housing through the government, but also sustainable neighborhoods."
Rankin, Lynn Keefe's opponent, said development is the most common issue he hears from residents. Rankin said it's important to attract health care professionals and young people to Easton while also keeping an eye on growth.
"It's really important that we properly manage these developments that are coming on to make sure that those potential concerns are mitigated," Rankin said.

stories.title: Dorchester County Ballot Questions Will Not Take Effect Due to 'Administrative Error'
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although Dorchester County voters who took to the polls in November voted on whether changes should be made to the county charter, those changes will not be made this year.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on March 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county had made an "administrative error" by not advertising the referendum questions for five consecutive weeks after the council approved them.
"With it not being advertised correctly per state law, it would not make those referendum questions valid to change the charter," Pfeffer said.
The error in advertising was an accident, Pfeffer said, and he apologized to county residents.
"As far as blame for this, this entire (council) and Dorchester County takes general responsibility for this mistake," he said.
Pfeffer said the error was discovered in the process of reclaiming the county's sanitary district. He said that during the bond review process, legal counsel for the bond review discovered the oversight.
Pfeffer said the county waited for additional legal review before telling the public.
In an interview with the Star Democrat March 5, Pfeffer said the council was notified of the error a little over a month ago. He said the county had previously been trying to have the amendments made to the charter by spring.
In November, county residents voted to amend four parts of the county charter. The changes amended the charter to:
Have the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term. Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.Push back budget-related due dates 15 days.Clarify responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies. Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.Include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Pfeffer said although these amendments cannot be made to the charter now, they could be voted on again in future elections.
"So it will be up to the wishes of the Charter Review Commission and the council before the next election on if any one, all of, or whatever list of referendum questions could get placed on the ballot next time," he said.
Dorchester County Attorney Chip MacLeod said the county is looking into whether the ballot questions that were approved by voters could be addressed through county code or policy changes.
MacLeod called the situation "unfortunate," but made it clear other opportunities might exist.
"One way or another, the county's going to be impacted by those charter amendments, even though they're not technically valid," he said.

stories.title: Election Judge Imbalance Stirs Concerns in Talbot County
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Election judge imbalance stirs concerns in Talbot County

 September 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1009
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Concerns over election judge appointments made by the Talbot County Board of Elections are being raised by residents and local officials.Adding an unexpected agenda item to the Talbot County Council's Tuesday meeting, Council Member Dave Stepp voiced such concerns, which deal with the party makeup of Talbot County's election judges for the November election. He said the elections board is not following a state law that requires an equal number of election judges from the two political parties.
"I feel like there's certain aspects of election law that are trying to be skirted here, from both an elections director from Talbot County as well as the majority of members of our Talbot County elections board," Stepp said.
According to Election Director Tammy Stafford, current judges consist of 62 Democrats, 50 Republicans and 11 unaffiliated, though that makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. Currently, she says there are no vacancies.
The 123 election judges, people who are responsible for running polling places and verifying voters, will work at 10 different polling places in the county.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
Stafford told the Star Democrat that election judge selection is "based on recruitment numbers," which has been a challenge for the county and something the board is "committed" to fixing. "Even if we use everyone on our list, it would be hard pressed to be 50-50," Stafford said.
"Our recruitment levels are still low, and the interest of certain parties is low," Stafford added. She said the board's goal is to "be as party balanced as possible."
Richard Osborne, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, says he's heard from many Republicans over the past two years that they had applied to be an election judge but were never selected.
This year, the central committee began to document those who were not accepted, Osborne said.
"We have a backlog of almost 30 Republicans who have applied to be an election judge over the last three to four months," Osborne said. "They have not been able to do any of the training. They have been turned down."
Stafford said since canvassing of mail-in ballots begins on Oct. 15, the county's elections board "will not have space for training" or the resources to train individuals who have applied to be judges but have not been accepted yet.
"We have a window of time when we train individuals," Stafford said. Those that have applied will be "one of the first groups of people that we contact for 2026," she said.
Other factors, such as prior experience, play a role. Stafford said the board is also "looking to diversify the age of the election judges throughout the county."
The five members of the Board of Elections are appointed by the governor to four-year terms, with approval from the House of Delegates. The election director is appointed by the county board.
Osborne said the issue boils down to the state code not being followed.
"It's just incredible to me that you have state employees and people that have been appointed to the state board knowingly agree to break the law," Osborne said. "Our committee is not done with fighting this battle."
COUNCIL DEBATETuesday's County Council meeting came after a special meeting held Tuesday morning by the Board of Elections to discuss election judges. Stepp and Council President Chuck Callahan attended that morning meeting and brought forth their worries to council members, leading to tense discussion.
In an agenda item added at the start of the council meeting, Stepp asked the council to send a letter reminding Stafford and the elections board to follow state law, garnering support from Callahan.
The council's three other members, who did not attend the elections board's special meeting that morning, were not immediately willing to send a letter to the election director.
"I understand your concern," Council Vice President Pete Lesher said to Stepp. "That's a serious allegation. But I'm not sure that I could substitute my lower level of expertise here for the judgment and command of the data that the Board of Elections has to take action."
Council Member Keasha Haythe said, "I cannot sign onto a letter that I haven't received any type of information regarding this going on or any constituent complaint," adding that council members typically have a draft of the letter to view prior to signing it.
Stepp said he's heard of citizen complaints and was aware of the Republican Central Committee's efforts to provide judge applications to ensure an even distribution between the two parties.
"I believe it's very timely that we do this because if we miss the opportunity today, I feel like it's going to be a totally missed opportunity," Stepp said of sending the letter.
"Witnessing what was going on this morning was concerning," Callahan said. "There's one thing us five don't want to do, is meddle into an election. That's not what we're here for."
"I think that's what you're doing," Mielke said to Callahan.
"With all due respect to the two councilmen, I think it's sort of based on hearsay and interpretation (of) what they saw," Mielke later stated, saying she didn't have enough information to sign the letter. "And you're tainting the public's view of this election."
"So we just don't bring it up at all then?" Callahan responded. Mielke followed, "No, we don't bring it up in the letter. We have other options."
Callahan and Stepp voted in favor of sending the letter, while Lesher, Haythe and Mielke all voted no.
After Stepp's motion to send a letter failed, he provided additional comment at the end of Tuesday's meeting, emphasizing that the Board of Elections is not in compliance with Maryland law.
"He's just tainted our elections," Mielke said. As Stepp continued, Mielke asked County Attorney Patrick Thomas, "is this appropriate to make accusations as a comment of council?"
Stepp finished his comment asking the Board of Elections to balance its selection of judges.
"Follow the law, do your job, be transparent and train more Republican election judges immediately, and have them ready to work our general election," Stepp said.

stories.title: Ridgely to Hold Commissioner Election on Monday
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
Ridgely to hold commissioner election on Monday

 April 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 859
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — There are three people up for one commissioner's seat in Ridgely. Incumbent John Hurley and two others, Chad Leister and Lakia Harris-Pierce, will face off in a town-wide election Monday.Candidates spoke to issues currently impacting the town as reasons they decided to run.
All of the candidates are aware of an ongoing investigation by the Office of the State's Attorney into the Ridgley Police Department, which resulted in the entire department being suspended in March. The Sheriff's Office has taken over the duties of policing the town while the investigation takes place. Details of the investigation have not yet been made available to the public.
Other big issues raised by candidates include giving the next generation a reason to stay in Ridgely and keeping the small-town character alive despite the town's growth.
LAKIA HARRIS-PIERCE"I am running because I have a vision of a vibrant and strong community moving forward for the next generation," said Harris-Pierce. "That is a community that engages with each other. They are part of the decision making process with the leadership. They would also volunteer their time to upkeep the community."
Harris-Pierce is a veteran and has a background in social work. She is the only Black candidate for the commissioner seat, which she said gives her perspective into the needs of Ridgely's Black community.
"When I am out in the world, I see that we are behind in education, infrastructure and technology," she said. "These kids are going to grow up and leave here one day. The only (way) to bring them back is to keep it growing. There is nothing here for the next generation to come back to and build on."
Harris-Pierce has a masters degree in cannabis studies. As a cannabis policy expert, she said she would work to change the town moratorium on cannabis businesses to attract these businesses to the town. "It will bring in revenue, and it will bring in jobs," she said.
Focusing on the suspension of the Ridgely Police Department, she said, "Right now there is no solution because we would just have to wait for the investigation to be over."
"We haven't had any crime go up. The residents are all getting along. I think it comes down to trust and authenticity. The community is at a loss about what happened with our police department. Not just the police chief but the commissioners too, they hired those people," Harris-Pierce said.
JOHN HURLEYHurley has been a Ridgely commissioner since 2012. He has lived on the Eastern Shore his entire life and has lived in Ridgely since 1987.
In an email to the Star Democrat, Hurley wrote, "I love my small town and try to make our town better. In my 12 years as a Commissioner, the town has gone from a deficit to a surplus without raising taxes."
He touted his record of fiscal discipline.
"(It is) A small town with only so much money to go around- without raising taxes. Taxes have not been raised in the 12 years. I have been in office and I don't plan on raising them," Hurley wrote.
Hurley has a long history as a firefighter, having worked on the BWI Airport Fire Department for upwards of three decades. He is also a member of the Ridgely Volunteer Fire Department.
He wrote about the Ridgely Police department, "It may be a year until the outcome of the investigation comes to a finish. Until that happens, there really can't be a solution."
CHAD LEISTERLeister, an electrician, said he hopes, if elected, to provide fresh perspective to the Town Commissioners.
"A lot of people in town positions, they have been there for a decade or more and always run uncontested," he said. "I don't think someone should be running uncontested for an office position like that."
He also had some fiscal concerns about the suspension of the Ridgely Police Department.
"We are paying our police department, which I understand because we don't know if they are guilty or innocent. It is innocent until proven guilty," Leister said. "And then we are also paying to rent police officers from the Sheriff's Department. We have to know a solution soon. We can't be doing both. I think the State's Attorney that is in charge of this needs to come forth with a little more than they are giving us."
He spoke to what he thinks the voters are concerned about.
"Safety overall. We have lots of concerns about traffic," he said. "There is an influx of people moving to Caroline County — a lot of people want to make it more, and a lot of people like how life is, or was."
"... A challenge is to figure out the right way to expand Ridgely. How to contain the influx of people coming over but still keeping the small-town values. Ridgely is a great town to live in. Being in the Lions Club and organizing the town flea market, I have met a lot of amazing people. I have put a lot of volunteer work into the town," Leister said.
The winner of Monday's election will serve a three-year term as the town's commissioner.
The polls will be open from 1 to 7 p.m. April 22 at 2 Central Avenue — the town hall.

stories.title: Easton Approves Restrictions on Campaign Donations
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton approves restrictions on campaign donations

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Candidates in future campaigns will face new fundraising restrictions and reporting requirements thanks to a new law passed by the Easton Town Council.After nearly six months of fine-tuning, Easton passed its first campaign finance ordinance on Monday.
It will limit campaign contributions to $1,000, ban contributions from political committees and organizations, and require campaign treasurers to submit detailed financial reports before and after the election.
Council members said the ordinance is a win for transparency in Easton's elections. All five voted in favor of the new regulations.
"I think that (we) have done an excellent job of putting together an ordinance which achieves our goals of providing transparency in elections," said Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook.
The ordinance was introduced in April, amid a heated and politically charged race between current Town Council President Don Abbatiello and former President Frank Gunsallus.
There were largely no requirements for candidates to report specific contributions made to their campaigns during this year's election. Financial disclosures submitted by candidates when they filed for candidacy didn't include campaign donations. Montgomery, Cook and others argued that there should be more transparency on which organizations and people make donations to candidates.
Now, future candidates must name a campaign treasurer, who is responsible for sending the town office documentation of each donation, whether from an individual, business or organization.
The council has made several edits to the campaign ordinance since April, including raising the maximum donation mark from $250 to $1,000 and exempting spouses or domestic partners of candidates from the $1,000 limit.
Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said Monday that concerns he had about a political committee donation ban in the ordinance breaching First Amendment standards were quelled after discussion with Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh.
Rankin said individuals involved in political organization can still donate on behalf of themselves. And the ordinance doesn't stop political committees from making "independent expenditures" supporting a candidate, as long as the money doesn't go to the candidate directly.
Political groups will be required to file reports to the town if their expenses for an election cycle are $100 or more.
Town elections are nonpartisan.
Resident Lance Simon, a vocal advocate for the ordinance, thanked council members for supporting the new restrictions and said he hopes it can be "up and running" soon to allow enough time for it to be properly implemented. The town's next election is scheduled for May 2027.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who expressed concerns with the first draft of the ordinance potentially blocking some residents from running for office due to fiscal limits, said Monday that the final version is in a better place.
Davis thanked Cook and Montgomery for sponsoring the ordinance and bringing transparency to future town elections.
"I think the work has been done," Davis said. "I think we have really mulled it over a lot."

stories.title: Talbot County's Cannabis Bill Fails, Goes 'Back to the Drawing Board'
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot County's cannabis bill fails, goes 'back to the drawing board'

 August 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A zoning bill for cannabis facilities in Talbot County failed to pass Tuesday after months of consideration, sending the County Council back to square one.Since recreational cannabis was legalized in Maryland in 2023, local jurisdictions have been tasked with creating zoning regulations for different types of cannabis operations. Talbot County planners have worked nearly a year on drafting a cannabis processing and growing bill, outlining rules on setbacks from homes, odor mitigation and more.
On Tuesday, council members voted down two proposed amendments to the cannabis bill and, eventually, the bill itself. Opposition from council President Chuck Callahan and member Lynn Mielke, along with abstentions from Keasha Haythe (and, in one instance, Dave Stepp), combined to defeat the legislation. Vice President Pete Lesher and Stepp supported the amendments, while Lesher was the sole yes vote on the unamended bill.
Lesher told The Star Democrat that he didn't expect the bill to fail. He believes without it, the county in a tricky spot.
"I think we find ourselves in an interesting position figuring out what the course forward is on regulating cannabis," Lesher said during the meeting. "The state has told us that we must do so, and we now don't have a plan."
As drafted, the legislation would have required processors and growers to locate at least 500 feet away from residential lots, mitigate cannabis odors so nothing is "detectible from adjacent properties" and obtain site plan approval from the county.
Multiple state cannabis license holders had advocated for a reduced setback and lessened odor mitigation requirements, citing that they may not be able to successfully open in Talbot County without those changes. But those edits didn't appear in legislation on the table Tuesday.
Stepp offered an amendment to harden the 500-foot setback so it couldn't be reduced by way of an agreement between affected neighbors, though that failed with only Lesher's support.
Lesher offered an amendment to make permits for processors available only through special exception, as well as increase minimum lot size for growers and processors from 20 to 40 acres. Those changes were recommended by the county's Planning Commission, but only Stepp joined the vice president in supporting them.
Council members who voted no on the legislation cited varying reasons.
Haythe said in an interview after the meeting that she needs more information and has concerns about the effects of odor on children.
"We're gonna have to go back to the drawing board and come up with something," Haythe said. On Wednesday, Haythe said she's working with council and County Attorney Patrick Thomas on drafting a new bill.
In an interview, Stepp said there were "too many moving parts" with the legislation for it to pass. The residential setback should be closer to 1,000 feet, he said.
"I feel like it wasn't the best product that we could've put forward yet," Stepp said. While he still has "a hard time believing" recreational cannabis passed statewide, he acknowledged the county is in a position where it must create some sort of local zoning law.
Many residents have weighed in on the legislation. The matter gained traction in Cordova after a license holder said she was in talks to buy the now-closed Triple Creek Winery. Property owners haven't confirmed or denied if that's still a consideration.
Some residents raised worries that a cannabis business could locate too close to Chapel District Elementary School. Haythe echoed that sentiment.
"Children are a huge concern as it relates to the odor that's smelled, the air that's breathed in the areas where the growing and processing will be done," she said. "We just don't want that to affect the children at that school."
Callahan wrote to The Star Democrat that his concern is land value. "The community doesn't want this," he wrote on Wednesday.
WHAT'S NEXT
It's unclear exactly how soon legislation may return to the council's desk. Any significant changes may necessitate a return to the Planning Commission and potentially a council-commission work session. The council already met with commission members in September to draft the now-failed bill.
In the meantime, the county will operate without clear zoning on cannabis processing and growing facilities. At Tuesday's meeting, Lesher asked how staff will deal with potential permit applications from cannabis license holders looking to locate in Talbot County.
Bryce Yelton said he believes the county "might have to hold it" based on the fact that zoning legislation is under consideration. He deferred to Thomas, the county attorney, for a firmer answer.
Thomas said state law requires cannabis operations to comply with local zoning. Prospective cannabis operators may not be able to make progress in this current limbo period, he said.
"If the county were to take the position that cannabis does not fall under existing agricultural use, then it wouldn't be permitted as such under the zoning code," Thomas said. "So without this (bill), they wouldn't be able to go forward under that position."

stories.title: Talbot's Cannabis Regulations Draw Mixed Reviews from Residents, Operators
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot's cannabis regulations draw mixed reviews from residents, operators

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 678
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CORDOVA — Debate over how strict Talbot County should be on cannabis operations has peaked in recent weeks, especially among Cordova residents.Last month, the county began to consider draft cannabis legislation focused on growing and processing operations. As originally written, such businesses would be barred from locating within 500 feet of residential properties.
Two Talbot County residents who were awarded state licenses for cannabis operations spoke out against strict "no odor" requirements and the 500-foot mark in the draft rules. They asked the council to consider dropping the residential setback to 200 feet as they look to acquire property to locate their cannabis businesses, potentially in Cordova.
Many residents disagree.
"We knew we were going to have agricultural smells," Cordova resident Donna Albright said in an interview. "We were not expecting the continuous odor of marijuana."
Albright and others have lobbied the Talbot County Council to reject the 200-foot setback and keep the "no odor" requirement as initially drafted. Albright said at a county meeting last month that around 150 residents signed onto a petition against any amendments relaxing the setback.
Some have objected to cannabis operations as a whole.
"I have grandchildren that come over, and I would like them to not have to look at this," Cordova resident Perry Davidson said at a July 22 meeting. "So I would ask you not to let something like this happen in Talbot County. It's just not a great idea."
Recreational cannabis use was legalized in 2023 in Maryland. Talbot County's legislation comes as neighboring jurisdictions have enacted regulations on growing and processing operations. The County Council is eligible to vote on the cannabis legislation at its Aug. 12 meeting.
Discussion on cannabis among Cordova residents largely began online and at county meetings after a cultivation license holder, Lori Yates, said at a July 8 meeting that she was potentially working on acquiring the Triple Creek Winery property.
The winery, now closed, is located on Three Bridge Branch Road in Cordova. An owner of the property did not respond to a request for comment.
Yates said in an email Thursday that her entity, Hanson Street Partners LLC, prefers to locate somewhere in Talbot County and plans to acquire property by the end of the year.
She wrote that a 500-foot setback is "quite burdensome," citing the fact that other jurisdictions use 200-foot marks for cannabis operations.
Yates says her motivation to open a cannabis site comes from her experience as a cancer survivor. She pointed out cannabis' use by cancer patients.
"Recreational use has gained increasing cultural acceptance and has shown itself to be less dangerous than alcohol consumption," Yates wrote.
For the residents opposed, the location of Chapel District Elementary School in comparison to the winery raised qualms. Albright also shared worries about groundwater contamination due to high water use.
Albright said she's not against cannabis use, but that "our biggest thing is about processing in our front yard." Speaking to the County Council last month, Albright asked that the county keep the "no odor" language.
"We are deathly opposed to the continuous odor," she said.
Zac Hopkins, co-founder of Lady Grace LLC, the county's other license holder for processing, said he's reviewed more than 10 potential sites in Talbot County.
"Unfortunately, if the current draft cannabis legislation is enacted as written, every one of these properties would be deemed noncompliant; effectively preventing the production of this Maryland state-certified agricultural product within our county," Hopkins wrote in an email.
While over 100 people signed onto the petition against reducing the setback, some Cordova residents have expressed their support for vetted cannabis operations.
"I know that these facilities are run clean," longtime Cordova resident Sylvia Carroll said in an interview. "They don't destroy the environment."
Carroll acknowledged that "the further away from a residence, the better." But she added that she sees much of the opposition coming from misunderstandings about the prospective operations.
"I've lived through the chicken factory and I've lived through the manure spreading and chicken houses being emptied," Carroll said. "I think people just aren't really informed as to what it is. I think they think they're just going to be selling drugs out the back door."

stories.title: Two Potential Dispensaries Compete to Open in Easton
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Two potential cannabis dispensaries are racing to secure final approvals from the Easton planners, but only one will be able to be built, at least in the location the business plans.Both potential locations sit near each other in the former bank locations near the Giant and Walmart on Elliott Road. State law will require one of the two dispensaries to find another spot.
"It was described at our hearing as something of a race to the finish at this point," said Lynn Thomas, town planner, in an interview. "The one issue that is at play for both of them is part of the state law requires minimum separation between other cannabis dispensaries.
"They obviously are right across the street from one another, so whoever gets their final approval first is going to prevent the other from opening at that location."
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, dispensaries are required to be 1,000 feet away from each other.
The applicant for 8223 Elliott Road is BGFY LLC and the applicant for 8171 Elliott Road is Driller Ventures LLC, Thomas said in an email.
Both business were approved for special exception by the town on different dates.
According to the town planner, BGFY LLC received its special exception on Dec. 17. A subdivision application for this property is currently under review, which would create a new parking lot surrounding the dispensary. Following the completion of the subdivision, the business will also need to submit applications for building permits.
According to Thomas, Driller Ventures LLC received a special exception on Jan. 25. The business' next step in the process is to apply for building permits.
The town planner states, "to my knowledge, we have not yet received any such applications."
The Star Democrat could not reach Driller Ventures LLC or BGFY LLC for comment.

stories.title: Caroline County Emergency Cannabis Bill Moved to Introduction
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County emergency cannabis bill moved to introduction

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their Tuesday meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed an emergency cannabis bill that would allow the county to set zoning regulations for cannabis facilities.The emergency bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
It would also create parameters for dispensaries, growers and processors and where they can grow, process and sell cannabis in the county.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches. Dispensaries will also not be allowed to be within 1,000 feet of another dispensary.
All state regulations are upheld in Caroline County's proposed emergency bill.
For cannabis growers and processors, Caroline County's proposed emergency bill will mandate growers and processors to be in the I2 industrial district of Caroline County.
The regulations will also mandate that growers and processors not be located within 1,200 feet of schools, religious facilities, public or nonprofit parks, recreation areas, playgrounds, civic centers, club, libraries, registered family daycares and group daycares. They also can't be within 300 feet of a residence.
Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter questioned if the distance in feet of the dispensaries, growers and processors could be increased to a further distance from the places the state suggested.
Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds responded, "For the processors and growers the distances, yes they can be increased, but for the dispensaries, no, they are covered by state law."
Porter made another suggestion that Caroline County make a color-coded map of the county to indicate areas where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located for when businesses put in an application.
"Yes, we can put something together to give a better visual where those areas are and what the setbacks look like," Dadds said.
The licensing of cannabis sales will be handled by the state. The counties have no control of applications, only the zoning of where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located.
The Caroline County Commissioners decided to move the emergency cannabis bill forward for introduction.

stories.title: Centreville Planning Commission Tables Cannabis Expansion
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
Centreville Planning Commission tables cannabis expansion

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 660
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Centreville cannabis dispensary Green Thumb Industries request for major site plan approval for a two-acre expansion was tabled Jan. 15 by the Centreville Planning Commission to address additional comments.The original facility final site plan was approved in 2021 with two-acres of outdoor growth, and Green Thumb is now requesting amended final minor site plan to expand with an additional two acres and include a new irrigation shed and incorporate drying trailers to enclose order, according to attorney Kevin Shearon, DMS Associates on behalf of the applicant.
The expansion is a permitted use and meets town requirements, he said.
Public comment was split on the expansion.
Several emails from citizens presented to the planning commission voiced support, citing Green Thumb as a job creator and revenue source for the town, as well as cannabis fitting into the expanding definition of agriculture.
In-person public comment largely played a different tune however, mainly residents of Symphony Village speaking against the odor.
Over the summer odors were described as minimal or not as noticeable, but during September to December of the harvest and drying time, residents claimed the order as "pungent" and "almost daily."
In operation in Centreville for a year and a half, Green Thumb has undergone major odor mitigations following previous community feedback, spending over $100,000 assessing, identifying and installing technology, according to Rebecca Brown, of Green Thumb's government affairs department.
Green Thumb has invested over $40 million in the building, she said.
The location had been vacant for eight years before Green Thumb moved in, Brown said. The location was chosen for the Green Thumb's ability to grow as expansion is a key component of the business model and needed to stay competitive, she said.
Green Thumb is considered one of the largest private employers in town and in the county, employing over 200 at the Comet Drive location, Brown said.
Byers Scientific performs the testing samples both indoor and outdoor for Green Thumb twice a year previously in June, Brown said.
While odor hasn't completely gone away, Green Thumb was doing everything it could to diminish odors, "and we're not going to stop doing that," according to Brown.
Smells have been identified as coming from harvesting and processing, not just budding outside, Green Thumb officials said, and mitigation has been applied where odors have been noted to be the most prevalent including the extraction lab, and the indoor kitchen hood, where edible products are created.
Green Thumb previously utilized a cost-prohibited hemp dryer, while moving forward, seeks to use fully enclosed drying containers with charcoal odor mitigation built in, according to officials.
Scrubbing the air, the 40-foot long, eight-foot wide containers perform roughly 42 air changes per hour and filters are swapped out every two weeks, officials said.
The same odor mitigation technology already employed will be utilized on a broader scale, she said.
Brown claimed with the expansion, twice that outdoor growing area would not double the odor, "It's sort of like when you bake two apple pies versus you bake four apple pies, you're not going to smell any additional pies, you're already smelling it."
Acknowledging she was not in the marijuana industry, planning commission member Wendy Emerson disagreed with the pie analogy, stating herself as a baker, and that "four pies will in fact provide more scent."
Emerson sought information regarding the industry's standards that she claimed should have been shared with the planning commission prior, including what was the odor level previously, where is it today, and what is the intended increase.
Noting existing technology to detect other odors such as carbon monoxide monitors, Emerson sought exploring technology to monitor cannabis odors and Brown said Green Thumb could look into technology as part of the expansion's approval.
The planning commission also noted the plan's public works agreement and tree canopy requirements need addressing.
Tabling a vote, the planning commission determined there was not enough information and sought additional comments to be addressed including testing data from other Green Thumb sites during the fall months and submission of the most recent Jan. 20 test results.

stories.title: Planners Send Short-Term Rental Regs to County Council with Major Revisions
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Planners send short-term rental regs to County Council with major revisions

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — New short-term rental rules proposed by two Talbot County Council members this spring will soon return to the council's desk, though the controversial draft legislation has been significantly changed by the county's Planning Commission.On Wednesday, commission members voted 3-0 to recommend a much different version of short-term rental rules originally introduced by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher.
Mielke and Lesher's proposals aimed to address what some say is a proliferation of rentals in the county, hurting small communities and villages. Rental owners and agents, though, have said the proposals are an unnecessary example of government overreach.
According to county data from June, there are about 185 short-term rentals in operation. That's largely even with the past two years.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years. Thirteen new licenses had been approved in 2025 as of early June, per county data.
Initially, Mielke and Lesher's proposed restrictions included mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
The Planning Commission gutted most of that.
Landlines, seven-night minimum stays, a class split for licenses and most of the stay log requirements were struck through by the commission in its recommendation.
In some areas, such as with a 60-day deadline for rental license holders to submit a renewal application, the commission is suggesting reduced regulation.
County staff prepared the edits that were presented Wednesday based on a lengthy discussion at the commission's July meeting. Commission member Chip Councell said the update was an accurate reflection of that meeting.
The County Council, though, will have final say on the matter and whether or not language struck by the commission is plugged back in. As of Friday, the short-term rental legislation isn't on the council's agenda for its Tuesday meeting.
"Of course, the ball's in the County Council's court," Councell said. "This is our recommendation. Obviously, they can do whatever they see fit."

stories.title: Fate of Talbot's Short-Term Rental Proposals Still Up in the Air
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Fate of Talbot's short-term rental proposals still up in the air

 July 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The future of short-term rental legislation in Talbot County remains uncertain as the county's planning commission and elected officials have yet to find a middle ground.In an ongoing debate since May, Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher are aiming to further regulate short-term rental properties in the county. But agents, owners and now county planners have indicated opposition to the proposals.
At its July 2 meeting, the Talbot County Planning Commission reviewed draft legislation line-by-line. Commission members delivered mixed thoughts on some of the rules, but for the most part, they provided negative reviews on changes they described as "onerous" and unnecessary.
And on a couple specifics, they discussed relaxing requirements instead of increasing them.
In an interview Tuesday, Mielke said it's clear the commission is "100% on the side of short-term rentals."
"Anybody who is affected negatively by short-term rentals doesn't have a voice," she said. "And those who are profiting from short-term rentals control."
The Planning Commission left written comment open on July 2, and it's unclear exactly when that body's amended version of the legislation will be officially sent to the council.
The commission's recommendation is likely to gut a number of the proposed regulations; however, the commission is only a recommending body in the matter, leaving the County Council with final say.
PROPOSED RULES
Proponents of the legislation, such as Mielke and some county residents, argue a proliferation of short-term rentals is hurting local communities, especially village zones. Opponents say the number of rentals hasn't significantly increased in the last few years and that changes aren't needed given a lack of formal complaints from neighbors.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years.
Some of the new proposed restrictions include mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Commission member Paul Spies said the class split is a "hard sell."
"I think the law as it is is fine," he said. "Two licenses, to me, doesn't make sense."
"It seems onerous on staff," Commission Chair James Corson said.
For renewal applicants, the proposed legislation lays out new logging requirements. Property owners would need to submit specific stay logs, including when the property was occupied by the owner or family members.
"I think that's a little bit too much of an overreach," Chip Councell said.
Mielke said the concerns around how much work will be put on staff and what would be asked of rental owners aren't totally valid. She said wording for the draft regulations was derived from Prince George's County.
"It had a basis," Mielke said, adding that for tax purposes, rental owners should already be documenting information that the new proposals would ask for.
The commission at times voiced that Talbot County's current short-term rental rules could be relaxed. Commission members said the council should make rental licenses transferable. Currently, new applications must be submitted if ownership of a property is transferred.
"The use hasn't changed. Zoning follows a land, it does not follow the owner," Councell said. "So it would seem to me that there would be a way that makes sense.
"I would say that a short-term rental license should be transferable" with conditions, he added.
Lesher and Mielke disagree.
"That's something that I don't support," Lesher said in an interview. "I think that who is running one of these matters, and that should not be automatic in the transfer and renewal."
Lesher said the council does pay attention to the commission's recommendation, and that with positive reviews of some smaller aspects of the proposals, there will be an update to the code no matter where some of the more major pieces land.
"I do think that something should pass here," Lesher said.
It's still unclear whether Mielke and Lesher's proposals will garner majority support from the council. Dave Stepp and Keasha Haythe both said they are waiting for the commission's official recommendation and further discussion.
Council President Chuck Callahan says he hopes to take the recommendations into account while coming "to a compromise" with all council members.

stories.title: Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot council, planning commission weigh in on controversial short-term rental restrictions

 June 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Planning Commission members are largely skeptical of proposals to increase regulations on short-term rentals in the county.During a joint workshop with the County Council on Tuesday, the commission reviewed legislation sponsored by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher. Planning Commission members said they struggled to understand why stricter rules for short-term rentals were necessary.
Commission Member Chip Councell said some of the proposed items are more of a "hindrance" than an improvement to the county's existing rules.
"I would almost support an easing of some of the restrictions more so than getting more stringent," Councell said. "I'm struggling to see this as a balance."
Mielke has previously said the legislation was drafted amid a "proliferation" of short-term rentals in Talbot County, noting her concerns for St. Michaels village communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista.
Mielke said Tuesday that in village zones, some communities don't have covenants or restrictions on the temporary rentals. County attorney Patrick Thomas, who helped draft the legislation, noted it can be "tricky" to change covenants since many require 75 to 80% of homeowners to agree.
"They can be overwhelmed by short-term rentals, so the idea was to sort of make a distinction," Mielke said.
Mielke added that an increasing number of short-term rentals are "being scooped up by investors," which she says is hurting the county's affordable housing stock. Planning Commission members disagreed.
"I don't see where this is a proliferation," Councell said, citing that the number of licensed short-term rentals hasn't significantly increased or reached 200 in the last few years.
"They're taking them from subpar to show pieces for people to come down and enjoy," said commission chair James Corson. " … I don't think the majority of these are even in that range of affordable housing."
Some of the new restrictions if the legislation is passed would include: mandatory landlines; more detailed stay logs for license renewals; a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts; and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
As drafted, properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence would face new license limits: one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
The proposals have drawn support from a number of residents around the county but sharp criticism from short-term rental property agents and owners who view them as government overreach.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license to operate a short-term rental. Most license requests are granted.
Corson raised qualms with how the proposed seven-night minimum stay could deter tourists from attending weekend events such as the Waterfowl Festival. Lesher acknowledged it's "largely a weekend business" and said he's comfortable keeping the current three-day minimum in place.
County Council member Dave Stepp weighed in against proposals for more detailed logs and required landlines.
"To have that legislation in there, it just doesn't make any sense," he said of the landlines.
No official changes were made to the draft regulations Tuesday. The commission will hold a public hearing and discuss the legislation at its July 2 meeting. A recommendation will then be made to the council, likely with significant revisions to the original proposals.
Planning Commission vice chair Michael Strannahan said the issue comes down to preserving the balance between economic benefits and maintaining the county's complexion.
"It's the old growth versus character thing we face all the time," Strannahan said.
