stories.title: Short-term Rentals Come Under Scrutiny in Talbot County with Proposed Regulations
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Short-term rentals come under scrutiny in Talbot County with proposed regulations

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 720
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As a proposal to increase regulations on short-term rentals in Talbot County draws sharp criticism from rental owners and companies, some residents are pushing back in support of the legislation.Leslie Steen, of Tilghman Island, says there are four short-term rental properties within 1,000 feet of her home. She's worried it'll become a domino effect for the "tight-knit" community if more rentals pop up.
"The more houses we lose, the less of a community we have," Steen said. "And that's not healthy."
Regulations proposed last month by County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher would introduce stricter rules on short-term rental operations and the licenses they receive. The proposal elicited divided opinions at a county meeting last month, and there's no clear middle ground as county planners prepare to meet with the council Tuesday for a workshop on the legislation.
Property owners already must go through a review board to obtain or renew a license. Most license requests are granted.
Proposed are measures that some rental owners argue go too far, including a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, an increase from the current three-night requirement.
Lesher says the seven-day minimum isn't a huge change — he says short-term rentals are "by and large a weekend business."
"It's really, how often can it be rented?" Lesher added, saying an increase from three to seven days still leaves 52 weeks a year on the table.
Michelle Hoyle, owner of the rental company Tidewater Vacations, says renters won't be likely to pay for seven days if they can only stay for less than a week. She says shorter stays have become more common since many of her renters have gone back to in-person work in Washington, D.C.
"This will shut me down," Hoyle said. "Three-day is hard enough. We understand the three-day."
Hoyle says the possibility of the change is already leading her to seek out homes in nearby counties. Currently, Tidewater Vacations operates seven short-term properties, all in Talbot County.
"It's something I don't want to do because I truly do love this county," Hoyle said. "But I don't have an option."
ADDED RESTRICTIONS
Draft legislation would amend the county's current short-term rental rules, which property owners largely say they understand and accept.
Along with the seven-day stay requirement, some of the proposed rule additions that have received divided reactions include:
Licenses would split into two classes — one for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and the other for non-primary residences. The latter class would limit one license per 500 or 1,000 feet, depending on zoning district.Landlines would have to be installed in all short-term rentals.Short Term Rental Review Board members would only be eligible for one immediate reappointment.Renewal applications would require logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
The ask to provide more detailed logging hasn't sat well with Easton residents Kevin and Angeline Hartmann, who often rent out a second home on the Miles River.
"To me, that's a total overreach," Kevin Hartmann said. "I still can't believe that lawmakers and the county attorney would put that in the legislation."
Keith Watts is chair of the review board and owns two short-term rental properties himself. He says the new restrictions would only add more stress on county planners tasked with reviewing and tracking licenses and applications.
"The amount of time that planning and zoning spends on short-term rentals is astronomical," Watts said.
Residents supportive of the regulations view them as an improvement from the current rules that they feel are "one size fits all." They hope the class distinction could help prevent clusters of short-term rentals from popping up in St. Michaels neighborhoods like Bentley Hay or on smaller residential roads in areas such as Tilghman Island.
"You may not need the same kind of restrictions for 10-acre lots as you do for houses that have 10-foot setbacks," St. Michaels resident Monica Otte said.
The revisions are still far from a potential vote. The commission and council will hold a joint workshop Tuesday at 2:30 p.m. Lesher said in an interview that he's listening to critics of the legislation, especially those who have specific objections.
Residents like Otte say they aren't looking for legislation to completely kill short-term rentals, but instead something to provide more balance.
"What we're looking for is a better balance, a more fair balance between Talbot residents and short-term rental owners," Otte said.

stories.title: In Packed Meeting, Short-Term Rental Owners Speak Out Against Proposed Regulations
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
In packed meeting, short-term rental owners speak out against proposed regulations

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over 40 people filled the room for Wednesday's Talbot County Planning Commission meeting, an unusually large turnout for the 9 a.m. event.Many of those in the crowd were property owners who came to oppose potential new regulations on short-term rentals.
In legislation drafted by Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher and subsequently referred to the Planning Commission, new restrictions would be placed on short-term rental operations and licenses.
Mielke says the proposed revisions come as there's a "proliferation" of short-term rentals that are hurting neighbors and communities. But owners argue some of the proposals will derail short-term rental businesses.
One change would mandate a seven-night minimum stay for short-term lease holders in some districts, while the other districts would maintain the current rule of a three-night minimum.
"That is absolutely a killer," said Bill Morrison, who operates a rental in St. Michaels. "It will drive business away."
Property owners called the potential revisions government overreach and a breach of privacy. Kathleen Schamel called the legislation a "non-starter."
Mielke, along with a handful of residents who spoke in support of the draft regulations, disagreed.
Tilghman Island resident Leslie Steen said short-term rentals "diminish the sense of community."
"Concentration is an issue," she said. "Four short-term rentals within 1,000 feet is too many. There's a domino effect. My neighbor goes short-term rental, I'm out of here. Then my house, guess what? It'll sell as a short-term rental."
THE LEGISLATION
In order to obtain a short-term rental license, property owners in Talbot County must go through the Short Term Rental Review Board. Most license requests are granted. The properties are often listed on sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo and leased out to tenants.
Once an initial license is approved, property owners must obtain renewal from the board one year later, and then every two years after the one-year mark.
Cindy Reichart, vice chair of the board, spoke in opposition to Mielke's proposed regulations Wednesday. Reichart noted the number of licenses hasn't significantly increased in recent years — there were 157 in 2018 and 164 in 2024, she said.
"I'm scratching my head trying to understand why all these changes are requested," Reichart said.
In addition to the seven-night minimum, the proposed revisions would:
Split licenses into two classes. Class A for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and Class B for properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence.
Limit Class B licenses to one per 500 feet or one per 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Require that short-term rentals install landlines.
Require that license renewal applications include detailed logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
Some short-term rental owners said having to provide logs of when family or friends stay will infringe on privacy or become an extra burden.
"Our renewal process is already plenty burdensome," said Steve Goldberg.
Mielke noted that the purpose of the revisions is to "strike a balance between residents and short-term rental owners." She said many residents moved into communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista not expecting much of the neighborhood to be flooded with short-term rental houses.
WHAT'S NEXT
The proposed revisions were introduced by the County Council April 18, then referred to the Planning Commission. A second version of the revisions — which added wording on the seven-night minimum stay — was created between April 18 and Wednesday's meeting.
Some property owners and representatives said the edited legislation should've never been reviewed by the commission since County Council didn't introduce it as edited.
"Councilwoman Mielke picked and chose what she wanted and presented it without council approval," said Martha Suss, a former Short Term Rental Review Board member.
The legislation would have to make its way back to the County Council's desk in order to be voted into law. Once the Planning Commission makes a recommendation on the revisions, they will likely appear on the council's agenda for approval.
The Planning Commission received over 70 written testimonies regarding the proposed changes. Wednesday, it held public comment for over 90 minutes, including remarks from commission member Ed Heikes, who recused himself from the dais to speak against the legislation.
Commission members agreed to leave written public comment open. The proposal will return when the commission and County Council host a joint workshop Tuesday, June 10, at 2:30 p.m.
Keith Watts, chair of the STR Review Board, said Wednesday the revisions shouldn't make it out of the commission.
"This should die a quiet and dignified death somewhere," Watts said.
But St. Michaels resident Monica Otte felt the proposal is an adequate effort to provide balance.
"Balance between the interests and rights of the short-term rental owners, and the neighbors, the full-time resident neighbors," Otte said.

stories.title: Dorchester Council Talks Juvenile Crime, Other Priorities with State Legislators
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Dorchester council talks juvenile crime, other priorities with state legislators

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Dorchester 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Council members provided a number of requests to local legislators on Tuesday in advance of the 2026 General Assembly, including an ask to tighten up on juvenile crime.During an annual meeting outlining the county's goals for statewide legislation this winter, Eastern Shore delegates and senators weighed in on the logistics of potential bills the county would like to see offered.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) acknowledged the request for more stringent laws on juvenile crime. She noted that she and others are looking to see what comes out of the state's juvenile reform commission, which was created last year.
"I hear you loud and clear and know that there's something needs to be done," Sample-Hughes said. "But I think we're in the trenches of trying to figure out what is in this task force."
Youth crime in Cambridge has raised concerns in recent weeks, especially from Dorchester County Sheriff Jimmy Phillips. On the second day of school at Cambridge-South Dorchester High School, two students were arrested after assaulting the school safety monitor.
Sample-Hughes noted that last winter, a failed piece of legislation would have increased the age minimum from 14 to 16 for a juvenile to be tried as an adult. County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said it should go the other way, if anything.
That legislation even being proposed last year is a sign that "the well's gonna be poisoned" for any commission or task force recommendations, Detmer said.
"This is not hypothetical. This is reality that unfolds weekly in our town," Detmer said. "And it's a hazard to people around and it's a hazard to them."
Council Member Ricky Travers said state youth justice laws are "setting up a whole group of juveniles for failure."
Meanwhile, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the county's warden has raised concern about separation requirements between juvenile and adult inmates.
"Our facility, being limited on staff, and size and logistics, sometimes finds it difficult to house a juvenile," Pfeffer said. "We have to sometimes bring in additional personnel above the normal shift size."
Pfeffer said it's a "one size fits all" conundrum, where the rural and small Dorchester County can't as easily comply with state regulations.
For his part, Detmer said he's "increasingly concerned about the legislature's encroachment on local control," noting he doesn't think the Eastern Shore legislators are responsible.
"We need to have something where there can be more nuance with blanket laws," Detmer said.
WORKERS' COMP
Pfeffer said the county is bound by state law to pay out equal workers' compensations to all fire service volunteers, whether they perform on-duty or administrative roles. He asked if there's a way for state law to be adjusted so those working in purely administrative roles, and with less risk of workplace injury, could be classified differently.
Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) addressed the council's request. He warned that a workers' comp bill won't be easy. He added that it's important the county doesn't get caught reducing workers' comp for someone who may switch between field service and office work.
"Don't get mixed up in these scenarios where you have an audit and/or you have a person that does clerical work on Monday through Wednesday, but then ends up on a fire call Thursday or Friday and then gets hurt," Adams said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) asked council members to take a look at workers' compensation laws that other counties are bound by to see if there's something that could work.
Other potential legislation discussed by the County Council and state legislators on Tuesday included:
Outlawing the use of shoulders to pass vehicles in left-turn lanes. Dorchester County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Robbie Larimer said there's been accident concerns.Reducing or removing the requirements for the county to advertise leases in newspapers. Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said he's tried to see through a bill on the matter multiple times, though it's never passed.

stories.title: Federalsburg Considers Former County Administrator for Contractual Town Manager Role
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Federalsburg considers former county administrator for contractual town manager role

 August 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 413
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Federalsburg Town Council hosted a special meeting Wednesday to consult with Ken Decker, a one time was the Caroline County administrator, about becoming Federalsburg's town manager on a contractual basis.The contract would be on a month-to-month basis to help the town address issues while seeking a candidate to permanently fill the position vacated by Sally Slook, who stepped back as town manager due to a family emergency.
"I think the first order of business is to kind of dig in and see what's really going on in terms of the town's finances and sort of their operational challenge," Decker said Thursday.
"The second is to start helping them get ready to hire a permanent town manager because at the moment, what I'm just doing is proposing to provide some contractual managerial administrative services to kind of help them get organized."
Decker has worked as a city manager or county administrator for just over 20 years in Delaware, Pennsylvania and Maryland. He served as the Caroline County administrator from 2011 to 2018.
During the meeting, town officials said current County Administrator Kathleen Freeman had recommended Decker for the role. However, Freeman told the Star Democrat on Thursday that she did not recommend Decker.
Decker and Freeman had a general conversation, in which Federalsburg came up, Freeman said. Decker approached Federalsburg about offering help.
The town councilmembers and Decker spoke about multiple issues at Wednesday meeting.
Federalsburg is in the process of paying off more than $5 million of debt, most of which comes from the town's wastewater treatment facility.
The facility was built to support a housing development in the town that was never constructed, making it outsized to the town's needs.
Mayor Kim Abner said the facility is built to handle 750,000 gallons per day, more than double the current usage.
The town has many issues with taking care of the facility due to improper usage and rates for town residents not being enough to cover the cost of the facility.
"The wastewater and water plant need a thorough look through," Decker said. "I mean, we've talked about the rate study, and even though that there's been a recommendation for that rate study out there, there's been no movement on it. No pun intended, but water and sewer is where you're leaking the most money right now."
While the town didn't make a motion to officially bring Decker on has a contracted town manager, they moved to go into closed session to discuss what a contract would look like for Decker.

stories.title: Trash Dumpsters Removed from Multiple Apartments in Greensboro Due to Undercharges
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Trash dumpsters removed from multiple apartments in Greensboro due to undercharges

 August 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 395
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council meeting, Town Manager Cindy Yost revealed that multiple audits have been conducted on different parts of the town's finances.Within the audits, multiple overcharges and undercharges were discovered.
Yost reported on audits of phone accounts showing the town paying for multiple inactive phone lines. The audit led to about $18,000-$20,000 in savings for the town.
Yost also reported School House, Maple Village, Rolling Meadows and Greensboro Heights apartments were underbilled for trash services for a 23-month period, amounting to more than $18,000 in under paid fees.
The underbilling was due to an error with the flat rate on trash bills. The bill was divided by dumpster size. The town was not charging enough for the dumpsters including when dumpsters were full and over the trash line, resulting in an extra $100 charged by Republic.
The undercharges were deemed by council members to not be the apartment complexes' fault, so they decided to pay up to $24,000 in fees. The town notified the apartment complexes that trash service will end on Sept. 2, and Republic has been notified.
In addition to the issues with the dumpsters, the town discovered that the apartment complexes were being billed a flat rate for water and sewer services, which has been corrected for the next billing cycle.
Yost stated the cost could go up or down depending on residents' usage.
While the town is disappointed this has happened, they are thankful that Yost came in and discovered savings for the town and multiple undercharges.
"This all started looking at a phone bill," Mayor David Spencer said. "We're trying to be as transparent with the citizens as we can be to let you know where we are and where we're going and where we're headed to.
"There's been a lot of mistakes and as the mayor I have to own that. We can't go backward, we have to move forward. I think that we're doing a good job at doing that, and we owe it all to Cindy. She has uncovered a lot of money, a lot of savings for the community. In the end, I think it will turn out well. It's going to hurt for a little while hearing some of the things that have happened. It's going to hurt for some of you that haven't been billed properly, but we need to make it fair to everybody in the community."

stories.title: Oxford Tackles Short-Term Rental Compliance Issues
stories.author: Lily Tierney
stories.content:
Oxford tackles short-term rental compliance issues

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Oxford currently has somewhere between 35 and 44 short-term rentals, but according to Town Commissioner Dave Donovan, only five are licensed.Donovan proposed an ordinance at Monday's Town Commission meeting amending town code to hold operators liable for non-compliance and gather accurate data on the number, location and rental frequency of short-term rentals in town.
The information will help commissioner make better-informed policy decisions, Donovan said.
He believes the primary issue with short-term rental compliance is operators forgetting or neglecting to register.
"I suspect that the real problem with compliance, at least in the last couple years, is that people in town just forgot," Donovan said. "And, obviously that's not okay, but also, you got to do something to make sure they remember."
The town's current short-term rental rules fine operators that are not licensed $100 to $200 every day they remain unlicensed. Donovan said this is difficult to enforce, especially considering unlicensed rentals are hard to track because they advertise online without physical signs.
The proposed ordinance would fine short-term rental operators who do not comply a flat fine of $1,000 a month, which Donovan said will likely be more effective. It would also make the act of advertising a short-term rental property without a license a violation, requiring owners to remove listings if not properly registered.
"The agents are the ones that really should, and most likely do, understand the requirements of the local ordinances, whether it's here, or Easton, or Trappe, or St. Michaels or the county. And so, there's really no excuse," Donovan said.
The current ordinance restricts licenses to "natural persons," which prevents corporations and investment groups from buying multiple properties for short-term rentals.
"I think it's very clever. It really provides a tremendous disincentive to the true out-of-towners, the true real estate investment companies that just want to come into a town like ours and buy up chunks of it and run a short-term rental business, because they can't," Donovan said.
There will be a public hearing on this proposed ordinance at the Oxford Town Commissioners meeting on Oct. 28.

stories.title: Ridgely Commissioners, Residents Weigh in on Potential of Reinstating Police Department
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Ridgely commissioners, residents weigh in on potential of reinstating police department

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Over a year after suspending the now-defunct Ridgely Police Department, town commissioners say reestablishing the force will cost the town nearly double its projected payment to the county sheriff for police coverage.At a workshop Wednesday, Commissioner Brad Sears told residents that restoring the department would cost an estimated $852,000. Ridgely currently receives dedicated coverage from the Caroline County Sheriff's Office based on a memorandum of understanding. Renewing that MOU for fiscal year 2026 would cost $493,000, per estimates.
A number of residents questioned the Town Council's openness to consider reinstating the department. Concerns raised stem back to the town's controversial decision to suspend and subsequently lay off the department last year amid a criminal investigation into the police chief that came up empty.
Residents were only permitted to testify in front of the commissioners Wednesday if they had signed up around a day in advance.
Heather Amador said the workshop felt like the town was "checking a box."
"I feel solid that your minds are made up," Amador told commissioners. "Some of you openly expressed that at the last town meeting. It feels pretty certain that my words and efforts will be for nothing."
"We're not going to make any decisions tonight," Sears said. "We're not really going to take questions, because we want to focus on what you, the public, have to say. And we want to take some time to properly consider what you have to say."
The commissioners suspended former Police Chief Jeff Eckrich and the entire department March 12, 2024, amid a state criminal investigation into Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office.
On July 25, 2024, an investigation report by the Office of the State Prosecutor found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution."
But by that time, the Ridgely officers had already been laid off with the start of the new fiscal year July 1. The town began selling and transferring its police vehicles and equipment in the weeks before the state prosecutor's report was released.
Since then, Ridgely has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town. Last week, the Sheriff's Office announced a third officer was assigned to the Ridgely patrol group.
At Wednesday's meeting, Sears explained why Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker and Chief Deputy Rodney Helmer weren't in attendance.
"They wanted to attend, but they were advised by their attorney not to attend because there is potential litigation outstanding," Sears said. Lt. George Paugh attended in their place.
While two residents submitted written testimony in support of maintaining Caroline County Sheriff's Office coverage, residents who spoke at the meeting largely asked for two other options: reinstating the town's force or ending the Sheriff's Office contract and operating like towns such as Goldsboro and Preston, which receive general county and state police patrol.
"Since the sheriff has taken over, we've had no community policing like before," said Christine Eckrich, wife of the former Ridgely chief. "And a lot of the hours have not been covered. So now my question is, what are we paying for? Why are we double paying for the Sheriff's Office to come to Ridgely."
Resident Anna Mansfield questioned if the budget estimates for a reestablished town force and the county coverage are comparable.
"Was the Ridgely Police Department afforded the ability to reduce their hours to meet the amount of hours expected for the desired budget?" Mansfield asked commissioners.
Sears, who assumed his seat in July 2024 after the department's suspension earlier that year, prepared the cost estimates by reviewing past police budgets, meeting with a consultant and comparing projections to other local departments.
He said it's key to have "rationale and cost effective reasons" when considering creating a police department.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad stood up to express her displeasure.
"We had a police department, and we don't need to start a new one because you illegally took ours away," she said, leaving the room.
President John Buckle said in an opening statement that "the commissioners will listen carefully to what everyone has to say." Commissioner John Hurley provided no comment at the workshop.
As the meeting closed, Sears emphasized that reinstating the police department would require infrastructure and safety improvements to the department's office within the town hall building.
"But the police department existed how many years without those features," resident Robin Martin said.
"Things have changed a lot over the last five to 10 years," Sears responded. "The racial incidents, the general degradation of respect for authority, COVID and so on has changed our cultural landscape. Violence is on the upswing."
"It's very difficult to be a police officer," he later added. "It's very difficult to attract and retain police officers."

stories.title: Everbridge Becomes Kent's New Emergency Alert System
stories.author: Will Bontrager
stories.content:
Everbridge becomes Kent's new emergency alert system

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Even at 3 a.m. from his home, with a tap of a button Emergency Preparedness Planner Brian Pearsall can send out an alert to a majority of Kent County residents.He hopes he never has to do that, but it's beneficial the option's there.
In the basement of the Kent County Sheriff's Office, where the Office of Emergency Services is housed, he demonstrates how efficient he can be in sending notifications with the department's new software, Everbridge.
On July 1, they made the switch from their old system Code Red, a commendable program in its own right.
Why the switch?
"It allows us to be more effective to the community with updated information regarding weather forecasts and gives us a larger environment to do that with their technology," Pearsall said.
Pearsall explained there are three levels of communication.
Everbridge is a TSP level 3 certification, designated Public Health, and receives restoration priority just under Federal government certifications. It is required to be backed up and restored in order to provide for public health.
He pointed out, Everbridge is used widely throughout the state right now making communicating between counties convenient.
"We can coordinate better as far as resource needs," Pearsall said.
Everbridge can target specific areas within the county as well.
In a simulation, a test, on his cell phone, Pearsall uses the map on the Everbridge application to send out a storm warning to just Kennedyville residents.
Narrowing it down even further, if needed, he could send notifications to just a specific housing community within Kennedyville.
These alerts are available to residents who have phones in a contract with Everbridge. But also residents can receive specific notifications by signing up to receive alerts at https://www.kentcounty.com/oes.
Those who sign up get alerts for weather conditions, tornados, flash floods, and even water line repairs and other infrastructure information.
So far, the new software has gone off without a hitch as they've sent out 10 alerts since the time of the interview in late August.
Along with other administrators, Director Pete Landon and Chief of Communications Brad Russum, Pearsall meets regularly over Zoom with the Everbridge team to increase their knowledge of technology which always seems to be adapting.
The emergency team is always looking to learn as much as they can to increase the public's awareness and safety.
Like for example, in a few months time they will be able to provide IPAUS, Integrated Public Alert and Warning System.
"When you receive an amber alert on your phone, you can't stop that from coming through. So soon I'll be able to provide this to our residents and visitors," Pearsall remarked.
In the case of an impending tornado for example, he can interrupt every phone in Kent County warning residents.
He's been taking FEMA courses online, and when the time comes, will take an exam for certification along with quarterly tests.
The team's also looking to expand public's awareness like the recent Maryland Mesonet Weather Station, set up at the back of the A.F. Whitsitt Center. It's one of 70 weather stations in the state in partnership with the University of Maryland, Maryland Department of Emergency Management, Maryland Environmental Service and Maryland Department of Health.
These stations are spaced about 10 miles apart and solar powered, measuring rainfall, snow, even the temperature of the top soil.
"It has all manner of capabilities and allows us to be more effective in predicting and forecasting weather events," Pearsall added.
Like the Everbridge program, the station provides opportunities to cooperate with various local, state and federal entities.
All these expansions are part of an effort, "To create a safer Kent County by getting the resources to the community, residents and visitors."
Pearsall noted, "We're doing everything we can to ensure the public is safe as possible."

stories.title: Talbot Police Accountability Board Releases Inaugural Report
stories.author: Natalie Jones
stories.content:
Talbot Police Accountability Board releases inaugural report

 January 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 749
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Police Accountability Board's first year was marked by challenges in adjusting to citizen oversight in policing, but "reluctant confidence" from law enforcement is believed to be growing, the board said in its inaugural report.The annual report, submitted to the Talbot County Council on Dec. 20, 2023, outlined the board's yearlong struggle in establishing a rapport with the county's four law enforcement agencies, which voiced concerns with the state-mandated legislation that created the board and a committee to review complaints of police misconduct.
Trends in call volume, arrests, struggles with recruitment and retention, use of force and police-community relations within each of the county's law enforcement agencies were analyzed in the report.
The board also asked the County Council to consider a number of recommendations to improve police accountability in Talbot County.
However, the board said most of the concerns from local police agencies centered on the Administrative Charging Committee, which is tasked with determining if officers should face administrative charges following a police agency's own investigation into the allegations. The committee also recommends appropriate discipline.
The committee is composed of five county residents and is helmed by Mitchell Ettinger, who also serves as the chairman of the Police Accountability Board.
Gaining the confidence of the county's law enforcement agencies proved to be the Administrative Charging Committee's great challenge last year, the report said.
Police questioned the wisdom of citizen oversight, the breadth of the committee's role and a lack of experience in law enforcement, which could translate to a gap in understanding the tasks and competing interests police officers face daily, according to the report.
In 2023, 15 complaints were submitted to the Administrative Charging Committee for review: 10 from the Sheriff's Office and five from the Easton Police Department.
Twelve complaints resulted in officer exonerations or were ruled as unfounded charges. Three complaints ended with varying disciplinary actions — two of which involved disagreements on recommended dispositions between the Administrative Charging Committee and the officers' respective agencies, the report said.
In one case, a Sheriff's Office deputy was administratively charged for undue use of force. According to the report, the deputy deployed pepper spray in an attempt to stop a juvenile who was improperly operating a mini-bike on the road.
The Administrative Charging Committee found it was unreasonable for the deputy to do so and imposed charges. The committee recommended two days' loss of pay, which the deputy accepted, according to the report.
The Sheriff's Office also revised its policy to clarify that deploying pepper spray on a moving motorist is inappropriate.
Use of force reports were a particular focus of the Police Accountability Board in 2023, according to its report. Law enforcement agencies now submit those reports quarterly.
The board's report said given the extensive interaction between police and the public, it was "remarkable" that officers only resorted to use of force on 10 occasions — six times by the sheriff's office, three times by the Easton Police Department and once by the St. Michaels Police Department.
Another case was heard against an Easton officer for unbecoming conduct off-duty, along with administrative failures to report conduct and a subpoena to testify. The allegations in that case were sustained, with the committee recommending two days' loss of pay or leave and a letter of reprimand.
The committee heard a third complaint against a sheriff's office deputy for speeding, which the deputy acknowledged. The deputy received a letter of reprimand.
Despite a year of building relationships, some distrust still lingers between the Administrative Charging Committee and local law enforcement.
"...The LEAs most certainly will maintain that they did not (and do not) need citizen oversight to exercise proper review and disposition of citizen complaints," the report said.
Though work remains to be done, the board believes the Administrative Charging Committee has established credibility with police through its "well-reasoned and supported" opinions on each of the complaints.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey acknowledged the lack of consensus between law enforcement and the committee on some case dispositions, but he said there was space for those disagreements.
"I think that we all want to be going in the same direction, and that is to have professional law enforcement in Talbot County," he said. "I've never gotten a sense from either entity, the PAB or the ACC, that they're looking to do in law enforcement like has been the narrative nationally for a few years of some groups — not all groups."
"We understand that it's important to have a rule of law in our community, and we just want it to be done well," Lowrey continued.

Easton department announces first Community Police Academy

 December 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 5 | Section: News

 The Easton Police Department announced its first Community Police Academy.The goal of this program, the department said in a press release, is to educate the public about the Easton Police Department and to increase the rapport between community members and police officers.The Community Police Academy will take place from 6 to 9 p.m. on the following eleven evenings: Jan. 17, Jan. 24, Jan. 31, Feb. 7, Feb. 15, Feb. 21, Feb. 28, March 6, March 13, March 20 and March 27.Most of the classes will meet at the Easton Police Department on 106 W.Dover St. in Easton. To "graduate," attendees may not miss more than two classes.The class curriculum will be different each week.Students will become familiar with the different functions in the police department and experience the decisions that officers must make in different situations, according to the release."We hope the graduates of the Community Police Academy complete the program with a better understanding of the Easton Police Department and will encourage others to participate in this rewarding program," EPD wrote in a release. "We invite Easton residents to apply and learn more about their Easton Police Department. If you are interested in attending, please contact the Easton Police Department. Class size is limited, so don't wait."Questions about this program can be directed to: EPDCareers@eastonmd.gov. Applications can be filled out at: eastonmd.gov/604/Community-Police-AcademyQUALIFICATIONSEligible applicants must meet the following criteria:. Resident of the Town of Easton. At least 18 years of age. Willing to sign a waiver of liability, consent to criminal history check form, and a limited confidentiality agreement form.An applicant may be disqualified from participating for any of the following reasons, including but not limited to:. Outstanding warrants of any type.· Having a conviction or being under indictment for, or currently charged with any violent felony offense.· Having a history of/or conviction for any sexual or family violence related offense.· Cannot be a suspect of any criminal case, regardless of the case outcome within the past three years.· Association with any person or organization which advocates hatred, prejudice or oppression of any person or group or which disseminates such material.· Association with any organization, association, movement, or group which advocates the commission of acts of force or violence to deny others their rights under the Constitution of the United States or which seeks to alter the form of government of the United States by unconstitutional means.· Has a pending lawsuit against the Department.Any other indications of criminal history, criminal involvement and/or previous law enforcement involvement will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis and considered in the application process.

stories.title: Serving, Protecting for 250 Years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office Celebrates Its Sesquicentennial
stories.author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
stories.content:
Serving, protecting for 250 years - The Caroline County Sheriff's Office celebrates its sesquicentennial

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 979
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - To mark the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, a new badge has been struck, containing symbols of its history dating to colonial Maryland.But the badge itself is a symbol of the long line of sheriffs who have held the office since 1773, when Thomas Hughlett of Greensboro was appointed by the British governor after the county was formed from parts of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.Bookending the long blue line is Sheriff Donnie Baker, who, like Hughlett, is also a Greensboro native. He's the county's 77th sheriff.Caroline County Deputy Lt. Jacob Andrew is the unofficial historian of the sheriff's office. And because he's the fifth generation of the Andrew family to serve the office during the past century, he's well-qualified for the job."Jake was just teaching me something," Baker said. "I didn't know that the first sheriff was buried up there (in Greensboro)." According to Andrew's research, Hughlett was a plantation owner appointed to a one-year term by the governor to be in charge of weights and scales because he was deemed trustworthy.Ironically, the next year he became captain of the Caroline County Militia Fifth Company, which encompassed Greensboro, Goldsboro and Bridgetown during the American Revolution.Hughlett later became a judge. He is buried in a crypt in a tiny, privately-owned graveyard in a Greensboro subdivision, the site of the Hughlett family farm.During the Civil War, John Wilson Saulsbury served a two-year term from 1861 to 1863 and was required to swear allegiance to the Union.Andrew said Sheriff James Temple, who served from 1923 to 1926 "was actually a pretty cool guy." A veteran of the Spanish-American War, Temple was known as the walking sheriff."He had the first Buick in Caroline County. He always told everybody that," Andrew said. However, "he hated driving it.So, if he had to go serve a warrant on somebody, he'd walk from Denton to Ridgely, lock them up and walk them back." "The original sheriff's office was pretty much a shed on the courthouse green, and it was very easy to break out of," Andrew said. The lynching on the green of Federalsburg blacksmith Marshall Price following accusations of murder in 1895 prompted the government to build a new jail across Gay Street on the Choptank River, where it stands today.In 1921, William Curtis Andrew, Jacob Andrew's great-great grandfather, became sheriff and served a two-year term. His son, William E. Andrew served from 1938 to 1946 and, following a four-year term by Saulsbury Sparks, served again from 1950 to 1961, dying of a heart attack in his office.William's son Louis C. Andrew served from 1961 to 1994, retiring when he was 70. His son, then-Deputy Charles Andrew, served as acting sheriff until Phil Brown was elected sheriff the following year.Back then, the sheriff and his family lived in the center section of what is now the Caroline County jail. Two wings were added to the large brick structure, but Charles Andrew remembers when the original section was home."I got to know a lot of inmates," he said.He recalls the night his "mother had a fit" when a naked woman was brought in by the state police."They had to come in the front door and walk down the hall which separated the living room and dining room directly back to that one-room office" at the back of the house, he said."I would have been seven or eight" years old, Charles Andrew said. "So, she made my father go to the commissioners, and that's when they put stairs on the side of the building to come in the outside door." "Back then, when my father started, he was only making $2,600 a year," he said. "They had to supply their own vehicle. The only thing the county gave them was a radio that went into their own private car." That center section of the current jail is called the Andrew Building today.Until 1994, both the sheriff's office and jail were under the jurisdiction of the sheriff, according to Charles Andrew. When Brown became sheriff, the county Department of Corrections was formed as a separate agency, and Charles Andrew served as the superintendent for 13 years, after serving in the sheriff's office for 20 years.Charles's son Jacob, now the fifth generation to serve in the sheriff's office, serves the county with almost 50 fellow deputies. After serving in the Air Force, Jacob Andrew joined the sheriff's office and has been on the job for 19 years. "I love it. I love my job," he said.The commemorative badge symbolizes not only his family's history of serving county citizens in the sheriff's office, but a long legacy of the office's commitment to public safety stretching back to the nation's founding.At the five points of the badge's star are a Revolutionary War soldier, the Caroline County Circuit Court building, the original courthouse before the renovations, the original sheriff's office on Gay Street, and the current office, completed in 2021 on Double Hills Road."One of the things that former Sheriff Randy Bounds wanted to do was have a wall of sheriff's (pictures)," Baker said."So I told him that Jake is going to fulfill that dream of his." The sheriff's office is seeking memorabilia from the public for a future museum or showcase. If you have any artifacts, photos or clippings you'd like to share, contact Lt. Jacob Andrew at 410-479-4124 or jandrew@carolinemd.org. 
 
 Caption: CONNIE CONNOLLY/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Sheriff Donnie Baker commissioned this commemorative badge for the 250th anniversary of the Caroline County Sheriff's Office
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Joining current Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker, center, are former Sheriff Phil Brown, left, and Sheriff Randy Bounds.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
H. Saulsbury Sparks served as Caroline County Sheriff from 1934 to 1938, and again from 1942 to 1946. Note the handcuffs on his desktop.
 
COURTESY OF CCSO
 
Charles Andrew, left, served as acting sheriff and was a deputy for 20 years with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office.

stories.title: Easton Farmers Market Retains Downtown Spot for 2025
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton Farmers Market retains downtown spot for 2025

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Farmers Market is set to remain at its normal downtown spot this season, though the location drew concerns at a recent town meeting.The market's public assembly permit was approved by the Easton Town Council March 18, allowing the market — operated by the Avalon Foundation — to run Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. on North Harrison Street behind Goodwill in the town's parking Lot 5.
But some business owners expressed worry about the farmers market limiting downtown parking on Saturday mornings.
Steve Mangasarian, owner of Breakfast in Easton, said at the March 18 Town Council meeting that there have been parking and trash disposal issues stemming from the farmers market.
In an interview, Mangasarian said while he's not against the market and acknowledged it has "many good actors," he believes the Avalon is not doing enough to police market vendors.
"We feel as if we have a right as taxpayers to be entitled to some parking spaces, to be entitled to the secure use of our dumpsters, and accessibility to our parking lot," Mangasarian said. "And nobody at the farmers market seems to worry about these merchants who are being negatively impacted by the market."
Marie Nuthall, the Avalon's outdoor event coordinator , argued the downtown location is crucial for community connection. The market has been in the same spot for more than 30 years, Nuthall said.
"Over that time, families get to know where to find us, generations, their kids, so forth," she said. "Longevity and consistency is very, very important to us."
"The town has a vested interest in the farmers market being there, because we are part of a tourism draw," she added.
Nuthall said vendors sign memorandums of understanding at the beginning of each season outlining proper garbage disposal standards and parking regulations.
"We do everything that we can to be really good neighbors to all the neighboring businesses," Nuthall said.
The public assembly permit first went through the Easton Police Department before it hit the Town Council desk. While the Easton Police Department recommended approval for the North Harrison Street location, it also suggested an alternative spot at the District Court parking lot on Dover Street.
That lot is larger and would prevent downtown parking from being unavailable on Saturday mornings, according to EPD recommendations.
Easton Sgt. Patrick Sally said while the Harrison Street setup is "as safe as it ever has been," the department explored another option because an unofficial parking lot on Washington Street at the site of the former Safeway is soon to be under construction.
In an interview, Sally said the district court lot may be more of a "long-term" consideration. "It is a safety concern because there (are) a lot of people that do walk there," Sally said of the current downtown location.
Crossing guards are typically stationed at the current location during peak hours to assist pedestrian traffic on Harrison Street and Brewers Lane.
Nuthall said it's a relief to have the market remain in Lot 5 this year. She said "if a move is inevitable" in the future, she hopes the market and vendors "have buy-in" during that decision-making process.
"It should be something that is done thoughtfully and collaboratively," Nuthall said.
The Easton Farmers Market kicks off its 2025 season Saturday, April 12, and runs through December.

stories.title: Cambridge City Council Hears Plans for Harriet Tubman Mural Area
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Cambridge City Council hears plans for Harriet Tubman mural area

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge mayor and commissioners spent a significant portion of their three-hour meeting Monday learning about Alpha Genesis Community Development Corporation's plans to revitalize the area surrounding the Harriet Tubman mural behind 424 Race St.Adrian Holmes, president and program director of Alpha Genesis, said the second phase project will help extend the stay of tourists in Cambridge.
"Right now, most people who go back there stay no longer than five or ten minutes because there's nowhere to sit, it's hot, it's just not really appealing," she said. "So this is what we want to do to help the people who come to the mural extend their stay. And when they extend their stay, they'll spend more money ... and they'll just have a better experience."
The plan, which extends into Cannery Way off Race Street, is to add two retail spaces adjacent the mural. One of the spaces will be a souvenir shop, Holmes said. The building itself will also include Alpha Genesis' headquarters, three other retail spaces that face Race Street and an exhibition deck.
In front of the mural will be the Harriet Tubman Pavilion, which will shield viewers from inclement weather. Near the pavilion, there will be a community garden.
"We affectionately call this project the North Star Village, a tribute in honor of Harriet Tubman," Holmes said.
Alpha Genesis has been working with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development, the Maryland Historical Trust, the Rural Maryland Council, state legislators and the City of Cambridge to make enhancements to the space. Alpha Genesis is still raising funds for the second phase of the project, which will cost around $1.5 million. The project has received funding from the Maryland General Assembly and the city.
"And then we have a couple grant opportunities that can cover the rest of it," Holmes said.
According to council meeting documents, the proximity of Alpha Genesis' property to city property has made the project a "joint venture" between the two. One document from Alpha Genesis states the city will improve Cannery Way and the adjacent parking lot, and Alpha Genesis will focus on 428 through 432 Race St.
Alpha Genesis is asking the city for the installation of public restrooms, the repositioning of the brick wall on Cannery Way and the addition of a replica of the Ben Ross Cabin on the Cannery Way property.
Holmes said restrooms would benefit tourists who come from far distances to see the mural. Alpha Genesis' proposal is to construct a "North Star Station" that includes two all-gender bathrooms, a 135-square-foot public meeting room and a small lobby space with digital kiosks that have information about the city.
RESTROOM DISCUSSIONCommissioners asked a variety of questions about Alpha Genesis' plans. Multiple questions focused on the restroom proposal.
Commissioner Brian Roche shared his concern with the North Star Station blocking the view of the water from Cannery Way. Holmes said a possible change to the proposal could be to remove the meeting room from the station to make it smaller.
Commission President Sputty Cephas asked who would be responsible for maintaining the public restrooms. Alpha Genesis Executive Director Jermaine Anderson said he thinks it would be a good idea to form a youth or recidivism program where those in the program would be tasked with maintaining areas around the mural.
"Now's the time," he said. "Let's get real creative. Let's continue planning, continue talking, developing relationships. ... I think we can find the solutions we need."
During public comment, Chuck McFadden said he supports revitalizing the area, but the city should be careful about how much it commits. McFadden also cautioned that bringing youth in to clean the public restrooms might not be an easy feat.
After council discussion, the City Council unanimously voted to have city staff work closely with Alpha Genesis on its proposal and make sure it gets through the Historic Preservation Commission and the Planning and Zoning Commission. The vote, which Cephas motioned, also called for a presentation on the fiscal impact of the proposal and made sure Roche and any other interested commissioners can work with city staff on the matter.

stories.title: St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board Holds First Meeting
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board holds first meeting

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After months of controversy surrounding its creation, the St. Michaels Tourism Advisory Board held its first meeting at the Boy Scout Cabin in St. Michaels Thursday morning.During this meeting, members of the board, the St. Michaels Business Association and residents of the town came together to discuss the future and current condition of the tourism industry.
The board discussed potential budgets, marketing and branding strategies including combining various websites, and getting a better understanding of the tourists who are visiting and the tourists the board would like to bring to St. Michaels.
Timothy Law, the representative of retail businesses on the board, said as a business owner he is really excited for the work the board will produce.
"I love St. Michaels, and today was a huge stride forward to really understanding tourism and promoting our spectacular destination. I think it's a great group of people and we've got a great diversity of thought and diversity of background. It was just a very positive first step."
The idea of a tourism board was brought forth during a commissioners candidate forum hosted by the St. Michaels Business Association last April, when representatives of the Business Associations stated a need for marketing assistance due to a decrease in revenues within the last year.
The purpose of the board, according to a town memo, would be to assist the town in its efforts to encourage businesses to locate or remain in the town and to make recommendations to the commissioners. The board would also "work closely with the Talbot County Tourism Board on a unified, regional marketing approach."
The board has seven members serving four-year terms, all appointed by the commissioners. Membership includes residents not associated with a business and representatives from the lodging, eating/drinking, retail or service, marinas, museums and nonprofit sectors.
The members of the board were elected by the Commissioners of St. Michaels and include:
Brian Ball, managing director for the Wildset Hotel, to represent lodging.
Chris Agharabi, chief executive officer of Ava's Hospitality Group, to represent restaurants.
Katie Blaha, advancement manager of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, to represent nonprofits/museums.
Michael Morgan, owner and president of St. Michaels Marina LLC, to represent marinas.
Timothy Law, owner of American Holiday Shop, to represent retail.
Craig Bertolett, chief operating officer of COLUMBIA Technologies, and Michael McMillan, associate clinical professor of accounting at the University of Maryland, as two representatives for the residents of St. Michaels.
Included in the board is St. Michaels Commissioner Katrina Whittington as acting representative for the commission.
On Thursday, the board discussed the importance of a unified marketing message and the potential benefits of public Wi-Fi for data collection. Board members emphasized the need for a clear target audience and suggested a short-term plan to focus on digital marketing.
Ball said it's important for people to understand how tourism effects all aspects of the town's economy.
"St. Michaels is very much a tourism-based economy and it really affects everything we do from local government to all the businesses and all the restaurants and hotels," Ball said. "I think that this (board) is a very valuable economic tool to use to help the town grow."
Plans were made for the next meeting to include presentations on budget allocation and marketing strategies. The next meeting will be held on Jan. 30.

stories.title: St. Michael's Council Moves Toward Marketing the Town
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
St. Michael's council moves toward marketing the town

 June 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 342
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — The Commissioners of St. Michaels is making moves to market the town, including creating a marketing and social media presence and establishing a tourism advisory board.After briefly advertising for bids from marketing firms, the commissioners unanimously approved Madison Enterprises LLC to provide strategic marketing for St. Michaels.
During the firm's June 12 presentation to the commissioners, representatives emphasized their previous experience working with 75 local businesses.
Maya Brandon, a representative of Madison Enterprises LLC, explained that she has been running all of the digital marketing assets, including Stmichaelsmaryland.com, an associated Facebook page called Experience St. Michaels and Instagram account @st.michaelsmd.
This past winter, Brandon created a mobile app called Experience St. Michaels that gives business directories, interactive maps and events that are going on around town.
The annual cost of this company's services will be $45,000.
After the presentation, Commissioner David Wojciechowski suggested going further than a social media presence.
"I would prefer that we consider more of a surgical strike than a shotgun approach in how we affect tourism," Wojciechowski said. "We do have the ability to form a St. Michael's tourism advisory board, and I'd like to be able to see that we have a method to communicate with the company that we hire and to answer that question 'what is our target market? What are we trying to achieve?' And right now, I don't think we have that answer."
He said a tourism advisory board would help prepare an outline of objectives and could consist of representatives from the hotel industry, businesses and nonprofits, and residents of St. Michaels.
Wojciechowski suggested that the commissioners postpone accepting marketing bids, stating that the town may not be ready to hire a marketing group.
After some deliberation, the commissioners decided to accept Madison Enterprise's bid but voted to approve amending the contract so that the marketing firm will collaborate with and report findings and plans through the new tourism advisory board going forward.
The commissioners will discuss the tourism advisory board further in a future meeting, Wojciechowski said, which could be as soon as the July 10 meeting.

stories.title: Lodging Tax Increase Proposed for St. Michaels
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Lodging tax increase proposed for St. Michaels

 May 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 578
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the Commissioners of St. Michaels discussed a new proposal to address a potential increase to the town's accommodation tax, the tax charged to travelers when they rent lodging.The topic raised controversy during the town election earlier this month.
Commission President David Breimhurst said the reason he added the subject to the agenda was due to concerns brought up during a Talbot County Tourism Board meeting that the town's new commissioners, who will be sworn in next month, "are likely to approve an increase in the accommodation tax."
Breimhurst said the new proposal would "level the playing field in a way that benefits all stakeholders."
The accommodation tax is currently 4% and could potentially increase to 6%, a 50% increase. Based on the town's current budget projections, the fiscal year 2025 budget real property tax revenue will raise about $1.68 million. Breimhurst said over a third of that revenue comes from commercial properties, and almost two-thirds comes from residential homeowners.
The current real estate tax rate is 47 cents per $100 of assessed value. The added accommodation tax revenue could be used to lower that rate to 35 cents per $100 for homeowners, lodging facilities and short-term rentals, while the remaining commercial properties would continue to pay the current rate.
According to Breimhurst, the $425,000 in added accommodation tax revenue would cover a $359,215 shortfall and leave $65,785. Breimhurst said the remaining money could be returned to the town's reserves or used for some other purpose.
"This proposal, I believe, has something in it for all stakeholders and fairly addresses the issue of unequal taxation while supporting a healthy business climate," Breimhurst said.
Commissioner Alfred Mercier raised questions about Breimhurst's proposal. Mercier asked how they are supposed to move forward with this proposal with the restrictions on how the town is supposed to use revenue from the accommodation tax.
"We have to use it for promoting tourism," he said.
Mercier also raised questions about the extent to which giving tax breaks to either residential properties or business owners would affect the town's ultimate goals.
Breimhurst responded that the tax statute states that the money collected would be paid to the municipal corporation's governing body to "alleviate costs associated with tourism." He went on to explain the associated costs taxpayers take to maintain the town such as a tourist attraction, including brick sidewalks, extra police and maintenance of parks.
Mercier proposed using some of the revenue for marketing the town, purchasing banners, replacing street maps or creating transportation to take tourists through major landmarks of the town. Breimhurst said, however, that their current budget already accounts for maintaining the town's infrastructure, and with the potential increase, they will have to figure out where to put that money.
Breimhurst said that no action would be taken at Wednesday's meeting and that he just wanted to record a proposal he came up with so people can review it and consider uses for that increase.
During the recent commissioner election, accommodation tax split candidates, with Breimhurst opposed to raising it.
Breimhurst and Commissioner Joyce Harrod both lost their bids for reelection earlier this month. Three new commissioners, Jay Hudson, David Wojciechowski and Alexis Roiter, will be sworn in in the coming weeks.
Hudson and Roiter did not respond to a request for comment on the issue in time for publication of this article.
Wojciechowski said he was open to the consideration of the raise.
"It needs to be taken under consideration to understand the impact it may have on everyone concerned," Wojciechowski said.

stories.title: Stronger Together: Rebuilding Together Wraps Up Rebuilding Month with Appreciation Lunch
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.
Providing more resources and personnel to help more residents, the recent merge of the Kent and Queen Anne's counties departments has made Rebuilding Together even stronger together, Thomas said.
Thomas started as a volunteer swinging a hammer 15 years ago and credited the non-profit as making a difference in local lives.
Before rebranding, Rebuilding Together originated nationally as Christmas in April in 1973 and started in Queen Anne's County in 1994 and in Kent Count in 2004, according to Executive Director Genevieve Croker in a presentation to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners April 22.
Keeping the human aspect along with the housing aspect, Rebuilding Together recognizes everyone has the right to live comfortably, and works to repair homes, revitalize communities, and rebuild lives, Croker said.
All work is done at no cost to the homeowners who meet the income limits and other criteria. Typical projects can include painting, installing ramps and grab bars, repairing floors, plumbing, electrical, and other areas needed to ensure safe and healthy housing for homeowners.
"We say what we're going to do," Community Service Coordinator Cory Palmer said.
Rebuilding Together seeks to establish safe homes and communities for all and addresses the housing crisis by improving property values and preserving affordable housing stock, noting it is often cheaper to repair a home than build a new one and help aging homeowners age in place, Croker said.
Helen Fisher, of Crumpton, was one such homeowner utilizing volunteer services including smoke detector installation, outside lighting installation, and improved home skirting. At the appreciation luncheon, Fisher credited volunteers as professionals who get the job done.
Rebuilding Together welcomes volunteers of all calibers, whether with repairs or behind the scenes fundraising. "There is a role available for you," Thomas said.
Palmer encouraged anyone struggling with home repair costs to apply for services, noting income requirements and guidelines can change.
Volunteer Dan Hercher, of Church Hill, recently celebrated his first completed project with Rebuilding Together. Experienced with repair work, he said he loved seeing the change made to the homes and what it means to the homeowners.
"Some people don't have the tools or resources, so it's nice to help," he said.
More information about Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore can be found at rebuildingtogethereasternshore.org.

stories.title: Idlewild Park's Cherished Tile Wall to Remain Up Until the Spring
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Idlewild Park's cherished tile wall to remain up until the spring

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 572
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town of Easton's plans to tear down an Idlewild Park walkway adorned with hand-painted tiles has brought back cherished memories for many Easton residents.Like many others, Easton resident Michael McCormack remembers painting his tile around 17 years ago. He was eight years old, and it included trees and grass, which fit with his then-involvement in Boy Scouts and camping outdoors.
His tile is one of hundreds that make up a winding path next to the playground at Idlewild Park — some include handprints, names or school classes. While the tiles remain, they are weathered and damaged from the time that's passed.
After the town initially announced on Sept. 25 that the tile walkway would be taken down in October, many town residents asked to retrieve their tiles, with others suggesting a new community art project go in its place.
The town has said the tiles have too much wear and tear to be retrieved without damaging the wall entirely. But the outpouring of community input led town officials to delay the removal of the tiles to the spring of 2025.
"It has been truly heartwarming to see all of the community response regarding the tile wall at Idlewild Park," the town wrote in a Facebook post on Sept. 27. " … Hopefully this way everyone who wishes to visit will have a little more time to make the trip and take photos before the tiles are gone."
McCormack said he's reconnected with old friends in recent weeks after going to Idlewild Park to look at the tiles.
"You bring back these memories that aren't necessarily attached to the tile, but they're attached to the person," McCormack said. "Just seeing their name and seeing what they did makes you laugh."
Mayor Megan Cook was a driving force behind Idlewild Park's construction in 2006. As co-chairman of Project Idlewild at the time, Cook helped spearhead a community-led effort to fund and build the park that opened in the summer of 2007.
"The whole thing from start to finish was a massive undertaking with so many volunteers," Cook said, "and then so many people came to build it over a two-week period."
Cook said hundreds of people showed up to help construct the park. There was even a dedicated team in charge of watching over the kids so parents could come chip in.
The hand-painted tiles cemented the park as a community-driven project, the mayor said.
"The hope had always been that, as a community project, … there would always be that link back in community," Cook said.
She said the town is considering ideas to incorporate the tiles into a new design once the tile wall is taken down. The town's Parks & Recreation department is "all ears" on ideas from residents, it said in a Facebook post.
McCormack hopes to see the piece of Easton history commemorated, even if all of the tiles cannot be saved.
"It would be cool to save the ones they can," McCormack said. "People my age are starting to have kids, so it'd almost be cool to have their kids paint it. And then you could connect two generations together out there."
"You can see the weather, you can see the time has taken its toll on those things for sure," he said. "So you can see why they need to be taken down. It's just one of those things that I don't think people in the town really appreciated until they realized it was going to be gone."

stories.title: Hurlock Opens Walking Trail, First of Three-Phases
stories.author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Hurlock opens walking trail, first of three-phases

 August 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Hurlock residents have a new place where they can soak up the final weeks of summer: a paved walking trail.Using funds from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the town has completed the first phase of a three-phase, 1.5-mile trail project. This first part of the project, a 2,080-foot trail, stretches from Jackson Street to Delaware Avenue.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery said the trail is a "relatively flat," six-foot-wide, paved asphalt trail with eight solar streetlights, three steel benches and trashcans placed along it.
Since its opening, the path gotten a lot of use. Avery said residents have reacted positively to the new public space.
"Everybody said that it's great they can have a place they can walk that's safe, that's lit at night," he said.
Hurlock Town Council Member Russell Murphy said in an email that the trail has been used "much more than expected."
"Every time I have been on it or ridden by it, there are people using it," he said. "We are so looking forward to completing phase two and phase three."
Murphy said he first introduced the idea for the trail as a way to light up Railroad Avenue and make it safer.
"Once seeing some of the rails-to-trails projects going on, it was brought up again as a way to provide a path from one end of town to another with safety and health also being in the forefront," he said.
Once all three phases of the project are complete, the trail will stretch 1.5 miles from one end of the town to the other, ending at North Main Street Park. To complete the last two phases of the project, Murphy said the county will need to take ownership of the railroad and then the town can ask for the county's permission to proceed with applying for grant funding.
Murphy said the Town Council hopes the trail will draw in visitors.
"We are hoping that anyone passing through will want to walk the trail and see what Hurlock has to offer," he said.
On Aug. 3, the town held a grand opening for the trail. Avery said the event went well, with Hurlock Mayor Rev. Charles T. Cephas and four of the Town Council's five council members in attendance.
Murphy called the grand opening "a monumental event." He said although the turnout was light, he hopes that word will get out and the trail will bring in prospective residents and businesses.
It took about two years for the trail to get built. Avery said the majority of that time was spent securing grant funding from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, which funded $82,000 of the approximately $105,000 project through the Community Parks and Playgrounds Program.
"The property is owned by Delmarva Power, so there was a joint-use agreement that had to go in place between Delmarva Power, the Department of Natural Resources and the town," Avery said. "And it took quite a while to get that worked out."
Avery said that after the agreement was worked out, the town was able to secure the grant funding for the project.
Murphy said the project could not have come to fruition if not for Avery and Cephas. He said the trail can bring residents closer together.
"When an activity, such as a park or trail, gets people outside, it will bring the community closer together," he said. "Its great to see neighbors and friends out and about so we can communicate and stay in touch with each other."
