stories.title: Easton Residents Look to Jumpstart Discussion of Soon-to-Be Vacant Lot
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Easton residents look to jumpstart discussion of soon-to-be vacant lot

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two Easton residents are seeking feedback on the prospects of a soon-to-be vacant one-acre lot on South Hanson St, which will be left when the Talbot County Health Department moves to a new location on Cadmus Lane later this month.Residents Greg Zimmerman and Joyce DeLaurentis created a survey to collect opinions of town residents on what the space could turn into. In the survey, it states that "with community support, there may be an opportunity for the Town of Easton to acquire this property" from the county.
Zimmerman, who has a background in business development and has lived in Easton for six years, feels this is a chance for community members to "lead on an issue rather than react to something later."
"The survey gives the community members a voice in the decision making process," Zimmerman said. "It'll also help the public officials understand community priorities."
The survey includes a list of multiple-choice questions measuring respondents' thoughts on potential uses for the space, such as a community pocket park, housing and small business startups. It also has open feedback questions for residents to fill out.
Thus far, Zimmerman has noticed many responses indicating residents would support a new community center, a multi-use park or a courtyard with small shops.Throughout his time in Easton, he also has noticed that the public's opinions are not always known, adding that the survey can "create a conduit between residents and public officials."
"When I have attended some of the meetings, I'm always wondering, 'What does the majority of the population feel about this?' Zimmerman said. "I don't know. And I don't really know if the town officials know either."
The property, which is owned by the county, is still operational and will be through most of June. County Manager Clay Stamp said the council will discuss the future prospects of the building and surrounding land "in the coming months."
"It's going to be a process that the County Council goes through," Stamp said. "I'm sure it's going to be a fairly open process. I'm sure they're going to be interested in getting input … That's going to be on their agenda in the coming months."
Stamp said the primary focus will be on moving the department into its new building, which will better house the department that has outgrown its current location.
"We're laser-focused on trying to get them into their new building, where they'll be able to better serve the community," Stamp said.
Talbot County Health Department spokesperson Justin Beall said a ribbon-cutting is set for the end of this month. The department's goal is to re-open at the new location by early July.
Results of the survey will be presented to Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council once county discussions concerning the property begin, according to Zimmerman. However, the survey will remain open for the foreseeable future to gather "as many responses as possible."
"We're not advocating for a specific outcome or on behalf of any interest group," Zimmerman said. "This is a grassroots effort to promote a process that encourages public input. Tell us what you think and we'll help amplify the collective voice of the community."
Residents can fill out the survey by emailing {span}eastoncommunitysurveys@gmail.com and filling out the anonymous form.

stories.title: Dorchester County Council Introduces Bill to Raise 911 Fees More
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Dorchester County Council introduces bill to raise 911 fees more

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 315
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester County Council will consider raising its 911 fee more after passing legislation to increase it by 50 cents earlier this month.On March 4, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. During a County Council meeting March 18, the council voted to introduce legislation to further increase the fee to $4.25.
Currently, the county is going through the process of preparing its budget for fiscal year 2026. At a budget work session Feb. 28, County Manager Jerry Jones said the county is facing a deficit of $6.2 million, with $87.7 million in estimated revenue and $93.9 million in estimated expenditures.
At the council meeting March 18, Council Vice President Mike Detmer said he wanted to introduce the legislation to increase the 911 fee because he thinks it is necessary.
"Unfortunately, because of the budgetary mandates that have been passed down to us and the need for us, as we discussed, to look to other sources to raise revenue, unfortunately I believe it's my duty to introduce another increase from $2 to $4.25," he said.
Detmer said the county's Emergency Communications Division has a budget of about $1.9 million. He said the $1.50 fee raised about $660,000 for the county last year.
"If we increase it out of necessity to $4.25 per line per month, it would bring fees to a total of $1.8 million, which would be a large part for funding that budget," he said.
The council will need to hold a public hearing before it can vote. Detmer said he thinks it's the county's duty to consider the bill and hear residents' opinions on the matter.
"I would love to be having a discussion about how we lower these things," he said. "That's not the world that we're living in right now. Certainly not the state we're living in."

stories.title: Talbot County Provides First Look at Draft Budget for FY26
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Talbot County provides first look at draft budget for FY26

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Manager Clay Stamp said one aspect was clear when drafting the county's fiscal year 2026 budget: it needed to remain flat.Speaking with the Talbot County Council at a workshop Tuesday, county employees presented a balanced draft budget coming in at $163.3 million. It comes in slightly below last year's budget of $163.8 million.
The county's total budget has ballooned in recent years. In fiscal year 2023, it was $112 million, and one year later, it rose to $128 million. It took a sharper jump to the $163 million mark last year.
Stamp said the increases were for good cause. "You've made incredible and important investments in public safety and education," he told council members.
But Stamp emphasized that given federal uncertainties, state cost shifts and recurring county costs, it is important to curb that recent upward trend.
"That was a mandate as we put this budget together," Stamp said of the belt-tightening.
Stamp said the draft fiscal year 2026 budget currently proposes no additional job positions. The county's capital improvement plan is also trimmed back, he said. He hopes the county can focus on finishing projects already underway, such as Chapel District Elementary School renovations and a new EMS station in Cordova.
When drafting the budget, Stamp and Finance Director Martha Sparks said they initially came in $6 million over their target. To remedy that, they're proposing delayed payments for postemployment benefits and correctional officers' retirements, respectively — the latter of which is to be expected to be included in fiscal year 2027.
Sparks mentioned that tax hikes proposed at the state level for wealthy individuals may have an impact on Talbot County revenues. Sparks said last time a similar tax increase was levied in 2009, it made a significant dent, partly due to the recession.
"We had an exodus of the wealthy in our county as a result of that," Sparks said. "And it took us approximately 10 years to recover."
Sparks added, however, that the county looks OK for fiscal year 2026 in terms of those tax proposals. She said she's "not sure what that will look like for us moving forward."
As for policy and funding shifts at the federal level, Stamp said "it's reasonable" to expect impacts will trickle down to Talbot County.
"We are cognizant of that," Stamp said. "Radars are up, antennas are up. We're watching closely."
The draft budget shows $55 million in funding for the Talbot Board of Education. Stamp said the county must contribute that mark since it's required by state funding formulas. Any additional education funding is left for the County Council to consider in the coming weeks.
Council members and staff will hold a number of workshops this month and in April before a budget proposal is officially introduced April 15.
Public budget hearings are scheduled for May 6, and the County Council is expected to enact a budget ordinance May 27.

stories.title: Mid-Shore Counties Advocating Against State Cost Shifts
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Mid-Shore counties advocating against state cost shifts

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council sent a letter this week to the Maryland General Assembly expressing its concerns regarding more than $1 million in county money impacted by the state's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act."The proposal to shift costs onto counties by sending invoices simply places the State's fiscal problem into other hands and threatens local services," reads the letter, which was unanimously approved by the council Tuesday.
Cost shifts are expected as the state aims to balance a budget with a nearly $3 billion deficit. Specific costs include contributions to teacher pensions and the state Department of Assessments and Taxation.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher said it's "simply a poor and inappropriate strategy for resolving the very real state budget crisis."
Lesher noted Tuesday that Talbot County isn't seeing the worst of the cost shifts — Dorchester County may be looking at more than $3 million affected, he said.
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he testified at a Senate budget committee meeting in Annapolis and talked with members of the governor's staff.
Pfeffer says Department of Legislative Services recommendations to double the costs for counties to pay toward teacher pensions is particularly alarming. For Dorchester, it would cost $1.1 million compared to the previously estimated $550,000.
Gov. Wes Moore has said solving the budget crisis is an "enormous task" only made more difficult by constraints from the federal government. At a Feb. 28 Senate budget committee hearing, he emphasized that the budget bill is nowhere near final.
"While I still remain locked in on the destination, I come in moving in partnership to be flexible on the journey," Moore said.
Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said the county may lose $1.1 million in income tax revenue if Moore's tax cut plan is approved.
Moore has maintained that giving middle-class families tax relief is a critical component to the budget and state's economic growth plan.
"Marylanders are being squeezed. They're being squeezed by rising prices," Moore said Feb. 28. "They're being squeezed by the rising cost of groceries, they're being squeezed by the rising cost of energy."
As session continues, Breeding says Caroline County has representatives in Annapolis fighting for relief from the potential cost shifts.
"We have a lot of heartburn with the proposed budget," Breeding said.

stories.title: Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A controversial proposal to raise the accommodation tax was voted down by the the Talbot County Council Tuesday.During an impromptu public comment period, lodge owners and community members expressed concerns over the increase in the accommodation tax saying it would hurt profits and tourism in the county. Additional comments concerning a lack of information were shared resulting in the proposal not passing.
The rise of the accommodation tax was presented by Cassandra Vanhooser, director of the department of Economic Development and Tourism, on Tuesday who gave an overview of the steps taken by her department to get a proposal in front of the council including approval for the Tourism Board of Talbot County and receiving support from Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels and Trappe.
"(Talbot County Council is) being called on to balance the effects on tourism businesses with the benefits to the towns and the county," Vanhooser said. "The Tourism Board has weighed the evidence, and they believe that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages."
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels and short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Despite voting down an increase, the council voted to strengthen the existing accommodation tax.
Martha Sparks, financial director for Talbot County, suggested removing the 120-day grace period for owners of short-term rentals to provide accommodation tax collected to the county before the county can impose a 10% penalty. Sparks proposed that the council approve a request to the legislature to reduce that period of time.
The council unanimously approved the proposal.
Prior to voting on a letter of support for the accommodation tax increase, several people began to raise their hands in order to get their opinions on record. Commission President Chuck Callahan opened the floor for public comment.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment, business owner Scott Wagner expressed concern on raising taxes saying that though the accommodation tax has not been raised in 20 years, prices of rooms for rentals have, which in turn provides more funds from accommodation tax.
Wagner said room rates have "ridden the wave of inflation" and described raising the accommodation tax to "feeding the monster."
"This is feeding the monster, and the monster is asking for a million dollars more next year, so when the monster is going to get fatter. I've never seen the tax go down, quite frankly."
In contrast, Jessica Bellis, a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed concern over the negative connotation with the accommodation tax.
"We can use words like the monster that you're feeding, but the monster is making sure that we do have the roads and the infrastructure and the police department and the marketing to be able to promote and sustain tourism, which is a major industry in Talbot County," Bellis said.
Included in public comment were concerns over information. Kevin Hartmann, Easton resident, said lodging providers were not asked for comment at the time of the town's vote. He said the towns were "significantly under-educated as to the ramifications."
According to Hartmann, two surveys were conducted to gather the opinions of lodging operators. One was done by the Talbot County Tourism Board and the other was conducted by Hartmann. The board's survey, he said, showed 75% of operators did not support the increase in tax. For the survey done by Hartmann it was over 84%.
The survey by the tourism board was released on Dec. 5 and the last town to vote on supporting the raise was on Dec. 4.
"You have in your package, letters from your five towns of Talbot County, each one of those voted for the increase," Hartmann said. "But the significant difference is this: None of those towns heard what you're hearing tonight, none of those towns have the results of the survey at the time of their vote. None of those towns held a public hearing on the matter."
After hearing the comment given by Hartmann, Easton Council President Frank Gunsallus, spoke and shared his thoughts on the information provided.
"Our vote already occurred, but after hearing all the testimonies tonight, and especially Mr. Hartmann's … perhaps we could have been better educated before we voted," Gunsallus said. "I believe that people reserve the right to change their mind, and I know our votes were cast, but I am, on your record, withdrawing my support for this accommodation tax."
After much deliberation from the council, the motion was denied in a 3-2 vote with Councilmembers Pete Lesher and Keasha Haythe voting in support of the proposal.
Vanhooser, director of Economic Development and Tourism, said Wednesday that the proposal failed and will not move forward this state legislature period.
"The Tourism Board obviously supports this, because they see it as a way to fund my department and tourism marketing and promotion, and the towns, you know, were in favor, despite what was said last night, because it raises their revenue, which they need for the various things they spend the money on."

stories.title: As Easton Election Nears, Campaign Finance Transparency Discussion Sparks
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
As Easton election nears, campaign finance transparency discussion sparks

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With a little less than a month until Easton residents elect their next council president, incumbent Frank Gunsallus said he is voluntarily reporting his campaign finances.Gunsallus' announcement came after Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Councilmember David Montgomery shared their efforts to draft a town ordinance related to campaign finances.
The ordinance would require campaign contributions be reported and would limit the amount someone can contribute to a campaign. The town doesn't currently have any campaign finance-related laws in place.
In an interview with The Star Democrat Monday, Cook said they hope to introduce a draft ordinance at the next Easton Town Council meeting April 21.
"We've been receiving questions from residents and neighbors," Cook said, "and here's a way that we can move forward and better the election process for the community."
Although Cook said this effort is an attempt to address an "overall general concern" that isn't specific to any one campaign, Montgomery raised concerns with the upcoming town election, which is set for May 6.
"In my opinion, the elections before this have largely been financed by the candidates themselves," he said. "The candidates have gotten out knocking on doors, sometimes through media, frequently in forums that are put on. ... Nobody before this has tried to flood the town and the roads all over the county with signs and other ways of publicizing their name."
"We don't want that to determine who wins," he said.
GUNSALLUS' STATEMENT
Gunsallus' statement, which he sent to The Star Democrat Monday afternoon, says he "agrees with and joins hands with" Cook and Montgomery in their efforts to ensure there is more transparency surrounding campaign finances.
"Transparency builds trust, and that's why I have made the conscious decision to voluntarily report my campaign finances annually through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System (MDCRIS)," the statement says. "All citizens are welcome to go to this public website at (https://campaignfinance.maryland.gov/Public/ViewCommittees) and review all elected officials' financial reporting. Open, consistent financial disclosure is essential to maintaining public confidence in our local government."
Gunsallus said he has been reporting campaign finance information on the website for years.
As of early Monday evening, the Friends of Frank Gunsallus page showed campaign activity from Jan. 11, 2024, through Jan. 8, 2025. Gunsallus announced his reelection campaign in December.
As of Jan. 8, the committee had paid $639 to APG Chesapeake, which owns The Star Democrat, for political advertising. The website showed only two contributions, each under $50, from individuals.
Current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who is running against Gunsallus for the council president seat, said he thinks transparency with campaign finances is important at every level of government.
"I think it's important that the residents, the voters know exactly who's donating to the candidates that they're thinking about voting for," he said.
Abbatiello said he wouldn't have a problem sharing his campaign finances with the public.
"I don't have any political party support in this race or any kind of political action committee," he said, "so it's all been from individuals donating to the campaign."
Abbatiello said he hasn't heard concerns from voters specific to campaign finances in the town's upcoming election.
"I know there were some people questioning about the number of signs around town," he said. "But nobody questioning specifically, 'Where'd the money come from?'"
Along with the council president seat, candidates are vying for Ward 2 and Ward 4 council seats. In Ward 2, Lynnette D. Keefe and Robert J. Rankin will go head to head. In Ward 4, the race is between incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, Moonyene S. Jackson-Amis and Cameron Keefe.
If the council votes to introduce a campaign finance ordinance, a public hearing will need to be scheduled before the council can pass it. As a result, it is unlikely to take effect before the May 6 election.

stories.title: Republicans Continue to Push Talbot Board of Elections on Election Judge Breakdown
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Republicans continue to push Talbot Board of Elections on election judge breakdown

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 775
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — County Republicans continued to push the Talbot County Board of Elections to equal its selection of election judges during the board's monthly meeting on Wednesday morning.The breakdown by party was 62 Democratic judges, 50 Republican judges and 11 unaffiliated judges in September, according to Election Director Tammy Stafford. Local officials have indicated at meetings that the number of judges for each party may now be closer to equal, but this has not been confirmed by the Board of Elections.
Election officials have said the makeup is "fluid" and will change up until Election Day. During Wednesday's meeting, Stafford said "judges are always needed" and that her office "continuously" accepts interest forms.
According to Sept. 18 meeting minutes read aloud Wednesday, staffing for the election began in June of 2023. Training for those who filled out interest forms began in early 2024.
In the last month, concerns have circulated regarding a party imbalance of election judges, or those who staff polling places on Election Day.
Local officials, including Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Talbot County Council Member Dave Stepp, have cited that the board is not in compliance with state law.
Maryland election code states "each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges" from "the majority party" and "the principal minority party."
State election law permits judges not affiliated with either party for precincts with six or more judges, as well as "one or more election judges who are minors." The number of unaffiliated judges "may not exceed the lesser of" the majority or minority party, law states.
These concerns led to a flurry of responses from state agencies emphasizing the security of the electoral process. In an Oct. 2 statement responding to a letter sent by Gamble to the Talbot Board of Elections, State Board of Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis said voters should feel "confident" in the state's election security and "compliance with the law."
Attorney General Anthony Brown weighed in as well, writing a letter to Gamble on Oct. 7.
"Even at the individual polling place level, while all local boards make best efforts to achieve exact party balance, this is not always possible for reasons outside the local board's control, including the number of judges from each party who volunteer," Brown wrote.
Stafford stated at the Sept. 18 meeting that the training for election judges can no longer be done after Oct. 8 since the room used for training is also used for canvassing.
During Wednesday's public comment, Gary Judy, a member of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee, said he's heard from Republicans who applied to be an election judge but were not told there are no vacancies for this year's general election. He said the fact that the board did not achieve exact party balance is "extremely alarming to Talbot County voters."
"We decided to keep close track on it this year," Judy said, "and can confirm that there were more than enough Republicans who signed up to be election judges to fill the available Republican positions of the equal representation required by Maryland election law."
On Wednesday, Judy provided board members with copies of a letter written by the Maryland Republican Party addressing election judge concerns in Talbot County. Adam Wood, executive director of the Maryland Republican Party, later told the Star Democrat that the letter was a "draft" letter and had not been sent to the state board.
Shari Wilcoxon, also a member of the Republican central committee, spoke during public comment, asking the board to ensure "parity" of election judges.
"I think that it is an actual embarrassment that this board is allowing the executive director free rein to break the law," Wilcoxon said. "It is your duty to hold her feet to the fire, and that she does what is Maryland law."
Wilcoxon questioned why election judge applications were denied in February and March.
"February and March had to do with the primary," Stafford responded. "Let's be specific here. That was the primary. Those were the first people who were contacted for the general (election)."
This led to tense back-and-forth between Wilcoxon and Stafford.
Board President Susan MacKinnon stepped in, asking Wilcoxon to stop speaking.
"You have had the opportunity to speak, you are now being disruptive," MacKinnon said to Wilcoxon. "You are being disruptive, and if you continue being disruptive, I will call a recess and have you removed."
Wednesday's meeting was the board's last regularly scheduled meeting before the election Nov. 5. During Stafford's report to the board, she said "logic and accuracy testing on the electronic equipment was completed" on Sept. 16. The Board of Elections will have its logic and accuracy testing documentation available for public inspection Friday at 10 a.m. at 215 Bay Street in Easton.

stories.title: Criminal Records on Cambridge City Council: Mayoral Candidates Give Their Takes
stories.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Criminal records on Cambridge City Council: mayoral candidates give their takes

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During a Cambridge candidate forum conducted by the League of Women Voters on Oct. 5, the city's three mayoral candidates gave their takes on whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being a mayor or commissioner in Cambridge.The question is one of relevance to the city's mayoral election, specifically.
Mayoral candidate Andrew Bradshaw, who served as Cambridge's mayor in 2021, resigned from the position in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. He later pleaded guilty to five of those counts.
Now that the mayoral term — which he started but did not finish — is ending, Bradshaw is running for mayor again in the city's Oct. 19 election.
Mayoral candidate and Cambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas has also faced legal issues. In 2022, she was charged with second-degree assault in connection with a domestic violence incident in her Cambridge home. The charges were dismissed in January 2023.
During the forum, mayoral candidate La-Shon Banks-Foster, who is running against Bradshaw and Cephas, said the answer to whether a criminal record should disqualify someone from being on the City Council is not a yes or no question. She said it depends on the crime, whether that person has been rehabilitated and what steps they've taken since.
Cephas said the question should be up to the voters. She added that one of a mayor's responsibilities is to meet with different people.
"Are they going to feel comfortable being in a photograph with someone that's known for a nation-wide headline that was, not only embarrassing to that person, but the victim and also that community that person represented?" she said.
Bradshaw said he felt the question was directed toward him. He said that in a city where many people have made mistakes, a large portion of the population shouldn't be disqualified from serving on the City Council because of the "errors of their past."
"And likewise, when people have overcome the failures that they've made, when they can move forward in their lives, we shouldn't turn away from the people that have talent and ability to contribute to a community," he said.
In response to Cephas' comments, Bradshaw said his convictions were withdrawn and removed by the state and his probation has been abated.
According to court documents, in November 2023, Judge Thomas G. Ross ordered that the judgements of guilt for Bradshaw's five counts of distributing revenge porn be stricken and Bradshaw be granted probation before judgement.
In an interview with the Star Democrat on Oct. 8, Bradshaw said he didn't want to go into detail on how this came about, but it was a decision made by his attorneys, the Office of the state Prosecutor and Ross.
A court document filed in June said Bradshaw's probation abatement date — the end to active supervision of the defendant — was May 13.

stories.title: League of Women Voters Holds Training for Election Info Website
stories.author: Tom McCall
stories.content:
League of Women Voters holds training for election info website

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — A group of women came together to get trained on how to run a spin-free election information portal called Vote 411. They came with laptops from as far as Frederick and St. Mary's counties to be ready for this year's primary election on May 14.This exacting and meticulous training is what the nonprofit the League of Women Voters is all about. They hold the power to vote as sacred and nonpartisan information about that vote to be integral.
"The goal is to provide training for the people that are going to be doing the voters guide and inputting information in the Vote 411 website," said the president of the Queen Anne's County League of Women Voters, Elizabeth Hammond.
"This is it for in-person training. There will be an online training on Saturday, Jan. 20. I think it is a good idea to do both of them," Hammond said.
She said the organization gets donations to do this work and create the voters guide both online and in print.
"We insert it in the Record Observer and then order about 500 extra copies and distribute them to towns and post offices and various other public places to pick up and get information to make intelligent decisions about what they want to vote for," Hammond said.
She is clear about the big picture of voting rights.
"Voting is one of the freedoms that we absolutely cherish. You want to be able to make a responsible decision and vote for the candidate that you think can do the best job. That is what we try to do with the voter's guide — to give the voters the best information possible in a nonpartisan way," Hammond said.
She said this primary election will be smaller than the general election, which will have a more involved voter's guide.
The state Board of Elections is the ultimate authority for the League of Women Voters.
"It amazing what the state Board does. What the election boards do is amazing, and they really deserve all the support we can give them and their thanks. That's why you watch the candidate listings on the state board, because that is what is going to show up, and then the proof comes when they send out the individual ballots for each county. The hard thing is you have to look through each one of those ballots. It is like 200 pages long," said Jeanne Halpin of the League of Women Voters of Maryland.
She led the training that took place at the Queen Anne's County Public Library in Centreville.
She tried to be less daunting to all the volunteers that showed up across the state.
"This is just a great learning opportunity. Don't get stressed, don't go crazy. The political parties are nominating candidates. They are asking people to run. In both the primary and the general," Halpin said.

stories.title: Residents Challenge Solar Project Over Zoning, Health Risks
stories.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
stories.content:
Residents challenge solar project over zoning, health risks

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Public Service Commission heard residents' concerns Tuesday over a proposed community solar project on 41 acres of a 199-acre property at 10066 Peacock Corner Road in Millington, owned by David Chance.The project, designated TPE MD KE51, is being developed by Turning Point Energy (TPE), a renewable energy firm that has spearheaded several solar initiatives in Maryland, including a second proposal in Kennedyville. According to company information, Turning Point focuses on sustainable, ground-mounted solar projects designed to expand clean energy access in the region.
More than a dozen residents gathered at Galena Elementary School at 7 p.m. for the PSC hearing, moderated by Chief Public Utility Law Judge Chuck McLean. In addition to Turning Point representatives, legal counsel, and project managers, officials from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, Kent County Attorney Tom Yeager and Planning, Housing and Zoning deputy Carla Gerber were in attendance.
After brief introductions by Turning Point's team, Yeager and Gerber outlined the county's position. Yeager noted that local zoning restricts solar projects in this agriculture district to five acres and contended that Turning Point should have applied for a special exception. Project manager Frances Yuhas said the company was aware of the five‐acre limit for utility-scale solar in the district and chose not to seek an exception, adding that final approval lies with the Public Service Commission under state preemption.
Resident Darryl Calloway expressed his concern, saying, "I would love someone to address the health concerns I have such as microwaves. Anyone who lives near these arrays, what happens to them?"
Certified solar thermal engineer Dick Durham raised additional issues about panel efficiency and recycling challenges, noting that the panels contain materials such as lead and cadmium telluride. He also warned that pending legislation, Senate Bill 0931, could reshape land-use controls in ways reminiscent of eminent domain.
When asked about the origin of the panels, Yuhas said production could occur in the United States but noted that international manufacturing — including in Mexico or China —remains a possibility. Maryland Department of Natural Resources official Ginny Rogers addressed environmental risk concerns, stating, "From what we see there is no risk at all involved," and outlined plans to plant native, pollinator-friendly ground cover to boost biodiversity.
Kennedyville resident Judi Gifford questioned the economic benefits of the array, asking, "Are there any savings for residents at all?" Yuhas replied that subscribers to the power would be guaranteed a 5 to 10 percent discount over a 25-year subscription. Gerber added that the county would likely reclassify the property as commercial rather than agricultural, potentially increasing tax revenue.
At the hearing, Turning Point announced they committed to a $52,000 donation to Kent County's agricultural preservation program — a request based on state law calculations of agricultural value. Representatives from the company stayed afterward to discuss next steps pending a PSC decision on their certificate of public convenience and necessity.
When asked how they felt the county received their project proposal, TPE representative, Attorney Margaret Witherup of Witherup Allen Law admitted, "It's hard to tell. Each site is different."
No other comment were received from Turning Point legal counsel, Attorney Witherup, or from representatives at Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. Kent County officials said they will continue to monitor developments in the project. More details can be found under Case No. 9742 at the Maryland PSC website.

stories.title: Caroline County Commissioners Discuss Multiple Solar Issues
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline County Commissioners discuss multiple solar issues

 February 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — At their meeting Tuesday, The Caroline County Commissioners discussed a solar application issue that led to the county intervening.An application for a 3.0 milliwatt solar facility near Federalsburg, filed by Chaberton Solar Pahar LLC, does not meet requirements laid out by the county, County Attorney Stewart Barroll said at the meeting. The company has requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area where such developments are prohibited by the county, the commissioners said.
Barroll said the applicant had been informed by the county prior to submitting the application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, Barroll said.
But other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
Barroll said the Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
"So the department of natural resources came in and over said a project that we said wasn't complete was complete," Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said.
"We're getting steam rolled by the state," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding added.
Next steps in the application process will include public hearings, which the commissioners have been invited to, Barroll said.
The Caroline County commissioners are concerned about the precedent this case may set for future solar applications, the commissioners said Tuesday.
"We have to draw the line somewhere," Porter said.
At the meeting, the commissioners also discussed another solar application in which they will be intervening.
An approximately 40-acre solar facility to be constructed on a farm near Greensboro does not meet a new setback regulation the county implemented, requiring a 200-foot setback from adjoining properties. The commissioners said they would not oppose the project, which meets all other county requirements, should that issue be remedied.
Along with the state's role in solar applications, the commissioner voiced anxieties about legislation making its way through the General Assembly.
The county also has concern about proposed Senate Bill 931, which would prohibit a county from enacting zoning laws or adopting regulations restricting or prohibiting the construction or operation of ground-mounted solar systems or facilities.
The county currently has a 2,000 acre moratorium in place for solar development, which is being neared but has not yet been met.
This proposed bill would put the county in another situation where legislation the county has enacted, including an acreage moratorium on solar development, could be overruled by state agencies, the commissioners said.
"We're gonna have to fight every application. We're gonna spend time and money fighting every application, and we're probably gonna get steam rolled every time, that's the way its looking," Breeding said.

stories.title: Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming
stories.author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a 3-2 vote, the Dorchester County Council passed a bill that addresses setbacks and buffers, ownership, and decommissioning plans for accessory, small scale and utility scale solar energy systems.After the bill was passed at a meeting on Nov. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said this is a start for solar legislation in the county.
"Laws can be amended and modified," he said. "But if we don't do something now, before the start of the General Assembly, we could be facing much worse without any safeguards in place."
Council members Rob Kramer and William Nichols voted against the bill. Council member Ricky Travers, Council Vice President Mike Detmer and Pfeffer voted in favor of it.
Under the new bill, solar developments located off scenic byways will need to be set back 100 feet from all property lines, and developments that are not located off of scenic byways will need to be set back 75 feet. Requirements regarding vegetative buffers, perimeter fencing, topsoil and site plans are also in the legislation.
The bill defines who the owners of a solar site are. Pfeffer said in an interview with the Star Democrat in September that the owners of the property and the operator of the solar development would both be considered the owner.
The bill was reintroduced in September after getting tabled in March. In the reintroduced bill, a section was added regarding decommissioning solar projects. Per the legislation, a decommissioning plan will need to be submitted and approved by the county prior to the building permit application.
In the September interview, Pfeffer said the bill was tabled so the council could wait for state solar legislation to go into affect and make sure the county was in line with it.
At the meeting Nov. 4, residents thanked the council for their efforts and shared concerns that the county bill doesn't do enough to restrict solar development.
The reintroduced bill left out a section in the original proposed bill that put a cap on how many aggregate acres of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems.
Beth Hill said although she feels the bill is a step in the right direction, she thinks there needs to be a cap on the number of acres in the county that can be used for solar development.
"Other counties around us do have caps," she said, mentioning Caroline County, which has a 2,000-acre cap on total rural land available for solar development.
Tracy Whitby-Fairall, who attended a town hall on the subject that Detmer hosted the previous week, said she recognized the county's efforts. She called the bill a "good foundation for a strong framework" for the county.
"I think there are some things that could be improved," she said, later adding, "I hope this isn't the end of the legislation. I hope this is the beginning."
Erick Windsor, who asked the council to vote against the bill, talked about the county's history of thriving tomato, dairy and lumber industries, which are now gone. He said that large solar operations take land away from grain farming.
"And this is going to affect all the other industries in this county that work around grain farming, like chicken farming," he said. "So you hurt the chicken farmers and you're going to hurt the industry in Hurlock that processes all this stuff."
Windsor said more restrictions need to be put on solar so it doesn't "decimate" the north part of the county.
Detmer said the bill — especially the decommissioning component — is "crucial" to have at the county level before the Maryland General Assembly session begins in January. He talked about the possibility of additional legislation coming down from the state.
"The Wild West of solar that we are in right now, I'm very bothered by it," he said. "I think we have to plant our flag here in this place that we're ready to go right now. If we don't act tonight, the law's not going to be in place when the session starts."
Detmer said this isn't the end of creating legislation around solar, but action needs to be taken now.
"We've got to put the seatbelt on," he said.

stories.title: Caroline Commissioners Hear Options for Landfill After 2030
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Caroline commissioners hear options for landfill after 2030

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County could remain the host of the regional landfill for 12 years longer than originally planned.At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday morning, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn, CPA and Queen Anne's County Consultant Joe Zimmerman and Queen Anne's County Commissioner James Moran came to speak about the possibility of using the Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill in Ridgely through 2042 rather than building a new landfill in Queen Anne's County for 2031.
During their presentation, Mohn said Maryland Environmental Service has been working with county administrators to evaluate the future of Mid-Shore II, and it has concluded that the landfill could "easily provide service" to the citizens of the region through approximately 2042.
The Mid-Shore II landfill, which was opened in 2011, provides services to Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties.
Mohn explained that in the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, if the partnering counties agreed, they could instead extend the lifetime of Caroline County's landfill.
During the presentation, Mohn listed reasons why Queen Anne's County feels this option makes sense. For Caroline County, he said that this option would provide economic stability for Ridgely businesses and that the county would get a host fee for the extension of service.
He said the option would also maximize the value of public infrastructure, defer liability for debt to construct a new landfill, maintain shorter haul routes for Talbot County and avoid the cost of a transfer operation.
Moran said landfills are at a premium.
"We want to maximize that," he said about the space in each landfill. "And if this (provides) us with an extra 30 years of life that we didn't have coming into this 80-year deal, then that's a good thing for the environment, it's a good thing for the Eastern Shore."
If this proposal moves forward, all of the partnering counties would need to come to an agreement on a modified arrangement, including the host fee for Caroline County.
At the meeting, Zimmerman presented three options for host fees and annual tipping fee increases for the Mid-Shore II landfill:
A host fee of $2 per ton of waste growing to $4 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.15% in tipping fees.A host fee of $3 per ton of waste growing to $5 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.35% in tipping fees.A host fee of $4 per ton of waste growing to $6 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.5% in tipping fees.
"We think these are achievable options," Zimmerman said about the three options. "It's really the question of how much risk the counties want to take on in terms of their competitive posture."
He said that historically, tipping fees have, on average, annually increased by 1.42%.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said he has made it clear to MES that he agrees with keeping the landfill operating in Caroline County for environmental and economic reasons, but he would like to make sure the county retains "any of the savings associated with the extension of the landfill."
He said the county's residents are the ones burdened with the affects of the landfill operations, including truck traffic and bad smells from time to time.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter spoke about the impact of MES operations on the county.
He said that although this proposal is an opportunity to generate more revenue without raising property taxes, having the landfill in the county has affected the condition of the roads where trash is being driven, including trash left on those roads. He said the extension of the landfill's services would be a hard sell to the public.
"For me, anything that we do is going to have to involve MES stepping up to the plate and fulfilling what I think the obligations and responsibilities are," he said, adding that roads would be part of that obligation, in his mind.
Porter asked the presenters if it appears that the other partnering counties are on board with keeping the landfill in Caroline County and paying a host fee. Mohn said everyone seems to be in agreement.
"The question is, what is that host fee going to be?" Mohn said.
Porter said the county will have a public hearing on this in the future. He did not give a date.

stories.title: New Year Ushers in Single-Use Plastic Bag Ban in Town of Centreville
stories.author: Staff Writer
stories.content:
New Year ushers in single-use plastic bag ban in Town of Centreville

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The town of Centreville instituted a single-use plastic bag ban that went into effect on Jan. 1.Centreville joins Anne Arundel and Prince George's counties and the City of Frederick whose plastic bag bans also started the first of the year. According to the Maryland Retailer's Alliance, more than 70% of Marylanders now live in jurisdictions with carry out bag policies in place.
On July 20, 2023, Centreville Town Council passed the ordinance to ban single-use plastic carry out bags within Centreville town limits.
For Town Council President Ashley Kaiser while the ban addresses single-use plastic bags the spirit of the ordinance is to encourage the use of reusable bags and eliminate the reliance on plastic bags, many of which end up polluting our highways and waterways.
"Consumers have an opportunity to play a significant role in the implementation of this bill. I don't think that anyone who is shopping at a local business wants to burden a local business, but instead wants to support them. If a paper bag fee is going to be a problem for you, decline the bag," says Kaiser. "There are things people can do to change their behavior like making a point to remember to always carry reusable bags with them," she adds.
Following that philosophy, the Town of Centreville launched a "Bring Your Own Bag" campaign in October in coordination with Plastic Free QAC. The campaign included specially designed reusable bags with a rack card featuring information on the bag ban as well as tips for how to remember to bring your bag to your next shopping trip.
Bags were handed out at Centreville Day in October and at the Centreville Farmers' Market Heck with the Malls market day in December and were made available at Town Hall. A limited supply of Town reusable bags and vintage farmers' market reusable bags are currently available for consumers to pick up at Centreville Town Hall from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday.
The Centreville single-use plastic bag ordinance stipulates that retail establishments with the exception of food service facilities "shall charge, collect and retain at least 10 cents for each paper carry out bag that it provides to a customer."
Exceptions to the ordinance includes, but are not limited to:
Nonprofit fraternal, civic, war veterans, religious, or charitable organizations and fire companies can still use plastic carry out bags.
Due to cross contamination concerns restaurants may not allow customers to use their own reusable bags. Restaurants will provide paper bags, but will not charge a paper bag fee.
The Centreville Market's Market and cottage food businesses can continue to use plastic.
Pharmacies and opticians will not charge a paper bag fee for prescription items.
Consumers and business owners who want to read the full text of the ordinance and frequently asked questions can visit townofcentreville.org and type "plastic bag ban" in the search window. For more information, please contact Carol D'Agostino, mainstreet@townofcentreville.org or 410-758-1180, ext. 17.

stories.title: Dorchester County Public Schools Faces Budget Deficit
stories.author: Maggie Trovato
stories.content:
Dorchester County Public Schools faces budget deficit

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 636
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County Public Schools prepares to submit its fiscal year 2026 budget to the county, it is also preparing for some tough conversations.With $86 million in expected revenues and $97.5 million in estimated expenses for fiscal year 2026, the district is facing a deficit. Currently, with carryover in funds from previous years, the estimated deficit is at $10.19 million.
"We've just got some difficult decisions to make as a district on how we're going to move forward with the current budget crisis that we're in," DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson said during a Dorchester County Board of Education budget work session Thursday.
Jodi Colman, district assistant superintendent of academics and student services, said the budget increases for fiscal year 2026 make it possible to keep the district's current staff in place.
"This would just be to basically maintain the programs that we have right now," she said about the draft budget. "All of those increases were due to just keeping our staff that we have for the most part."
Thompson said "a whole host of things" has caused the deficit, mentioning fixed costs and unfunded mandates from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a plan passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state.
Board of Education Member Brandy Dawson Cumberland said that although the board likes a lot of what the Blueprint aims to do, there are "certain unfunded mandates that are going to cut other things."
Thompson said the district is still waiting on exact numbers from the state and county. He said once they have those numbers, it is possible the deficit could be lower than $10.19 million.
"But I don't think that it will be higher than that," he said.
So far, the district has taken a number of actions to reduce the deficit, Thompson said. This includes:
Reducing some positions added with Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief fundingSending emails about non-essential spendingDeciding not to hire for vacated positionsReducing the central office custodian scheduleReducing student support monitorsMerging some job dutiesEliminating the education specialist position
"We did try to make some significant changes," Thompson said. "And there's more that I didn't put up that we have done. But the reality is it's not enough."
The district is looking into more actions that can be taken to reduce the deficit. Some possible actions include revisiting who should have board vehicles, auditing and reducing the number of programs and platforms the district uses, revising overtime policies, sharing resources with the county and reducing staff.
"No one wants this one," Thompson said about reducing staff.
While listing different "cost containment options" Thompson and board members made it clear that the district hasn't made any decisions yet, and is just looking at potential cost-cutting options.
"We are just at the beginning of starting to think about what things we can do to attack that number," Board of Education Vice President Talibah Chikwendu said.
"And that's why we really would like to have public input to know what the public feels are areas we should focus on if possible," Board President Sheri Hubbard said. "Because we want to do what's best for kids, bottom line."
The Dorchester County Board of Education will host another budget work session on Feb. 13. It will also hold one in March. The district's proposed budget must be submitted to the county in June.
Board Member Chris Wheedleton said that if community members are able to do anything, they should talk with their representatives in Annapolis.
"Because we need their help," he said.
Thompson urged that this is the time to work together and not be divided.
"Because at the end of the day, we know that $10 million deficit that we're in, that's going to hurt the kids," he said. "That's going to have a profound impact on how we can provide resources for our students."

stories.title: Sale of Daysprings Townhomes Will Come Soon Caroline County Says
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Sale of Daysprings Townhomes will come soon Caroline County says

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 326
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have discussed the sale of Daysprings Townhomes throughout 2025, now the sale looks like it may happen.At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting on Tuesday, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman said that paperwork with legal teams are being prepared and negotiations are ongoing on the potential sale of Daysprings Townhomes.
"We're down to just what I would say wording, not much left to get that contract finished and I don't need to speak for Stewart, but he's drafted up the letters to notify the tenants and all of those things. So we're making really good progress on Daysprings," Freeman said.
The Dayspring Townhomes complex is located just outside Ridgely on School Street. The initial property was built in 1994 by Interfaith Housing Development, a former local nonprofit that worked with the county.
That nonprofit ceased operations a handful of years ago, leaving the low-income housing complex in the hands of its owners, Caroline County, and the contracted property management company, East Coast.
According to Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding, the decision to sell is due to a lack of funding to properly repair the complex.
"There's limited state money available to renovate the apartments that are there, and it's very difficult to get a hold of the money. So really the the best path moving forward is to sell it to a private company and just have them renovate as needed to make it fair market value housing," Breeding said.
According to Freeman, once the contract is signed, the county will notify tenants of the sale and advise them with an option to extend their lease for one year. The apartments will be sold to a private entity who will rent the units at market rate.
According to Freeman, the purchaser intends to renovate the apartments, but the timeline is unknown. The county will offer relocation assistance to all tenants.
The county will follow state requirements with the sale of Daysprings Townhomes and the movement of the tenants.

stories.title: Assessments and Taxation Discussion at Caroline County Meeting
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett
stories.content:
Assessments and taxation discussion at Caroline County meeting

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 485
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — In anticipation of changes to the division of costs for property assessment, the Caroline County Commissioners asked questions of Keith Bobbick, Caroline County supervisor of assessments and taxation, about some general operation of the department.A part of Gov. Wes Moore's proposed budget is a shift of more expenses for property assessment services to the county.
Counties will be responsible for 90% of operational costs for their assessment offices if the budget is passed as written, according to Commission President Travis Breeding. Currently, the county and the state split the cost of operation evenly.
The commissioners' questions dealt with how things were assessed and the process of assessment. In particular, the commissioners wanted to know what the process looked like for having agricultural properties reassessed for commercial uses.
The tax money paid for a property goes up when agricultural properties turn into commercial properties, making the taxes more expensive for the land owner and generating further revenue for the county and other taxing agencies.
"That happens once a year," Bobbick said. "It's usually in July, and it happens whenever the change actual starts from agricultural use to some other use."
By law, the towns and counties are supposed to provide permits about new operations in their area. A problem the assessment office faces is not receiving information on properties from the towns in a timely manner.
If the properties are not reported by the town, the assessments office will have no knowledge of the property, which could cause the reassessment to be delayed until after the July deadline, limiting the taxes that can be collected.
The county suggested the assessment office make a list of the towns it is having trouble with so the commissioners could encourage them to remain on top of reporting new developments.
Another big concern from the county is that a lot of taxpayers are showing up in the county tax office with assessment questions. The taxpayers are saying that the voicemail of Caroline County Assessment Office is directing them there.
"When you call our main line, it does have a bit in that in there," Bobbick said. "It says 'if you have a question about your tax bill, call the tax office.' When people come into our office, we try to help them as much as we can. If they have a question about their tax bill, we're gonna try to help them."
Commissioner Frank Bartz also questioned the assessment office's hybrid work schedule.
By state law, the assessment office employees are only required to work from the office three days a week.
Commissioner Frank Bartz questioned whether when the staff is working from home, they can accomplish all the necessary tasks.
"Anything we can do in the office, we can do from home," Bobbick said. Bartz responded, "expect answer the phone."
Bobbick informed Bartz that there is always someone in the office to answer the phone.
The county commissioners suggested that the language in the voicemail be changed to not confuse taxpayers.

stories.title: Body Cam Video Released of Cambridge Officer-Involved Shooting
stories.author: Staff Report
stories.content:
Body cam video released of Cambridge officer-involved shooting

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Dorchester 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BALTIMORE — A man who was shot and killed by a Cambridge police officer asked the officer to shoot him as he charged the officer with a knife.On Thursday evening, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General released the body-worn camera footage from the fatal officer-involved shooting that occurred Sept. 4 in Cambridge.
The preliminary investigation released in the days following the incident revealed Jacob Weber, a corporal from the Cambridge Police Department, fatally shot 30-year-old Ryan Garcy of Cambridge after Garcy charged at Weber with a knife.
The nine-minute video released by the attorney general's office includes footage from the body-worn cameras of three police officers — Weber and two officers identified only as "witness officer from the Cambridge Police Department."
The footage shows an exchange between Weber and Garcy that lasted under a minute.
During the interaction, Weber repeatedly tells Garcy to drop the knife he is holding and to stay back. Garcy, who was naked, can be seen slowly approaching Weber's police vehicle before pausing and asking Weber, "Will you just f------ shoot me?"
Garcy can then be seen rapidly approaching Weber. Weber is seen deploying a Taser, which is ineffective, then running from Garcy before firing five shots in Garcy's direction.
"I can say that I'm very proud of the officer that, from what I see, with all his training and knowledge of the job, he did what he, unfortunately, had to do to survive, and that's about all I can say about that for now," Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said Friday.
Garcy was transported by Maryland State Police Aviation to Tidal Health Peninsula Regional Medical Center in Salisbury, where he later died.
Weber, who has been with the police department for six years, has been placed on paid administrative leave until the investigation by the attorney general's office is finished, Todd said.
According to Todd, this is Cambridge's first fatal police shooting in about 15 years.
"I can say my condolences for the family of Mr. Garcy having to go through that and have that video out there. I can't imagine the pain and heartache," Todd said. "Mental health is a real problem."
Todd said he has been in contact with Garcy's family via email since the incident and considers the experience traumatic for both the family and the officers involved.
"We all sign up to do this job, and yes, we know it can come to that, but I don't think anyone can speak for it until you actually have been through something like that," Todd said.
Todd does not know when the investigation from the independent investigations division will conclude, but he said the investigators have been in touch and have been great to work with.
This article was updated to add comments from Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd.

stories.title: '25 Kids Should Not Take This Whole City Down' - Cambridge Council Grapples with Youth Crime in City
stories.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
stories.content:
'25 kids should not take this whole city down' - Cambridge council grapples with youth crime in city

 September 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Youth issues were the overwhelming theme for the third Cambridge City Council meeting in a row.At the Sept. 12 meeting, residents and commissioners alike made comments about juvenile crime.Lance Cephas, who is the father of Commission President Lajan Cephas and Commissioner Sputty Cephas, said crime is affecting everyone, including the children and families who aren't part of the problem.He further noted the children who aren't contributing to juvenile crime are being punished for the actions of about 25 children, "25 kids should not take this whole city down," he said.Lance Cephas stressed the importance of educating the kids that are caught doing things they shouldn't be."Because if you send them back home to that same environment, ain't nothing going to happen," he said. "A lot of police officers, they'll pick them up, they'll let them go, and soon as they're around the corner, they've done something else to somebody else. So you've got to get them and educate them." He said he understood both his children's, Lajan and Sputty, and Mayor Stephen Rideout's points of view regarding the juvenile curfew but said the council shouldn't be "at each other's throats" and "controlled by 25 kids." "We've all got to come together," he said.In late August, Rideout vetoed a juvenile curfew ordinance which commissioners had passed Aug. 14.Before that, in July, Rideout had proposed an alternative curfew ordinance which had additions and changes from the original curfew ordinance. These included adding definitions and altering language on enforcement procedures and penalties.Since Rideout vetoed the original curfew ordinance, Sputty Cephas has made amendments to Rideout's alternative ordinance in an effort to compromise and "find middle ground." According to council meeting documents, Cephas plans to recommend these amendments Sept. 25 when Rideout's proposed ordinance will be read for a second time.During the meeting, Sputty Cephas talked about finding that middle ground."Commissioner Atkiss made a point to say that $100 is a lot of money for a struggling parent," he said."My day job is in banking, so I understand that struggle as well." Sputty Cephas said he would like to keep fines as part of the penalty for not following the curfew, but said he cut them in half in his amendment. Instead of a $100 fine, it would be $50.At the end of the meeting, Rideout suggested to Sputty Cephas that the two of them get together to talk about the proposed amendments to the alternative ordinance. Sputty Cephas agreed to meet.Two presentations were given during Monday's meeting, as well. One presentation was given by Pam Gregory, president and CEO of United Way of the Lower Eastern Shore, and one by Lisa Molock, chief executive director at Let's Thrive Baltimore and an organizer for Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America.Molock talked about the work she has been doing in Baltimore, and Gregory talked about the economic issues that many Marylanders face. She shared data from a report that focused on asset limited, income constrained and employed (or ALICE) Marylanders and shared data on Dorchester County residents specifically. Gregory said that in Dorchester County, 45% of residents are below the ALICE threshold.During public comment, Theresa Stafford said poverty is a "lead driver" for many other issues in Cambridge."We need to get serious about fixing the problem of poverty," Stafford said."Bringing in industries or businesses that will pay good wages, and of course, supporting getting kids educated because that's the other key driver that keeps driving up the crime." 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT

stories.title: ICE Outlines Immigration Enforcement as QA Officials Explore 287(g) Agreement
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein and Hannah Combs
stories.content:
ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement

 August 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Grabenstein and Hannah Combs | Section: Local News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Stevensville — As Queen Anne's County leaders weigh the possibility of entering a formal partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, community members and officials remain divided.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agent James Brooks spoke to a full room July 30 during a Queen Anne's County Republican Central Committee informational session, offering a nonpartisan overview of ICE's operations, national enforcement protocols and local implications.
Brooks, the community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices, outlined the agency's primary focus on enforcing immigration law as enacted by Congress. ICE is tasked with identifying, arresting, detaining and removing individuals unlawfully present in the United States.
Underscoring the complexity of the issue at hand after decades of interpretation and practice by several White House administrations. "Immigration law is the second most complex set of codes next to tax codes," Brooks said.
reviewing options
In separate interviews, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann said the county's intent is to "fully comply" with federal mandates. They noted that many components of the 287(g) program — through which local jurisdictions partner with ICE on immigration enforcement — are already being fulfilled within the scope of current capabilities.
For example, there is a designated desk for ICE agents at the county sheriff's office, and at least one recent transfer has been made from the county detention center to immigration officials, officials said.
In July, county leadership assembled a task force to study the 287(g) program. The group — composed of Corchiarino, Hofmann, legal counsel and a representative from the detention center — is evaluating the purpose of such an agreement, the potential fiscal impact and any legal liabilities.
Corchiarino said the county commissioners would be required to vote before entering into any agreement. That vote could take place as early as this fall. He added that any needed funding could be drawn from the existing budget.
"As a sheriff, my commitment is to foster a safe environment for all members of our community, regardless of their citizenship status," Hofmann said. "We recognize the complexities of immigration laws and the impact they can have on federal funding. Our priority is to protect our citizens from gangs, criminals and violent offenders while also showing compassion and support for our immigrant community."
Understanding ICE operations
Brooks explained that ICE's operational components include Enforcement and Removal Operations, which conducts arrests and removals, and Homeland Security Investigations, which investigates transnational crimes.
"We don't go out and see who we can arrest," Brooks said. "We already know who we are targeting when ICE is going out to effect arrests."
He stressed that ICE detention is meant to streamline the deportation process, not to punish.
However, due to Maryland's "Dignity Not Detention" law, ICE must seek out-of-state facilities for detainees, oftentimes in Pennsylvania or Virginia.
Maryland has no ICE detention centers, only field holding offices — meaning the Baltimore and Salisbury centers for ICE do not contain beds and are not designed to house detainees past a temporary hold. The goal aims to transfer individuals "within hours," Brooks said. But he could not confirm what current protocol and practices are at those offices.
At press time, ICE had not responded to follow-up inquiries about these procedures.
The removal process, he noted, is far more involved than simply returning an immigrant to their country of origin. It often includes considerations for asylum, travel documentation, legal proceedings before an immigration judge, and agreements with third-party countries.
Brooks said while ICE officers often face criticism, morale remains high within the Baltimore field office. "Officers are busy but good. They know they're making a difference in their communities by going after the worst of the worst," he said.
He added that some officers choose to wear masks when in public as a personal safety measure due to the agency's current public image.
Community perspectives
The presentation was meant to provide factual, nonpartisan information, according to QACRCC President Helen Bennett.
"I think it counter-balances the misinformation that is out there," Bennett said. "And really, knowledge is power and we need to get information that is real, viable and truthful."
Bennett said she was particularly surprised to learn about the lack of ICE detention centers in Maryland, calling out-of-state transfers "a pretty penny." She noted that many attendees expressed interest in learning more about forming a 287(g) agreement.
Committee member Rick Bowers voiced his personal belief that the county should "fully engage" with ICE to enhance public safety and federal resource access.
Conversely, Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee Chair Elaine McNeil said her committee opposes entering into a 287(g) agreement.
"They just want a new start. And we're all trying to enjoy that ourselves," McNeil said of immigrants. She expressed concern that individuals could be "unlawfully processed and treated in a manner like some kind of criminal."
The topic remains under discussion by the Democratic committee, she said.
