stories.title: 'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent
stories.author: WILL BONTRAGER
stories.content:
'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 912
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In a recent interview, Jamie Williams noted that in Kent County, businesses are coming and going regularly."It's a churning process," she acknowledged.
For instance, Rock City Cafe's last day was Oct 12. Then Oct. 15, at that same location, 21536 Rock Hall Ave., Little Lemon Leaf Diner is advertising a hiring event, for kitchen and dining room.
Some new businesses moved in recently as well. Starbucks is now open for business, and It's Masala Time, an Indian restaurant at 3 Washington Square, had its soft opening on Wednesday, Oct. 2.
As director of Kent County Department of Economic and Tourism Development for 11 years, Williams sees this turnaround daily, offering support and creating opportunities for businesses to thrive.
While working with the Economic Commission, business owners and leaders in the community appointed by the county commissioners provide guidance and insight.
Their goals line up with the county's comprehensive plan: to retain and expand businesses while supporting start-up businesses.
With a hefty schedule to close out the week, Williams, highlighted some projects her staff is working on.
Millington Senior Housing: The Millington Senior Village is a project that will provide 52 one-story apartments for people age 62 and up.
The project is located on land once part of the Millington Elementary School property.
The county is working with Millington during the grant search process. If successful, they hope to build a community resource center, food pantry, church and daycare center, centralizing services in one location.
With all that activity, Williams hopes to have Delmarva Community Transit services to accommodate residential needs.
"The more density we have the more services we can build there," Williams commented.
Railroad Upgrade: Williams pointed out the Worton railroad system, services five companies and was in a state of disrepair for quite a while. The county had received funding from the state to fix the tracks in May of 2020.
Williams was happy to announce that in September 2024 that project is finally completed.
The fact that from the time they had received the funding to the actual repair was four years, she said, should give an indication to the public of how slow-going these processes sometimes take.
Brownfield Properties: Williams and staff has identified 12 brownfield properties — places contaminated and needing remediation.
Most of these properties, the director said, were dry-cleaning establishments, dealing with chemicals. One of these is in Chestertown, Admiral Cleaners, located across from the 7-Eleven on 212 Maple Ave.; a building that sits dormant with graffiti on the walls.
Williams asked, is it worth the county adopting a brownfield credit, a state program. Is it worth going through that kind of process to redevelop the properties?
They are seeking answers to those pressing questions.
Recreational Cannabis: Beginning July 1, 2023, individuals in Maryland at least age 21 could legally use and possess the personal use amount of cannabis. Licensing is issued by the State for those who aim to start a dispensary.
Currently, Williams said the county issued only one micro-license, for a cannabis dispensary in Millington.
According to earlier reports, the establishment is under Rahul "Rocky" Dutta and if meeting all the requirements, will be located in the vacant Truist Bank building at 400 Cypress Street.
In talking with Dutta earlier in the week, Williams reported everything is moving forward.
Short-term rental tax:The county has been working with the municipalities to collect short-term rental tax from properties where AirBnb's or Vrbo properties or other rentals of that nature are located.
Williams acknowledged that is an extensive process involving lots of moving parts.
She had worked with her administrative specialist Rose Osborn to locate the properties throughout the county. They purchased software to track these properties more efficiently as well as send out notices.
Now it seems like they are seeing positive results.
According to the July report, Williams said "64 percent of properties are in compliance."
The director expects higher in the future.
"We feel we're going to see the biggest impact after the September numbers."
Other than using the tracking software, they worked closely with the municipalities to coordinate their memorandum of understandings for short-term rental tax, so they are all on the same page.
The county collects the taxes monthly and remit it to the towns. The towns receive 90 percent of the revenue with 10 percent going to the county for administrative costs.
Even before they purchased the software, Williams and Osborn have been working steadily on this issue since November 2022.
She was thankful for the cooperation that occurred since then.
"Getting all five towns together is an example of what we need to be doing for a lot of other projects," she said.
Business Retention and Expansion: Williams maintained they have always responded to the needs of business owners. However, now, that attention and focus is being formalized as they launch their Business and Retention Visit Program, starting last week.
The department has reached out to 10 or 11 businesses so far, refining their data-gathering process and consulting with business owners.
They've been all over the county, visiting KRM Development, Hickory Stick and Blue Heron Oyster House to name a few.
The qualitative information they gather will be assessed and used to help the community.
All of this would not be possible without Economic Development Manager Katie Abbott, the Kent County Chamber of Commerce and many others, Williams noted.
"It takes a collaborative effort from everyone; that's how economic development happens."
As a team, they are helping businesses find their niche area to succeed in a region specific to rural concerns.
"We're not an area to put up a big distribution center," Williams said."We're here to promote businesses focusing on what's unique and special in Kent County."

stories.title: Coffee with the County Brings Representatives and Businesses Together
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Coffee with the County brings representatives and businesses together

 April 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON — Tuesday, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted Coffee with the County, bringing county agencies and business together to discuss different resources.Tracey Snyder, executive director of the Caroline Chamber of Commerce, highlighted the event as one of many planned to allow government representatives and business to meet each other and make connections. About 30 people attended.
"We love doing this. The main reason why we do it is to build communication," Snyder said. "Everybody's doing all their great things in their towns, but we don't always reach over to the next town, and I don't know why that is. So as chamber director that serves the whole county, my goal is to try to build that communication."
The chamber and county representatives participated in a speed-dating-like event Tuesday. For 10 to 15 minutes, a group of representatives would sit with chamber members and discuss their positions and what they offer to their town or to the county.
After hearing from all sitting at the table, representatives would ask different questions to each other on what they could improve and how to help each other.
Multiple business cards were passed around, and connections were made.
"It's giving those businesses more resources," Snyder said. "It's also giving the businesses more resources within our county that they may not know exist. So that's really what it's all about.
"I feel like the chamber is a conduit. That's really our role. We connect others together through networking, marketing and things like this."
Multiple county representatives attended the event and enjoyed the conversation and feedback that was given about the work in the county.
"I mean it's good to interact with the community and the towns to get feedback from them," said county Commissioner Frank Bartz. "The department head directors communicating what they do on a day-to-day basis, which they might not know, and they get to put a face with somebody they haven't met yet. So, that gives them a little bit of a one-on-one to where they can feel free to contact them. They don't feel like, 'Oh, I don't want to bother anybody.' So, that's good on that end of that."

stories.title: Old Middle School Moves Closer to Reuse
stories.author: Andrea Grabenstein agrabenstein@chespub.com
stories.content:
Old middle school moves closer to reuse

 July 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 New life for the former Sudlersville Middle School took a step forward after the Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved Queen Anne's County Economic and Tourism Development's application for another Rural Maryland Council Grant for up to $50,000 July 9.The grant application through the Rural Maryland Council seeks to fund predevelopment consulting costs up to $50,000 for the reuse of the former school, according to Economic Development Director Heather Tinelli.
Currently owned by the Sudlersville Volunteer Fire Company, both parties have had a great working partnership as they take the planning and pre-development steps needed to develop a feasibility study and adaptively reuse the former Sudlersville Middle School building, she said.
A request of $50,000 will fund consulting fees for developer outreach, identification of anchor tenants/users, and issuance of request for proposals to bring on an established development partner via a Master Developer Agreement.
A community laundromat currently operates out of the facility with several part-time employees and is doing well, she said.
The fire department will supply the match to this grant so there will be no out of pocket funding required from the county, according to Tinelli.
A Community Development Block Grant was completed in early 2023 to conduct a feasibility study of the property, and determined that the building is an ideal candidate for reuse.
The goal is to create a regional facility that will be an economic driver for the area, according to Tinelli.
Through the CDBG, the first part of the project explored what the building could potentially be used for and a study identified the facility in great shape and gauged community interest in 2022, she said.
Through the second phase of the project, the county received a $30,000 award from Rural Maryland Council in FY2024 to complete a market analysis that includes a financial model and redevelopment strategies; all of which are on track to be completed in partnership with the Maryland Economic Development Corporation and identify affordable lease rates and uses are needed for the area.
Phase Three is the final initial component that includes assistance with the state to identify developer relationships and funding opportunities, Tinelli said.
The former middle school has gained visibility through recent bus tour stops with the Secretary of the Department of Housing & Community Development, and Maryland Association of Counties as the county lays the groundwork for awareness and future state support of the project, Tinelli said.
"There are all kinds of entities that have looked at it to say, how can we support the community," she said.

stories.title: Greensboro Will Not Bring Northern Towns onto Wastewater System
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Greensboro — Caroline County is creating a plan to address septic system concerns in Henderson, Marydel and Templeville by building a wastewater treatment facility, but there is still a long way to go, officials say.The county has been brainstorming ideas since the May 6 commissioners meeting, where Commission President Travis Breeding announced the town of Greensboro would not take the towns onto its wastewater treatment system.
Greensboro Mayor David Spencer said the Greensboro Town Council came to that decision because of the wear and tear the facility would take by adding three new towns.
"I don't know that the council had absolutely said that they didn't want to be involved in the process. I think that they preferred not to be because of the additional responsibilities and potential expenses that may incur on our residents," Spencer said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Monday.
"I know that they were going to come back and give some more numbers... I don't know that the door has been absolutely closed, but I don't think the council had any appetite to try to move forward at this time," Spencer said.
The discussion arises after multiple north county residents complained about problems with their septic tanks. One resident brought their concerns to the county commissioners in April.
"My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Kia Pierce said at an April meeting. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The commissioners are working on a plan, Breeding said, but it all depends on government permits and funding.
"We're talking to Maryland Department of Environment about other options, whether it be individual plants for each town, which we don't think is feasible, or one new plant in a centralized location that all three towns, Templeville, Henderson and Marydale, could connect to," Breeding said.
"We are looking at options as far as locations of a potential plant and what kind of discharge permit MDE would be willing to give us... Then also we're looking at what kind of funding MDE or (U.S. Department of Agriculture) may have available to help us construct a new plant up there."
While the county is working with MDE and USDA, Breeding said there is no time table for when the county will have a solidified plan.
"It's all pretty much funding-dependent, and one thing I've learned in the two years I've been in the office, it takes a lot longer than you think it's going to take," Breeding said. "So, we're working through it."

stories.title: Ann O'Connor
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Ann O'Connor

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Ann Oconnor 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Ann O'Connor, 55, is a resident of Easton. She is running for the District 2 seat on the Talbot County Board of Education.She is a former teacher and has six children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the school board because I am deeply passionate about children's education. As a former teacher and mother of six, I have dedicated my career to helping children reach their highest potential.
Having witnessed my six children go through (Talbot County Public School), I have observed a decline in academic rigor, expectations and accountability, both in behavior and academics. This experience drives my desire to make meaningful changes on the school board. The fact that our students are scoring 18% proficient in math and 55% in reading indicates a pressing need for new perspectives on our educational strategies.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities are the ABCs of education: advancing academics, boosting accountability and cultivating character. The focus is on the whole child. We cannot advance academics without discipline.
When students develop self-discipline, good character naturally emerges. This requires daily practice and consistent reinforcement of rules and clear expectations for all students across all buildings. Disruptive behavior must be addressed promptly and effectively.
Regarding academic accountability: A 95% graduation rate when less than ¼ of our students are proficient in math skills, and less than ½ are reading on grade level is inconsistent — something is broken here and we need to fix it.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue is the steady decline of academic rigor. We need to make sure we continue to implement early intervention in elementary schools to support those who need that extra push. It's essential to send home books and ensure that our children have access to/and are accountable for reading materials throughout elementary, middle and high school.
We should place greater emphasis on traditional learning — using pencils and paper, cursive writing, fostering reading and critical thinking skills, while reducing reliance on computers. We need to offer pathways for middle school students interested in college or the workforce, including advanced/honors classes.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards received in the mail are snapshots of where our schools stand. No one wants these scores, they are abysmal. It's a wake up call to attack the problem and change the way we have been doing education here in Talbot County.
We need to put our focus on reading, writing and math. Our students are distracted. Let's eliminate anything that detracts from our mission as educators and focus on what truly matters — educating the child. Let's get back to basics with my ABCs of education.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
Simply changing a name doesn't lead to improvement. Over the last two decades, this initiative has gone through four name changes. Although there are many wonderful proposals in the Blueprint, I don't believe that top-down programs created by education experts would make our local schools better.
The Blueprint is a blanket principle mandated for all 24 counties in Maryland. The counties have no say in how it is implemented. It removes the schools from the control of locally elected school boards and puts control in the hands of unelected officials. I believe we want control over our local schools.

stories.title: Anna Howie
stories.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
stories.content:
Anna Howie

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Anna Howie

 Anna Howie, 49, is a resident of Easton and the current District 5 member of the Talbot County Board of Education. She was appointed to the post by Gov. Wes Moore in October, 2023.Howie is the assistant principal at Federalsburg Elementary School. She is married and has three children.
Why are you running for office?
I am running for the District 5 seat of the Talbot County Board of Education to represent students, families and other stakeholders. We are making gains in our school district, and I want to continue to ensure that our students and teachers have access to high quality instructional materials that will have an impact on student achievement and success.
What are your priorities if elected?
My priorities align with the goals set by the members of the Board of Education and the superintendent, Dr. (Shraron) Pepukayi. My two main areas of focus are increasing student achievement in the areas of mathematics and reading, and recruiting and retaining quality teachers.
Having teachers that provide outstanding instruction to our students will ensure that our students will be academically successful.
What is the most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools faces, and how do you think the board needs to address it?
The most important issue that Talbot County Public Schools face right now is providing exceptional education opportunities for all students while being fiscally responsible.
Currently, the curriculum coordinating committee has brought high quality resources to the board for approval in the areas of reading and mathematics. These resources are paid for through educational grants. Utilizing grants is a responsible way of ensuring that we are providing our students with high quality instructional materials while being fiscally responsible.
Talbot County residents have been receiving postcards in the mail criticizing education in the county. What are your thoughts on the postcards and how should these concerns be addressed?
The postcards that have been mailed out focused on student test scores as well as other concerns. In terms of student test scores, we have purchased new high quality instructional materials. Our 2024 data reflects growth in all subgroups as well as certain subject areas and grades.
Student test scores are not just a concern for our district but across the State. Through the Governance and Accountability pillar of the Blueprint, expert review teams will be visiting schools across the state to review literacy and mathematics instruction in our classrooms and provide quality feedback for improvement.
What are your thoughts on the Blueprint For Maryland's Future? What concerns or benefits do you see?
I believe that the pillars of the Blueprint reflect the areas that all Maryland Schools want to address. Those pillars address early childhood education, high quality and diverse teachers, college and career readiness, more resources for students to be successful, and governance and accountability.
The Blueprint identifies and prioritizes the needs that we see in our district and across the state. In order for our students to be college and career ready by 10th grade, we need to start addressing their needs in pre-Kindergarten and ensure that they are receiving the resources they need to be successful in every grade.

stories.title: Easton Police Chief: Traffic Stops Bill Would Have 'Drastic' Impacts on Police Work
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
Easton police chief: Traffic stops bill would have 'drastic' impacts on police work

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 478
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Police Chief Alan Lowrey raised concerns over a proposed bill in the state legislature that would limit police officers' abilities to make traffic stops for certain violations.Senate Bill 292, cross-filed in the House of Delegates, would shift many primary offenses to secondary offenses, including improper use of headlights and taillights, failing to use turn signals, missing or improper license plates, and excessive noise.
That change would mean police officers can only cite a driver for those offenses if they pull over the driver for a different, primary offense.
During an Easton Town Council meeting Monday, Lowrey, also serving as the interim town manager, said the bill's proposed changes would be "drastic" and negatively impact police in detecting crime.
"There's a number of concerns on my part as the chief of police, and I've spoken with my staff about this," Lowrey said.
Lowrey said offenses such as driving without headlights are common signs indicating potential impaired driving. He said all of the offenses that would be reclassified are safety issues.
"I personally have arrested a number of people, based upon traffic stops, for serious crimes," Lowrey said.
As written, the bill seeks to make evidence gathered during traffic stops inadmissible if an officer fails to state their name, identification number, agency and reason for the stop. Lowrey called that measure "drastic" as well.
Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) is the bill's sponsor. At a Jan. 28 Senate Judicial Proceedings hearing, Sydnor noted Baltimore County statistics that indicated Black and Hispanic drivers face inequities in the rate of citations issued.
"It is these disparities that spurred me to seek and introduce a legislative remedy," Sydnor said.
Sydnor said he worked with the Maryland Office of the Public Defender on the drafted bill. Moving primary violations to fall under secondary violations make way for technologies such as cameras to detect traffic violations, the senator said.
"Technology that can be modified to do what people do today," Sydnor said. "So really, this bill kicks off a conversation about, I would say, a reimagining of how we deal with traffic offenses on the highways."
At the hearing, though, some legislators and law enforcement officials from around the state spoke unfavorably of the legislation.
Those conversations around Maryland have continued in the weeks since. Last month, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed the bill at a meeting and expressed intent to write a letter in opposition.
Monday in Easton, Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said the job of being a police officer is "tough enough as it is."
"We don't need to make it any tougher," Abbatiello said. "So I would support anything that the town would like to do in order to try to prevent this from passing."
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Lowrey how the town could express its concerns regarding the bill. Lowrey suggested drafting a letter.
Following discussion, Easton councilmembers voted unanimously to send correspondence to committees in Annapolis opposing the bill.

stories.title: Ridgely Not Planning to Reinstate Police Department
stories.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
stories.content:
Ridgely not planning to reinstate police department

 September 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 735
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Despite a state criminal investigation against Ridgely's police chief coming up empty, Ridgely commissioners announced on Monday that they have no plans to reinstate the town's police force, which has been suspended since March.A report from the Maryland Office of the State Prosecutor stated an investigation was opened into Ridgely Police Department Chief Jeff Eckrich due to "suspected" perjury and misconduct in office. The investigation found no "sufficient evidence of criminal activity warranting further investigation or prosecution," the July 25 report said.
The commissioners suspended Eckrich and the entire department on March 12, providing minimal explanation to residents. Since, the town has entered into an agreement with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to provide police coverage in place of the suspended officers. With the start of the new fiscal year July 1, the Ridgely officers were laid off.
Chip MacLeod, an attorney representing the town, read aloud a statement at the beginning of Monday's town meeting.
"The commissioners recognize the pain this unfortunate situation has caused their friends and neighbors in the town," MacLeod stated. "At the same time, the commissioners are pleased that most of the former Ridgely Police Department employees have secured employment elsewhere. Thus, the commissioners realize that those employees would be unlikely to return to their former positions even if those positions were available."
"The commissioners recognize that reestablishing the Ridgely Police Department would be a complex and expensive undertaking," MacLeod later said. "Such an effort would require a high level of citizen support, not just political support, for operating the Ridgely Police Department, and a commitment to funding and seeing the process through. Accordingly, the commissioners believe that it is in the best interest of the town to continue the present arrangement with the sheriff and the county through at least fiscal year 2025 and to reevaluate the sheriff's engagement when preparing the fiscal 2026 budget."
MacLeod said commissioners and town staff will provide no additional comment regarding the police department.
Many residents reacted negatively after the statement was read. Some asked why there wasn't an apology provided to the officers, and others pointed out the town didn't acknowledge the police chief was cleared of wrongdoing.
One resident asked the Caroline County Sheriff's Office sergeant in attendance which three officers are currently assigned to the town for coverage.
"We're not answering no questions. I'm in charge," Commissioner John Buckle said.
Resident Jennifer Nesselroad spoke during public comment, asking the commissioners for an itemized list of police and town vehicles. She also expressed frustration with the commissioners' statement.
"You never apologized for disbanding our police department, not even issuing an apology for everybody being exonerated," Nesselroad said. "That was very, very rude and inconsiderate to us and those police officers that gave every day around this town, even for you all, everybody sitting up here. That was very cowardly."
Heather Amador asked commissioners why the town did not follow its charter, which states the commissioners must hold a vote to remove an officer or town employee.
"A criminal investigation's going to trump anything in the town charter," MacLeod said.
"Absolutely, against one, against the chief," Amador said. "The others were never under investigation."
"You heard the statement I read," MacLeod said. Amador responded, "I did, but it doesn't answer my question."
In an interview with the Star Democrat, Ridgely resident Robin Martin expressed concern over the fact that the commissioners have not clearly stated who directed them to suspend the police department back in March.
Monday's statement from the commissioners noted that on March 12, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office executed a search and seizure warrant issued by the county's circuit court. It stated that "commissioners were directed to order all RPD officers to surrender" firearms, vehicles and other equipment to the town, but did not clarify who provided that direction.
The decision to suspend the department came "without guidance" from the state prosecutor, according to the state prosecutor's report.
"I think we have a distrust for the commissioners of the town," Martin said. "We've been way more involved in things that are happening in the town, because we don't trust that they have our best interests at heart anymore."
During public comment, Martin asked commissioners for "less closed-door activity and more community involvement" in town decisions. After the meeting, Martin said her heart breaks for the officers.
"They participate in everything around town, and I think that's kind of what Ridgely should be about, community policing," Martin said. "This has been something so shameful for the town."

stories.title: Caroline Commissioners Weigh Potential Locations for New Lockerman Middle
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Caroline commissioners weigh potential locations for new Lockerman Middle

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During the Caroline County Commissioners' open comment report Tuesday morning, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter brought up the discussion on Lockerman Middle School's proposed locations.Porter said he preferred that the new middle school go on the North Caroline High School property, one of two locations being considered during the design processes for the building begin. The other location, near the county sheriff's office on Double Hills Road, presents several challenges, Porter said.
"I think at this point I would like to say that I am in favor of the North Carolina location as opposed to being built in town," Porter said.
Commissioners Frank Bartz agreed with Porter and cited traffic and safety concerns on Route 404.
The commissioners also had discussions about the school's location at their meeting two weeks ago.
At that meeting, County Administrator Kathleen Freeman presented the two location options. Commissioners President Travis Breeding sparked a conversation about how much sway the commissioners have over the school's location.
"How much influence do the commissioners actually have over where the school gets constructed?" Breeding asked two weeks ago. "As part of the funding of this, other than a survey, we haven't really been consulted."
Breeding then explained the issues they would run into with each potential location.
"From what I gather, it seemed like a lot of people really preferred the Double Hills location. But, with Double Hills, we've got to work out a ton of details with the Town of Denton as far as sewer, water allocation for that to work, potentially pump station upgrades," Breeding said.
He then mentioned traffic issues on Route 404 with beach traffic towards the end of the school year and students from northern county towns like Marydale, who would have to take the bus a long distance to the potential Double Hills location.
Porter, said he didn't recall that "the county did not have a lot of input" on the design of new county buildings in the past.
Freeman assured Breeding that the county will be involved with the full feasibility study for both sites to determine which site makes the most sense.
Breeding also brought forward discussion of how much influence the commissioners will have for the design of the school.
"Then also, how much input do we have over the the design?" Breeding asked. "I mean, we don't want a situation where we're building something that's way more expensive than it needs to be or making it as functional as we can and keeping the cost as low as we can."
Bartz raised an issue where if the county has to build a new detention center, a school on the Double Hills Road site would cause a problem. The Caroline County Sheriff's Office is located near that Double Hills Road site, making the location logical for a detention center, he said.
The county is in talks with Queen Anne's County about a new 388-bed regional detention center that would house all Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent county prisoners. After conversations about control and cost of the center, discussions between the three counties have slowed down.
Lockerman name
Porter pointed out conversation that are being had about the Lockerman's name staying at the location of the current building instead of being attached to the new school.
Though the existing building will no longer be used as a school when the new school is built, Porter said he was in favor of keeping the Lockerman name attached to the facility in the interest of honoring its history.
"I think it's going to be important that the history of the school and the name of Lockerman be retained," he said. "I don't know what the future use is going to be for that building, but it's important, I think, from the alumni standpoint, from the community standpoint, that the history be be kept there for whatever use is going to be done in the future."
Breeding suggested drafting a letter of intent to the Caroline County Board of Education stating that it would be the commissioners' intention to retain the name of the building.

stories.title: County Council Introduces Bills to Improve Auditorium Lights, Athletic Fields
stories.author: Konner Metz
stories.content:
County Council introduces bills to improve auditorium lights, athletic fields

 January 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council introduced three pieces of capital-enabling legislation during Tuesday's meeting that would dedicate funds for school improvements.Bills 1580, 1581 and 1582 were introduced by all five council members. If passed at a future meeting, they will approve a combined $1.5 million in funding for three projects: new auditorium lights at Easton High School ($817,321), light replacements at St. Michaels Middle High School ($556,000) and athletic field improvements across the district ($116,679).
The fiscal year 2025 budget already accounted for the capital costs, County Manager Clay Stamp noted. The three bills would simply authorize the usage of funds for those three projects, respectively.
Talbot County Public Schools Director of Operations Kevin Shafer said Easton High's auditorium lights date back to the school's renovation in 1997.
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher said he's noticed "how desperately needed this lighting system is."
"In order to put on some of the really quality student productions that we've seen at Easton High School, I believe that some of the lighting directors have been bringing equipment in from … the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and other places to supplement the antiquated equipment that the auditorium itself has," Lesher said.
"We've moved into an era of LED lighting, which didn't exist back in 1997," Lesher added. "This is going to be a huge leap forward."
Shafer said the light replacements and improvements at St. Michaels Middle High School will complete the ongoing LED conversion product across the entire St. Michaels campus. Grant funding allowed for new side lights at St. Michaels Elementary, Shafer said.
The $117,000 for athletic field improvements will help the district move forward with its grass field upgrades.
"Generally speaking, the athletic field improvements are going to be surrounding the current fields that we have, grass fields," Shafer said. "(We are) doing some longstanding improvements related to some issues or concerns that came up."
A public hearing on the three bills will be held during Talbot County Council's Feb. 11 meeting at 5:30 p.m.

stories.title: Federalsburg Police Chief Resigns; Sheriff's Office Takes Over Leadership
stories.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
stories.content:
Federalsburg police chief resigns; sheriff's office takes over leadership

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 375
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — At the July 7 town meeting, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner announced Police Chief Joseph Gasser resigned from his position on June 25."The mayor and council would like to announce the resignation of Chief Gasser from the Federalsburg Police Department effective June 25," Abner said. "We want to thank Chief Gasser for his service to the town and wish him well on his future endeavors."
Within the announcement, Abner said that the Caroline County Sheriff's Office would take over leadership of the Federalsburg Police Department to give the mayor and council time to figure out police department leadership.
"I was contacted by the mayor and council and asked to take over day-to-day operations and management oversight of the department," Sheriff Donald Baker said to the Star Democrat in an interview Tuesday. "I agree to do that on an interim basis for 30 to 60 days until the mayor and council decide what they are going to do moving forward and what that looks like for the Federalsburg Police Department."
The mayor also announced a public forum meeting for July 21 at 6 p.m. at the Federalsburg Town Hall to discuss their options moving forward with the police department, public safety and policing.
While the sheriff's office and the town of Federalsburg are in the early stages of conversation, Baker believes all options are on the table for the Federalsburg Police Department, including an memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office that could discontinue the police department.
"I believe that everything is on the table to include signing an MOU somewhat like Ridgley's, directly with the sheriff's office of the county," Baker said. "Again, everything is on the table. and we are really early in this stage, but we absolutely could absorb any officers that were left."
Gasser was appointed to police chief position in January. He came into the position with a military background, and he had been serving the Town of Federalsburg for almost 30 years.
Ridgley has maintained a contract with the Caroline County Sheriff's Office to have assigned officers covering the town since last year. In March 2024, the town suspended its police department amid a state investigation.
More recently, Ridgley has agreed to continue the memorandum of understanding with the sheriff's office for the next fiscal year.
